Sudan rejects US stance on legitimacy of authorities, says it will not accept externally imposed solutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:57:39 UTC
00:57:39 KST

Adel Abdelrheem, Lina Altawell
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieddin Salem on Friday rejected a US position that the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and their leaders do not represent legitimate or constitutional authority in Sudan, saying his government is “open to dialogue” but will not accept externally imposed solutions.
Salem made the remarks at a news conference in New York attended by Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi and other Sudanese officials on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
“The Sudanese government is open to dialogue, but it does not accept foreign interference or externally imposed solutions on the government of Sudan, which represents the Sudanese people,” Salem said.
“Khartoum’s position is based on its commitment to national sovereignty and the territorial integrity of Sudan,” he added.
The US State Department said: “Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan.”
In response, the Sudanese government rejected the US statement Wednesday, reaffirming its commitment to national sovereignty and calling on Washington to “engage positively” with it.
Addressing the war, Salem said the conflict that erupted on April 15, 2023, had been “imposed on the people of Sudan,” accusing external parties of financing and arming it and the RSF of rebelling against the army.
“The government participated in Jeddah negotiations in May 2023, which resulted in understandings that could have helped contain the conflict at an early stage, but the RSF reneged on them,” he said.
The army and the RSF signed the “Jeddah Declaration of Commitment to Protect the Civilians of Sudan” on May 11, 2023, which included commitments to respect international humanitarian law and facilitate humanitarian work.
The Sudanese Foreign Ministry said the news conference also addressed Khartoum’s position on the US not issuing an entry visa to Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan to attend the UN General Assembly meetings.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed concern over the failure to issue the visa, while Khartoum raised the issue of US obligations as the host country of the UN headquarters.
Sudan has been engulfed in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023 that has killed tens of thousands of people and caused one of the world’s largest displacement crises.

Truckers, commuters protest in Portugal against soaring fuel prices
LISBON, Sept 25 - Hundreds of truckers took part in a "go-slow" convoy along a motorway in north-central Portugal on Friday, while commuters blared their horns on Lisbon's main bridge to protest against soaring fuel costs.
Fuel prices have reached all-time highs in Portugal due to supply disruptions related to the Iran war and refinery attacks linked to the war in Ukraine. Prices at the pump increased 24% in August year-on-year, with diesel hitting more than €2 ($2.28) per litre, according to Eurostat data.
Trucks slowly rolled along the A1 motorway in a 150-km (93-mile) convoy from Paredes in the north to the central Portuguese city of Coimbra. Demonstrators demanded eligibility for the partial refunds of the tax on petroleum products enjoyed by freight and passenger transport companies.
Video from state broadcaster RTP showed a truck leading the convoy bearing a sign reading: "Today, the trucks are stopping — but their importance isn't."
Speaking to reporters in Cascais, Minister of Infrastructure and Housing Miguel Pinto Luz acknowledged the trucking industry had been "overlooked in some ways" in the measures taken so far to limit the impact of rising fuel prices.
He pledged to review their proposals and scheduled a meeting with the movement's representatives at the ministry next Monday.
In Lisbon, commuters launched a honking protest at 8 a.m. local time (0700 GMT) while crossing the April 25 bridge, which connects the capital to the working-class outskirts on the southern bank of the Tagus river.
They called for the reinstatement of remote working — a policy temporarily applied during the COVID-19 pandemic – as well as the suspension of toll payments and the 23% value-added tax on fuel, Aristides Teixeira, spokesperson of the Ponte 25 de Abril Users' Association, told Lusa.
The group also seeks the resignation of Environment Minister Maria Graça Carvalho over comments in which she suggested citizens drive more slowly to reduce their fuel consumption. REUTERS

Exhibition by Kharkiv artist Zorkin opens at Khanenko Museum
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:55:45 EEST
00:55:45 KST

The "Anabasis" exhibition by Kharkiv artist Kostiantyn Zorkin has opened at the Khanenko Museum in Kyiv.
"Anabasis" began as a joint project with Kharkiv Literary Museum entitled "In the Name of the City," Zorkin told journalists on the eve of the exhibition opening.
According to him, the central part of the exposition is the "Hold" installation, created in 2023-2024 during a difficult period for Kharkiv. It transports the viewer into the hold of a ship, where a creative team of artists descended. On a large wooden table sits a toy that appears as a symbol of the city in wartime, where all the figures are connected by a single rope: pull one, and you disrupt the fragile existing balance.
"Guests also sat at this table, including Timothy Snyder (American historian and writer)... Over time, the city-ship, whose course is heading west, became a country-ship, and its story found continuation at the Khanenko Museum," Zorkin noted.
Since the spring of 2026, the Khanenko Museum team, together with Zorkin, has been exploring the concept of the "In the Name of the City" project, working with its archive, graphic art, and works.
"Anabasis" turns the gaze back to man – his resilience, wisdom, and conscience – through images and symbols that humanity has used for millennia. The exhibition project explores the search for oneself and those nearby, connections, and the strength of community at a time when the world is experiencing the loss of its footing, the museum's press release notes.
The exhibition will run until November 29.

Minister for Food Security, Fisheries and Horticulture Silvio Erkens to visit India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:55:26 UTC
00:55:26 KST

From 27 September to 2 October, Minister Silvio Erkens from the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Food Security and Nature will be visiting India. The purpose of the visit is to further strengthen the relationship between the Netherlands and India, especially in terms of international cooperation in the areas of agriculture, horticulture, sustainable food processing and innovative value chains.
‘India is a rapidly growing country and the agriculture sector is very important from an economic perspective,’ Minister Erkens explains. ‘And when it comes to agrifood innovation, India is quickly becoming a major world player. This presents economic opportunities for the Netherlands, owing in part to the country’s scale. We have a lot to offer India in terms of knowledge and innovation in areas such as seed improvement and greenhouses. The aim of this trip is to strengthen our trade relations and our broad partnership and to open the door for Dutch business in India.’
Trade partners
The Netherlands-India partnership focuses on sustainability, innovation and trade. More than 350 Dutch businesses are active in India, for instance in the potato and seed sectors, the poultry sector, the dairy industry and in horticulture. Opportunities for Dutch entrepreneurs in India lie mainly in the areas of seeds, sustainable crop protection, logistics, technology and knowledge sharing. The 18 Dutch businesses and organisations participating in this trade mission are all hoping to explore opportunities and strengthen ties in one of the most dynamic economies in the world.
First government visit
This will be the first time since the announcement of the Strategic Partnership between the Netherlands and India during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit in May that a member of the government is travelling to India. It will also be the first visit by a minister from the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Food Security and Nature since 2018.
In January 2026 negotiations on the EU-India trade agreement were concluded. This is important for the Netherlands, the EU and India from both geopolitical and economic perspectives. Now is therefore a good time for this visit and for the Netherlands to foster relations and strengthen cooperation with India.
Programme
The visit will begin on Monday 28 September with a substantive programme at the official residence of the Dutch ambassador in Delhi, and will include meetings with the Minister of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare and the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying.
On Tuesday 29 September Minister Erkens will visit Mumbai, where there will be a round-table breakfast with key business players, followed by the opening of the Anuga FoodTec expo, meetings with the Maharashtra government and a meeting with the seed sector.
From there the minister will head to Bangalore for a trade visit on Wednesday 30 September with a delegation of 18 Dutch businesses and an informal meeting with the Minister of Horticulture of the state of Karnataka.
On Thursday 1 October Minister Erkens will open the Agricon HortiConnect Expo and the Dutch pavilion. He will also visit the cold chain company NewCold from Breda, which is working hard to pave the way for the professionalisation of cold chain transport in India. The minister will conclude his trip with an agrifood innovation event with start-ups and scale-ups.

Russia’s ruling United Russia party secured 349 out of 450 seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, in last weekend’s legislative polls, the head of the country’s electoral authority said Friday.
In a Moscow press conference on the results of the Sept. 18-20 election, Ella Pamfilova said United Russia got 50.79% of the vote, followed by the Communist Party, which won 37 seats, while the Liberal Democratic Party, New People, and A Just Russia secured 23, 19, and 17 seats, respectively.
The Rodina party, as well as four independent candidates, won a single seat apiece in the State Duma, she added.
Voter turnout was 59.8%, and some 67.4 million people voted, she said, adding that over 7 million people within Russia voted remotely via e-voting.
Pamfilova said over 280,000 people took part in the elections from abroad, and 333 polling stations were opened in 152 countries.
The percentage of invalid ballots was 1.36%, and the results of regional elections in one district in the Kirov region were declared invalid, she said.
The election, held on Sept. 18-20, was Russia's first parliamentary vote since 2022 and was held amid the ongoing Ukraine war. Voting also took place in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine, a move condemned by Kyiv and some Western governments.

South Lebanon children return to school destroyed by Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:52:50 UTC
00:52:50 KST

Breadcrumb
South Lebanon children return to school destroyed by Israel strike
In southern Lebanon, eight-year-old Yara Ajami started the academic year this week in a doorless, windowless classroom after her school was destroyed by an Israeli strike.
Well known in the area for its excellence, Ajami's primary school in Burj Qalaway was struck by Israel in May, two months after Hezbollah dragged Lebanon into the Middle East war by attacking its southern neighbour.
"We are happy to be back (to school), but we were happier before. We used to draw, play, but now there are no desks or chairs," the young girl with braided hair said as she climbed a bare concrete staircase.
Rather than go to their old school building, Ajami and the other students returning to classes after the summer break on Monday were diverted to a nearby structure still under construction that was being built to house preschoolers.
The sun shone through unglazed windows into unfinished classrooms as children followed their lessons, while outside clumps of twisted rebar jutted from the ground like dead bushes where walls used to stand.
The students come from areas heavily hit by Israeli attacks and most were displaced during the war, with some - like Ajami - returning to find their homes damaged or destroyed.
'Sadness in their eyes'
"There is sadness in their eyes, each one of them has a story," school principal May Mehdi told AFP from the courtyard.
"But I am happy they are here," she said, showing on her phone what the school, her pride, once looked like.
Mehdi does not have an office in the current building, which does not even have a teacher's lounge.
Around 250 students are registered in the 24-classroom school, which used to have at least 600 school-goers before the start of the latest war in March, when Hezbollah attacked Israel in support of Tehran, following US-Israeli attacks on the Islamic republic.
Israel responded with major airstrikes and a ground invasion that killed more than 4,300 people, including 261 children according to Lebanese authorities.
More than a million people were displaced, but more than 800,000 returned since June, when a US-Iran memorandum of understanding and a Lebanon-Israel framework agreement significantly reduced the violence.
In some schools in the south that have been converted into shelters, displaced people and students now share the space, with floors reserved for each group.
The Israeli army has accused Hezbollah of using civilian buildings, including schools, to launch attacks or hide weapons.
Rights groups, however, have accused Israel of possible war crimes in its war with Hezbollah.
Lebanese authorities accuse Israel of systematically destroying villages in the south, including homes, schools, places of worship and water and electricity infrastructure.
'Destruction, insecurity, displacement'
Many of Burj Qalaway's children were unable to start the school year, being still displaced or fearing to return to the town, less than a kilometre (mile) away from Israeli troops occupying a swathe of the south.
On Thursday, an Israeli strike hit Qantara, a nearby village.
Earlier this month, UNICEF said that nearly 100,000 students in Lebanon were unable to return to their schools for the academic year due to "damage, destruction, insecurity, or displacement".
The UNICEF report also stated that 436 schools were damaged by the war, while 37 were completely destroyed.
The Burj Qalaway school previously boasted a laboratory, a computer room, and an interactive room.
Government-funded prefabricated units are being installed on the school premises where rubble has not yet been cleared.
'Make my father proud'
Teacher Hoda Najdi gave her class while emphasising to her students the importance of continuing their education and achieving good results despite the difficult circumstances.
"My home was destroyed and so was my school... (but) the students give us the strength and will to continue," the 42-year-old told AFP.
Student Mohammed Mozannar, who was displaced from one place to another in Beirut during the war, said he was "very happy to be back to make up for" the lost year.
"I had no books, no phone and no internet" to follow lessons online, he said.
"I now want to make my father proud."
But the return to school also brought back painful memories for some, like 14-year-old Rawan Fakih.
"I remembered the activities we used to do, I remembered how stressful exams were... and I remembered my friend who was killed" by an Israeli strike, she said.
(AFP)

UN expands list of companies linked to Israeli settlements

Breadcrumb
UN expands list of companies linked to Israeli settlements
The United Nations human rights office issued a list on Friday adding 61 more companies operating in Israeli West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
The database is highly sensitive as firms could be targeted for boycotts or divestment to pressure Israel over settler expansion in the territory that is home to over 3 million Palestinians.
The database, first released in 2020, now includes 214 firms, mostly from Israel, but also from 10 other countries including France, Germany, China and the US.
Newly added firms included Israeli pesticides maker ADAMA, part of Chinese-owned Syngenta Group, Israel-based real estate investment holding company Alony Hetz and Spain's Salvat Logistica.
They did not immediately respond to a request for comment on their inclusion in the UN database.
They joined companies such as travel agency Expedia and home-rental company Airbnb already on the list.
Israel has previously claimed that the list unfairly vilifies companies working legally.
"This is a distorted mechanism - created by a deeply flawed body with an automatic majority against Israel," Israel's diplomatic mission said on Friday, alleging that the database was establish to "persecute" the Jewish state.
There has been a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians as outposts proliferate, prompting Britain, France and Canada to block imports from settlements this month.
The UN rights office assessed companies active in a group of sectors including energy, food, hospitality, transport and agriculture, based on confidential submissions to the UN rights office.
Another 60 or so companies were assessed but not included since they did not meet the UN criteria of involvement in activities that violate the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Examples include supplying demolition equipment to destroy Palestinian buildings, provision of surveillance for settlements and other services like transport that help maintain their existence, according to the UN website.
Other companies, like British-registered online travel company Opodo and Spanish-domiciled online travel agent eDreams, have been dropped from the original list after submitting a reassessment request.
The UN found that there were reasonable grounds to believe they were no longer involved in the activities that previously justified their inclusion.
eDreams said last year it had withdrawn and would continue to block listings of accommodation in Israeli settlements, saying that some had appeared on its website automatically after owners uploaded them.
Palestinians want the West Bank to be part of a future independent homeland.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right government has largely backed settlers, with building ramped up since the Hamas-led attack on Israel in October 2023 and the ensuing Gaza war.
Travel firm Expedia has previously said that the listings in what it called "disputed areas" were clearly labelled, complied with international laws and sanctions and undergo enhanced due diligence guided by UN standards.
(Reuters and TNA staff)

Salam also stressed the need for Israel to fully withdraw from Lebanese territory and for Beirut to move forward in extending state authority over its entire territory, ensuring "weapons (are) held by the state alone."
Lebanese group Hezbollah has so far opposed disarmament.
Lebanon and Israel reached a US-brokered framework agreement in June, providing for the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces and the disarmament of Hezbollah, but its implementation has stalled.
The agreement is aimed at ending decades of Israeli aggression against Lebanon while safeguarding the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Microsoft packages business AI in single app as it tries to compete with Anthropic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:51:25 UTC
00:51:25 KST

Microsoft is shifting its strategy for its Copilot AI platform as the software giant keeps looking for momentum in enterprise AI, where Anthropic has been gaining traction.
On Friday, Microsoft introduced an updated Copilot app that can both code and handle complex productivity tasks, a move the company hopes will entice more of its Office 365 customers to pay for the advanced tools.
While Microsoft maintains a dominant position in business software through Office, its flagship work AI product hasn't taken off. Of more than 450 million existing commercial Office 365 seats across the globe, fewer than 7% have licenses for the AI addition.
Microsoft has, to this point, offered its 365 Copilot AI assistant for knowledge work separately from its GitHub Copilot coding agent. The market has been consolidating around easy-to-use products from OpenAI and Anthropic that bundle various functions. Microsoft's launch comes after CEO Satya Nadella, in June, talked up a future Copilot "super app."
Rather than charging for subscriptions like it does for most of its software — the commercial Microsoft 365 Copilot costs $30 per user per month — Microsoft says clients will pay for the Cowork, Code and Autopilot portions of the new app based on usage, similar to how they buy other AI products.
"We're holding a very high bar," Jacob Andreou, Microsoft's executive vice president for Copilot, told CNBC. "This product is at its best when it's just optimizing for user value and for the quality of the output and what it's able to deliver." Cost efficiency is less important, he said.
Microsoft shares are up 3% this year as of Thursday's close, underperforming the Nasdaq and most of the company's megacap peers.
The new Code feature makes it easy for non-technical users to start simple AI-driven programming projects, and is based on the same technology as GitHub Copilot. An Autopilot tab will allow users to create custom agents that can take care of assignments and communicate in Teams and Outlook.
David McLaren, enterprise data and AI leader at consulting firm GHD, said his company has given Microsoft Copilot to 12,000 employees, with around 200 experimenting with Copilot Cowork, which can handle more complex tasks.
McLaren told CNBC that he's excited for the new app "because it makes GitHub-like capability simpler for more people to use."
Microsoft faces an increasingly crowded AI agent market. Meta's Muse app, introduced earlier this month, has shot up to the top of Apple's App Store, following the rising popularity of tools like Instinct and the open-source OpenClaw.
"The problem is that these agents have been almost impossible to bring into the enterprise," Andreou said at a Wednesday product preview for customers in Seattle. He acknowledged to CNBC that adding the coding element to the app is an instance of Microsoft playing catch-up.
And in catering to user demands, Microsoft is still leaning on the foremost models from OpenAI and Anthropic even as it invests in its own models.
With the new app, users of the coding product can manually select which model they want to use, including a cost-efficient offering from Microsoft. In the Home tab, where users go for productivity requests like generating a report and scheduling changes, there's no Microsoft model available.
Companies enrolled in Microsoft's Frontier program, which provides access to the newest features, will be able to use the Home and Code tabs in the coming weeks, with the Autopilot available in private preview by the end of this month.
"When I think about the Frontier program, this is not about any one frontier model," Nadella said at Wednesday's event. "It's about the frontier ecosystem that we want to ensure, where every firm is able to take their human capital that's in the flow of AI, and then being able to build out this continuous learning system."

Italian truck drivers threaten strike over soaring diesel prices

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Italian truck drivers could go on strike over soaring diesel prices if the government fails to convene road haulage associations for talks, an industry representative said Friday, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
“If the government doesn't convene the road haulage associations to address the rising cost of diesel, we can't rule out a strike,” Claudio Donati, general secretary of the Assotir road haulage association, said at a press conference in Rome.
Donati said a strike would be “the ultimate weapon,” warning that stopping for even one day would mean “stopping the country.”
He said any decision to strike should be made jointly by the sector as a whole, adding that the association wanted to avoid such action.
“We would like to avoid it at all costs,” Donati said, calling on the government to “show a sense of responsibility.”
Assotir national president Anna Vita Manigrasso said the economic situation was so difficult that some truck drivers could stop working because they could no longer cope with rising costs.
“There may not even be a chance to call a strike,” she said.
The consumer group Adusbef said strikes and protests were not an appropriate way to address rising fuel prices.
“A general strike in the road haulage industry would only harm citizens and the country, without, however, resulting in a reduction in diesel prices at the pump or any benefits for the community,” Adusbef President Antonio Tanza said.
He called for a steering committee involving all parties affected by high fuel prices to develop “realistic and immediately applicable measures” to limit the impact of rising costs.
Starting Wednesday, farmers staged a three-day tractor rally near Rome to protest rising fuel prices, with about 10 vehicles initially taking part on Via Aurelia, according to ANSA.
Organizers said more farmers were expected to join the protest, including from outside Rome, and called for government support.
“We expect a real response from politicians for the well-being and stability of the sector,” organizers said.
Massimiliano Dona, president of Italy's National Consumers Union (UNC), said diesel prices were set to approach €2.40 ($2.73) per liter on regular roads and €2.50 ($2.85) per liter on highways following an increase in excise duties.
According to UNC, diesel prices would rise by about 6.1 cents per liter including VAT, reaching €2.399 ($2.73) per liter on regular roads and €2.482 ($2.83) per liter on highways.
Dona said diesel prices would exceed €2.40 ($2.73) per liter in nine of Italy's 20 regions, or 10 if the autonomous provinces of Trento and Bolzano are counted separately.

				     During the visit, the delegation made stops at the National Library of Ireland and Leinster House, the seat of the Irish Parliament, where they were welcomed by Senator Joe Conway, chair of the Italian-Irish Interparliamentary Friendship Group.

Starlink station fire in Poland investigated as sabotage, Russian intelligence link suspected
Polish prosecutors are investigating a fire at a Starlink ground station in the village of Wola Krobowska as an act of sabotage and a terrorist-related crime. Investigators suspect the arson may have been carried out on the orders of Russian secret services.
Source: Polish news agency PAP, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Prosecutor Przemysław Nowak, spokesperson for the National Prosecutor's Office, said criminal proceedings had been opened "regarding acts committed on 23 September this year in the village of Wola Krobowska in the interests of a foreign intelligence service against the Republic of Poland, as well as the commission of sabotage and a terrorist-related crime by causing a fire at a Starlink satellite communications ground station, resulting in significant property damage".
He also said that, based on the information available at the time, the fire had been caused by arson.
Quote: "Furthermore, in this case there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the perpetrators acted on the orders of Russian secret services and in the interests of a foreign intelligence service against the Republic of Poland. The aim of their actions was to disrupt the operation and internet connectivity of the Starlink system in Poland and other countries in Central and Eastern Europe."
Details: Nowak said that on Thursday, prosecutors carried out the necessary activities at the scene, including an examination of the site and interviews with witnesses. The activities were conducted jointly with officers of the Internal Security Agency and the Central Bureau of Police Investigation.
"An investigation is underway in this case. No one has been charged so far," Nowak added.
The investigation has been assigned to the Internal Security Agency and the Central Bureau of Police Investigation.
Background:
- The fire at the Starlink satellite communications ground station in the Polish village of Wola Krobowska broke out on the evening of 23 September.
- Commenting on the incident, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he "does not like to make definitions without 100% certainty as to what constitutes sabotage and what is an accident", but added that "it does not look good".

Protests against rising fuel prices erupt in EU countries — Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:48:56 UTC
00:48:56 KST

BRUSSELS, September 25. /TASS/. Protests against the sharp rise in fuel prices are taking place in several European countries at the same time, according to Politico.
In Portugal, hundreds of trucks took part in a protest on Friday against the rising cost of diesel. Organizers had aimed to gather around 500 heavy vehicles. The protesters moved at low speed along three highways toward the city of Coimbra, causing significant traffic disruptions. Representatives from companies involved in construction, underground works, and materials transport participated in the protest.
Organizers state that since the end of February, the price of diesel in Portugal has risen from approximately 1.59 euro to 2.22 euro per liter. They estimate that for some businesses in the sector, fuel expenses account for more than half of their production costs.
Protests against rising diesel prices also took place in France. Fishermen blocked the ports of Nice, Sete, and Le Grau-du-Roi, as well as an oil depot in Frontignan in the south of the country. Protesters demanded lower fuel costs and increased state support for the industry.
Amid the protests, French authorities were compelled to expand aid programs for citizens and sectors hardest hit by the rising cost of fuel.
Automotive fuel prices in EU countries rose significantly in 2026 due to disruptions in the supply of oil and petroleum products following the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran in February. The European Commission acknowledges that instability in the Middle East has led to significant price volatility, particularly for diesel and jet fuel. According to Reuters, by September, European market prices for diesel had more than doubled compared to levels at the start of the year - a trend driven by reduced supplies of petroleum products from the Middle East and the EU's policy of phasing out energy imports from Russia.

The Ukrainians and the U.S. citizen are allegedly suspected of involvement in the illegal “import of large shipments of drones from Europe to Myanmar via India” for the use of “ethnic armed groups.”
Indian authorities accuse the Ukrainians of having ties to armed groups in the border region.
In addition, they are accused of violating immigration laws, specifically of staying illegally in an area closed to foreigners and of possibly crossing the border with Myanmar without proper authorization.
It later emerged that Russian intelligence agencies were monitoring the Ukrainians in India and passing on information about their movements to local law enforcement.

Over 60% of Armenians favor keeping Russian military base — poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:47:37 UTC
00:47:37 KST

YEREVAN, September 25. /TASS/. A total of 64.4% of Armenians favor keeping Russia's 102nd military base in the country, according to a survey presented by Gallup International's Armenian office.
"Some 39.7% said Armenia needs the 102nd Russian military base to ensure the country's security. Another 24.7% believe the base should remain in Armenia, but the terms governing its presence should be revised. In other words, around 65% think it should stay," Aram Navasardyan, head of the Armenian office, said while presenting the results.
More than 28% of respondents said Russia should withdraw the base, while 6.8% were undecided, he added.
President Vladimir Putin earlier said Russia was willing to keep its military presence at the base in Gyumri for further work and cooperation if the Armenian people wanted it. If Yerevan saw no need for the contingent, he said, personnel could "leave as early as tomorrow." Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan responded that the country was ready to discuss options for the 102nd base to remain or withdraw, although it had not raised the issue.
Russia's 102nd military base has been stationed in Armenia under a 1995 interstate treaty. The facility has around 5,000 personnel. A 2010 amendment extended its term from 25 to 49 years, until 2044. The base has two garrisons, near Gyumri and Yerevan.

HACC Appeals Court upholds UAH 7 mln bail for ex-Sense Bank board chair
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:47:34 EEST
00:47:34 KST

The Appeals Chamber of Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC Appeals Chamber) upheld the UAH 7 million bail set for former chairman of the supervisory board of state-owned Sense Bank Mykola Hladyshenko, the Anti-Corruption Action Centre (AntAC) reported.
The defense had asked the court to overturn the investigating judge's ruling and reject the detective's motion to impose a preventive measure, while a prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) objected to the appeals being granted.
The defense argued, among other things, that during the period of the actions Hladyshenko is accused of committing, he had recused himself from his duties as chairman of Sense Bank's supervisory board.
The SAPO prosecutor, for his part, noted that during a meeting between Hladyshenko and another suspect, Valentyn Yelizarov, at which the posting of bail for former Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko was discussed, the case materials recorded a reference to "pounds." In the prosecutor's view, this indicates that Hladyshenko was aware of the matter.
According to AntAC, as of September 25, the UAH 7 million bail set for Hladyshenko had not been posted.
As reported, on September 8 the HACC imposed a preventive measure on Hladyshenko in the form of UAH 7 million bail. He was required to post it within five days; otherwise, the prosecutor could ask the court to impose a more stringent preventive measure.
The court also ordered Hladyshenko not to leave Kyiv, to surrender his passports for travel abroad for safekeeping, to refrain from communicating with individuals involved in the criminal proceedings, and not to visit the premises of Sense Bank, the National Bank of Ukraine and the State Financial Monitoring Service of Ukraine.
The prosecution had asked the court to remand Hladyshenko in custody with the possibility of posting UAH 20 million in bail. According to the prosecutor's version, Hladyshenko, acting on behalf of Sense Bank, controlled the process to ensure that there were no obstacles to posting bail for Halushchenko and involved the bank's financial monitoring department director, Liudmyla Snihur, in this.
As part of the NABU and SAPO "Forrest Gump" operation, law enforcement authorities are investigating the circumstances surrounding the posting of UAH 150 million in bail for Halushchenko. Sense Bank appears in the investigation materials, with some of the relevant transactions conducted through its accounts.
On September 2, the HACC imposed a preventive measure of UAH 15 million bail on Sense Bank Chairman of the Management Board Oleksiy Stupak, and on September 4 it imposed UAH 3 million bail on Snihur.

Manchester City found guilty of almost all Premier League financial breach charges: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:46:41 UTC
00:46:41 KST

Halis Sünnetci
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Manchester City have been found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations, The Athletic reported on Friday.
The ruling by an independent commission comes more than three years after City were charged in February 2023 following a four-year investigation.
The Athletic reported that sanctions have not yet been decided on and City are expected to appeal.
The case includes breaches of rules requiring clubs to provide accurate financial information over a nine-season period from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as charges that City failed to cooperate with the Premier League's investigation.
City have consistently denied any wrongdoing.
"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023," a City spokesperson told The Athletic.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," the spokesperson added.
City had expressed "surprise" when the charges were announced in 2023 and said they had a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" supporting their position.
A 12-week hearing before the independent commission ran from September to December 2024.
City have won eight Premier League titles since Sheikh Mansour's takeover in 2008, as well as their first Champions League in 2023.
No sanctions have yet been announced, with the disciplinary process set to continue as City prepare to appeal the ruling.
Possible sanctions available to the independent commission include fines, points deductions, suspension or expulsion from the Premier League.

Italy raids neo-Nazi network over synagogue attack plot, finds bomb manuals and weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:45:25 UTC
00:45:25 KST

Italian security forces on Friday searched the homes of 17 people, including 14 minors, as part of a nationwide investigation into an online neo-Nazi and white supremacist network whose members allegedly spread antisemitic propaganda, praised Adolf Hitler and discussed attacks on a synagogue, mosque and school.
The suspects are being investigated on allegations including incitement to commit crimes, propaganda and incitement based on racial, ethnic and religious discrimination, as well as training for terrorist activity and terrorism-related aggravating circumstances.
According to Italian investigators, the probe grew out of prolonged monitoring of online groups and profiles linked to neo-Nazi, white supremacist and accelerationist ideology. Members allegedly circulated material glorifying Hitler, the SS and other Nazi symbols, alongside antisemitic, racist and homophobic content.
The groups also shared manifestos written by far-right mass killers including Anders Breivik, Brenton Tarrant and Stephan Balliet. Investigators said they found instructional material related to homemade explosives and the use of knives and firearms, which they described as presenting a “real danger” because of the way such material was being distributed alongside operational guidance.
Two extremist groups
Investigators focused on two main online groups.
One, called the “New European Order Chat,” allegedly distributed Nazi and white supremacist propaganda, Holocaust denial, antisemitic material, manifestos written by mass killers and manuals on explosives.
The second, called the “Italian Fascist Front,” allegedly circulated racist and antisemitic material targeting Jews, Black people and gay people, as well as videos of executions and massacres of minorities and propaganda linked to The Base, a U.S.-founded neo-Nazi organization.
The Italian Fascist Front allegedly had an internal hierarchy. Its founder and administrator used the title “supreme commander,” while other members were assigned titles including “secretary,” “Blackshirt” and “SS corporal.” Recruitment was conducted through Telegram, with prospective members required to fill out an application form, and participants referred to one another as “comrades in combat.”
According to the investigation, conversations in the groups included threats and proposals involving attacks on a synagogue, a mosque and a school, as well as talk of a “mass reset” and Holocaust denial.
Police searches across several Italian cities uncovered knives and other bladed weapons, Nazi flags and memorabilia, as well as phones, computers and other electronic devices investigators suspect were used to distribute extremist material.
Authorities are continuing to examine the seized devices and the role of each suspect as they seek to determine whether the online activity developed beyond propaganda and discussion into preparations for violence.

Eni sets price cap of €2.19 for diesel, €1.99 for petrol
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:45:03 CEST
00:45:03 KST

Italian energy giant Eni on Friday
announced a price cap of €2.19 per litre for diesel, €1.99 for
petrol, running for 30 days from Monday September 30 and
extendable until the end of the year.
                                    
                                       
				"Eni has set a maximum price (price cap) for fuels sold by
Enilive at €2.19 per liter for diesel and €1.99 per liter for
petrol (approximately 17 cents lower than current average
levels)," it said in a press release.
                                    
                                       
				"The price cap is linked to the current excise duty relief and
will apply starting September 28 for an initial period of 30
days, with the possibility of extension until the end of the
year, depending on market trends and supply conditions.
                                    
                                       
				"The contraction in the supply of refined products on the
international market resulting from ongoing geopolitical crises,
combined with a shortage of refining capacity across Europe
(with nearly 30 refineries closing over the last 15 years), has
driven fuel prices to levels that place an extreme burden on
Italian households and businesses," the company writes.
                                    
                                       
				"Against this backdrop," the statement continues, "Eni intends
to offer further support to the country, consumers, and its own
customers.
                                    
                                       
				"This move complements initiatives the company has pursued since
last March—specifically, passing on only a portion of rising
international market prices to the recommended retail prices at
its service stations, thereby absorbing a significant share of
the cost increase.
                                    
                                       
				"Eni is also committed to operating the biorefineries
established in Venice and Gela," the statement concludes, "as
well as to the development and transformation of sites in
Livorno and elsewhere in Italy.
                                    
                                       
				"In doing so, it is safeguarding jobs and the environment,
investing significant capital locally, and preserving refining
capacity—specifically for sustainable products—that would
otherwise have been lost to the market."
On September 16 Giorgia Meloni's government extended a
diesel duty cut to October 5, but lowered it from 17 cents a
litre to 12.2 cents and then to 6.1 cents.
                                    
                                       
				The measure, introduced to address rising fuel costs amid the
Iran war, had already been extended twice.
                                    
                                       
				It said the reduction in excise duties (and VAT) on diesel will
drop to 12.2 cents per liter from September 18 to 25, and then
decrease further to 6.1 cents from September 26 to October 5.
                                    
                                       
				The decree is aimed at providing economic support and mitigating
the impact of the ongoing rise in fuel costs.
                                    
                                       
				The measure stipulates that from September 18 to September 25, 
2026, the excise duty will be 572.90 euros per thousand liters, 
and from September 26 to October 5, it will be 622.90 euros per
thousand liters.
                                    
                                       
				The "standard" excise duty is 672.90 euros per thousand liters.

Asian Games | Roundup: China wraps up seven golds in gymnastics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
23:44:15 CST
00:44:15 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's Zou Jingyuan claimed his third consecutive Asian Games gold medal in the parallel bars on Friday, while his teammate Tian Hao won the horizontal bar title as the gymnastics competition at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to an end.
Zou, an Olympic gold medalist and four-time world champion, was the first gymnast to perform in the parallel bars final and posted a score of 15.500. None of the following competitors could surpass him, giving Zou the gold with a clear advantage.
"Overall, I think my performance at the Asian Games was quite good. I had prepared for the worst before coming here, so I'm actually satisfied with the result. It proves that our previous efforts were not in vain," he said.
"But finishing one competition does not mean the end. As long as I keep going, there will always be another competition. I don't think I can be the champion forever," Zou added.
In the horizontal bar final, several gymnasts fell from the apparatus. Tian topped the standings with 14.700 points, while Paris Olympic champion Shinnosuke Oka of Japan took silver with 14.033.
It was Tian's first Asian Games appearance after an injury kept him out of the Hangzhou Asian Games. He said the fact that most of China's key gymnasts had already completed their events left him with relatively little pressure in his final competition on Friday.
"I was able to showcase the horizontal bar more fully, and it is also my strength," Tian said. "I'm in good form now. I hope I can maintain this at next month's world championships so that our team can achieve a better result."
In the women's floor exercise final, Japan's veteran gymnast Aiko Sugihara won another gold with 14.033 points after she ended China's straight 13-title run in women's all-around on Tuesday. Her teammate Misa Nishiyama took silver, while China's Zhang Yihan won bronze.
South Korea's Hwang Seo-hyun won the balance beam title, with China's Qiu Qiyuan taking silver.
In the men's vault final, the Philippines' Carlos Edriel Yulo claimed his second gold after also winning the men's floor exercise title.
China finished the artistic gymnastics competition with seven gold, two silver and four bronze medals. The Chinese team had earlier swept the men's and women's team titles and also won gold in the men's individual all-around, men's rings and women's uneven bars. ■

Asian Games | Athletics roundup: Boonson, Chen Yujie storm to 100m golds in Asian Games record times
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
23:44:11 CST
00:44:11 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Puripol Boonson and China's Chen Yujie broke Asian Games records to win the men's and women's 100 meters on Friday, capping a night of seven athletics finals in Nagoya.
The 20-year-old Thai clocked 9.90 seconds, lowering the 9.91 he had run in the semifinals. Both times beat the previous Games record of 9.92 set by China's Su Bingtian in the 2018 Jakarta Games. Oman's Ali Al-Balushi took silver in 10.04, while compatriot Malham Al-Balushi claimed bronze in 10.11. Defending champion Xie Zhenye finished seventh in 10.30.
"My goal is to break the Asian record, I would like to see a Thai person set an Asian record," Boonson said after the race.
Chen, 17, won the women's 100 meters final in 11.06 seconds, cutting 0.09 seconds off the Games record set by Sri Lanka's Susanthika Jayasinghe in 2002. Singapore's Veronica Shanti Pereira was second in 11.21, with Bahrain's Edidiong Odiong third in 11.33. Chen's victory kept the title in Chinese hands after Ge Manqi's win in Hangzhou three years ago.
"Although I've gone from being a challenger to a defending champion, holding on to an Asian Games title will be difficult. I want to keep the mindset of a challenger and set my sights on the World Championships and the Olympics. I hope women's sprinters from China and across Asia can achieve better results on those stages," Chen said.
The home crowd had a gold medal to celebrate in the women's pole vault. Japan's Morota Misaki cleared 4.55 meters to improve her national record and beat China's Asian record holder Niu Chunge, who took silver with 4.50m. India's Baranica Elangovan won bronze with 4.15m. It is the first time in Asian Games history that an athlete from outside China has won gold in the event.
Japan also took the top two places in the women's heptathlon, with Yuri Tanaka winning on 5,920 points ahead of Nanaka Kajiki on 5,673.
China's Song Jiayuan won the women's shot put at the Asian Games on Friday, with teammate Zhang Linru taking silver as China claimed the title for a 13th consecutive edition. Song, the Paris Olympic bronze medalist, had finished second to compatriot Gong Lijiao at the previous Games in Hangzhou.
"We've inherited the competitive spirit of the older generation, who taught us a great deal," Song said. "Techniques have advanced, and I've switched to the rotational technique. But I think the support of our coaches and team officials is the main reason Chinese women's shot putters have performed so well in Asia."
Bahrain's Birhanu Balew retained his Asian Games men's 10,000 meters title on Friday, crossing the line in 28:27.51 to finish 1.87 seconds ahead of India's Gulveer Singh. Singh, a bronze medalist in Hangzhou three years ago, took silver in 28:29.38, while Bahrain's Albert Kiptoo claimed bronze in 28:34.38. China's Wang Wenjie finished fourth in 28:38.14.
Uzbekistan's Sukhrob Khodjaev won the men's hammer throw with 74.38m, while defending champion Wang Qi of China finished sixth. ■

Thailand's exports jump 24.3 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
23:44:06 CST
00:44:06 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's exports expanded for the 26th consecutive month in August, mainly driven by overseas investments in infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI)-related industries, which in turn fueled demand for electronic products, official data showed on Friday.
Exports, a key driver of the Southeast Asian country's economic growth, expanded 24.3 percent year-on-year last month to 34.62 billion U.S. dollars, up from a 21.6 percent gain in July, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
Industrial product shipments soared 27.1 percent year-on-year, marking the 29th successive month of expansion, with the fastest growth recorded in video recording, telephones, and printed circuits.
The August data also indicated that imports surged 25.1 percent from a year earlier to 37.10 billion dollars, resulting in a monthly trade deficit of 2.48 billion dollars.
Looking ahead, Thai exports are expected to continue their upward trajectory through the remainder of 2026, supported by steady demand for AI-related products and clarity on U.S. tariff policies, said Natiya Suchinda, deputy director-general of the ministry's Trade Policy and Strategy Office.
However, geopolitical risks, energy prices, and freight rates remain downside pressures on global trade that warrant close attention, Natiya said in a statement. ■

TEHRAN, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian late Thursday reaffirmed his country's commitment to dialogue and diplomacy while accusing the United States of repeatedly disrupting the negotiation process.
"We have favored dialogue and continue to do so. However, if there is any recommendation (regarding the need to pursue diplomacy), it must be conveyed to the American side, as at various junctures, the dialogue process was disrupted by the United States," he said.
Pezeshkian made the remarks at a meeting with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten on the sidelines of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, according to a statement published on the website of his office.
On Thursday, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi also underlined the country's "responsible" approach towards using diplomacy for resolving issues related to its "peaceful" nuclear program during a meeting with his British counterpart Ed Miliband on the UNGA sidelines, according to a statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry on Friday.
At a UNGA press briefing on Thursday, he said Tehran had proposed to Washington a seven-day plan to cease hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and then begin comprehensive talks on its nuclear program, according to The New York Times.
The minister added that the proposal closely reflected commitments in the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between Tehran and Washington in June on ending the war and expressed Iran's readiness to begin implementing it once the United States agrees, saying that "it would be better" if a deal was reached before the U.S. midterm elections.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the June MoU, negotiations were scheduled within 60 days, which ended on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the talks' fate remains unclear following recent escalations. ■

Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:43:59 UTC
00:43:59 KST

Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.
In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.
Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.
Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.
The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.
“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.
In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.
On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.
Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.
Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US.
In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible.
It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.
Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.
Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.
He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

LONDON, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Children in youth custody in England and Wales continue to face high levels of violence, prolonged confinement in cells and inadequate access to education, according to official findings highlighted by the Youth Justice Board on Friday.
The board was responding to a report released earlier this week by HM Inspectorate of Prisons on the experiences of 12- to 18-year-olds in custody.
The report found that children at most establishments spent too much time locked in their cells, with boys at some sites unlocked for less than four hours a day on average.
Education provision was also inadequate at most establishments. Across the youth estate, 16 percent of children surveyed said they were not taking part in education, work or programs aimed at addressing offending behaviour.
Violence remained a regular feature of daily life, with 39 percent of children saying they had felt unsafe at some point in custody. Only 26 percent said they would report bullying or victimization by other young people.
Steph Roberts-Bibby, chief executive of the Youth Justice Board, said the problems were systemic rather than isolated failures, calling for a shift towards smaller, child-centered facilities with a stable specialist workforce.
The findings have renewed concerns over whether the current system is adequately preparing children for life after custody. The British government has said children entering the justice system often have complex needs and face significant barriers to rehabilitation, and is seeking to strengthen early intervention and ensure custody is used only as a last resort. ■

The "C909 Airplane Hospital" project represents a significant development, opening up new opportunities for bilateral cooperation in civil aviation.
"I am confident that Chinese-Kyrgyz cooperation in healthcare will continue to strengthen the centuries-old friendship between our peoples and further advance the high-quality cooperation between the two countries," Sun said.
The C909 aircraft used in the project is reportedly one of the highlights of the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China, Ltd. (COMAC). The aircraft is available in various configurations, including emergency response and medical versions.
On the same day, a Kyrgyz woman who had suffered from allergic rhinitis for two years underwent surgery aboard a Chinese C909 aircraft parked at Manas International Airport in Bishkek.
"Everything went very well. I didn't expect it to be so quick," she said. "I express my deepest gratitude and appreciation to all the doctors."

The month-long action provides free diagnosis and treatment, academic exchanges and telemedicine services in ophthalmology and otolaryngology. It is expected to benefit more than 2,000 local patients, with over 170 surgeries to be performed free of charge. ■

Germany approves fuel tax cut to reduce energy costs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
23:43:25 CST
00:43:25 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Germany's two houses of parliament on Friday approved a law to temporarily cut fuel taxes, clearing the way for lower costs on petrol and diesel as record-high fuel prices weigh on households and businesses.
The Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, and the Bundesrat, which represents the country's 16 federal states, both approved the measure. It will take effect on Oct. 1 and run through the end of this year, the federal government said in a statement.
Under the measure, taxes on petrol and diesel would be cut to provide relief of around 17 euro cents (0.19 U.S. dollars) per liter, similar to a temporary reduction introduced in May and June.
The total cost of the tax reduction is estimated at around 2.5 billion euros (2.85 billion dollars), with federal states contributing half of the amount, the government stated.
Citing renewed escalation of the Middle East conflicts, the government said higher energy and fuel prices had placed a heavy burden on consumers and the German economy.
Berlin is also planning further measures to contain fuel costs. The government said it would hold talks with the oil industry to introduce a temporary cap on petrol and diesel prices by Jan. 1, 2027 at the latest.
Higher energy costs have added to inflationary pressure in Europe's largest economy. Germany's inflation rate rose to 2.9 percent in August from 2.8 percent in July, while energy prices jumped 10.5 percent year-on-year, official data showed. ■

Estonian household deposits rise by €1 billion in a year as housing lending grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:42:00 UTC
00:42:00 KST

Estonian households held €1 billion more in bank deposits in August 2026 than a year earlier, according to Eesti Pank. Banks issued €237 million in new housing loans during the month, €39 million more than in August 2025. The average interest rate on new mortgage-backed housing loans also rose, reaching 4.18%.
Deposits and bank assets grow
Total deposits in Estonian banks reached €34.5 billion in August, up €389 million from July and €1.9 billion from a year earlier. Time deposits held by Estonian households and companies amounted to €7.6 billion, an annual increase of 8%.
Non-resident deposits fell by €157 million over the year and accounted for 15% of all deposits. Banks’ combined balance sheets stood at €49.6 billion, up 6.1%, or €2.9 billion, from August 2025.
Housing lending remains above last year’s level
Banks issued €237 million in housing loans to households in August. That was €29 million less than in July, but €39 million more than a year earlier. The outstanding stock of loans and leases to Estonian households reached €16.3 billion, up 9% year on year.
The average interest rate on new mortgage-backed housing loans was 4.18%, compared with 3.57% in August 2025. This measure covers new loan contracts and excludes renegotiated agreements. Households also took out €28 million in car leases during August, €8 million more than a year earlier.
Corporate borrowing increases
Estonian companies received €365 million in long-term loans and leases in August, €70 million more than a year earlier. The largest annual increases in new lending were recorded in infrastructure and retail, while lending to the primary sector, which includes agriculture, forestry and fishing, declined.
The outstanding stock of corporate loans and leases reached €14.2 billion, up 8% year on year. The average interest rate on new long-term corporate loans was 4.96%, compared with 4.67% a year earlier. Meanwhile, the assets of leasing companies totalled €3.9 billion, down 6.3% over the year.
The figures come from Eesti Pank’s August 2026 statistics on banks and leasing companies.

Evan Gershkovich Says His Arrest in Russia Was Carefully Planned FSB Sting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:41:59 UTC
00:41:59 KST

U.S. reporter Evan Gershkovich, in his first detailed published account of his arrest in Russia in 2023, says he was the victim of an elaborate sting operation by the FSB security service.
In an extract from his book "This Cursed Beautiful Land," Gershkovich says that while working on a story for The Wall Street Journal about Russian military production, he held two meetings with the union boss of a factory in Yekaterinburg, a major defense-industry hub.
At their second encounter, in a steakhouse, the source produced papers with hand-copied tables of figures, telling the reporter that they related to the production of tanks.
As he jotted down notes, Gershkovich said, he heard the sound of marching feet and looked up to see a group of masked men approaching their table.
"A pang of guilt ripped through me: Had I compromised a source? But panic immediately replaced that thought. Instinct took over, my hands moving to hide the papers in the gap between the bench and the wall," he wrote in the book extract, published by the Journal on Friday.
"The men quickly descended on us. An arm was yanking my neck, pulling me off the couch... Someone shouted: 'You are under arrest by the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation'."
A long sentence, then a prisoner swap
Gershkovich, then 31, became the first U.S. reporter arrested on espionage charges in Russia since the Cold War. He was later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
He writes that he and his editors had considered the risks of the reporting trip and agreed that the source should not bring any documents to the meeting; if he did so, Gershkovich should not accept anything from him.
But at the meeting, the source had "thrust the papers into my hands."
Although he had reported on the arrests of other Americans in Russia, and on the targeting and even murder of Russian journalists, Gershkovich writes that the "unspoken rule" was that foreign correspondents enjoyed a degree of immunity: they might be expelled, but not arrested.
Reeling with shock, he was handcuffed, had a black sack placed over his head and was whisked into a van where he was placed in a chokehold and punched in the abdomen while being questioned, he writes.
FSB 'backup plan'
Gershkovich said that since his release he had learned of evidence that the FSB had a "backup plan" to arrest him on another of his planned reporting trips, to Siberia, if the Yekaterinburg operation had failed.
He said he believes the two meetings with the source in Yekaterinburg were designed to help the FSB persuade President Vladimir Putin that he was a spy and secure approval for his arrest at the second meeting.
"Putin, it seems to me, fully bought into this narrative," he said.
The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Putin said in a February 2024 interview with U.S. television host Tucker Carlson that Gershkovich had been "caught red-handed" while collecting confidential information.
The journalist, his newspaper and the U.S. government all strongly deny the allegation that Gershkovich was a spy.

Seventh person killed by bear in Russian region in a month as spate of attacks grows

Seventh person killed by bear in Russian region in a month as spate of attacks grows
MOSCOW, Sept 25 - A Russian woman has been fatally mauled by a bear in her garden, the seventh such death in her Siberian region this month, state investigators said, amid a nationwide spate of killings that experts blame on climate change and human incompetence.
A video released by investigators in Siberia's Krasnoyarsk region some 3,000 km (1,864 miles) east of Moscow showed them walking through a wooded area and inspecting the corpse of the brown bear which carried out the attack.
The state TASS news agency said the bear had killed the 51-year-old woman in the village of Voznesenka after she saw the creature trying to get into a pen in her garden where she kept domestic animals.
"The bear lunged at the woman. The predator was shot dead by a neighbour of the deceased," TASS reported.
Experts cited in Russian media said that bears — which have attacked humans in at least 11 regions across Russia this year and killed at least 20 people — have been forced to look further afield for food this year because an early and dry spring meant there was a lack of berries for them to feed on in September.
People are also guilty of leaving food waste out in the open where it attracts bears and of ignoring safety rules, the experts said, while in at least one region the authorities stand accused of failing to keep bear numbers down.
BEAR POPULATION HAS RISEN SHARPLY
Shorter and milder winters, among other factors, have seen bear numbers more than double from 130,000 in 1990.
Investigators in Krasnoyarsk, home to nearly 27,000 of Russia's 308,000 brown bears according to environment ministry data, said on Wednesday they had opened a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing it of negligence that led to the deaths of six people — now seven, including the woman in her garden — in the region in September alone.
It said the ministry and other agencies had a responsibility to monitor and control the bear population and act promptly if people's lives were at risk.
"Despite numerous warnings of danger, officials from the ministry and other authorised officials failed to take measures to regulate the predator population and prevent their appearance in areas inhabited by people," investigators said in a statement.
"Monitoring data show that the brown bear population in the Krasnoyarsk region has increased 2.5-fold, reaching over 26,000 animals. Residents... have submitted more than 120 reports of brown bears entering the boundaries of settlements in more than 15 districts of the region, as well as in the cities of Krasnoyarsk, Zheleznogorsk and Zelenogorsk," they said.
Investigators warned people to avoid visiting forests and to postpone any plans to go mushroom and berry picking in the woods, a popular Russian pastime.
"If you encounter a large predator, you have virtually no chance of survival," the statement said.
Other people killed by bears in the Krasnoyarsk region this month include a 39-year-old male logger and two women out picking mushrooms.
OTHER REGIONS ALSO AFFECTED
In Siberia's Irkutsk region, a male pensioner who also went out mushroom picking was killed by a bear this month as were two men gathering wild plants in a forest.
In one of the most high-profile attacks this year, a bear attacked two tourists in their tent in the Altai region in August. It dragged one of the tourists, a 29-year-old woman, out of the tent, killed her, and then buried her in the forest.
And in the Siberian region of Tuva, ice hockey coach Alexander Kuzmenko — father of NHL player Andrei Kuzmenko — was killed this week by a bear while on a fishing trip.
The environment ministry has sought to play down the spate of attacks.
"In recent years, around 20 to 30 cases of bear attacks have been recorded annually," it told the RBC news outlet.
"The only abnormal spike was in 2014, when there were 166 cases. The thing is, nowadays everyone has a smartphone, and information spreads quickly via the internet and social media, which creates the impression that the problem is widespread." REUTERS

Speaking at the Elysée, the pontiff set the tone for his first visit to France; dialogue with the Republic, warnings over AI and a call for peace, while acknowledging ongoing disagreements.
French President Emmanuel Macron's meeting withPope Leo XIV gave the French leader an opportunity to revisit the fundamental principles that shape dialogue between the state and religions, while addressing the upheavals confronting contemporary societies.
In his speech, Macron placed the encounter within the framework of the traditional dialogue between France and the Holy See, while recalling the principles of the Republic.
The French president placed particular emphasis on secularism, presented not as a way of distancing society from religion, but as the framework that guarantees freedom of conscience and enables everyone to express themselves.
The meeting also comes as both interlocutors identify artificial intelligence as one of the major challenges of our time. The Élysée stresses that climate and AI were at the top of the global issues discussed during the pair's talks.
On the international stage, Emmanuel Macron defended an engaged France, standing for "peace, multilateralism and respect for international law."
"Every life is worth the same, and all peoples must be defended," said the French leader, referring to the raging wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, which he believes are central to the concerns of both Paris and the Vatican.
He also affirmed that France stands "on the side of peace, active multilateralism, respect for international law and the United Nations Charter."
'AI, peace and human dignity'
In his address, the pontiff placed human dignity at the heart of his message.
Speaking to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on Thursday, Leo XIV had already warned of the risks linked to artificial intelligence, pursuing a reflection that has become one of the hallmarks of his pontificate.
He warned in particular against a technology liable to be used "for purposes of surveillance, manipulation and discrimination", while calling for technological progress to remain subject to human responsibility.
"The greater our power to transform the world, the greater must be our ability to discern what truly serves human dignity," he said.
The Pope also assigned France a particular responsibility in a world marked by wars and tensions, especially within Europe.
"Faced with the sound of marching boots and the multifaceted crises shaking our world, France has the vocation to remain a tireless artisan of peace and multilateralism," he said.
He further challenged the idea that nuclear weapons constitute a security guarantee, calling for a break in the arms race and for a deeper emphasis to be placed on dialogue and justice.
On secularism, Leo XIV argued for a concept that he sees as compatible with the presence of religious convictions in the public sphere.
"True secularism does not consist in excluding religion from the public space," said the Head of the Catholic Church, as he addressed bioethical issues on which the Vatican is at odds with developments in France.
He slammed Paris' recently adopted and controversial assisted death bill, and reaffirmed his commitment to protecting every human life. He also opposed surrogacy, in a speech whose guiding thread was the defence of human dignity.
After the meeting at the Élysée, Pope Leo XIV visited the UNESCO headquarters in the French capital, where he will deliver an address on artificial intelligence, youth, peace and interreligious dialogue.
He is then due to celebrate vespers at Notre-Dame cathedral before leading a prayer vigil with young people at the Stade de France.
On Saturday, the Pope will visit the Bakhita House, dedicated to support and social integration, before a Mass at Place de la Concorde ahead of his departure for Lourdes. There, he will celebrate Mass on Sunday and meet bishops, locals and the faithful.
Finally, on Monday Leo XIV will travel to Metz for an interreligious meeting and a session devoted to the "roots of Europe for peace and unity", before a final Mass at Saint-Étienne Cathedral.
