Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
16:36:22 BST
00:36:22 KST

Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
- Published
School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.
One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service".
At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made boosting Germany's military a priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
A new law introducing voluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers.
However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag.
Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces.
One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's armed forces]".
"That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on."
The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service.
The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms.
The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt.
A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007".
This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam.
During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain.
Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011.
But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army.
The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences.

Russia Can Restart 80% of Black Sea Grain Export Terminals if Attacks Stop – Analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:36:14 UTC
00:36:14 KST

Russia could quickly restart up to 80% of its grain terminal capacity in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov if diplomatic efforts to halt mutual attacks by Russia and Ukraine result in a ceasefire, a Reuters analysis of industry data showed on Friday.
But three terminals accounting for about 20% of Russia's grain export infrastructure in the area have suffered heavy damage and could take months to repair, the analysis showed.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan is leading an international effort by grain-importing countries to restore Black Sea grain trade, which has been stalled by attacks on ports and vessels in recent months.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that India, Egypt and other Middle Eastern countries were also involved. The Kremlin acknowledged diplomatic contacts but said Russia was finding alternate export routes in the meantime.
Reuters analyzed the condition of Russia's nine major grain terminals in the region, as well as smaller facilities in the Sea of Azov and Don river delta, using information from four sources familiar with terminal operations.
The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue. Before the attacks, the route handled up to 70% of Russia's grain exports.
Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, and disruption to shipments has driven up global grain prices and renewed concerns about food security linked to the war in Ukraine.
The analysis found that three of nine major terminals had suffered serious damage in Ukrainian attacks, affecting about one-fifth of grain-loading capacity in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
Extent of damage
One of Russia's three largest grain terminals, NKHP in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, suffered serious damage in an Aug. 12 attack. The terminal has annual capacity of 7.1 million metric tons and repairs could take up to six months.
"At NKHP, that conveyor gallery was completely destroyed. It actually collapsed onto the road and was lying across it," one source at Novorossiysk told Reuters.
"The staff were sent home for six months. I don't even know how long the shutdown will last," he said, adding that damage at the other two Novorossiysk terminals, KSK and NZT, was minor and that both were ready to resume operations.
The company said repairs at NKHP could take up to four months.
The other damaged terminals, ZTKT at the Black Sea port of Taman and a terminal in Taganrog on the Azov Sea, have halted operations although the full extent of the damage could not be established. Together, ZTKT and Taganrog have annual capacity of 6.7 million tons.
ZTKT, which has annual capacity of 5.5 million tons, was hit on July 30 and is unable to load grain, another source said, adding that it was unclear when operations could resume.
The analysis showed that terminals with combined capacity of about 53 million tons are currently idle because of security risks but could resume operations. Total grain terminal capacity in the region is about 67 million tons.

PLATFORM: a steel bed frame reimagined as a piece of architecture
Amsterdam architect and designer Rik Frans Jansen presents PLATFORM, a bed made from stainless steel and aluminum and dressed by Berlin bedding label Brut Studios at Paris Design Week 2026. Its bolted metal panels and exposed aluminum profiles draw from building construction, bringing materials usually concealed behind walls and ceilings into the domestic interior.
Presented at GOOD SELECTION, an exhibition organized by designer Lucas Zito during Paris Design Week 2026, PLATFORM measures 250 × 220 × 50 cm. The bed consists of an aluminum profile frame clad in bolted stainless-steel panels, lifting the sleeping platform above the floor and giving it a distinct spatial presence.
Exposed joints and soft sateen contrast across the PLATFORM bed
The same panel system continues into a low headboard with integrated power outlets, while joints, bolts, and profile ends remain visible. The approach reflects Jansen’s architectural background and his interest in materials typically encountered during construction before they are concealed within a building. Here, these structural elements become the visible language of the furniture.
The rigid metal construction is paired with Brut Studios’ 600-thread-count sateen made from extra-long-staple Egyptian cotton, presented in Ashen Stone and Concrete Blue. The colors reference the tones of the steel, creating a contrast between the hard metal frame and the soft textile surface.
RIK FRANS JANSEN’S uses Brut Studios’ bedding in exhibition settings
Designed in Berlin and made in Egypt, Brut Studios develops bedding through material, proportion, and a restrained palette of architectural colors. For the presentation, the bedding extends the PLATFORM concept into the softer elements of the bedroom while maintaining its material and tonal relationship with the bed frame. PLATFORM is available to order.

The Kyiv Independent will host a live storytelling event in London on Oct. 2, bringing together its journalists and readers for an evening of firsthand accounts of reporting, working, and living through Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.
We spend most of our time reporting from Ukraine for an audience we don't actually see. And this October we are set to change it, and are inviting you to spend an evening with us in London — to hear the stories behind our reporting, ask us questions, and meet our team in person. The event will also bring together media colleagues, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and others united by their desire to support Ukraine and independent journalism.
Buy tickets here
The event, to be held on Oct. 2 at Kings Place, will be hosted by Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko and feature talks by CEO Daryna Shevchenko, Deputy Chief Editor Toma Istomina, war reporter Francis Farrell, video creator Olena Zashko, and business reporter Dominic Culverwell.
The stories you'll hear that evening range from personal experiences amid Russian attacks, to a war reporter's firsthand experiences of documenting war crimes to the reasoning of choice to stay and live in Ukraine.
As Olga says, "Live storytelling is a very special and intense experience for us as journalists — we come before people stripped of the usual barrier of paper or screen. It works for a different level of connection and allows us to offer more. It's also, frankly, a little scary. But it's so great to be able to do it in London, where we have many followers, and Ukraine has many allies."
We rarely get to meet the people who read our stories and make our work possible — which is exactly why evenings like this matter to us.
As Francis puts it, "The most powerful way to communicate remains face-to-face. In recent months, the war has only become darker and more confusing, and the need to cut through the narrative noise has only become more acute."
"Since the full-scale invasion, London has been an unrivalled hub of people who understand what this struggle is about, and I am more than excited to see everyone there, old friends and new."
The war is not only what we report on. It also shapes our own lives in ways that are sometimes difficult to put into words.
For war reporter and video creator Olena Zashko, years spent filming the war meant documenting soldiers holding their positions, families evacuating, and the suffering and loss inflicted on Ukrainian communities. Then, one day, it was her own family evacuating as Russian forces closed in on her hometown.
"That experience became one of the most terrifying of my life."
At the London event, Olena will reflect on that experience and what it means to tell stories about a war that has reached into her own family.
"War is not only about weapons and explosions. War is about people. And we are people who still live, work, dream, and exist during this time in Ukraine."
As the Kyiv Independent team makes its final preparations for the London event, Russia's war against Ukraine continues to intensify. Russian attack drones are striking Kyiv day and night, alongside regular ballistic missile attacks. The stories our journalists will bring to London are unfolding against the backdrop of a war that continues to shape every aspect of life in Ukraine.
We look forward to meeting you in London on Oct. 2.

More than 100 “shadow fleet” oil tankers have switched to the Russian flag since the start of 2025, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:31:26 UTC
00:31:26 KST

Between January 2025 and June 2026, Russia moved around 100 “shadow fleet” tankers to its flag registry amid mounting sanctions pressure. By the time most of the vessels switched to the Russian flag, they were already subject to sanctions, according to a new report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
The center’s analysts counted 107 tankers that have switched to the Russian flag since the start of 2025, boosting Russia’s overall registry by 36%. The peak came in December 2025, coinciding with a U.S. campaign against Venezuelan crude and threats to detain oil tankers.
At the time they changed flags, 93 tankers — 87% of the total — were already under sanctions. More than half of them had sailed under false flags between the time they were added to sanctions lists and the time they switched to Russian jurisdiction.
CREA confirmed sanctions were a key factor behind the rise in tankers switching to the Russian flag. Throughout the first half of 2025, “shadow fleet” vessels were actively being registered in the Comoros and Gambia, but the company managing their registrations was placed under European sanctions that summer. As a result, both countries reduced the number of tankers they registered, and some of those vessels switched to the Russian flag instead. Panama also cut the number of “shadow fleet” vessels in its registries by nearly two-thirds starting from May 2025.
CREA’s analysts said the case of the Arctic Metagaz gas carrier (IMO: 9243148) may also have made third countries less willing to register vessels that, in practice, operate on behalf of Russia. The gas carrier was struck by a drone this spring and was left drifting in the Mediterranean. The report’s authors said the incident highlighted Russia’s inability to meet its obligations to countries that allow “shadow fleet” vessels to sail under their flags, prompting those states to increasingly refuse registrations.

2027 UP assembly polls: Fight against BJP or Congress? Why Akhilesh’s ‘rath’ show in Raebareli is message for Rahul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:29:59 UTC
00:29:59 KST

Samajwadi Party national president Akhilesh Yadav during a visit to Raebareli. (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: Is Uttar Pradesh all set to go the Bihar way for the opposition’s INDIA bloc? Wait, we are not talking about the results yet. This is about the all-too-familiar alliance strains between INDIA bloc allies - the Samajwadi Party and the Congress in the run-up to UP assembly elections early next year.On Thursday, Akhilesh Yadav unveiled the Samajwadi Party's 'PDA Rath' which he will use for a statewide campaign in the run-up to the 2027 assembly poll. While his fight is against the BJP, the first stop of his rath was Raebareli - a Congress bastion represented by the Gandhis for decades.Also, while Akhilesh targeted the BJP, he had a clear message for the Congress also.“Alliance will happen. We will also go with the alliance. Winnability will be the criteria for deciding seats. For us, it is not about seats, it is about victory. Whosoever can win can take the seat.”The BJP was quick to take digs at both allies and suggested that now Congress should start its campaign from Yadav bastion Mainpuri.This was not an isolated remark. The SP and the Congress have been engaged in a war of words over seat sharing for quite some time now. The open fight has an uncanny resemblance to how events had unfolded between the INDIA bloc allies in Bihar.
INDIA bloc's failed Bihar experiment
Cut to the 2025 Bihar assembly elections.INDIA bloc allies - the RJD and the Congress engaged in a continuous war of words in Bihar over seat-sharing and CM face, while the BJP-led NDA managed a smooth division of seats. What started as public posturing between INDIA bloc allies ended up in public sparring between them as the divided opposition alliance was decimated in the polls.The two parties campaigned separately for most of the time as they could not agree on seat sharing. They took out separate yatras across the state. While Rahul Gandhi undertook the “Vote Adhikar Yatra,” RJD’s Tejashwi Yadav went across the state with his “Bihar Adhikar Yatra.” Ironically, it was the success of the two yatras that boomeranged on the alliance as it made seat-sharing bitter and difficult.In the run-up to the Bihar elections, Tejashwi Yadav was confident of a sweep. The Congress was also not willing to budge, guided by its improved showing in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections in the state. The two parties used pressure tactics against each other. So much so that the INDIA bloc went into the elections as a divided house despite last-minute agreements and adjustments to keep the alliance intact.Uttar Pradesh appears to be headed the same way, at least as of now. We have already seen a lot of public posturing and sparring between the leaders of the INDIA bloc partners. Both the Congress and the SP have repeatedly claimed that the opposition’s fight against the BJP can be led only by their respective leaders.The SP and Congress contested the 2024 Lok Sabha polls together in Uttar Pradesh and won 43 seats between them, with the SP winning 37 and the Congress six. The alliance also won the Faizabad seat, which includes Ayodhya, where the BJP won in 2019.And that is perhaps where lies the genesis of this power tussle. Both the SP and the Congress feel that it was their party and leader who played a greater role in the 2024 electoral success and hence want the advantage to flow accordingly in seat sharing for the assembly elections.
Rahul or Akhilesh vs BJP
One look at the latest broadside between the two parties and we know why seat sharing between them may not be smooth.Recently, Samajwadi Party MP from Kairana Iqra Hasan and Congress MP from Saharanpur Imran Masood, both elected in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls as part of the SP-Congress alliance, publicly pitched their respective party leaders to take on the BJP."Only Rahul Gandhi is the opposition voice across the country, which unnerves the BJP. Rahul ji has done the hard work and created a favourable atmosphere. So make no mistake, nothing is possible without Rahul ji, and no one should have any doubts about this," Masood said.Days later, Hasan responded and pitched SP chief Yadav as the key to the alliance's prospects."Only Akhilesh Yadav is capable of defeating the BJP. On its own, the Congress won't be able to achieve much," she said.Last week, Congress Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam signalled a firm stance regarding upcoming electoral negotiations and said that any seat-sharing arrangement with the Samajwadi Party (SP) must be built on mutual respect and equal standing.Clarifying reports regarding seat distribution, Gautam claimed that formal discussions with the SP have not yet begun. While expressing open flexibility for minor adjustments, he stressed that the Congress would not compromise its organisational self-respect or dignity in any prospective deal."We have made one thing very clear. The Congress is the country's oldest party. It was the Congress that led the freedom struggle. Any alliance formed will be based on mutual respect; there will be equal partnership and dignity. Sure, we can show some flexibility; there might be minor adjustments, but we cannot compromise on our dignity," the Congress leader said.The contrasting assertions come despite messages of unity from both sides of the divide. Akhilesh is riding high on SP’s Lok Sabha success in Uttar Pradesh. The Congress, which is trying hard to revive its lost electoral fortunes, does not want to compromise on its expansion plans in one of the most politically important states.
The Owaisi factor
The problem is that both the parties are wooing the same social base in the state - minorities, Dalits, women, youth. Akhilesh is missing no opportunity to expand his PDA’s - Pichda Dalit and Alpsankhyak - base by making concerted attempts to include Pandits, Aadhi aabadi (women) and other social groups. The Congress is also wooing the Brahmins, the Dalits and the women in a big way.What the two bickering allies don't realise that there are several other parties who are also reaching out to the same social base. For instance, Mayawati and Chandrashekhar Azad are also going all out to woo Dalits. Then there is Owaisi, who has already put both the parties in a Catch22 situation by offering them an alliance against the BJP. Owaisi's proposal is like a double-edged sword for the two parties. If they accept his offer, the BJP will gun for them.
If they reject the offer, Owaisi will use the rejection to rally the Muslims against them.
Lok Sabha gains, assembly pains
The Samjawadi Party and the Congress may do well to learn lessons from the Bihar debacle before it’s too late. Lok Sabha elections and assembly elections are two very different games and success in one does not automatically translate into success in another. There are numerous instances to show that alliances which did well in Lok Sabha elections failed in assembly elections. Maharashtra is a case in point. The Maha Vikas Aghadi of the opposition parties - Congress, Shiv Sena and the NCP did very well in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, putting the BJP on the backfoot. But a year later in 2025 - the opposition alliance was decimated by the BJP in the assembly elections. So, Akhilesh and Rahul need to decide if they want to keep on flexing muscles at each other or unite in time to pose a challenge to the BJP.

Attacks on Ukrainians in Poland growing – envoy

Attacks on Ukrainians in Poland growing – envoy
Attacks on Ukrainians in Poland have continued to rise as public attitudes toward Ukrainian refugees deteriorate, Kiev’s ambassador to Warsaw, Vasily Bondar, has said. His remarks came a day after a Ukrainian man was detained over a deadly knife attack at a Catholic abbey in southeastern Poland.
Polish police recorded 180 attacks or acts of aggression against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, Bondar told RBK Ukraine in an interview published on Friday. There were 275 such incidents in all of 2025, up from 267 in 2024.
“We do see an increase of around 30%,” the diplomat said. He added that more incidents are now being classified as hate crimes against Ukrainians rather than ordinary domestic offenses.
Bondar also said Ukrainians committed 10,800 offenses in Poland during the first half of 2026, but argued the figure was statistically insignificant given that around 2 million Ukrainian nationals live in the country.
His comments came a day after a 31-year-old Ukrainian man allegedly stabbed five people at a Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, killing a priest and injuring four others. Polish authorities have said they are still investigating the motive and circumstances of the attack.
The incident comes amid worsening Polish attitudes toward Ukrainian refugees and continued tensions between Warsaw and Kiev over historical disputes, including Ukraine’s veneration of nationalist figures associated with the WWII-era massacres of ethnic Poles.
Bondar acknowledged that Polish society has a “consolidated public opinion” that is “highly negative” toward some historical figures regarded as heroes in Ukraine. He nevertheless argued that Kiev “could not give up its national interests” for the sake of better relations with Warsaw.
A July survey by polling agency CBOS found that, for the first time since it began tracking the issue, a majority of Poles opposed accepting Ukrainian refugees. Some 52% were against taking them in, compared with 42% in favor.
A separate CBOS survey conducted in July found that 53% of Poles believed reconciliation with Ukrainians was possible – the lowest level recorded – while 38% said it was impossible.

UN identifies 214 firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:27:39 UTC
00:27:39 KST

The United Nations on Friday released a fresh update of its database of companies with activities in illegal Israeli settlements in Palestinian territories, listing 214 firms from 11 countries.
Since last year's update, the UN rights office added an additional 61 companies to the database and had removed five companies.
But major firms like Airbnb, Booking.com, Motorola Solutions and TripAdvisor remained on the list.
The report, which was harshly criticised by Israel, served as a "reminder to companies that they have human rights responsibilities", UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
Firms, he said, "are expected to conduct due diligence to ensure that they do not become involved in human rights violations or abuses".
Two Spanish companies removed from the list
While most of the companies were based in Israel, others were based in Canada, China, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Britain and the United States.
There were two Spanish companies removed from the database since last year, along with one each from Canada, Israel and Portugal.
The list was first produced in 2020 after a UN Human Rights Council resolution called for a database of firms that profited from business in illegally occupied Palestinian territory.
The UN rights office was asked to list companies found to be taking part in any of 10 activities, including construction, surveillance, demolitions and destruction of agricultural land in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
Database updates limited
Despite a requirement for the database to be updated annually, it has been revised just twice before, in 2023 and 2025.
The list is not exhaustive. It only reviews companies about which it received submissions during set timeframes, the last of which closed in June 2024.
In all, it has received submissions about 596 companies, of which it has so far reviewed 381.
Around 750,000 illegal Israeli settlers live in 156 settlements and 360 settlement outposts in the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem.
The UN considers Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories illegal under international law and has repeatedly warned that settlement activity undermines the possibility of implementing a two-state solution.

Five people are missing after an explosion caused a building to collapse in Athens’ historic Plaka district on Friday morning, Greece’s Fire Department said, according to the Greek state news agency AMNA, as search operations continued at the scene.
The explosion and subsequent fire broke out on Lysikratous Street shortly after 7.30 am local time (0430GMT).
A large number of firefighters, including personnel from the Special Disaster Response Unit, were searching the rubble using specialized equipment, thermal imaging cameras and a trained search dog.
The five missing people are believed to have been staying on the first and second floors of the building, according to the Fire Department.

It was not immediately known whether they were inside the building when the explosion occurred. “There are missing persons. This is a very complex situation, and the search is in full progress,” Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said after arriving at the scene.
Drones were also being used to assess the situation, while municipal services remained at the scene to assess damage to neighboring buildings, Doukas said.
Asked about the cause of the explosion, Doukas explained: “I understand that it was caused by gas, and the force of the explosion was terrifying. This means that there was a very serious fault. Something went completely wrong,” he said.
Police officers and ambulances from Greece’s National Centre for Emergency Care were also at the scene.
Construction machinery provided by the Municipality of Athens was being used to remove debris from the collapsed building.

Saudi grand mufti urges troops to sacrifice their lives for ‘complete defeat’ of Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:27:02 UTC
00:27:02 KST

Saudi Arabia’s top religious authority has issued an unusually forceful appeal to soldiers stationed on the kingdom’s borders, telling them to remain ready to sacrifice their lives in the fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and praying for the group’s “complete defeat.” The message comes amid mounting questions over whether Riyadh could be preparing for a broader military campaign in Yemen after weeks of escalating missile, drone and air attacks.
Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh bin Fawzan Al-Fawzan said protecting Saudi territory and punishing those who attempt to seize even part of it were among the highest religious duties, “for which lives and souls are sacrificed.” His statement, addressed directly to troops on the front lines, drew heavily on Quranic verses and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad about sacrifice and fighting in defense of God.
“We ask God Almighty to grant you all his support, and to protect our countries and beloved Yemen from all harm,” he said. “We also ask him to bring about the complete defeat of the Houthi group and those who assist and support them.” He urged soldiers to remain constantly prepared, obey Saudi rulers and field commanders and “carry out orders with the utmost precision.”
The rare intervention comes as fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis intensifies sharply. The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that it intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed toward Taif and the strategically important Red Sea port of Yanbu. The Houthis later claimed missile and drone attacks against what they described as a sensitive target in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. The extent of any damage from the Houthi-claimed strikes has not been independently established.
Saudi Civil Defense has repeatedly issued emergency warnings across parts of the kingdom during the latest escalation, including Jazan, Jeddah, Yanbu, Taif, Mecca and Tabuk. The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi military positions in Jazan, while Saudi Arabia has continued airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
Religion enters an escalating conflict
The grand mufti’s message also appears to reinforce an increasingly religious dimension in Saudi Arabia’s public presentation of the conflict. Saudi state television has aired footage of what authorities said was a Houthi attack on a mosque in the kingdom’s south, while Riyadh has accused the Houthis of attempting to strike Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. The Houthis have rejected Saudi accusations surrounding attacks on holy sites.
Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since a Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in 2015, months after the group seized the capital, Sanaa. A 2022 truce largely reduced cross-border fighting, but hostilities have surged again, with the Houthis expanding their position around the Red Sea and Saudi Arabia resuming airstrikes. Recent fighting has increased concern over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Saudi energy infrastructure, including Yanbu, which is particularly important when oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted.
France has now pledged military assistance to protect Yanbu. President Emmanuel Macron said Paris would send soldiers, radar equipment and defense systems to help safeguard the strategic oil-export site, stressing that the deployment was defensive and was not intended to draw France into the fighting.
Riyadh is also pressing its newer defense partners for support. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan announced an urgent meeting of their military chiefs to discuss assistance to the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which provides that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all three. The countries signed the pact in August and have since begun building the mechanisms needed to implement it, although no specific military deployment has yet been announced.
The combination of repeated Houthi attacks, the grand mufti’s appeal to frontline troops and Riyadh’s increasingly urgent search for outside military support has added to speculation over the kingdom’s next move. For now, Saudi Arabia continues to strike Houthi positions from the air while reinforcing defenses at home, as both sides signal that a confrontation once held largely in check could be entering a more dangerous phase.

Bundeswehr Received First Puma IFV From Second Batch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:26:47 UTC
00:26:47 KST

The Bundeswehr received the first Puma infantry fighting vehicle from the second production batch ordered as part of the re-equipment of German armored infantry units and the gradual replacement of the Marder IFVs.
PSM, a joint venture between KNDS Deutschland and Rheinmetall responsible for the Puma program, announced the delivery of the vehicle.
The first Puma from the second batch, in the S1 configuration, was delivered to the Bundeswehr on August 28, 2026.
Meanwhile, on August 27 and September 3, the government contractor officially accepted the first two vehicles from this batch. They will be sent for further testing to the WTD 81 and WTD 91 military-technical centers.
In May 2023, the Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support (BAAINBw) signed an agreement with PSM and simultaneously ordered 50 new Puma IFVs.
The delivery of new vehicles and the modernization of existing Pumas are part of the re-equipment of the Bundeswehr’s armored infantry units. The Puma is gradually replacing the older Marder IFVs, and the German military is simultaneously working to bring the Puma fleet up to the uniform S1 standard.
The Puma is a tracked infantry fighting vehicle with a crew of three and space for six infantrymen. The vehicle is equipped with a remotely controlled unmanned turret featuring a 30 mm MK30-2/ABM automatic cannon, a coaxial 5.56 mm MG4 machine gun, and, in the VJTF and S1 versions, a MELLS anti-tank system with Spike LR missiles. Its maximum speed is 70 km/h, its engine power is 800 kW, and it weighs 43 metric tons.
The S1 configuration also features digital communications and control systems, improved observation equipment, and a 360-degree surveillance system that combines daytime cameras with thermal imaging channels. The Bundeswehr plans to extend this standard to all armored infantry units and training units equipped with the Puma.
The vehicle’s primary armament is a stabilized 30 mm MK30-2/ABM cannon with an effective firing range of up to 3 km. The Puma’s modular protection system is designed, in particular, to counter mines, improvised explosive devices, shaped-charge munitions, and anti-tank guided missiles.
At the same time, Germany continues to expand its fleet of these vehicles. In December 2025, the Bundeswehr ordered another 200 Pumas from PSM, with a total value of approximately €4.2 billion. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2028.

Pakistan's Sharif rails against India, praises Trump at UNGA

Pakistan's Sharif rails against India, praises Trump at UNGA

Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.
Sharif blames India for 2025 clashes, calls for 'just and fair' Kashmir resolution
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took aim at India in his speech as he discussed the limited military clashes between the uneasy neighbors last year.
"A year ago, Pakistan faced external aggression from India under a false pretext," the prime minister alleged. "Pakistan exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations charter."
He praised the country's military saying, "They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attack, and taught it a lesson it shall never ever forget," as the UN's TV feed cut to an Indian observer in the assembly shaking his head as he listened.
Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, that ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retalliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in late April. New Delhi had accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, which Islambad denied.
Sharif praised US President Donald Trump's "resolute and visionary leadership," crediting it with saving "hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia" by intervening and helping to broker a truce "when two nuclear neighbors stood at the brink of all-out war."
Sharif asked "who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place" without Trump's "clarity of thought and action" at a critical moment.
He said it was necessary to ensure that South Asia "never reaches this precipice again," and said that doing so would require "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute."
He said Kashmiri people had been waiting eight decades for the UN to "fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices." He also criticized recent "attempts to alter the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir through demographic reengineering and other illegal measures."
He also criticized India for its decision to hold a treat on the Indus River System in abeyance, saying this move had "no legal basis whatsoever."
Pakistan's Sharif: Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb are 'arteries of global economy' and 'must remain open'
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif touted his country's efforts to mediate in the war between the US and Iran since February, particularly in reaching the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding that brought an uneasy calm to hostilities for a few weeks earlier this year — albeit without resolving many of the wider issues in the conflict.
"Regrettably, Mr. President, recently we have witnessed a dangerous surge of hostilties," Sharif said. "Yet amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger."
"The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are arteries of the global economy," Sharif said, also referring to the western entry to the Red Sea coming under increasing pressure from the Iran-aligned Houthis. "They must remain open, connecting nations, not becoming the chokepoints of confrontation."
Sharif said these waters "must carry the promise of prosperity, not the perils of war."
He said Pakistan condemned recent "deplorable" Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia "in the strongest possible terms," not least the reported attempted drone attack on the holy city of Mecca, which he said had "outraged Muslims across the globe."
Albania's Rama tells of 'Flamingo Revolution,' warning not of a rogue AI, but one following rogue orders
Prime Minister Edi Rama told the chamber that while Albania was not a developer of "frontier models" in AI, "we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating," given how outside actors had tried out the technology's darker capabilites on its citizens.
Rama said he felt he owed the chamber a "simple message," if not necessarily the one most commonly discussed during the week.
"The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity. The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly," he said.
"The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators," Rama said. "But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts, they multiply ours. They have no ambition of their own, they serve the ambition of others. They carry no flag, but they can be deployed by a state. They tell no lie for their own benefit, but they can tell a billion lies on others' behalf."
Rama mentioned how Albania had become the first government to launch an AI minister. He said this showed his government's belief that "inside an accountable state," the technology could be used to "reduced the distance between citizens and public services."
But he said Albania had also learned how "artificial intelligence outside accountability can be used to eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind."
He relayed the story of the so-called "Flamingo Revolution," a "fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast."
This entirely fictional invasion "was manufactured, was personalized and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted." Rama explained how the details of the overarching story were personalized to maximize their impact with the individuals reading them.
"Different fabriactions entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie," he said. "The consequences were real. Citizens had their own reasons to protest — don't take me wrong. But suddenly, they started to protest also against a phantom enemy. Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse for the first time ever."
Rama said that amid the AI disinformation drive, "fear became anger, anger became mobilization and fabrication became political reality."
"And this was not a laboratory experiment. I'm not talking to you about a science fiction movie. It was a Tuesday, in Tirana, our capital city."
Rama said it wasn't an algorithm that invented the objective, but rather a human actor. The algorithm didn't develop hatred, but "it discovered how to activate ours."
He called this particular use case "systematic fraud as a service," and warned its potential for use in scenarios like elections were just as real as in trying to amplify animosity to war in the Middle East.
St. Lucia urges assembly not to forget Haiti in war-torn world
Prime Minister Philip Pierre from the Caribbean island of Saint Lucia said his country "laments the continued conflicts and human suffering across the globe," listing some of the most notable wars in Ukraine, Gaza, the wider Middle East and Sudan.
He said his country of around 184,000 people called for the establishment of a Palestinian state with full UN membership.
Pierre then turned to a Caribbean conflict that has featured rather less this week in New York, Haiti.
"Member states of this organization must act in a manner that will restore the trust of the people of Haiti in the United Nations," Pierre said. "Some member states have failed to meet the commitments and pledges to the gang suppression force in Haiti, whose one-year mandate ends this month."
He urged the Security Council to renew the force's mandate, and called on member states to provide it with sufficient "resources to operation effectively and successfully."
He said that while gang violence was "the main factor to be resolved," the crisis in the country was "multidimensional."
"The international response must include long-term socio-economic assistance that will help restore an acceptable quality of life for the people of Haiti," he said.
Pacific archipelago Tuvalu appeals for climate finance, Taiwanese UN membership
Tuvalu's Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski told the assembly that climate change "is and remains the single, greatest existential threat to Tuvalu's survival, security and sustainable development."
He said the low-lying archipelago of some 10,000 people acknowledged global efforts to contain the climate crisis but said the "pace and scale of global actions remain insufficient."
Mickoscki called for a "fast, fair, just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels."
He called for moves to provide climate financing "as grants" to allow countries like his to better prepare and adapt for coming changes.
He said his country was keenly anticipating the pre-COP meetings this October, prior to the main UN COP31 summit in Turkey in November.
"Tuvalu may have only 26 square kilometers of land," he said, "but we are custodians of some 750,000 square kilometers of ocean, which makes Tuvalu a large ocean state."
Tuvalu joins Palau in appealing for Taiwanese membership
Tuvalu is also known as one of just 12 countries in the world to retain full diplomatic relations with Taiwan, rather than having formal ties to China.
Mickoscki said that the UN "must also uphold the principles of dignity, inclusion and equality" for everyone.
"Yet, too many communities remain outside the structures designed to serve all humanity," he said. "Tuvalu therefore calls for arrangements that enable the meaningful participation of the 23.3 million people of Taiwan in the United Nations and its specialized agencies and mechanisms."
He said that Taipei had consistently demonstrated that it was an "able, trustworthy and constructive partner," saying its UN exclusion "undermines both the spirit and effectiveness of multilateral cooperation."
The People's Republic of China took over the Chinese seat at the UN — and the Security Council veto that came with it — in 1971, more than two decades after the Chinese Communist revolution. Since then, Taiwan has been excluded from the UN for more than half a century since then, with no clear route towards membership, given that it is only possible with Beijing's blessing.
Not far away, during his state visit to Washington DC to speak with President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping on Thursday appealed to Trump to change the US stance on Taiwanese independence from not "supporting" it to openly "opposing" it.
Lebanese prime minister says 'the problem is not the absence of rules'
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told the UN that "without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among states, nor can competition among them flourish."
He said that the UN was founded, more than 80 years ago, on "the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force."
But Salam said that wars and conflicts still plague a world that spends more on armaments than on development.
"The problem is not the absence of rules," Salam said. "It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application."
He did not mention Israel by name in his preamble but did later in his speech.
Salam said his government had three commitments to fulfil, and argued that all three were interconnected:
- Restoring trust and credibility in Lebanese authorities after the economic collapse and vast port explosion in Beirut of August 4, 2020
- Ensuring that only the Lebanese government held weapons and made decisions of war for the country — comments seemingly aimed at the pro-Iranian Hezbollah group, which he did not name
- Reclaiming occupied Lebanese territory from Israel under the terms of UN Resolution 1701 adopted to end the Second Lebanon War between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006
"Our position on the war has been clear from the outset," Salam said. "We want it to end. We want the ceasefire consolidated. We want Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognized borders, in accordance with the 1949 General Armistice Agreement and as affirmed by Resolution 1701. We want the release of all our detainees, the safe and dignified return of our people to their villages and towns, and a reconstruction of what the war destroyed."
Under the tense ceasefire deal between Lebanon and Israel, brokered by the US, Israel is supposed to withdraw its forces from a self-declared "buffer zone" in southern Lebanon. In turn, Lebanon's government is supposed to move its military fores into these areas and stop Hezbollah from using them to launch attacks into northern Israel. The current goal is to create so-called pilot zones where the Lebanese army moves in and Israel's troops move out.
The process is making only gradual progress, as both sides accuse the other of failing to meet their obligations.
Lebanon PM calls for peacekeeping troops after UNIFIL mandate ends
Lebanon Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called for the UN to keep its UNIFIL (UN Interim Force in Lebanon) peacekeeping troops in place after their mandate expires at year's end.
"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," he said.
The UN's troops, currently numbering 7,500 from 46 different countries, have been in Lebanon since 1978.
Last year, however, the US pushed the UN Security Council to terminate the mandate when it ran out.
UNIFIL's expected departure comes as Israel maintains troops in its own self-declared "security zone" extending some 10 kilometers (6 miles) into south Lebanon.

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's young prime minister stood at the podium of the UN General Assembly to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.
"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," said Balendra Shah as he began his address to the UNGA on Thursday.
Nepal's leader calls for international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas
The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.
"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a "Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism," which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.
Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.
Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Shah noted that his country only contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he wasn not blaming any nation or continent.
"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.
Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery
The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of "Responsibility, Reparation and Resilience" as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.
Shah said that vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure
Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten, addressing the General Assembly on Thursday, said the International Criminal Court, which is based in The Hague, was "under attack."
Jetten did not name the US or President Donald Trump, who on Tuesday urged countries to leave the court, the latest move in his administration's campaign against the ICC.
"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?" Jetten asked the assembly, drawing loud applause from the delegates.
"I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order. Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity."
Washington has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on ICC staff, with officials reportedly preparing additional sanctions that could curtail the court's ability to operate.
Yemen, Kuwait stress freedom of navigation at UNGA
Yemen and Kuwait, both heavily impacted by the Iran war and its regional spillover, have used their General Assembly addresses to stress the importance of the freedom and safety of navigation, while condemning Iran and its proxies in the region.
Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer, vice resident of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, represents the internationally recognized government, which has been at war with the Iran-backed Houthirebels for more than a decade.
Alimi-Bawzer devoted his address to highlighting recent Houthi actions and their impact on global trade.
The Houthis' conflict with Saudi Arabia, which has led a coalition against them, has recently escalated, with the Yemeni rebels declaring a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial global shipping route. This has further squeezed the Saudi kingdom as Iran continues to block access through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Ensuring security at sea begins with eliminating the source of the threat on land," Alimi-Bawzer said, in an apparent reference to the Houthis.
Kuwaiti Crown Prince Sheikh Sabah Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Sabah stressed that freedom and safety of navigation, as well as the right of passage through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, must be guaranteed.
"To inflict harm on the economies of the region and the world, and to disrupt global trade and oil markets, Iran is obstructing maritime navigation and closing the Strait of Hormuz, using it as a bargaining chip in the war, in violation of international law and relevant Security Council resolutions," he said.
Kuwait has been among the countries targeted by Iranian strikes since the start of the war, in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes.
Nigeria says don't 'surrender our technological future to paranoia'
Nigeria's Vice President Kashim Shettima addressed the assembly on behalf of President Bola Tinubu.
Among a range of issues, he weighed in on the question of AI with an appeal for an optimistic and proactive approach more than what he deemed undue caution.
"We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia," he said. "An invention can be destructive or beneficial, depending on the purpose it serves and the judgment of those who use it. A knife can take a life in the hands of an assailant, and can save one in the hands of a surgeon."
He said that while AI could be used to wage war, it could also "transform" an array of areas like healthcare, education and agriculture.
"Much of the anxiety surrounding AI reflects the distrust we have allowed to grow amongst us," Shettima said.
He said Nigeria wished to invite the world "to work with our inventive, resourceful and enterprising young people to direct AI towards humanity's advancement rather than its destruction."
Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'
Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Tawakecolati Lalabalavu addressed the chamber on behalf of one of the low-lying island nations at severe risk from climate change on Thursday.
He said that many of the UN's sustainable development goals remained off track with 2030 approaching and said that aid and financial assistance often did a poor job of reaching remote islands exposed to more natural disasters than average. But then he called for a wider financial system that would better enable Fijians to help themselves.
"There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly," he said. "Remittances are now Fiji's third-largest source of foreign exchange."
Lalabalavu said these funds paid for school fees, rebuilt homes after cyclones and sustained families between harvests.
"Your excellencies, they are not aid. They are earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home. Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money."
He noted how the chamber had in May committed to work to keep such transfer costs below 3% and to eliminate corridors costing more than 5% — he said that Pacific countries like Fiji wanted this to be "treated as an obligation and not an aspiration."
"Labor mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people that we have trained," the president said. "Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those recruit our nurses, our teachers invest in the systems that recruited them."
Lalabalavu also alluded to Fiji recently declaring a national HIV emergency and said that organized crime and drug trafficking was exacerbating this problem. He said that as a small impoverished country, Fiji had three requests for the international community:
"That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. That the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resources at a level that does not force triage between regions, and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is."

Ukraine's steel industry is nearing collapse — and calling for help from abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:23:45 UTC
00:23:45 KST

Ukraine's steel industry is nearing collapse — and calling for help from abroad
An employee shows processed iron ore at an iron ore processing plant operated by the Metinvest Group in Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine, on April 14, 2026. (Giulio Piscitelli / AFP via Getty Images)
Ukraine’s largest steel company, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, said on Sept. 25 that it cannot restart steel production amid a surge in Russian strikes on factories, as the embattled sector calls for more domestic and international support to prevent its total collapse.
Since the summer, Moscow has launched a widespread campaign of attacks on Ukraine’s economy to shut down key industrial centers. The metallurgy sector, which contributed 7% of Ukraine’s gross domestic product (GDP) last year and employs tens of thousands of people, has been one of the biggest victims, suffering at least nine separate ballistic missile attacks since August.
The recent attacks have likely cost steelmakers close to $100 million, Oleksandr Kalenkov, president of Ukrmetallurgprom, a Ukrainian steel association, told the Kyiv Independent. This is the sector’s worst year since 2022, when Russian forces occupied and destroyed the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, wiping out 40% of Ukraine’s steel production.
During the attacks, Russia launches precise strikes that damage critical equipment like blast furnaces, preventing Ukrainian steelmakers from producing pig iron — a key material for steel. Metinvest, Interpipe, and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih — Ukraine’s top three companies — have all suspended steel production.
Now teetering on the brink of survival, the steel industry wants far more support from international partners and the state.
"We don't really have another choice. Otherwise, we will have to stop production until the end of the war, which could last for many years, and I have doubts that we would be able to save our employees in that time," Kalenkov said.
The direct missile attacks on steel plants are only part of the problem. Russia’s campaign has also shut down Ukraine’s seaports, preventing companies from exporting or importing goods via the Black Sea. At the same time, Brussels’ new trade rules have limited Ukraine’s access to the EU market, while Europe’s anti-carbon policies have made it more expensive to sell there.
Moreover, some major metallurgy companies are ineligible for funding support from international financial institutions because they are owned by oligarchs, while overland trade routes are too expensive for companies that are currently hemorrhaging tens of millions of dollars per month.
As the industry warns of a potential collapse, the knock-on effect would be felt beyond the factories in the east and south of the country. Building firms will have to import more expensive steel from Europe, hiking construction prices, fueling inflation, and ultimately raising the costs of reconstruction, Denys Sakva, a senior analyst at Ukrainian investment firm Dragon Capital, told the Kyiv Independent.
But instead of supporting Ukraine’s steel industry as it nears total destruction, the EU is undermining it, Karin Karlsbro, a member of the European Parliament (MEP), told the Kyiv Independent. Karlsbro, who toured Ukraine’s steel plants in the spring, is urging Brussels to urgently review its trade policy and remove Ukraine from its tariff regime introduced in June.
read also
"If we seriously want to support Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, we must do what we can to support the industrial infrastructure," she said.
"If Ukraine’s economy collapses, Ukraine will have much more difficulty defending itself and will be much more dependent on support from the EU."
Saving Ukrainian steel
At the start of September, steel sector representatives warned Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi that the situation was at a breaking point and proposed solutions. One idea being discussed in parliament is a steel fund akin to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund, which would pool financing from partners to help affected companies procure critical equipment from Europe.
"A recovery fund could help affected producers finance emergency repairs, restore production capacity, and make operations more resilient," Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO’s office at Metinvest, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Large industrial employers near the front line face some of the heaviest attacks while sustaining tens of thousands of jobs and their regional economies."
Kyiv also needs to open up negotiations with financial institutions like the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) to allow financing for oligarch-owned metallurgy companies, like Metinvest, which is owned by Ukraine’s richest man, Rinat Akhmetov, Kalenkov said.
The other issue burdening metallurgy companies is sky-high logistics costs caused by the closure of the Black Sea ports. Companies are paying 50%-60% more to transport some goods, like coal, by rail or via Polish and Romanian ports, Metinvest’s Chief Operating Officer Oleksandr Myronenko told Forbes Ukraine.
The government and European countries could split the cost, Kalenkov said. Kyiv needs to keep railway tariffs high to bring in budget revenue, but EU partners could instead provide financing to help the government cover part of the cost, he said.
Cheaper logistics would also lower import costs, allowing companies to import foreign pig iron and slabs to roll in Ukrainian plants and produce steel, Kalenkov added. Currently, logistics prices make importing goods unfeasible, he said.
At the same time, Ukraine also needs unrestricted access to the EU’s steel market and relief from the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism — known as CBAM — which adds additional taxes to carbon-heavy imports, like steel, Vodoviz stressed.
"Ukrainian producers cannot finance large-scale decarbonization while repeatedly rebuilding after missile attacks," he said.
But the biggest boost to Ukraine’s steel sector would be reopening the Black Sea. That would not only shave off logistics costs but also allow companies to resume exporting iron ore, a key ingredient in steel, to bring in some cash if they can’t restart steel production.
Ukraine’s calls for a renewed Black Sea trade route have received international support, with 51 countries backing Kyiv in a joint statement on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 23. For now, however, Russia hasn’t shown any interest in slowing down attacks on Ukraine’s seaports and civilian vessels.
Nevertheless, even if Ukraine’s steel sector gets the support it needs from the government and partners, it will still take many months and tens of millions of dollars before it can relaunch steel production, assuming Russia won’t strike again, Kalenkov said.
Right now, it’s just about finding a way to survive, he added.

US national VanDyke was arrested by the NIA in a case involving an alleged terror conspiracy linked to Myanmar-based ethnic armed groups.
NEW DELHI: The release of US national Matthew Aaron VanDyke, who was arrested by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in March in a case involving an alleged terror conspiracy linked to Myanmar-based ethnic armed groups, has triggered a political row, with the Congress questioning the circumstances of his release and alleging that US diplomatic pressure influenced the outcome."Our compromised PM has does it again. The PM has failed to protect India’s elections, institutions and our national security," Congress said in a post on X.
VanDyke and six Ukrainian nationals were arrested by the NIA on March 13. According to the agency's allegations, the accused had entered India and travelled to restricted areas in the Northeast before crossing into Myanmar, where they allegedly came into contact with ethnic armed organisations and were involved in drone-warfare training. The NIA had initially registered the case under provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).The agency's March court submissions alleged that the accused supported anti-India insurgent groups. The NIA later told a Delhi court that the seven foreign nationals were allegedly linked to a drone attack on a civilian aircraft in Myanmar, although the investigation remained underway.The case took a fresh turn on September 8, when the NIA filed a chargesheet against the seven under Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, without invoking UAPA provisions in the chargesheet.
The agency said the UAPA investigation had not been closed and that a supplementary chargesheet could be filed if further offences were established.A Delhi court subsequently granted VanDyke default bail, observing that the chargesheet was "piecemeal" while the investigation into the UAPA offences remained pending. The 180-day statutory period for completing the investigation had also elapsed.
On September 24, the court allowed VanDyke and the six Ukrainian nationals to travel to their respective countries for a month, subject to conditions. The court also released their passports.Congress has alleged that the development followed US pressure and questioned whether diplomatic intervention played a role. The party has also raised questions over how the foreign nationals obtained Indian visas and were able to travel to restricted areas of the Northeast before allegedly crossing into Myanmar.The government has maintained that the terror investigation against VanDyke and the other accused remains open.

One in three women in Finland received mental health support by age 28
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
18:22:05 EEST
00:22:05 KST

One in three women born in Finland in 1997 had received mental health-related sickness allowance, disability pension or rehabilitative psychotherapy by age 28, according to an analysis by Kela. The corresponding share among men was 15.3 per cent, compared with 33.9 per cent among women.
The findings cover more than 57,000 people and track their use of the selected benefits and psychotherapy from age 16 until the end of 2025.
Kela said the analysis is believed to be the first in Finland to measure the use of these forms of support across a single birth cohort during adolescence and early adulthood.
Mental health-related sickness allowance was the most common form of support included in the study. A quarter of women had received the allowance, compared with 12 per cent of men.
The difference was larger for rehabilitative psychotherapy. Some 16 per cent of women, or around one in six, had received Kela-supported psychotherapy. The figure among men was below four per cent. Half of those who had received rehabilitative psychotherapy had also received sickness allowance.
“What stands out in particular is how common the use of rehabilitative psychotherapy was among young women. At the same time, the large gap compared with men raises questions,” Kela head of research Miika Vuori said.
Disability pensions showed a different pattern. Some 3.5 per cent of women and 3.4 per cent of men had received a temporary or permanent disability pension, leaving little difference between the groups.
The diagnoses associated with those pensions differed. An intellectual disability or neurodevelopmental diagnosis formed part of the grounds for a pension among 62 per cent of male recipients and 37 per cent of female recipients.
Kela uses mental health as a broad category in disability pension statistics. The classification also includes neurodevelopmental conditions and intellectual disabilities.
Vuori said benefit registers should not be treated as a direct measure of the population’s mental health.
“Official registers measure the use of benefits and services, not mental health or mental health problems directly,” he said.
Researchers examined more than 28,000 women and 29,000 men born in Finland in 1997 who were alive and living in the country when the follow-up period began.
Kela said further research is needed into how support needs among young women and men are identified and how education, workplaces and other settings respond to those needs.

8 sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide, Navy tells Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

8 sailors assigned to USS Abraham Lincoln attempted suicide, Navy tells Congress
Trump and War Minister Hegseth had dismissed suicide attempts as ‘fake news’
Eight US Navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier attempted suicide during a period that included when the ships undertook combat operations in the war against Iran and the carrier set a modern record for its time at sea, according to a letter from the service’s acting secretary, which was obtained by CNN.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao revealed the number, which has not been previously reported and covers crew members from several ships that travel together, including the carrier, in written responses to questions posed by Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand about the morale and mental health of the USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew. Cao wrote that no service members had killed themselves during the deployment.
“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote to Gillibrand, a Democrat and member of the Senate Armed Services, in a letter dated Tuesday. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.”
Between 6,000 and 7,000 US Navy sailors were deployed as part of the Lincoln strike group across roughly a half dozen ships — with the carrier kept out of port for over six months while conducting a high rate of combat operations against Iran.
“Eight attempted suicides is incredibly high,” one US military official told CNN, noting recent carrier strike group deployments have had one or two per year. “The strain of combat ops is much higher than normal deployments. No port calls, constant alerts, etc.”
The Navy did not respond ahead of publication to a request for comment about the letter.
“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a statement Wednesday to CNN. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”
CNN previously reported that two sailors assigned to the Lincoln strike group, one from the carrier and one from another ship, had jumped overboard in recent months. Both were rescued, US officials said. Others were prevented from jumping, according to reports from the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.
In his letter to Gillibrand, Cao also confirmed that a sailor assigned to the airwing went overboard from the ship in early August but was “quickly recovered” and treated by the Lincoln’s medical department. “Additionally, one sailor attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates. That sailor was also provided immediate medical care and subsequently returned to homeport.”
The Navy previously said in a statement to CNN, “We have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise.”
A US official also previously told CNN that the Navy does not believe there is a correlation between deployment length and thoughts of self-harm, and that man overboard incidents are not unique to this group.

New Data: More and More Companies Are Using AI  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:21:18 UTC
00:21:18 KST

TALLINN - According to recent data from Statistics Estonia, 34 percent of companies are already using artificial intelligence (AI), one and a half times more than last year.
However, alongside the opportunities, this rapid spread is increasingly raising questions about what the rules for using AI should be: what can be entrusted to it, what data can be shared, and where a human must remain the decision-maker.
In addition to official corporate use, the results of a 2025 study by KPMG and the University of Melbourne provide a more detailed picture of employee habits. The study included more than 48,000 people from 47 countries, with at least 1,000 adults participating from each country.
According to the study, 70 percent of working respondents in Estonia said they consciously use AI at work. This is precisely why the rapid spread of AI requires clear agreements within companies, according to Astrid Maldre, Head of the Small Business Segment at Swedbank. "AI has become a daily tool for many people, as employees quickly find ways to make their work easier with it," Maldre said. "For a business owner, it is important to have clear agreements for using AI. This way, employees know which tools they can use, what information to input into them, and where to be cautious."
In a joint workshop by Swedbank and Eesti.ai, Lembit Loo, founder of the AI strategy and training company Portata.ai and a machine intelligence strategy advisor, spoke about how to safely implement AI in a company and what principles help to better manage its use.
According to the KPMG study, 40 percent of Estonian respondents have used AI in a way that contradicts their organization's rules or guidelines. Thirty-one percent found that compliance and privacy risks have increased due to the use of AI.
"If a company is worried about data security or trade secrets, the first thought might be to simply ban the use of AI. However, an employee might find another solution and use a personal account for business matters instead. It's better to bring AI out of the shadows and create clear guidelines for its use," Loo said.
The use of AI applications not managed by the company to perform work tasks is called "shadow AI." In such cases, work-related information can end up in environments over which the company has no control.
According to Loo, when implementing AI, how the change is explained to employees and what rules are established from the outset is just as important as the technology itself.
New tools can also raise questions about how a person's own role and work will change in the future. "AI brings with it completely new fears. When a manager says we are now going to use AI, an employee's first thought might be that they are going to be replaced. Therefore, it is crucial to think very carefully about how to introduce AI into the company and how to talk about it with employees," Loo added.
The adoption of AI can be started with small steps. Loo recommends first choosing a suitable tool and giving more freedom for experimentation to those employees who have a greater interest in it.
Loo compares introducing AI to bringing a new colleague onto the team. "Even if the CV is good and the interview goes perfectly, it takes time to get to know each other. AI can also make mistakes, so trust in its work is built through experience and verification," said Loo.

European parliamentarians call removal of Russian oligarchs from the EU sanctions list a dangerous precedent and urge that the sanctions remain in place  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:21:04 UTC
00:21:04 KST

RIGA - The removal of Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the European Union (EU) sanctions list sets a dangerous precedent, as emphasized in a joint statement signed Friday by parliamentary representatives of several European countries and members of the European Parliament, in which EU member states are urged to continue a coordinated and effective sanctions policy.
As the Saeima Press Service informed LETA, the statement notes that easing sanctions in exchange for concessions on issues unrelated to Russia’s actions undermines the very logic of the sanctions regime.
In support of Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion and in advocacy for the effective and consistent implementation and maintenance of the sanctions regime, the statement was signed by Evika Silina (New Unity), Chair of the Saeima’s European Affairs Committee; Inara Murniece (National Alliance), Chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee; Raimonds Bergmanis (United List), Chair of the Committee on Defense, Internal Affairs, and Corruption Prevention, as well as Member of Parliament Juris Vilums (United List).
In the statement, the parliamentarians express concern over the removal of Usmanov and Fridman from the EU sanctions list. The parliamentarians emphasize that these individuals are subject to the sanctions regime as key financial and material pillars of the Russian regime. For decades, these individuals have directly benefited from the Kremlin system, contributed to destabilization in Ukraine, and supported the economic base that enables Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, the parliamentarians states.
Removing individuals from the sanctions list raises serious concerns about the consistency, credibility, and effectiveness of the EU policy on restrictive measures. Any such decision must be based on a thorough and case-by-case assessment, taking into account the applicable criteria, the evidence underlying the decision, and any new circumstances that could serve as a legal basis for removal. As the parliamentarians emphasize, there is no information regarding such an assessment with respect to these individuals.
Removal from the sanctions list would send a signal both to thousands of other individuals on the list, as well as to third countries that support them, that sanctions can be lifted through sustained lobbying or diplomatic pressure. This could lead to a steady stream of new requests to remove individuals from the list, increase pressure on individual EU member states, and weaken the deterrent effect of EU sanctions overall, the statement said.
The European parliamentarians who signed the letter highlight Latvia’s principled stance on this issue and its decision to impose sanctions at the national level, calling on other countries to follow this example.
The parliamentarians call on EU member states to continue a coordinated and effective sanctions policy. The policy of restrictive measures must be legally justified, evidence-based, consistent, and effectively enforceable for as long as the circumstances that led to the imposition of these measures persist.
