Association of Lithuanian Banks President Eivile Cipkute said banks were prepared to operate in emergency situations without internet or electricity.
"On the banking side, institutions are properly prepared in accordance with Lithuanian law. Major banks have signed agreements with the Bank of Lithuania and adapted their systems for 'offline' mode. If there is no internet, card payments will still be possible, and all cards have been adapted for this," Cipkute told reporters.
"The financial sector is pleased to have completed its work in this area," she added.
Furthermore, Sinkevicius said the government was ready to cooperate with banks to develop public skills in both saving and investing.
Regarding government plans for a national strategy to combat digital fraud, it was announced that the Centre of Excellence in Anti-Money Laundering was developing an information-sharing platform for payment institutions.
The Association of Lithuanian Banks believes the platform should be implemented by the state.
Lithuania is already developing a card payment system for use during mobilisation if internet connectivity is lost. In June, the Seimas passed amendments to the Law on Payments allowing the purchase of essential food, hygiene products, medicine and fuel during communication disruptions.
Such transactions will require specially configured cards and payment terminals, with spending limits set on the cards. Residents will not need to replace their cards; banks will be required to record the limits on existing cards.
The meeting also addressed broader financial sector issues, service accessibility in the regions and the government's planned national strategy against digital fraud.

European Commission sends formal notice to EU member states  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:20:54 UTC
00:20:54 KST

TALLINN – The European Commission is sending letters of formal notice to several EU member states, including Estonia, for failing to notify the Commission of measures taken to transpose certain EU directives into their national law.
The transposition deadline for these directives recently passed. Under the EU treaties, the Commission may launch infringement proceedings against an EU country for failing to apply EU law. Sending a letter of formal notice is the first step in this process.
Directive on electricity market design
The European Commission has decided to send letters of formal notice to Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovenia, Finland, and Sweden for failing to notify the complete transposition of the new electricity market design rules concerning the free choice of supplier and energy sharing rights, as laid down in Directive (EU) 2024/1711.
The aim of these provisions is to strengthen the position of consumers in the electricity market by expanding their opportunities to choose and switch suppliers, access more competitive and innovative offers, and participate more actively in the energy system.
Rules on hydrogen and decarbonized gas markets
The European Commission has decided to send letters of formal notice to Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden for failing to notify the full transposition of the recast Hydrogen and Decarbonised Gas Directive (EU) 2024/1788.
The new directive updates the rules for the EU natural gas market and establishes a legal framework for a dedicated hydrogen infrastructure. The rules aim to facilitate the uptake of renewable and low-carbon gases, including hydrogen, while ensuring security of supply and energy affordability for all EU citizens.
Anti-Money Laundering Directive
The European Commission decided to send letters of formal notice to Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Cyprus, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, and Finland for failing to fully notify national measures transposing certain provisions of the sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/1640).
This would allow member states to give competent authorities, self-regulatory bodies, obliged entities, and persons with a legitimate interest access to beneficial ownership registers. Member states were required to transpose most of the directive by July 10, 2026.
Right to Repair Directive
The European Commission has decided to launch infringement proceedings by sending letters of formal notice to Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, and Sweden, as these countries have not notified the full transposition of the Right to Repair Directive (Directive (EU) 2024/1799).
The directive promotes sustainable consumption by making it easier to repair products instead of replacing them. It gives consumers the right to demand repairs for products such as smartphones, washing machines, or refrigerators, even after the legal guarantee has expired. Manufacturers must offer repairs within a reasonable time and at a reasonable price, and provide clear information about their repair services.
The Commission has also decided to launch infringement proceedings by sending letters of formal notice to Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Estonia, Spain, France, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Finland, and Sweden for failing to notify the full transposition of Delegated Directive (EU) 2026/74, which amends the Right to Repair Directive.
The delegated directive extends the scope of the right to repair to include domestic indoor heating appliances, such as fireplaces, portable electric heaters, or underfloor heating systems.
Rules on reducing pollution from industrial installations
The European Commission decided to launch infringement proceedings by sending letters of formal notice to Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden for failing to notify measures for the full transposition of the Industrial and Livestock Emissions Directive (amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1785).
The updated directive tightens emission reduction rules, aims to reduce the use of hazardous chemicals, and expands the scope of the previous Industrial Emissions Directive. In addition, it strengthens public rights and creates a new right to claim compensation for health damage caused by illegal pollution.
The member states have two months to respond to the letters and complete the transposition of the directives. Otherwise, the Commission may, as the next step in the infringement procedure, issue a reasoned opinion.

Transit of grain from Russia and Belarus must be completely banned - LLKA  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:20:52 UTC
00:20:52 KST

RIGA - Latvia’s security and the interests of its agricultural sector can be safeguarded most effectively by completely banning the import and transit through Latvia of grain originating from Russia and Belarus, Rolands Feldmanis, chairman of the board of the Latvian Agricultural Cooperatives Association (LLKA), told LETA.
He believes that the decision adopted by the Saeima on Thursday - to impose stricter border controls on grain shipments from third countries as a matter of urgency - is a step in the right direction, but controls alone are not enough.
"The Saeima’s decision to impose stricter border controls on grain shipments from third countries is a step in the right direction, but it is not enough. The reality on the ground shows that inspections and attempts to trace the true origin of these shipments will quickly turn into a game of cat and mouse. The simplest, safest, and most effective solution is to ban these shipments entirely," Feldmanis notes.
He emphasizes that it will be particularly difficult to determine the true origin of a shipment in cases where grain of different origins has been deliberately mixed into a single shipment.
Feldmanis notes that the liability of the cargo owner and the penalties for non-compliant or falsely declared cargo must also be seriously considered. In his view, when non-compliant cargo is detected, it must be possible to immediately detain and confiscate it, while those responsible must face real economic and legal consequences.
"If the cargo owner faces no real financial losses or criminal liability, there is a significant risk that the infrastructure will be deliberately flooded with questionable cargo. Such a scenario could paralyze both the control authorities and the grain terminals, physically halting Latvia’s own transit and export capabilities," Feldmanis emphasizes.

If there is no significant progress in implementation of Rail Baltica by 2034, it will be more difficult to defend the project politically - Zile  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:20:33 UTC
00:20:33 KST

RIGA - If the implementation of Rail Baltica does not make significant progress by 2034, it will be more difficult to defend the project politically, Roberts Zile (National Alliance), Vice President of the European Parliament (EP), told LETA.
He noted that other sources of funding must also be sought for the implementation of Rail Baltica, including public and private financing options. The politician did not rule out the possibility of making significant progress on the project by 2030, but emphasized that it is particularly important to ensure the project's progress through 2034, when the next European Union (EU) multiannual budget period will conclude.
According to the EP Vice President, even if the full scope of the project is not implemented by 2034, it would become politically more difficult to advocate for the project's continued implementation not only in the EP but also elsewhere. He explained that when drafting the next EU multiannual budget, covering the period from 2035 to 2041, member states advocating for cuts to EU budget spending, such as Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Finland, might oppose further funding for the project, citing its prolonged implementation.
Zile also stated that failure to complete Rail Baltica by 2030 would most likely not, in and of itself, require the repayment of EU funding that has already been allocated. He is not aware of any precedents where funding would have to be repaid in such a situation.
As reported, the Baltic states have agreed to extend the deadline for the first phase of Rail Baltica railway project to 2034, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) told members of the press on Tuesday.
The prime minister noted that the Baltic states have drafted a final document - a statement to the European Commission (EC) - outlining the trilateral agreement among the three Baltic states to continue the Rail Baltica project.
"The project deadline, which had been set for 2030, is not realistic, and all three Baltic states have agreed on a 2034 deadline for the first phase," Kulbergs emphasized.
In the Baltic states’ declaration, the heads of government affirm the importance of Rail Baltica as a joint strategic project for European security, military mobility, connectivity, and competitiveness, and commit to working together to ensure that construction of Rail Baltica main line under the next EU multiannual financial framework proceeds as closely as possible to the agreed schedule.
The Baltic states will strive to secure EU funding for the project, maintain the EU co-financing rate at 85 percent, and create the conditions for uninterrupted construction until the start of the new EU financial programming period. Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia agreed to jointly advocate for an allocation of at least EUR 10 billion for the Rail Baltica project in the EU’s multiannual financial framework. The prime ministers also agreed to instruct each country’s transportation ministers to review the project’s costs and meet regularly to coordinate efforts to reduce them.
They also plan to collaborate to reduce project costs, improve project management, and ensure closer coordination of their actions. The leaders of the Baltic states agree that the potential of the Rail Baltica project can only be realized through a continuous cross-border rail connection linking the Baltic states with the rest of Europe.
The joint declaration of the Baltic states states that the Baltic states are committed to ensuring that the main line of Rail Baltica begins operations during the next EU multiannual financial framework period (2028-2034), while maintaining the intention to continue construction, adhering as closely as possible to the currently agreed timeline of 2030, as set forth in the European Commission’s implementing decision.
To achieve this, the project partners will commission the necessary integrated systems in a timely manner, establish their construction schedules and investment priorities, as well as each country’s commitments, in order to jointly move the project forward. This process will be closely coordinated with the EC and Poland, ensuring consistency regarding the Rail Baltica connection, financing mechanisms, comprehensive work plans, and unified implementation deadlines.
LETA also reported, the first phase of the Rail Baltica project’s main route in Latvia is planned within the current scope, which calls for establishing a Rail Baltica cross-border connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as to complete construction work at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Train Terminal to ensure the connection between Rail Baltica and the existing rail network.
The cost of the first phase of Rail Baltica in the Baltics could reach EUR 14.3 billion, of which EUR 5.5 billion would be in Latvia; however, depending on inflation, this amount could rise to EUR 6 billion.
According to the cost-benefit analysis, the total project cost in the Baltic states could reach EUR 23.8 billion. A previous cost-benefit analysis conducted in 2017 estimated that the project would cost a total of EUR 5.8 billion.
The Rail Baltica project aims to build a European standard-gauge railway line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border, thereby enabling the Baltic states to be connected by rail to other European countries. In the Baltic states, plans call for the construction of a new 870-kilometer-long European standard-gauge (1,435 mm) railway line with a maximum train speed of 240 kilometers per hour.

TALLINN - Collective agreement negotiations in the healthcare sector have ended without results, and healthcare workers' unions are turning to the public conciliator to resolve the resulting labor dispute.
The reason for the failure of the negotiations is the decision by Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller and the Health Insurance Fund to use the sum intended for raising the minimum wages of healthcare workers in 2027 to balance the Health Insurance Fund's budget.
"A balanced budget doesn't treat patients, healthcare workers do. Nurses are not satisfied with their pay. The average salary is often cited, but it is earned through many hours of overtime and by working nights, weekends, and holidays. Due to the shortage of nurses, many also hold multiple jobs. If the state cancels the pay raise, it is telling these people that they are not valued or needed. A salary increase is an essential condition to ensure that there will be nurses in hospitals to help patients tomorrow," said Kätlin Lillemaa, president of the Estonian Nurses Union.
The basic salary for care workers is over a third lower than the national average, and their pay only approaches the average thanks to night work and overtime hours. As the population ages, the demand for caregivers is not expected to decrease in the coming years.
"In the hospital, care workers are the ones who are with the patient the most and are the first to notice if something is wrong. They certainly deserve higher pay for their physically and mentally demanding work. Each of us wants our loved ones to be well cared for. This cannot be done by a tired person working for two employers just to make ends meet," said Ulvi Tasane, president of the Estonian Health Care Professionals' Union.
Estonia is already facing a shortage of doctors, nurses, and other healthcare specialists. If wages do not correspond to the workload and responsibility, there is a risk that the number of workers will decrease even further.
According to a recent survey by paramedic Kevin Lumi, the national healthcare system could lose 740 healthcare workers if the 2027 pay raise is canceled. That is how many respondents plan to leave for private clinics, go abroad, or change their profession altogether. This means longer waiting lists, and accessing care will become even more difficult. The minister's promise that the accessibility of treatment will remain the same does not hold true, as there is no medical care without staff.
Minister of Social Affairs and chairwoman of the Health Insurance Fund's supervisory board, Karmen Joller, is responsible for the functioning and financing of our healthcare system, which is why her presence at the collective agreement negotiations is crucial. Unfortunately, the minister did not see fit to sit down at the same table with healthcare workers and employers.
The appeal is signed by the Estonian Nurses Union, the Estonian Health Care Professionals' Union, the Estonian Medical Association, the Estonian Union of Clinical Psychologists, the Estonian Association of Clinical Speech Therapists, and the Estonian Association of Physiotherapists.

EC takes action against Latvia over transposition of EU directives  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:20:24 UTC
00:20:24 KST

RIGA - The European Commission (EC) has launched six infringement proceedings against Latvia for failing to notify the full transposition of six European Union (EU) directives into national law, the Press Office of the EC Representation in Latvia informed LETA.
The EC decided to open infringement procedures by sending a letter of formal notice to Latvia for failure to communicate the full transposition of the new electricity market design rules on free choice of supplier and the right to energy sharing. These provisions are intend to strengthen consumers' positions in the electricity market by expanding their ability to choose and switch suppliers, access more competitive and innovative offers, and participate more actively in the energy system. Member states were supposed to notify the EC of the transposition of these provisions by July 17.
Latvia has also missed the deadline to notify the EC of the full transposition of the recast Hydrogen and Decarbonized Gas Directive. The directive, together with the regulation, updates the rules for the natural gas market and introduces regulations for hydrogen infrastructure to promote the use of renewable and low-carbon gases. The deadline for transposing the directive was August 5. In this case, the EC sent letters to 25 other member states besides Latvia.
Meanwhile, the revised Anti-Trafficking Directive provides for stricter criminalization, strengthens the ability of authorities to investigate new forms of exploitation, including online, and improves assistance to trafficking victims. Member states must also formalize a national mechanism for referring victims to assistance services and designate a contact point for the cross-border referral of victims. Latvia has not notified the EC of the full transposition of the amendments by the July 15 deadline.
Two separate infringement cases concern the repair of goods. The first directive gives consumers the right to request repairs for certain goods, such as smartphones, washing machines, and refrigerators, even after the statutory warranty period has expired. Manufacturers are obliged to offer repairs at a reasonable price and within a reasonable timeframe. The second, delegated directive, extends these provisions to local room heaters used in households. Latvia has failed to notify the EC of the full transposition of both directives by July 31.
The sixth infringement case concerns the transposition of amendments to the Industrial and Livestock Rearing Emissions Directive. These amendments strengthen pollution reduction requirements, expand the scope of the regulation, and provide for the right to claim compensation for health damage caused by unlawful pollution. Full transposition of the amendments was due by July 1. In this case, the EC has sent letters to all EU member states.
The letters of formal notice sent by the EC constitute the first stage of the infringement procedure. Latvia has two months to respond, complete the transposition of the directives, and notify the EC of the measures taken.
If the EC does not consider the response satisfactory, it may issue a reasoned opinion requiring the infringement to be remedied. If the country still fails to fulfill its obligations, the EC may bring the matter before the Court of Justice of the European Union. In cases where a country has not notified the EC in a timely manner of the measures taken to transpose a directive, the EC may ask the court to impose financial penalties. If a country fails to comply with a judgment of the court, the EC may refer the matter to the court again and request that financial penalties be imposed.

Trump hails ‘very productive’ talks with China’s Xi Jinping

During a tea ceremony at the White House on Friday, Xi – who was on his first visit to the US in more than a decade – said, “We invite the president and his wife to visit China,” also noting that the two leaders could have two further opportunities to meet this year.

Earlier on Friday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that “tremendous things will be happening” between the US and China, adding that his meetings with Xi were productive for both sides, emphasising the issue of artificial intelligence.
“[Xi] seemed to like calling the poorly and inaccurately named Artificial Intelligence to a far more accurate and important name, SUPER INTELLIGENCE. That would be ‘SUPER!’ Everyone last night agreed, also,” said the US president.
Trump told the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week that the US would rename artificial intelligence “super intelligence” in all US government documents.
AI, Iran war
Trump hosted a lavish state dinner on Thursday for Xi, which included high-profile guests like Amazon’s Jeff Bezos and Tesla head Elon Musk, who was seated at the main table alongside the Chinese and US presidents.
Despite being locked in a fierce strategic rivalry over AI, Trump and Xi have rebuffed recent calls from inside the US tech sector to slow the pace of development over concerns about controlling the rapidly advancing technology.
On Friday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher that creating channels of communication on AI is one of the main challenges Washington and Beijing are seeking to overcome.
“I think with every government in the world right now, there isn’t a department of AI, and so there can be a question of who do you call when you have an issue,” Greer said, adding: “When I think about it, I think about the red zone between the Kremlin and the White House during the Cold War.”
Greer said another meeting on AI is planned within the next month between the representatives of both countries.
Separately, Greer told US media on Friday that the current talks did not cover the sale of a small amount of high-quality US-made chips requiring licences.
“These are the crown jewels of American technology. It’s the way we stay ahead in the race for superintelligence, or AI, and so those conversations … [are] not really happening in these negotiations,” Greer said.
On the Iran war, David Perdue, the US ambassador to China, told US-based business news network CNBC that Trump told Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was “totally unacceptable”.
Perdue later told Fox News that China was already moving away from supporting Iran, saying, “That’s what the commitment is. They assured us yesterday they’re not doing that.”
Xi and Trump made a show of working to preserve harmony between the world’s two largest economies during the visit, though there were no major breakthroughs on issues such as trade or AI safety.

Capalo AI has passed 1 GW of contracted battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity in the Baltic States. Just over twelve months ago, the company’s first asset in the region was a 1 MW BESS in Latvia. Today, close to 400 MW of BESS and close to 400 MWp of solar are under live optimization across Lithuania and Latvia.
The Baltic portfolio includes some of Europe’s leading infrastructure investors and developers. Several have returned to Capalo AI with second and third projects, including the owner of the company’s very first Baltic asset, who has since signed two more.
The live portfolio includes 13 hybrid parks, where battery storage and solar generation share a site and a grid connection. Capalo AI optimizes these parks as a single asset, deciding when to sell solar output directly, when to store it, and how to allocate battery capacity across Day-Ahead, Intraday, and balancing markets.
All Baltic assets run on Capalo Zeus VPP™, the company’s turnkey service for battery and hybrid asset owners. Zeus VPP™ covers route to market, multi-market trading and optimization, and Balance Responsible Party (BRP) and Balance Service Provider (BSP) services, taking assets from prequalification through to lifetime value maximization. For owners, that means one partner handles market access, trading and grid obligations, while the asset is continuously positioned across the markets that pay best at any given moment.
Alongside Lithuania and Latvia, Capalo AI is now bringing its optimization and trading expertise to Estonia, with plans to go live later this year.

1 GW is not the ceiling, Capalo AI’s Baltic portfolio continues to grow.

Complaints from the Belgian depository were filed with the Moscow Arbitration Court on September 24. Euroclear intends to appeal the court ruling issued on May 29.
In December 2025, the Bank of Russia filed a claim against Euroclear for 18.2 trillion rubles with the Moscow Arbitration Court amid the European Union’s plans to use blocked Russian assets to fund Ukraine. This amount includes frozen funds, the value of blocked securities, and foregone profits. On May 15, 2026, the court upheld the Bank of Russia's claim to recover 18.2 trillion rubles from Euroclear Bank. On May 20, the Bank of Russia filed a motion with the Moscow Arbitration Court for immediate enforcement of the ruling.
In July, the 9th Arbitration Court of Appeal rejected Euroclear’s appeal against the recovery of 18.2 trillion rubles in the Central Bank’s lawsuit.
The Bank of Russia is also considering the possibility of protecting its interests in international courts and arbitration tribunals, with subsequent enforcement of the decisions of such courts in UN member states. The EU and G7 countries have frozen around 300 bln euro of Russian assets. Roughly 180 bln euro is held in the Belgian depository Euroclear. The European Commission is seeking approval from EU member states to use Russian assets for Ukraine.

Couple jailed for at least 21 years for murder of vulnerable man in their care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:15:36 UTC
00:15:36 KST

A couple convicted of murder after inflicting “deliberate cruelty” on a vulnerable 28-year-old man in their care, who at the time of his death weighed just 40kg (6st 4lb), have been jailed for life.
Rubin Blount was made to stand for long periods of time, left to lie in his own urine and forced to eat out of bins by his stepbrother Kenneth Newton and Newton’s partner, Melanie James, at a property in Tamworth, Staffordshire, Stafford crown court heard.
Newton, 58, and James, 64, both from Birmingham, who had filmed themselves mocking and abusing the victim, were convicted by a jury in July of his murder.
Jailing them each for a minimum of 21 years, Mrs Justice Jefford said they had been in a position of trust which they had abused and had shown an “abject failure to help him when he was in pain and suffering”.
Blount was severely dehydrated and malnourished when he was taken to hospital after he became unwell, and he had a cardiac arrest upon arrival. He died three days later on 30 November 2022.
Doctors found he had extensive pneumonia, severe infection, fractures to his ribs and spine, and burns, lesions and grazes. He had 50 rib fractures, 47 of which had been inflicted in the weeks leading up to his death.
Jennifer Josephs KC, prosecuting, told Friday’s sentencing hearing that Blount had been described as “considerably mentally impaired” and was particularly vulnerable, and that the defendants’ “cruel” behaviour towards him was demonstrated in videos shown to the jury.
Josephs said Blount must have been in “extreme pain and suffering” before his death, and the couple had denied him access to medical care until he was “beyond help”.
“Mr Blount’s death was the culmination of a prolonged course of conduct perpetrated against a man who was unable to speak for himself,” she said.
Blount’s mother, Jeanette Blount, said in a victim impact statement that her son was vulnerable and deserved “compassion, dignity and a chance to live his life”.
“We all believed they loved him and would take care of him. We had no reason to believe otherwise,” she said.
The judge said a series of videos made by the defendants on 2 November 2022 “show Rubin emaciated, gaunt, stooped and broken, standing in the doorway”. Videos showed the pair mocking him and flinging abuse at him while he was “unable to defend himself or even walk away”.
“The first 25 rib fractures were inflicted before or shortly after this recording was made,” she added.
James sobbed as the court was told that the abuse and violence inflicted on Blount went on for months.
Rebecca Wade KC, defending James, said: “No one could fail to be disgusted by Melanie James’s actions towards this vulnerable man. She is a woman who has had a difficult life of her own.
“There is some evidence to show that at one point she did care for Rubin and did love him, and him her.” Something “shifted”, she said, due to James’s “ability to cope with the stresses and strains of life and that was much to Rubin’s detriment”.
Mark Heywood KC, defending Newton, said Blount was, through no fault of his own, a “challenging” person to care for. The circumstances leading to his death “can’t be dealt with as simply as saying he was financially advantageous for them, or that he became a burden”, he said. The couple were “ill-equipped”.
Speaking outside the court, DCI Ian Fitzgerald, of Staffordshire police, said: “The extent of the injuries Rubin suffered, the state that he was in and the arrogance [of the defendants] in the way they thought they could try and get away with it and blame him for his injuries was shocking and very, very distressing.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Zelenskyy discussed the framework in an interview, noting that Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on energy infrastructure if Russia did the same.
He also floated the upcoming G20 summit in Miami as a possible venue for leader-level talks.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on September 25 that Ukraine's Drone Deal agreements with partners can extend beyond equipment transfers to include sharing air-defense experience and deploying specialists.
He made the comments while speaking with journalists on September 25. The question concerned whether Ukraine might send units to NATO member states amid the threat of Russian hybrid and drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"We have offered our help to various countries," Zelenskyy stated, adding that priority goes to nations already assisting Ukraine during the war.
He noted that partner governments are aware of that assistance.
Zelenskyy explained that the bilateral Drone Deal format applies regardless of NATO membership, since eligibility depends on partnership rather than alliance status.
He described the agreements as covering drone and missile sales, co-production, and the exchange of operational experience.
The Ukrainian leader did not indicate that Kyiv would deploy units to NATO territory, framing the cooperation instead around shared expertise.
He pointed to recent hybrid and drone attacks against Moldova, which belongs to neither NATO nor the European Union.
Similar incidents, he told journalists, have also targeted Germany and Romania. Zelenskyy emphasized that such attacks are not limited to NATO members, calling it part of a broader pattern of Russian hybrid warfare.
He cited Ukraine's earlier deployment of specialists to the Middle East as an example of that exchange. Those specialists, he added, helped protect critical facilities in the region.
Zelenskyy described the initiative as an ongoing framework that continues to expand to new partner countries.
The Drone Deal framework Zelenskyy referenced has expanded rapidly since its introduction. Ukraine had signed long-term Drone Deal agreements with nine countries by early August, with another fifteen under negotiation.
Separate deals had already been concluded with the European Union, alongside a bilateral framework with the US covering drone technology cooperation.
Under the format, Ukrainian teams assess a partner's air-defense needs before proposing solutions drawn from Ukraine's wartime experience, with agreements structured to run for at least a decade.

Steel Giant ArcelorMittal Halts Kryvyi Rih Operations Following Deadly Russian Attacks

Steel Giant ArcelorMittal Halts Kryvyi Rih Operations Following Deadly Russian Attacks
Global steel giant ArcelorMittal announced it will indefinitely suspend operations at its Ukrainian subsidiary, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, the company reported in an official statement on September 25.
It informed the Government of Ukraine that it can no longer safely and sustainably run the facility following a wave of deadly Russian bombardments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The shutdown at ArcelorMittal is reflective of a devastating pattern of Russian strikes targeting Ukraine’s commercial and industrial infrastructure. In recent months, intense bombardments have crippled major factories, logistics hubs, and other heavy steelmaking facilities, while simultaneously destroying an estimated 90% of the country’s retail warehouse capacity and disrupting vital supply chains.
According to an official statement released by the company, the Kryvyi Rih plant has been targeted by four missile strikes over the past five weeks, with the most recent attack occurring on September 21. The strikes caused extensive damage to production facilities and resulted in severe casualties.
ArcelorMittal confirmed that the four attacks claimed five lives and injured 17 employees, one of whom remains in critical condition.
“It is with deep regret that we have concluded that we are no longer able to operate ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih safely,” said Mauro Longobardo, CEO of ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, in the company’s statement.
“Since the war started, our people in Ukraine have worked tirelessly to keep the mines and plant operating. They have been the embodiment of bravery, in circumstances most of us cannot begin to imagine,” he continued.
Longobardo added that the company is currently in talks with the Ukrainian government regarding the facility’s future. The immediate focus will shift to preserving the plant’s remaining infrastructure so that “when peace finally returns, options for restarting production remain available.”
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, ArcelorMittal reported providing over $700 million in financial support to maintain continuity of operations at the Kryvyi Rih plant, prioritizing the safety and economic security of its local workforce, the company wrote.
However, the recent destruction has forced a massive financial write-down. The company expects to record a non-cash impairment charge of about $1 billion, primarily reflecting the impairment of property, plant, and equipment at the Ukrainian facility.
ArcelorMittal is the largest steel producer in Europe and one of the leading integrated steel and mining companies globally, generating $61.4 billion in revenue in 2025.
As Russian missile strikes force major Ukrainian industrial sites like ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih to shut down, Ukraine has been calling for the EU to sanction Russian steel and nickel tycoons Vladimir Lisin and Vladimir Potanin.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, sanctions advisor to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, stated that listing Lisin (owner of NLMK) and Potanin (owner of Nornickel) is essential to restricting Russia’s war economy, particularly after the EU set a “risky precedent” by delisting oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.

====================================================================================================

Burnham’s AI agenda is already in disarray thanks to Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:14:38 UTC
00:14:38 KST

Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets with US President Donald Trump during a meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly on September 22, 2026 in New York City. | Pool photo by Toby Melville via Getty Images
LONDON — Andy Burnham flew to New York this week with a dream: the U.K. would set itself up on the world stage as a leading light in AI safety.
He didn’t bank on Donald Trump immediately tearing that idea to shreds.
The new U.K. prime minister said the country would use its upcoming G20 presidency to set international principles on AI, and use its world-renowned AI Security Institute to test the latest AI models and cement its role as a global AI power player.
Advertisement
Within the space of a week, however, Trump trashed any hopes that America will participate in global agreements on AI and POLITICO revealed that AISI’s usually privileged access to new AI models is now being delayed by the White House – which told leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their models with the U.K. until U.S. testers have finished ascertaining that they don’t pose a threat to American systems.
So if Burnham wants to stick to his plan of making U.K. the center for brokering international AI harmony he has to figure out how to bring the U.S. onside, or else press on without the U.K.’s closest ally.
When approached by POLITICO, a U.K. government spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a world leader in AI security, and the AI Security Institute continues to work closely with the U.S. government, international partners and leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.”
Special relationship problems
The U.K. already has a track record for convening global meetings on AI safety, but it has also tended to stick by the U.S. when deciding whether to sit out specific international agreements.
In 2023 the U.K. hosted the Bletchley Park Summit on AI safety, which produced an agreement on the opportunities and risks of AI signed by 28 countries, crucially including the U.S. and China.
However, at the Paris iteration of the summit in 2025 the U.K. declined to sign a new declaration on the ethical development of AI alongside the U.S.
Advertisement
This week at the U.N. General Assembly, Finland and Norway brought a declaration on frontier AI safety to ensure human oversight and suggested a global supervisory regime. It was adopted by 22 countries on the sidelines of the UNGA, but not the U.S. or U.K.
Bringing the U.S. to the table on any international agreement will now prove a delicate dance. According to a person familiar with U.K. government thinking, granted anonymity to disclose private discussions, the Burnham administration does want to drive international cooperation but is worried that signing up to formal pacts at this point could alienate the White House.
The risks of sticking by Trump
Mounting political frustration with the U.K. on AI means there are also concerns that the likes of France, Canada and EU “will cut us out [of brokering] if they can,” said Wendy Hall, computer scientist and a U.K. representative in U.N. efforts on AI.
One of the countries that did sign the 22-country pact earlier this week was Australia, whose prime minister Anthony Albanese used an address at the U.N. to reveal his country’s Medicare site had been hacked by OpenAI agents and health records stolen.
“That's not a ‘rogue agent,’” said Gina Neff, executive director of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, “It's literally a cybercrime against a state. Now, if the U.S. won't rein in these companies, other countries will be faced with no choice: they have to defend the realm.”
Testing times
Both Burnham and his foreign secretary Ed Miliband stressed at UNGA that the U.K.’s AISI gives the country an edge on AI safety, but the reports that AISI’s access to models is being delayed by America cast doubt over that claim.
Advertisement
AI companies hand their models over to AISI voluntarily, on the basis that it has a deep bench of expertise. But AISI continuing on a voluntary basis is “going to be difficult to sell to domestic audiences if frontier AI companies are no longer playing ball,” said Neff.
Hall said that she “can’t see a U.K.-led effort being very strong at the moment but we need to be part of the conversation. Our strong card is AISI. If that is weakened, then our efforts to lead on AI assurance and safety are weakened.”
The U.K. government spokesperson said: “We will continue to work closely with the U.S. and other partners on the testing of advanced AI, while building our own rigorous scientific understanding of these systems and ensuring our approach is grounded in the evidence.”
The China question
China has shown a lot more appetite for global agreements around AI than America, and when President Xi Jinping met with Trump on Thursday the technology was high on the agenda.
“Burnham’s call for collaboration on AI standards provides Xi with an opportunity to demonstrate the gulf between the present U.S. administration,” said Aled Lloyd Owen, chief of staff at Responsible Ai, a non-profit for international responsible AI research.
“China is seizing the initiative by advocating for relatively uncontroversial measures and a cooperative approach that will be increasingly challenging for other advocates of cooperation to ignore,” he added.
Advertisement
That means if the U.S. refuses to be brought to the table on AI, the U.K. could turn increasingly to China as the next largest global power.
The U.K and China already have ties on AI, said Isabella Wilkinson, Senior Research Fellow for the Digital Society Initiative at Chatham House. “The U.K. and China have had very close exchanges on issues of technology, policy, and cybersecurity in the past,” Wilkinson told a briefing ahead of Xi and Trump's meeting.
Bridging the divide between China and the U.S. could be a way for the U.K. to bring America into the fold, Neff said.
“Burnham has some great diplomatic tools in the toolkit to be able to offer the Americans a way of third-party evaluation for safety, while coordinating with allied countries to ensure that their own systems are safe and secure,” she said.
For Burnham to achieve his goal of the U.K. being treated as the world’s “honest broker” on AI, he’ll have to decide how much pressure he wants to exert on its largest, and at present most unpredictable, ally.
“As the prime minister said, we are going to put AI at the heart of our G20 presidency and will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness – and to ensure that AI development is safe,” the U.K. government spokesperson said.

Merz faces pension mutiny after election disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:12:10 UTC
00:12:10 KST

Merz faces pension mutiny after election disaster
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s humiliating run of regional election defeats has reignited a bitter fight over his unpopular pension reform, with his Social Democratic coalition partners pushing back against plans that could make Germans work longer, national media have reported.
Merz’s Christian Democrats suffered a historic drubbing this month, culminating in what the chancellor himself called a “disaster” in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The CDU failed to clear the 5% threshold for the state parliament, while the right-wing, anti-immigration and Euroskeptic Alternative for Germany (AfD) came first. The AfD also topped the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, while in Berlin the CDU was pushed into second place behind the left-wing Die Linke. The SPD also suffered significant losses.
The defeats have complicated Merz’s already contentious reform drive. At the center of the fight is the so-called “pension at 63,” which allows people with 45 qualifying years to retire early without deductions. A government commission recommended scrapping the scheme, citing Germany’s aging population straining pension finances and the workforce. Merz, who has repeatedly urged Germans to work more, backs the reform.
Opponents, however, have argued abolition would punish people who started work young and paid into the system for decades. The issue is particularly sensitive in eastern Germany, where incomes and private savings tend to be lower. An INSA poll published last month found 68% of Germans opposed scrapping the scheme.
The election rout has given those opponents fresh leverage, including within Merz’s conservative camp, German media has reported. An SPD strategy document circulated this week argued there are “open questions” on proposed early retirement changes. SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch has called the entitlement after 45 years a “fundamental issue of justice,” while Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s Minister-President Manuela Schwesig argued that people who have worked and paid contributions throughout their careers should retain the right to retire early without deductions.
The coalition is now scrambling for a compromise. According to Bild and Spiegel reports on Thursday, options include preserving deduction-free early retirement for physically demanding jobs, such as roofing, or raising the qualifying period from 45 years to 46 or 47. Hardship exemptions and transition periods for workers nearing retirement are also under discussion.
Alexander Hoffmann, parliamentary group leader of the CSU, the CDU’s sister party, argued there could be no pension reform without scrapping the early retirement scheme, telling Bild: “We have a clear agreement in the coalition: hardship cases yes, standard cases no.” However, nearly four hours of coalition talks this week reportedly failed to produce an agreement.
The clash threatens more than the pension scheme. Merz came to power promising sweeping reforms to revive Europe’s largest economy after years of stagnation, but the election defeats have sharply narrowed his room for maneuver. Analysts say SPD lawmakers whose votes he needs have less incentive to embrace unpopular measures after the governing parties were punished at the ballot box, while resistance is also reportedly growing within the CDU itself, particularly in the east. Merz, however, has responded to the election defeats by insisting that “the reforms must come.”
The chancellor’s own standing has plunged amid economic weakness and dissatisfaction with his government. Earlier this month, just 10% of respondents told pollster Forsa they were satisfied with his performance, against 88% who were dissatisfied. A YouGov poll published ahead of the latest elections found 48% of Germans expected him to be out of office by year-end. German media have also discussed the possibility of a Kanzlertausch, or “chancellor swap,” if the CDU suffers further setbacks.

Africa must have a say in global AI rules – South Africa
Africa must have a say in shaping global rules that govern artificial intelligence, South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola has said, arguing that the continent should play a greater role in emerging technologies.
Speaking at the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday, Lamola linked Africa’s role in AI development to the continent’s vast reserves of critical minerals and its young population. He said these resources could help narrow the gap between richer and poorer countries, while African states could contribute to AI research and innovation.
“Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and deployment of artificial intelligence,” the minister said.
Lamola also renewed Pretoria’s push for broader reform of global institutions, particularly the UN Security Council. Africa accounts for more than a quarter of UN member states, yet has no permanent seat on the council.
Earlier this month, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa proposed that BRICS establish an international mechanism for the independent scientific assessment of AI. Speaking at the group’s summit in New Delhi, he also called for AI companies to face formal external checks and government oversight.
South Africa is also developing its own AI industry. Johannesburg-based company Lelapa AI has built language technology designed for African languages, focusing on smaller and more resource-efficient models that can operate with limited computing power.
The African Union (AU) has also sought to give the continent a greater role in global AI governance. Its Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy, adopted in 2024, calls for an Africa-centered approach to the technology and the development of common governance frameworks to ensure its responsible use.
Earlier this month, the AU brought together African diplomats in Geneva to coordinate the continent’s position in international negotiations on AI and digital policy. The bloc said African countries could help shape global AI standards and rules by presenting a common position in international talks.

‘Major milestone’: TfL to launch new public bus operator in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:04:56 UTC
00:04:56 KST

A publicly owned company, Buses for London, will start running services in the capital next year, Transport for London has announced.
TfL said the launch was a “major milestone” in its plans to improve buses for drivers and passengers.
The new public company will take over a handful of London’s bus routes, which number nearly 700 in total, from late 2027, starting with route 6, which runs between Willesden and Victoria station.
A further four routes to be run by the public company from 2028 are to be announced.
TfL said the creation of a publicly owned bus company would give it greater control over how services were run, allowing it to make buses more reliable and safe, and to reinvest profits into improving the transport network.
At present, TfL contracts bus services to eight privately owned operators.
The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “This is an opportunity to reimagine our bus network so that it provides better value for money, supports our climate goals, makes our roads safer, and overall just works better for passengers and drivers alike.”
London’s buses have been getting gradually slower and passenger numbers have fallen over the past decade, as they battle with congestion and demands on road space in the capital.
Lorna Murphy, TfL’s director of buses, said the public company marked “an exciting new chapter”, with a depot in the Old Oak regeneration area that would be “the first home of a new generation of zero-emission buses … helping us to build on the progress we’ve already made towards a more sustainable transport system”.
Unions welcomed the move but private operators said the taxpayer would foot the bill for investment and take on more risk.
The Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “Unite has long been calling for London’s bus services to be returned to public ownership. Outsourcing to private companies hasn’t worked well for workers or passengers.
“For too long, bus workers have been subjected to intolerable working conditions and passengers have experienced worsening services, while bus firms and their shareholders rake in huge profits.”
The union’s national officer for passenger transport, Wayne King, said it was “only the beginning”. He said Unite expected Buses for London to “lead the way in workers’ pay, terms and conditions and treatment and will hold TfL and the mayor to account on this”.
The Confederation of Passenger Transport, representing bus firms, said it would not fix London’s buses. Graham Vidler, the chief executive of CPT, said: “Passengers don’t need a new public bus operator. They need faster, more reliable journeys and investment should be made where passengers will actually feel the difference: tackling congestion, giving buses priority and getting London moving.
“Regardless of who operates the service, buses typically travel at just 9 mph in London – slower than the average cyclist.”
He said private operators had made significant investment in London’s bus network, including new vehicles and technology, adding: “The uncertainty created by a new publicly owned operator risks making it harder for private operators to make the case for continued investment in London in the future.”
Labour’s bus overhauls since 2025, which push wider franchising and public control of services, have also made it possible for local authorities nationwide to establish new publicly owned companies. A few municipal companies, such as Reading, Blackpool and Nottingham, survived deregulation and privatisation in the 1980s.

Trump backs Hormuz alternative but his Iran war is blocking the route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:03:40 UTC
00:03:40 KST

Trump backs Hormuz alternative but his Iran war is blocking the route
The US has put the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) back at the center of its Middle East strategy as shipping and energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain disrupted. US President Donald Trump told a meeting of Arab leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that attacks on commercial shipping showed the need to shift the Middle East’s energy infrastructure away from “Iranian checkpoints.”  
“That’s why my administration strongly supports the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor,” Trump said earlier this week, while calling for other ways of moving oil, including pipelines. 
The corridor was jointly unveiled at the G20 summit in New Delhi in 2023 by the US, India, Saudi Arabia, UAE, EU, Italy, France, and Germany. The IMEC would combine maritime routes, railways and other infrastructure, alongside planned energy and digital links. It has two broad sections: an eastern leg connecting India to the Gulf, and a northern leg linking the Gulf to Europe. 
Cargo would sail from India to the UAE, move by rail across Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel’s Mediterranean coast, and then travel by sea from Haifa toward European ports. However, the IMEC is not by itself a single oil pipeline designed to replace Hormuz, as Trump’s comments seemed to imply. It is a trade and connectivity network. 
What’s the IMEC’s geopolitical significance?
When the IMEC was announced, it was seen as a challenger to another route, which has been in the making for decades – the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC). Conceived in 2000 by India, Iran, and Russia, the 7,200-km INSTC will move freight from Mumbai through Iranian ports such as Bandar Abbas and Chabahar, across Iran and Azerbaijan – or via Caspian Sea routes – into Russia and onward to Northern and Western Europe.
Its main advantage over other routes is speed: the INSTC is said to be between 20% and 67% faster than existing corridors, while also avoiding the Suez Canal and Bab al-Mandab.
Since 2022, it has become one of Moscow’s highest-priority alternative logistics routes, as it allows Russia to maintain trade links with partners in South Asia.
The corridor’s development, however, has been slow, largely because Iran, and later Russia, came under unprecedented Western sanctions. Even so, work has continued. India has invested around $120 million in Iran’s Chabahar Port, widely seen as a strategic anchor of the INSTC.
However, work at Chabahar has also been stalled by unilateral US sanctions against Iran.
Washington gave New Delhi a sanctions waiver in 2018, allowing India to develop and use the port for Afghanistan’s reconstruction and regional trade. A second six-month waiver given in October expired in April, making it harder for India to continue to work on the port.
Chabahar is more than 500 km away from the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz. However, it still came under attack from US forces, with airstrikes targeting Iran’s maritime infrastructure and surveillance facilities in July. New Delhi clarified at the time that the Indian-operated Shahid Beheshti terminal itself was not damaged.
For India, Chabahar – and INSTC – remain the best options to access the Central Asian, Russian, and European markets, even if Washington and Tehran end hostilities tomorrow and open up Hormuz. A lot of work has already been done and the impact from any regional instability or political uncertainty would be far less than in the case of IMEC.
Why Hormuz actors still matter and the full corridor cannot be built now
It is difficult to imagine that the IMEC, if and when it becomes a reality, would move trade fully away from Hormuz. Saudi and UAE ports in the Persian Gulf that are key hubs on the route would still be impacted by any tensions around the strait.
The route will have to be recalibrated to ports like Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, to make it bypass Hormuz. However, in the last few months ships have been attacked off the coast of Oman and as far west as Yemen. 
Even the land corridor may not be fully safe in a regional conflict, as shown by the many Iranian missile hits on Saudi Arabia. That is a point missed by Trump, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who in April called for advancing the IMEC to diversify export infrastructure away from the Hormuz bottleneck.
The IMEC’s viability depends on much more than physical infrastructure, such as ports and railway lines. Making the land connectivity part work requires deeper transport and political cooperation across the Middle East, and specifically Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel. 
That is no longer easy to pull together after Israeli forces invaded Gaza. The widespread public anger in the Arab world makes it nearly impossible for the Gulf monarchies to agree to such collaboration with Israel, the war with regional rival Iran notwithstanding. Finance is another issue, with no firm overall funding commitments or construction timelines in place. The corridor remains a long-term proposal rather than an operational alternative to existing energy and trade routes.
So where does IMEC stand?
India and its partners are still backing the project. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni reaffirmed their commitment to the IMEC in May and called for a first ministerial meeting on the corridor to take concrete steps toward its implementation this year.
Still, despite the urgency created by the Middle East conflict and Trump’s comments, a fully functioning IMEC is years away.

Trump sees no urgency for Canada deal as trade dispute deepens, USTR says
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 - President Donald Trump's administration is comfortable maintaining its trade standoff with Canada even as new US import bans on Canadian products take effect next week and Washington threatens 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, parts and steel from January, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Friday.
His comments to CNBC signal Washington sees little need to compromise despite a deepening dispute that has strained relations between the longtime allies, triggered retaliation on both sides of the border and raised fresh questions about the future of the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement.
The looming US import bans are on a broad range of Canadian goods, including alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products. The January increase on tariffs to 50% could carry significant consequences for North American auto production.
Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect earlier this month. Canadian tariffs followed 50% tariffs that the US imposed on some $20 billion of Canadian goods last month, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.
"We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We're shipping (agricultural products) back and forth across the border, so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," Greer told CNBC. "We're comfortable with where we are. ... They call us now and then, and we have good conversations about potential deals. But it's not – there's no urgency on our side, I would say."
The Canadian Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.
The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, who have blamed each other for the failed talks, spurred Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from Canada's biggest trading partner, and cast doubt on the viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
Some experts think the Trump administration wants to first reach a deal with Mexico, which could give the US more leverage to get a better agreement with Canada. The next round of talks with Mexico could occur in October, Mexican officials said this week. REUTERS

Africa rejects new scramble for minerals – Ghanaian president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:30 UTC
00:00:30 KST

Africa rejects new scramble for minerals – Ghanaian president
Africa will not accept another era of colonial-style resource extraction as global demand for critical minerals grows, Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama has told the UN General Assembly (UNGA), calling for structural reforms to address historical injustices.
The remarks come as the US and EU pursue deals with African governments to secure minerals such as copper, cobalt, and lithium for electric vehicles, batteries, and power grids, while seeking to reduce their reliance on China.
African countries hold substantial deposits but often export raw minerals. A UN Trade and Development report published in June says many minerals agreements still focus heavily on extraction, warning that resource-rich African countries could miss out on the value generated by processing and manufacturing.
“Africa will not remain a passive arena for a new scramble for resources,” Mahama said on Thursday. He said African countries must process their minerals at home, build local industries, and retain more of the wealth they generate.
Several African governments have moved to tighten control over their mineral resources in recent years. DR Congo, the world’s largest cobalt producer, has banned exports of copper and cobalt concentrates to encourage local processing under an order reported in August. Zimbabwe also suspended exports of raw minerals and lithium concentrates in February.
Ghana has required licensed aggregators to refine gold locally since September 1, with Mahama pledging to end raw mineral ore exports by 2030. In July, the West African nation’s neighbor Mali created a state body to oversee artisanal gold sales and curb smuggling, while Niger nationalized the Somair uranium venture operated by French state-owned Orano last year.
Aside from critical minerals, Mahama also renewed the call for slavery reparations in his role as the African Union’s champion for the campaign. In March, Ghana secured a UN resolution recognizing the transatlantic slave trade and chattel slavery as the gravest crimes against humanity. It passed with 123 votes. The US, Israel, and Argentina voted against it, while 52 countries abstained.
Mahama welcomed what he called “positive overtures” from countries, particularly the Netherlands, Germany, and France, as well as from institutions, on reparatory justice and restitution following the passage of the “historic resolution.”
The Ghanaian leader, however, said real repair requires “structural transformation,” including “dismantling the persistent engines of exploitation: unfair global trade regimes, predatory resource extraction, discriminatory credit ratings, [and] unsustainable debt burdens.”
“Africa does not seek charity. Africa seeks equal partnership,” Mahama declared.

Diverse autism genes converge to disrupt shared biological pathways, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:18 UTC
00:00:18 KST

A new mapping of how proteins interact in the brain suggests that many different genetic mutations linked to autism spectrum disorder end up altering the same underlying biological networks. By determining how specific mutations rewire these protein connections, the research offers a potential roadmap for finding targeted treatments for neurodevelopmental conditions. The findings were published in Science.
Autism spectrum disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by varying challenges with social communication and repetitive behaviors. The genetics underlying the condition are highly complex, with hundreds of different genes implicated. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2016 found that thousands of genes might contribute to the condition in different ways. Despite identifying so many risk factors, scientists have struggled to understand how such a wide variety of genetic changes leads to similar developmental outcomes.
“Over the past 15 years, large-scale sequencing studies have identified hundreds of genes associated with autism,” study co-author Nevan J. Krogan, a researcher at the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at the University of California, San Francisco, told PsyPost. “That progress was initially very exciting; in 2012, only a few genes had been clearly implicated, whereas today the list includes several hundred.”
“However, identifying genes and mutations has not, by itself, produced a sufficiently detailed understanding of autism biology or led to many new therapeutic strategies,” Krogan continued. “A list of genes is somewhat like a parts list for a machine. To understand how the machine works, and what happens when one part is altered, you also need to understand the proteins those genes produce and how those proteins interact inside cells. That was the gap we wanted to address.”
To bridge this gap, scientists look to proteins, which are the microscopic machines that carry out most of a cell’s functions. Proteins rarely act alone. Instead, they bind to one another to form larger complexes, much like interlocking puzzle pieces. A 2026 study showed how a single autism-linked mutation can physically disrupt the binding between two partner proteins, impairing how brain cells communicate. Similarly, a 2026 preprint study that has not been peer-reviewed indicated that turning off different autism-associated genes in human brain cells disrupts shared biological pathways.
Mapping these physical connections can be highly useful for medical research. In fact, research covered by PsyPost in 2022 used protein interaction networks to identify existing medications that might counteract the biological processes underlying autism.
Building on this concept, a research team that included Krogan and lead author Belinda Wang sought to map the physical interactions of proteins associated with autism risk genes at a massive scale. They wanted to see if different mutations might converge on the same biological complexes, selectively rewiring how these proteins connect rather than simply destroying their function altogether.
“Through this work, we generated what we believe is the largest protein-protein interaction map assembled for a neuropsychiatric disorder,” Krogan said. “The map provides a molecular framework for understanding how autism-associated mutations may disrupt cellular systems. Importantly, it has also revealed potential therapeutic directions that would not have been visible from genetic information alone.”
“We are now following up on several of those opportunities through drug-development programs,” he noted. “The broader goal is to move beyond cataloging autism-associated genes and toward understanding the underlying biology well enough to identify new strategies for treatment.”
The team focused on 100 genes identified as high-confidence risk factors for autism. They introduced the protein versions of these genes into human embryonic kidney cells. This cell type is widely used in laboratories because it is easy to grow and allows for large-scale analysis of protein interactions. Using a technique called affinity purification and mass spectrometry, which acts like a microscopic fishing hook to pull out a target protein along with everything attached to it, they identified which other proteins bound to their targets.
The resulting map uncovered 1,881 total interactions, 87 percent of which had never been reported before. On average, each autism risk protein interacted with 11 other proteins. The researchers observed a highly interconnected network, meaning that the different autism risk proteins tended to bind to the same central hubs.
To determine which proteins touched directly rather than indirectly, the team used AlphaFold, an artificial intelligence system that predicts the three-dimensional shapes of proteins. They then tested one of the central hubs, a protein complex involving the molecules DCAF7 and DYRK1A, in living systems. They edited the genes of Xenopus, a type of frog often used to study early development, as well as human neural progenitor cells, which are stem cells that develop into brain cells.
Disrupting this shared protein complex impaired the multiplication of the progenitor cells and resulted in a smaller forebrain size in the frog models. This provides evidence that different autism risk proteins work together in the same physical machinery to regulate early brain growth.
The researchers then looked at the impact of the disease-linked mutations themselves. They introduced 54 specific genetic mutations derived from autistic patients into 30 of the risk proteins. They repeated their protein-fishing experiment to see how these mutations changed the interaction network compared to the typical, unmutated proteins.
The mutations caused 253 interactions to be altered, with some connections strengthening and others weakening. The researchers found that completely different mutations often caused the exact same changes in the protein network. For example, three different mutations in a gene called FOXP1 all caused its resulting protein to lose its connection to a partner protein called FOXP4.
To see how this specific severed connection affects brain development, the team grew human forebrain organoids. These are miniature, three-dimensional bundles of brain tissue grown in a dish from stem cells, which mimic the early stages of human brain development.
In organoids carrying the FOXP1 mutations, the loss of the FOXP1 and FOXP4 connection led to the partner protein attaching to the wrong sections of DNA. This biological misstep caused the brain cells to mature too early. The premature maturation altered the proportion of specific types of neurons in the organoids and increased their overall electrical activity.
This overlap in downstream effects was exactly what the researchers were looking for. “The most surprising finding was the degree of biological convergence,” Krogan noted. “We began with roughly 100 genes associated with autism, but the corresponding proteins were not acting independently. Many were connected within a smaller number of shared biological networks.”
“That suggests we may not need a separate treatment for every individual genetic mutation,” he added. “A smaller number of therapies targeting common pathways could potentially benefit multiple groups of patients. That possibility has significant implications for future drug development.”
The findings provide independent researchers a new lens to interpret the thousands of rare mutations identified in recent years.
Lisa Bradley, a senior research associate at The Centre for Applied Genomics at The Hospital for Sick Children Research Institute who was not involved in the study, noted that the research complements existing genomic efforts. “This large-scale study of bona fide high-risk genes specifically looks at the very real possibility that ASD-associated mutations rewire specific protein-protein interactions,” she told PsyPost. “For me, the key takeaway is that this strategy provides a way to move from many different ASD-associated genes toward a smaller number of convergent molecular mechanisms, which otherwise could have remained hidden.”
Bradley found the study’s experimental validation using human forebrain organoids particularly persuasive. “For me, the FOXP1 story was the most convincing because they took an ASD-associated mutation from disruption of a specific protein interaction with FOXP4 through to downstream effects on gene expression and neuronal development in brain organoids,” she said. “Other ASD studies have implicated altered cortical layer development, so this provided an important proof of principle that altered protein interactions can translate into meaningful cellular neurodevelopmental consequences.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The initial protein mapping was conducted in kidney cells rather than brain cells. While the researchers validated key interactions in brain-specific models later, the initial environment might lack some specialized proteins found only in developing neurons.
Bradley cautioned that the findings offer early-stage evidence for molecular mechanisms, “rather than demonstrating that they are causal mechanisms.” She added, “Some of these genes and mutations could also be associated with complex ASD, including co-occurring intellectual disability, so the molecular changes identified may include broader NDD [neurodevelopmental disorder] biology rather than mechanisms unique to autism etiology.”
The study focused on 100 high-confidence autism risk genes, but hundreds more have been linked to the condition, meaning the current map represents only a fraction of the total biological picture. “In this study, we examined a small number of genes and mutations in depth using stem cells, neurons and brain organoids,” Krogan said. “We have now built a pipeline that allows us to apply the same approach more systematically and at a larger scale. Our next goal is to identify which autism-associated mutations and biological pathways are most suitable for therapeutic development.”
Before new therapies can be developed, these molecular interactions must be observed in broader behavioral contexts. “While the molecular and mechanistic evidence is very compelling and is likely to be highly relevant to complex ASD etiology, I would like to see this tested in a mammalian developmental model where social and ASD-relevant behaviors can be examined alongside learning and cognitive impairments,” Bradley said. “This would allow more direct tests of causality for the FOXP1-FOXP4 interaction and how these molecular changes ultimately translate into social behavior.”
Additionally, artificial intelligence predictions of protein structures are estimates and sometimes miss the nuance of how proteins bend and fold in a living organism. Beyond refining these models, future research could expand this network and test additional drug candidates that might stabilize these weakened protein connections. The researchers believe the principles established in this study could eventually stretch to entirely different fields of medicine.
“The concept of biological convergence may extend beyond autism,” Krogan pointed out. “We are applying these tools to other neuropsychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive disorder, to look for shared pathways. We are also seeing overlap between some genes and proteins implicated in autism and those studied in cancer.”
“Because drugs already exist for certain cancer-related targets, there may be opportunities to investigate whether some of those compounds could be repurposed for neurological or psychiatric conditions,” he continued. “That possibility is still at an early stage, but it opens an unexpected avenue for collaboration and therapeutic research.”
Ultimately, the research team views this extensive protein map as a foundational resource for the scientific community, moving the field past simple catalogs of genetic risks.
“This is an important step between identifying a genetic change and developing a potential treatment,” Krogan concluded. “It is not the final step, and new therapies will still require years of research and testing. That said, our study provides a clearer biological framework for identifying therapeutic opportunities that were not apparent before.”
The study, “Autism mutations rewire protein interaction networks to drive neurodevelopmental pathology,” was authored by Belinda Wang, Rasika Vartak, Kelsey M. Hennick, Yefim Zaltsman, Zun Zar Chi Naing, Benjamin J. Polacco, Ali Bashir, Manon Eckhardt, Mehdi Bouhaddou, Jiewei Xu, Nawei Sun, Micaela C. Lasser, Yuan Zhou, Justin McKetney, Keelan Z. Guiley, Pawel Gniewek, Una Chan, Naufa Amirani, Owen Griffiths, Nishant Chadha, Reshmi Tognatta, Merve Cakir, Martin Gordon, Prachi Khare, Sam Drake, Vanessa Drury, David F. Burke, Silvano Gonzalez, Sahar Alkhairy, Reuben Thomas, Stephanie Lam, Montana Morris, Ethel Bader, Mélanie Dos Santos, Anastassia V. Komarova, Maxwell Bennett, Craig Ennis, Octavio Castillo, Yvonne Lim, Robert Martin, Meghan Seyler, Tierney Baum, Rebecca Krasnoff, George Wang, Sagnik Middya, Sheng Wang, Presley Pham, Juan Arbelaez, Dexter Pratt, Sofia Bali, Shivali Chag, Julia A. Kaye, Nadir Mahmood, Lee Spraggon, Thomas Rolland, Shawn Hervey-Jumper, James S. Fraser, Thomas Bourgeron, Steven Finkbeiner, Caroline Demeret, Danielle L. Swaney, Sourav Bandyopadhyay, Trey Ideker, Pedro Beltrao, Helen Rankin Willsey, Ruth Hüttenhain, Kirsten Obernier, Tomasz J. Nowakowski, Matthew W. State, A. Jeremy Willsey, and Nevan J. Krogan.
