Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane | Brigid Delaney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:09 UTC
00:00:09 KST

Think of your online life as a garden. At first it’s just a few seeds here or there – a Facebook profile where you created entire albums from a night at the pub, or maybe a Tumblr or a Myspace page listing your favourite bands. It is fun – something just for you and your friends to enjoy.
Then the garden grows. You get an Instagram account and document moments from each day on Stories, use LinkedIn for networking and sharing career triumphs, and check your X/Twitter hyper-vigilantly in case you wrote something that just got you cancelled.
Your online garden grows more sprawling and complex; now it’s no longer just a fun project for yourself on weekends and weeknights. As it grows, you start to view it through the eyes of others.
How will this garden be seen? Will people like it? What can I plant in this garden that will make more people like it?
A few more years pass. And now, instead of working on the garden here and there, you’re in there all the time. You have discovered if your garden is really enticing, you can make money off it. You want – then need – big numbers coming in there. You look at other people’s gardens all the time and you get jealous. They have better gardens.
When you’re not in your garden, you’re still somehow tending to it – looking at the number of people coming in, and comparing them with what it used to be, and being worried that maybe you didn’t plant the right things. But people will tell you if you’re doing it wrong. They’ll spray paint all over the garden walls how much your garden sucks, how you’re a loser, how ugly it all is.
And with all this activity going on you hardly notice how, over time, the world outside your garden has shrunk, until soon there is no outside world. The garden is your home now.
When this current moment ends and a more enlightened time kicks in, descendants looking back will see that millions (or is it billions?) of us have spent the last 10 years or more migrating our lives and identities, and our political, communal and social selves, to a digital realm that has sent many of us insane.
The (digital) signal that we are living a better life has been imbued with more energy and importance than living a better life itself.
Those descendants will see what we can’t really see now – a massive serf culture has emerged, where people have become servants to these gardens.
They’ll see how truly unfree so many of us are – allowing the rich, real, tactile world to recede, while the digital gardens have sprawled to take up all our time and energy (the average user spends about 2 hours and 39 minutes a day on social media.)
And it will become apparent that the real elite won’t be the people with the most popular digital gardens. They’ll be the people who never had gardens. Or people who had small private gardens, where they only let a few friends in.
Brand strategists and trend forecasters are saying that, in 2026, the true measure of status is privacy and a low or no digital footprint.
This is a different way of living off-grid.
You experience a rich and interesting life in the real world and don’t feel the need to post about it.
Your sense of self worth is not linked to how many people see that you’ve been somewhere, hung out with someone or worn something.
Your income, status and financial security is not dependent on your social media account.
Your attention span has not been corrupted or shortened by chronic social media consumption and AI use – and this gives you almost superhuman powers such as the ability to read long, difficult novels, think critically, and retain information in your head.
Your emotional stability is not dependent on how your content is performing.
You have not internalised the digital panopticon where everything you do is with an eye to how it is perceived.
You have a healthy social life in the real world, meaning you have less time or inclination to post.
Brand strategist Eugene Healey in his Substack wrote a recent series on “post-luxury status symbols” and said “the greatest privilege is to be chronically offline” and “in this culture of overexposure – it’s only natural that it becomes desirable to opt out”.
The ultimate flex is not needing social media, walking away from your digital garden and back into your real life.

War Bros Didn’t Always Rule Silicon Valley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

In September 2015, the Founders Fund hosted a retreat at an eco-resort in British Columbia. Most of the attendees were VCs and people from the companies the firm was backing, but they also invited a few outsiders, including computer pioneer Alan Kay, writer Neal Stephenson, and me.
One morning at breakfast I was sitting across from Kay at a long table. The man who conceived the Dynabook—basically the modern computer that we all use—was expounding on his exploits when Founders Fund leader Peter Thiel plopped down next to him. As Kay, in full raconteur mode, spun stories of optimizing the mouse and advising Steve Jobs, Thiel listened with increasingly visible incredulity. Finally, he couldn’t take it. “Who ARE you?” he demanded of Kay.
The mustachioed legend was stunned. He began stumbling out his bona fides, but quickly realized that for someone unacquainted with his résumé, it would have sounded ridiculously overblown. It was like asking Einstein or Mick Jagger to explain themselves. Kay stopped mid-sentence and sighed. “I’m just an old has-been,” he said and went back to his breakfast. Two worlds had collided, and failed to connect.
I thought back to that moment a couple of weeks ago while reading an op-ed in The New York Times headlined “Silicon Valley Was Right From the Start,” by Sharon Weinberger. The essay claimed that the portrait often painted of the Valley as driven by the counterculture and a desire to make the world better was a sham. Today’s bare-knuckled approach to accumulating massive wealth, kowtowing to an authoritarian leader, and embracing lethal military technology simply exposes the industry for what it always was. (Weinberger’s essay was promoting her new book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War.)
“Silicon Valley’s values haven’t changed, just its customers,” she wrote, calling the industry’s current love affair with military tech “less a story of political conversion than of market adaptation.” In that reading, all that hippie stuff about free expression and democratization during the 1980s PC revolution and the 1990s Internet boom was a mirage, an opportunistic feint by Big Tech to push its wares and garner the loot.
I disagree. The story as I see it is that beginning in the late 1970s, a new generation of technologists, identifying with the counterculture, operated with a set of values that unleashed innovation and ironically set the stage for the industry’s current wealth. Yes, that movement carried a torch from the field’s defense industry roots. But even as DOD funding kept fueling innovations (Darpa grants provided dough for the GUI, the internet, and Google Search), that new generation was characterized by idealism, a hackerish love of building things, and disdain for conventional practices.
That mindset changed not only the course of the computer industry, but the culture of American business. (Before Apple Computer, a CEO wouldn’t dare come to work in anything but a suit.) Denying the existence of that idealism is not only inaccurate, but it conveniently lets the new generation of defense contractors off the hook for their pivot toward deadly materiel.
When I shared my views with Weinberger, she acknowledged that I’d probably studied tech culture more than she had from her perch in Washington, DC. Still, she gamely defended her op-ed. “We’re all products of what we grow up in,” she says. “If you were growing up in the peace-dividend era, with defense tech jobs disappearing, the money from defense was less important, and you start to have different values.”
By that standard, the market shift from missile control modules to Macintoshes was driven not by values but by greed. Likewise, she says, the recent return to high-tech weaponry doesn’t represent a philosophical repositioning but a fortuitous opportunity to sell to a Pentagon eager to exploit the Valley’s innovations. “It's not like everybody in the workforce in Silicon Valley woke up and went, like, ‘Defense is cool,’” says Weinberger. That impulse to go where the money is, she argues, is the defining ethos of Silicon Valley. “Your prime directive is for your company to succeed,” she says. “Why didn't Apple work with the military? Because they didn't need to. They had the consumer marketplace.”
Actually, Apple and its cohorts invented the consumer marketplace for computers. And the shoulders that Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, and others stood on were not those of pocket-protector-wearing nerds clocking into jobs at Lockheed, but young and freaky computer scientists. My friend John Markoff’s book What the Dormouse Said is all about how the counterculture set the tone for the Valley during its tremendous growth years. When we spoke this week, Markoff noted that the Valley’s transition point from a defense-oriented industry to one shaped by counterculture values rose from three pivotal computer labs—AI pioneer John McCarthy’s Stanford lab, the Stanford Research Institute, which hosted Douglas Engelbart’s groundbreaking GUI innovations; and Kay’s Xerox PARC, which essentially set the foundation for the computers that we all use today.
These influential institutions were hippie havens. In fact, says Markoff, many of the researchers in those labs worked there in order to get draft deferments to avoid the Vietnam War. “Money was not the motivating factor for these people,” he says. “The Valley’s entrepreneurial culture emerged from a fusion of the counterculture hackers and engineers who believed that technology would change the world, and the more traditional semiconductor culture, which quickly escaped its military roots.”
While those labs were thriving, a ragtag group of engineers met at the Homebrew Computer Club, hosted by a political radical named Lee Felsenstein. That was the bunch that invented the personal computer industry, notably Apple. When I first became exposed to the computer world in the early 1980s, the countercultural nature of the enterprise blew my mind, and drew me into covering that world full-time. I saw for myself how, working within the infrastructure of big business, techno-idealists like the early Macintosh team built the products of their dreams.
No, the Valley did not turn from defense to consumer products because that’s where the money was. Well into the ’80s and ’90s, Apple in particular had to fight the image that their products were like toys, because they eschewed the macho industrial vibe of previous machines in favor of a friendlier look and feel. It took decades for the company to significantly break into the corporate market. (It’s ironic that the current War Bros that Weinberger writes about in her book are obsessed with masculinity.) Google was founded by iconoclasts who thumbed their noses at Wall Street even as their company pursued its IPO.
The most nuanced study of the relationship between the Valley’s military past and the counterculturists who built the modern industry is historian Margaret O’Mara’s book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America. When I spoke to her this week, she agreed with me that the Valley's counterculture shift wasn’t a mercenary pivot but a genuine movement toward making the world better. The market’s move from defense tech to consumer, she says, was a reflection of a generational political shift. In the presidential elections of 1980 and 1984, the Valley voted decisively for Reagan. But as the Valley increasingly tilted toward the counterculture, that all changed, and for many recent cycles those tech-heavy zip codes have been tattooed in deep blue hues. While Trump-affiliated War Bros are currently getting attention, they represent only a small cohort of self-interested multibillionaires. Essentially, they’ve hijacked the values of the Valley.
“I feel like the wealth and the concentration of power has warped everything so profoundly,” says O’Mara. “When you’re in a bubble, whether you’re a president or a billionaire, you have a very hard time understanding how the rest of the world is receiving you.”
I’m sure that the War Bros themselves believe they are acting out of patriotism—though at least some of them have fetishized cool war movies and shoot-’em-up computer games to the point where they get a kick out of making products with spectacular kill functions. But for the past 40 years or so, Silicon Valley typically wanted nothing to do with killing, even though there was always money to be tapped from the Pentagon budget. Ignoring that history or, worse, denying it, takes the War Bros off the hook.
It’s too bad that Peter Thiel didn’t bother to understand what made Alan Kay tick or even know who he was. Thiel himself is a beneficiary of Kay’s idealism, as well as the ethos of countless hackers and founders. They strived for something more lofty than a Valley of Death. Don’t pretend otherwise.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

These are the first feathers ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

These are the first feathers ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop
The plumage may help explain why only some birds survived dino doomsday
Exquisitely preserved feathers, the first ever found in fossilized dinosaur poop, are providing a peek into how some ancient birds lived — and possibly went extinct.
Dense bristles suggest some of the feathers could repel water, possibly as well as those of modern pelicans, researchers report September 10 in Current Biology. And their central shafts are filled with air pockets, a trait that in modern birds keeps plumage lightweight yet stiff enough for flight. “That’s something we’re seeing for the first time in the Age of the Dinosaurs,” says vertebrate paleontologist Jingmai O’Connor of the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago.
The find also offers a clue that might explain why, among birds, there were winners and losers in the mass extinction that ended the dinosaurs’ reign about 66 million years ago. The ancestors of modern birds survived the asteroid-triggered event while many other types of birds, including the group these feathers came from, died out.
One of O’Connor’s colleagues unearthed the fossilized dung, or coprolite, in 2016 in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. If it weren’t for a “lucky break” on the coprolite’s surface that put one feather on full display, her team might never have known it had feathers inside, O’Connor says.
The scientists used micro-CT scans to 3-D map the coprolite’s inner contents. Leg bones and fish scales suggest the bird was aquatic — a member of a group called hesperonithiforms — and that it had eaten shortly before its demise. And while some of the feathers resembled those of modern birds, others were more primitive and stringy, which could have made it difficult for the bird to maintain body heat.
Poor insulation might explain why hesperonithiforms and their close kin didn’t survive the deep chill that followed the asteroid impact, O’Connor says. But researchers need more feathers from various bird species during that time period to test the hypothesis. And fossilized feathers are incredibly rare.
Now that it’s clear poop can be an excellent guardian of plumage, O’Connor says, “people should start looking.”

MOSCOW – Russia said on Sept 25 it had arrested a respected political scientist – who has commented extensively about recent elections – on drug charges that carry up to 20 years in prison.
Alexander Kynev, 51, is a well-known commentator on Russian domestic politics, studying Moscow’s political system for years.
He has remained in Russia during the war against Ukraine, which has seen tens of thousands of others go into exile, despite being critical of the political system built by the Kremlin and of the war.
Since the conflict began in 2022, Moscow has increased repression and censorship to levels comparable with those of the late Soviet period.
Russia state media said a Moscow court had ordered Kynev’s arrest, on accusations that he illegally sold and distributed drugs – a charge that carries between 10 and 20 years in prison.
His arrest was made public the day the authorities said the final results of the national parliamentary elections showed that Putin’s United Russia party had increased its supermajority in the Duma, the assembly’s lower chamber.
In recent days, Kynev had published social media posts commentating on voting procedures in the tightly controlled parliamentary polls, saying he had conducted “intensive monitoring”.
In February, he was designated a “foreign agent” – a tag with Stalin-era connotations that the authorities use against Kremlin critics.
Alexei Venediktov – a media guru who remained in Russia – said on social media that Kynev, now in custody, was not admitting any guilt.
Fellow political scientist Konstantin Kalachev defended Kynev.
“I can associate him with anything but this,” he said on Telegram of the drugs charges.

Mariupol defender, 22, describes his captivity in letters
Mark Mykhailov, a 22-year-old Mariupol defender, has been held captive in Russia for four years after being captured at the Azovstal steel plant. His family and friends can communicate with him only through letters. In one of them, Mark sent a poem to his mother.
Source: Mark's friend Zlata in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life)
Details: Zlata also shared the letters Mark has sent from captivity.
"I have known Mark since school. We were in the same class and also lived in the same block in Mariupol. He always brought a smile to people's faces near the drama theatre, performing card tricks – he was fascinated by them. He also loved playing football," the young woman recalled.
On 24 February 2022, 18-year-old Mark went to defend his native Mariupol, The Bridge Media reports. In April, he suffered a shrapnel wound to his neck during the fighting, as well as other injuries and concussion. A month later, after the defence of Mariupol, Mark was taken prisoner.
His loved ones managed to establish correspondence with him only four years later, in April 2026. At the time, he said he weighed just 54 kg. His family does not know his current weight.
His health has deteriorated significantly during his time in Russian captivity. Mark has been diagnosed with tuberculosis and damage to both lungs requiring urgent treatment.
On 18 March 2026, a Russian court sentenced Mark to five and a half years in prison on charges of participating in a "terrorist organisation". This is how the Russian side classifies his affiliation with the Azov Brigade.
In one of his letters, Mark described being transferred from Volgograd. On 11 September 2026, he was taken away for transfer. He later ended up in Izhevsk. Before the journey, Mark tried to take care of the most important thing – making sure his loved ones received word from him.
"Having written a letter to my mum and my friend Zlata, I was left alone with my thoughts," Mark said.
The young man said he is glad to have the opportunity to communicate, at least through correspondence, which had not been possible before.
"Reading the letters from my friends and loved ones, I realise that ordinary life is going on, with its intrigues, quarrels and life as usual. I reread a letter from my friend and realised how much he has grown up," Mark wrote.
In his letters, the young man reflects on his life after 2022.
Quote from Mark: "Reading these stories, you immediately begin to live in your mind the life that disappeared in 2022… You take your mind off things for a while, and then you become sad. That is why I try not to reread the letters.
Sitting in this place, I've begun to realise how I simply wasted my time on unnecessary things and people I did not need. Everything is now in the past, the present is here, and the future – you can try to grasp it with your hands, but if the circumstances are stronger, you can end up in trouble."
Details: In another message, the young man dreamed about how he would spend his day if he were free.
"Without bars, with a thermos and the person I love, it would make for a wonderful weekend," Mark wrote.
He also wrote a letter to his mother, urging her not to grieve for him and to stay strong. The young man dedicated a poem to her.
Background: Russia previously sentenced three teenagers from Melitopol for "terrorism". The three young men from temporarily occupied Melitopol, who were accused of "terrorism", received harsh sentences in fabricated cases. They were 16-17 years old when they were detained.

In parcels from the United States, customs officers discovered Apple devices worth approximately UAH 1 million
Kyiv • UNN
Customs officers discovered 35 undeclared Apple devices in parcels from the United States. Their total value is approximately UAH 1 million.
At a customs post in Lviv, customs officers discovered undeclared goods worth approximately one million hryvnias in international parcels. The State Customs Service of Ukraine reports this, according to UNN.
Details
On September 24, 2026, at the Lviv-Postal customs post, customs officers discovered 35 Apple devices in international postal shipments from the United States addressed to Ukrainian citizens that had not been listed in the customs declarations. The violation was uncovered through an analysis of preliminary information on international postal shipments conducted by employees of the Coordination and Monitoring Customs Office
During the customs inspection, it was established that the information stated in the declarations did not correspond to the actual contents of the parcels.
The discovered equipment included 17 iPad tablets, 9 iPad Airs, 1 iPad mini, 2 iPad Pros, 5 MacBook Pro laptops and 1 MacBook Air. The total value of the equipment is approximately UAH 1 million. These actions show signs of a violation of customs rules предусмотреного by Part 1 of Article 473 of the Customs Code of Ukraine
Employees of the Coordination and Monitoring Customs Office are currently taking measures to document the violations that were discovered.

Kyiv customs officers seized rare bronze artifacts dating from the time of Kyivan Rus from a parcel. The items in question are seven pieces of bladed weapons and their decoration dating from the 2nd–12th centuries AD.

US to reveal details on China trade talks on Monday
The United States is expected to release details on the outcome of trade negotiations with China on Monday, according to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
"We're in a managed trade situation ... we've had progress, and we will release on Monday, I think, a lot more details about what we've accomplished over the past few weeks in negotiating with the Chinese," he told CNBC on Friday.
Greer also said that the US has agreed with China to exempt some key goods from trade disputes.
He added that the US would export agricultural products and medical devices, and import consumer goods and other "non-sensitive" items from China.

US President Donald Trump on Thursday rolled out the red carpet for China's Xi Jinping on the Chinese president's first state visit to Washington in over a decade.

A few hundred protesters gathered near the White House to rally against Xi Jinping's visit to the US.
Protesters highlighted a number of issues, from calls for religious freedom and autonomy in Tibet, Hong Kong and the Xinjiang region to demands that China refrain from interfering in Taiwan.
Protesters gathered in Lafayette Park, north of the White House, while other groups gathered outside the Chinese embassy. Pro-Xi rallies were also held in Washington.

US President Donald Trump continued to heap praise on his guest, Chinese President Xi Jinping, during a White House state dinner on Thursday.
"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."

Names such as Nvidia's Jensen Huang, former Apple CEO Tim Cook, and once again Musk, were hosted by the Chinese president at a state dinner in the Great Hall of the People.
But Chinese CEOs are conspicuously missing on the guest list this evening in Washington as bringing Chinese firms to the US may raise more questions than it answers, experts said.
The Associated Press reported that US and Chinese planners did discuss including notable Chinese companies, but that one obstacle was that the US side was slow to suggest protocols and what roles the Chinese CEOs would have in the state visit.
Just like on Thursday, despite the star-studded business attendance, few major deals were announced during Trump's visit to China.

ORIGIN and Anduril sign memorandum on counter-drone air defence solutions for NATO’s eastern flank during LIAA trade mission to the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:58:07 UTC
23:58:07 KST

US defence technology company Anduril, which develops autonomous systems and command-and-control software, and defence technology company ORIGIN, which develops autonomous unmanned aircraft systems, have agreed to assess the integration of their technologies to strengthen deterrence on NATO’s eastern flank. Under the memorandum of understanding, the companies will explore integrating Anduril’s Lattice software platform with ORIGIN’s autonomous BLAZE interceptor drone as part of a layered counter-drone air defence solution for Latvia. The memorandum was signed during the Latvian business trade mission organised by LIAA as part of President Edgars Rinkēvičs’ official visit to the United States.
Lattice is Anduril’s software platform, which brings data from different sensors and unmanned systems into a single environment. It gives operators a real-time view of the battlefield and enables them to assign tasks to connected sensors, vehicles and other assets. Under the memorandum, ORIGIN and Anduril will assess how BLAZE, together with deployed radars and other sensors, could be integrated into this environment. They will also develop a concept of operations for counter-drone missions.
The companies have agreed to conduct joint technology testing, demonstrations and validation in Latvia. They will develop a concept of operations, enable data exchange and assess the solution’s effectiveness in different counter-drone scenarios. This cooperation could allow interceptor drones to operate as part of broader defence infrastructure rather than as standalone systems. As threats become increasingly coordinated, integration within a common command-and-control environment is becoming essential to comprehensive air defence.
Mārtiņš Mārenis, Chief Commercial Officer at ORIGIN, said: “We want to work with industry leaders and innovators to develop counter-drone systems that make a real contribution to strengthening the defence capabilities of NATO Allies. Integrating BLAZE with Anduril’s Lattice platform would allow our interceptor drones to operate within a unified system, giving allied forces better situational awareness and a faster response to evolving drone threats. These are precisely the capabilities that modern air defence and countries on NATO’s eastern flank need to protect their airspace effectively.”
The memorandum was signed during the LIAA-organised Latvian business trade mission to the United States, which is taking place alongside the President of Latvia’s official visit. The mission runs until 27 September and covers New York, Los Angeles and San Diego. It brings together representatives of companies and organisations across four sectoral tracks, including defence and dual-use technologies.
“The memorandum of understanding between ORIGIN and Anduril is a significant outcome of this trade mission. ORIGIN came to the US with defence technology developed in Latvia and a concrete proposal for cooperation, while the signing of the memorandum demonstrates Anduril’s interest in developing that cooperation. Latvian companies aim to carry out joint projects with US partners, secure orders and attract investment. LIAA will continue to help advance this cooperation,” said Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.

Cheetah cubs survive powerful storms, mother's illness at zoo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Cheetah cubs survive powerful storms, mother's illness at Prague Zoo, but curator warns "it's still a long run"
Five cheetah cubs had to survive a weather scare and the illness of their mother after their birth at the Prague Zoo. But they are doing well now, the zoo said on Friday.
The zoo said the quintuplets — four males and one female — that were born on June 18 had faced a tough time from the start.
Their mother, Daenerys, opted to give birth in an outdoor enclosure with a period of strong storms hitting Prague soon after.
Despite her inexperience, Daenerys took "exemplary" good care of her first cubs under such weather conditions, the zoo said.
Daenerys protected the five from torrential rains, licking water from their fluffy fur to keep them dry, curator Pavel Brandl said.
"Thanks to the mother's attentiveness, all five cubs survived the heavy downpours," the zoo wrote in a statement. "Soaking and subsequent pneumonia — along with predation — are common causes of mortality in cheetah cubs in the wild. It appears, however, that the mother dried her young by licking water from their fluffy coats with a characteristic dorsal mantle."
To make things worse, Daenerys suffered from an intestinal infection in August.
But despite all odds, the five looked lively and healthy on Friday.
"At this moment, everything seems fine, but it's still a long run," Brandl said. He said it might take a year before it's clear they will survive the crucial period after their birth.
"The mother of the cubs continues to surprise us," Brandl said after the cubs were born. "She arrived from France several years ago in poor physical and mental condition, and at the time, I was convinced we would never see offspring from this female."
Scientists say every cub is critical to saving the species, which is threatened with extinction.
Cheetahs, the fastest land animals in the world, can reach maximum speeds of between 70 and 75 mph. It's estimated that fewer than 7,000 of them remain in the wild.
Since 2020, the number of cheetahs in European zoos has declined by 25%, according to the zoo.
"Every successfully reared cub is therefore both an achievement and a source of hope," the zoo said.
Last October, 11 cheetah cubs were rescued from illegal trade in Somaliland in what a conservationist described as "one of the largest confiscations of the species."

Dutch opposition party votes to join European Socialist family
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:55:32 UTC
23:55:32 KST

Dutch GroenLinks party leader Jesse Klaver attends the launch of the name "Progressief Nederland" for an upcoming merger of GroenLinks and PvdA parties, at the Sugar Factory in Halfweg on March 26, 2026. | Remko de Waal/ANP/AFP via Getty Images
The largest opposition party in the Netherlands has chosen to join the European Socialists rather than the Greens in an internal vote, the results of which were announced Friday.
Some 65% of votes cast by members of Progressive Netherlands (PRO), which was formed earlier this year when the Dutch GreenLeft (GroenLinks) and Labour (PvdA) parties merged, backed joining the Party of European Socialists instead of the European Green Party.
Before voting began, an advisory committee to the party recommended joining the PES, arguing that membership would give the party greater influence at the European level.
Advertisement
“There are only three European political families represented at all three levels [of the EU],” the advisory committee wrote in a report, adding that the PES has “prime ministers, the President of the European Council, European Commissioners, and leaders of national parties.”
“The Greens … have fewer ministers, no members of the European Commission, and no heads of government; consequently, their preliminary consultations carry less weight,” the report went on.
PRO leader Jesse Klaver joined a PES meeting ahead of the European Council summit in June, alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
What about the MEPs?
European political parties and political groups in the European Parliament are closely linked, but they are not the same thing.
A PRO spokesperson told POLITICO that the party’s eight MEPs are likely to remain in their current parliamentary groups: four in the Socialists and Democrats and four in the Greens/European Free Alliance.
The spokesperson said PRO would likely review the arrangement ahead of the next European Parliament election in 2029.
Advertisement
The choice of European party will, however, have implications for the allocation of EU funding.
Most EU cash for European political parties is distributed according to their share of MEPs. Under the rules, the PES could count all eight PRO MEPs toward its funding share, even if four remain in the Greens.
The Dutch party told POLITICO one option would be for the four MEPs from the former GroenLinks side to technically leave PRO, allowing them to be counted separately under the funding rules.

'Moldova is the best performer in my class': EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:54:29 UTC
23:54:29 KST

'Moldova is the best performer in my class': EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
The EU has gone through seven waves of enlargement since 1973, but there has not been one since Croatia joined in 2013. Indeed, there are not likely to be any new members in the club before 2028 – some 15 years after Croatia entered. But 2026 undeniably has momentum, and is on track to be a record year in terms of opening and closing new chapters for existing applicants. That is why our guest, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, sees this as "the year of the enlargement."
"Montenegro, which is really the frontrunner, could finish technical negotiations at the end of the year, and then become a member in 2028," Kos says. "Albania is well on the way. Moldova is delivering better and better and, of course, also Ukraine. So these are the four frontrunners. But when we say that this is the year of the enlargement, I mean that in the nine months of this year, we have opened and closed more chapters than in any previous year in the last 25 years."
But there's a distinction between the frontrunner and the best student. Kos says that Moldova "is the best performer in my class," taking into account that it started the process much later than applicant countries in the Balkans.
Speaking of the Balkans, Kos admits that there is uneven implementation of reforms, which could lead to €330 million in EU funding shifting away from the weakest performers.
"We will see how much money we will reallocate," Kos says. "Montenegro, for instance, has a 91 percent implementation rate of reforms to date. But then we also have Bosnia and Herzegovina with a zero (rate), because their politicians are not able to ratify two important agreements which would enable us to pay the money," Kos explains. "You know, our European Union is not a charity. So in order to be able to help their economies and societies to develop, they have to deliver the reforms, and we only give the money if they are doing this."
We turn to Serbia, which has been an EU candidate since 2012, but which has had a turbulent relationship with Brussels. According to Kos, "the trust between EU member states and Serbia was broken even more with the glorification of the war criminal Ratko Mladic at his funeral, which is really unacceptable. And that's also why I cancelled my planned mission to Serbia. We can have different opinions on how fast a country should make reforms. But there is no space for the glorification of a war criminal, or for denying the genocide in Srebrenica. We expect all the EU candidates, especially those from the Western Balkans, to walk the way of reconciliation. But sometimes I have the feeling that, instead of healing the wounds of the past, leaders are rubbing salt into those wounds."
Of course, enlargement is not only about the EU's closest neighbours. While Georgia's EU bid has stalled, Armenia is increasingly eyeing EU membership as an attractive option – even though it has not formally applied.
"We are helping Armenia, especially now when Russia stopped importing many Armenian products. So we are helping Armenia to redirect its exports to the European Union. We are also in the process of visa liberalisation. This means that Armenians would be able to travel to the EU without a visa. So now they have to align a lot of legislation, and they are doing great work. I'm full of admiration for the people of Armenia. It is not easy but, with the result of the last parliamentary elections, they have clearly shown that they want to be on the European path."

Everyone's Still Talking About Climate Change, Actually
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:54:15 UTC
23:54:15 KST

For a brief moment last year, it seemed like the anti-climate atmosphere created by the Trump Administration might kill New York Climate Week. Ahead of the September gathering, business executives and advocates waffled. Was the U.S. still the place to get together to talk about climate? Would going put a target on their back?
This year, it felt almost as though those questions disappeared. Leaders from the world’s biggest companies hopped between panels, engaging in serious discussions about AI-driven electricity demand, geopolitical disruptions to energy markets, and the state of energy and climate policy. Protesters hit the street—as well as disrupting a panel I moderated—to point out that things were moving too slowly. Even Trump Administration officials showed up at some sessions (though they may have framed their participation around the concurrent United Nations General Assembly not Climate Week).
Take a step back from the chaotic mix of roundtables and dinners, panels and meetings, and it’s clear that the climate agenda, broadly construed, has persisted. There’s no question that anticipated Democratic victories in the fast-approaching U.S. midterm elections have created a sense that much of the administration’s barking will remain just that. But there’s perhaps an even simpler explanation for the continued engagement: the implications of climate change and the related energy issues have only become more important for companies and the economy.
The energy-market disruption that has resulted from the war in Iran featured prominently this week. So did the political backlash to data centers, the related issues of higher power prices. And the role of new energy technologies in addressing the problem came up early and often in discussions. On top of this, the effects of climate change—storms, heat waves, and fires—have begun to extract real economic damage that even the most resilient firms can no longer ignore.
“People are now looking at the things that cause volatility, and they’re putting it together,” Sarah Kapnick, head of climate advisory at JPMorgan, told me on a Climate Week panel. “They’re putting geopolitics together with sustainability, climate, and AI.”
Still, the apparent vitality of New York Climate Week comes with caveats. I shared my sense that New York Climate Week has rebounded with a European climate leader, who pointed out that American participation may be strong but the presence of leaders from outside the U.S. has diminished somewhat, particularly from Europe. Simply put, many Europeans don’t want to travel here, instead putting their efforts into London Climate Action Week and other gatherings across the Atlantic.
The climate conversation has also survived in part by shedding some of its old vocabulary. Climate action, net zero, and emissions were mostly out. Energy security, competitiveness, and affordability were in. That may represent a retreat from the sweeping ambition of earlier Climate Weeks. But it also reflects a deeper reality: even when companies stop using the language of climate action, they cannot escape the problems rising emissions have created.
To most of those I discussed the topic with, it remains an open question whether that new framing is a good or bad thing. Emissions reduction paired with economic growth should be celebrated even if climate isn’t mentioned. At the same time, a conversation that avoids getting to the heart of the matter doesn’t feel all that sustainable. For the past several decades we’ve been holding a ticking time bomb, waiting for the effect of climate change to hit. Now, how society responds to the unfolding crisis—embracing adaptation, pushing back against the sources of emissions, or simply turning to populist backlash—may be the new climate time bomb.

Concerns over ‘missing’ British explorer Ranulph Fiennes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:53:00 UTC
23:53:00 KST

Concerns over ‘missing’ British explorer Ranulph Fiennes
LONDON – Mystery has engulfed the fate of legendary British adventurer Ranulph Fiennes, after relatives and friends went public claiming he was missing and his wife was isolating him – with one reportedly even asking King Charles for help.
Fiennes, the first person to cross the Earth pole to pole in the early 1980s, was last seen publicly nearly two years ago, months after opening up about a Parkinson’s diagnosis he received years earlier.
Last week, the Daily Telegraph reported the 82-year-old had been placed in a succession of care homes by his wife, Louise Millington-Cotes, who has allegedly put strict conditions on his care.
In a follow-up on Sept 25 in its months-long probe, the newspaper said a care sector watchdog in Wales had concluded he was “unlawfully deprived of his liberty” when housed at a facility there earlier in 2026.
Meanwhile, Fiennes’s stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, this week launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to “locate and safeguard” him.
“You may have recently heard the deeply concerning news: Sir Ranulph Fiennes is missing,” he wrote online, adding he had “tried multiple avenues to find” him.
Calling Fiennes “a national treasure”, he described his stepfather as “a man of immense heart, kindness, and selflessness”.
Swiss-based ex-explorer and Fiennes collaborator Michael Kobold has joined the campaign to “help lift the veil of secrecy” around his whereabouts.
“My friend of almost 30 years has gone missing and nobody besides a tiny handful of individuals seems to want to do anything to change this disgraceful status quo,” he wrote in a lengthy blogpost in September.
‘Not well’
Fiennes has long been a towering figure in exploration, acclaimed by the Guinness Book of World Records as the “greatest living explorer”.
His epic 1979-1982 Transglobe Expedition saw him proclaimed the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means.
He later became the first to cross Antarctica completely on foot and also ran seven marathons on seven continents within a week.
Hailing from one of the most storied families in England – which counts actors Joseph and Ralph Fiennes among its extended ranks – he has been friends with King Charles for decades.
His 34-year marriage to first wife Virginia ended with her death in 2004, and he wed Millington-Cotes the following year. The couple have a daughter and stepson.
In his last public appearance – a pre-recorded video played at an October 2024 Royal Geographic Society event – he read from an off-screen script apologising for not being “well enough” to attend, The Telegraph said.
The daily reports Millington-Cotes was granted lasting power of attorney that year and has become his legal guardian, placing Fiennes in care homes in London, Wales and then north-west England.
It claims she has refused to allow some friends to visit, while also insisting any visitors sign non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).
‘King ‘concerned’
Arabella McIntyre-Brown, Fiennes’ former sister-in-law, in 2025 checked herself into the London care home where he was living and made contact.
“He was lucid – personality intact, memory clear,” she told The Telegraph, adding he had stressed he wanted to see his friends.
However, after the visit, Fiennes was moved and later placed in a Welsh home, according to the newspaper.
“It’s absurd,” McIntyre-Brown told the Telegraph.
“It’s like we’d stumbled into a John Le Carre novel.”
The Welsh care-home owner told the paper Millington-Cotes had failed to provide the legally required paperwork designed to protect vulnerable adults, so sought advice from the industry’s regulator.
The Care Inspectorate of Wales responded in January that Fiennes was “being deprived of his liberty unlawfully” without the paperwork, it reported.
The Inspectorate told AFP “it would not be appropriate” to comment.
Meanwhile an old friend of Fiennes, Anton Bowring, claims he had contact with Buckingham Palace in 2025, when a staff member told him “the king was concerned for Fiennes”, the Telegraph said.
Buckingham Palace declined to comment to AFP. Millington-Cotes could not be reached for comment.
“It’s the extraordinary final chapter in a remarkable life,” Bowring told The Telegraph.
“I know he’s still out there, alive. But I’ve grieved for him. I’ve said goodbye.” AFP

The UN Security Council has condemned Houthi attacks targeting Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure that wounded civilians, including women and children.
Council members reiterated their condemnation of attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandab, stressing the need to protect vessels and their crews.
The council demanded that the Houthis “immediately cease their military escalation” and attacks affecting civilians and civilian objects.
Members expressed grave concern over reports of civilian casualties and noted that at least 125,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the beginning of September, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
They warned that further escalation could worsen Yemen’s severe humanitarian situation and called for full, safe, rapid and unhindered humanitarian access.
Council demands Houthis release detainees
The council also demanded the unconditional release of detainees, including 73 UN personnel and staff from NGOs, civil society groups and diplomatic missions.
Members called for cooperation with the Yemeni government to prevent the Houthis from obtaining weapons, technical assistance, training and financing for military activities. They also reminded UN member states of their obligations under the targeted arms embargo.
The council expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and affirmed its inherent right to self-defence under international law.
It also reaffirmed its commitment to Yemen’s unity, sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, stressing that sustainable peace “cannot be achieved through violence, coercion, or the use of force”.
Fighting threatens fragile calm
Council members backed UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg’s efforts to pursue a negotiated, inclusive and Yemeni-led political settlement and urged all parties to engage constructively with UN initiatives.
Saudi Arabia has faced missile and drone attacks attributed to the Houthis in recent days amid escalating regional tensions.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis has also intensified since early July, ending a period of relative calm that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce took effect in April 2022.

UN expands list of companies linked to Israeli settlements
GENEVA – The United Nations human rights office issued a list on Sept 25 adding 61 more companies operating in Israeli West Bank settlements, which the global body considers illegal.
The database is highly sensitive as firms could be targeted for boycotts or divestment to pressure Israel over settler expansion in the territory that is home to more than three million Palestinians.
The database, first released in 2020, now includes 214 firms, mostly from Israel, but also from 10 other countries, including France, Germany, China and the US.
Newly added firms included Israeli pesticides maker ADAMA, part of Chinese-owned Syngenta Group, Israel-based real estate investment holding company Alony Hetz and Spain’s Salvat Logistica.
They joined companies such as travel agency Expedia and home-rental company Airbnb already on the list.
Israel, which views the West Bank as disputed rather than occupied, has previously said the list unfairly vilifies companies working legally.
“This is a distorted mechanism – created by a deeply flawed body with an automatic majority against Israel,” Israel’s diplomatic mission said on Sept 25, alleging that the database was establish to “persecute” the Jewish state.
There has been a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians as outposts proliferate, prompting Britain, France and Canada to block imports from settlements in September.
The UN rights office assessed companies active in a group of sectors, including energy, food, hospitality, transport and agriculture, based on confidential submissions to the UN rights office.
Another 60 or so companies were assessed but not included since they did not meet the UN criteria of involvement in activities that violate the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Examples include supplying demolition equipment to destroy Palestinian buildings, provision of surveillance for settlements and other services like transport that help maintain their existence, according to the UN website.
Other companies, like British-registered online travel company Opodo and Spanish-domiciled online travel agent eDreams, have been dropped from the original list after submitting a reassessment request.
The UN found that there were reasonable grounds to believe they were no longer involved in the activities that previously justified their inclusion.
eDreams said in 2025 that it had withdrawn and would continue to block listings of accommodation in illegal Israeli settlements, saying that some had appeared on its website automatically after owners uploaded them.
Palestinians want the West Bank to be part of a future independent homeland.
But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s nationalist government has largely backed settlers, with building ramped up since the militant Hamas group’s attack on Israel in October 2023 and the ensuing Gaza war.
Travel firm Expedia has previously said that the listings in what it called “disputed areas” were clearly labelled, complied with international laws and sanctions and undergo enhanced due diligence guided by UN standards. REUTERS

AfD, CDU ban new Holocaust 'stumbling stones' in Heidenau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:51:00 UTC
23:51:00 KST

AfD, CDU ban new Holocaust 'stumbling stones' in Heidenau
September 25, 2026
The town of Heidenau, near Dresden, has banned new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) on public streets, with the center-right CDU and the far-right AfD voting together to stop the installation of new memorial plaques bearing the names of Holocaust victims.
The Stolpersteine are comprised of a concrete cube with a metal plaque on top that bears the victim's name. They are often seen in German streets, installed just slightly higher than the surrounding walking surface, often near the houses of people targeted by the Nazi regime.
German artist Gunter Demnig started the project in the early 1990s. While most of the 128,000 such paving stones were installed in Germany, they have also been placed in 30 other countries affected by the Nazi regime, making them the largest decentralized monument in the world.
Creator of Stolpersteine pledges to keep on working
The initiators of the Heidenau ban argue that, while remembering Holocaust victims is an essential task, the placement of stones leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring Holocaust victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead.
Demnig, now 78, has rejected this argument. The artist said that remembrance must be visible where people used to live, and that stumbling stones make history tangible for local young people. At the same time, he said he saw the ban coming due to the outcome of recent state elections in Germany.
"After the electoral successes of the AfD, something like this was completely expected," Demnig was quoted as saying by the DPA news agency. He expressed hope that the Heidenau ban would remain an exception and pledged to "push on now more than ever" with his work.
Demnig also accused the center-right CDU (Christian Democratic Union) of abandoning Christian values. He said the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz "should maybe drop the C" from their acronym "because they have dropped Christianity already."
CDU's support of AfD in Heidenau 'a scandal'
Many others also responded with outrage to the CDU's decision to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion. The move comes with Chancellor Merz already facing a political crisis over his party's poor electoral performance, and raises questions about the political "firewall" against the far right which mainstream political parties in Germany have maintained to keep the AfD out of power.
On Friday, one of the top two leaders of Germany's Green Party, Felix Banaszak, described the move as "a scandal."
Banaszak pointed to the current debate on right-wing extremism and the rise of the AfD, saying that everything must be done "to keep alive the memories of those who were persecuted and killed."
The International Auschwitz Committee also slammed the CDU support to the motion as scandalous.
"This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery," said Christoph Heubner, the organization's executive vice president.

Pope Leo warns that the UN risks turning into a "farce"
Kyiv • UNN
Pope Leo said that the UN and multilateral organizations are experiencing a crisis of effectiveness. He also criticized the disregard for the rule of law.
On Friday, Pope Leo stated that the United Nations and other multilateral organizations are experiencing a crisis, warning in his speech at the Paris headquarters of UNESCO (the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) that international dialogue risks turning into a "farce," UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The first-ever American pope, who is visiting France at a time when a tense session of the UN General Assembly is underway in New York, also criticized world leaders who disregard the rule of law, although he did not name anyone specifically.
"Instead of respecting the law, those in power invoke it when it serves their interests and ignore it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself as a commodity that can be bought or sold," the pontiff said.
The UN and other multilateral organizations are "experiencing a crisis of effectiveness," he said. "Dialogue is perceived as an obstacle to action, rather than as a resource for peace; as a farce, rather than as an opportunity to seek the common good together."
Leo, who became pope in May 2025, earlier that year provoked the displeasure of U.S. President Donald Trump by criticizing the war with Iran.
This year's session of the UN General Assembly, which concludes on Monday, has been accompanied by heated disputes. In his speech on Tuesday, Trump threatened to destroy Iran if it did not agree to terms for ending the war. On Thursday, dozens of delegates left the chamber during a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In 2025, Trump announced that the United States would withdraw from UNESCO.
Leo is making a rapid visit to three French cities, seeking to restore the Church's standing in the country after scandals involving abuse cases that shocked society.

Asian Games | Day 6 roundup: Thai Boonson clocks 0.90s to win men's 100m, Chinese swimmer Zhang secures 7th gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:50:01 CST
23:50:01 KST

by Sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- A new generation of sporting stars took center stage at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday. China's 17-year-old sprint sensation Chen Yujie and Thailand's 20-year-old Puripol Boonson claimed the women's and men's 100m titles, respectively, while 19-year-old swimmer Zhang Zhanshuo capped off an incredible campaign with his seventh gold medal.
Chen led all the way to win the women's 100m title in a Games record of 11.06 seconds, also setting a new U-20 Asian record. Singapore's Shanti Pereira and Bahrain's Edidiong Odiong took silver and bronze in 11.21 and 11.33, respectively. Boonson timed 9.90 to win the men's sprint, a new Games record. Oman runners took silver and bronze. China's Zeng Keli and Xie Zhenye finished sixth and seventh, respectively.
China extended its remarkable dominance in the women's shot put, claiming a 13th consecutive title at the Asian Games. Song Jiayuan threw a season-best 19.40 meters to grab the gold, while teammate Zhang Linru took silver with a mark of 18.14 meters.
"I'm very excited and emotional because I had surgery last year," Song said after her victory. "This time my coach didn't come here with me, so I am very proud and happy to have performed that well on the field."
China missed out on an eighth consecutive women's pole vault title after Niu Chunge, the Asian record holder, took a silver with 4.50m. Japan's Misaki Morota jumped a personal best 4.55m to win the gold medal. In the hammer throw, Uzbekistan's Sukhrob Khodjaev won the title with 74.38m. Meanwhile, on the track, Bahrain's Birhanu Balew brought home gold in the men's 10,000m, clocking a time of 28:27.51.
In swimming, China's Zhang Zhanshuo capped off a remarkable campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asiad, completing a seven-gold haul with a victory in the men's 400m freestyle at the Tokyo Aquatics Center on Friday.
The 19-year-old sensation won seven of the eight events he entered. His individual triumphs included the 800m and 1,500m freestyle, as well as an Asian-record finish in the 200m freestyle. He also propelled China to three relay golds: the men's 4x100m medley, the 4x200m freestyle (in an Asian record of 7:00.17), and the 4x100m freestyle (in another Asian record of 3:10.60).
Zhang became the first swimmer to win seven gold medals at a single edition of the Asian Games. More significantly, his haul equaled the Games record for most gold medals won by an athlete at a single edition, a mark set by DPRK shooter So Gil-san in 1982.
"Of course, I'm very happy to win these seven gold medals, and I will turn them into greater motivation going forward," he said.
Also in the pool, butterfly veteran Zhang Yufei won the women's 50m butterfly, while world champion Qin Haiyang successfully defended his title in the men's 50m breaststroke. Freestyle specialist Li Bingjie staged a brilliant comeback to win the women's 800m freestyle, and the Chinese quartet triumphed in the women's 4x100m medley relay in a Games record 3:54.55 to round out another golden night for the team.
Elsewhere, Wang Kuan-hung of Chinese Taipei secured the men's 200m butterfly title, while Japan's Kodai Nishiono touched first in the men's 200m backstroke, leaving China's Xu Jiayu to settle for bronze.
With the swimming concluded, China firmly established its sheer dominance in the sport, claiming 30 gold medals in a total of 41 events.
Away from the pool, at the weightlifting venue, China's Yang Liuyue claimed two new world records in the snatch and total of the women's 61kg event, hoisting 112kg in the snatch for a gold-medal total of 251kg. In the clean and jerk, silver medalist Pak Jin Hae of the DPR Korea set a new world record with a lift of 139kg, which Yang later matched. Meanwhile, DPRK's Oh Kwang Ok took home the women's 57kg title.
In gymnastics, China added more hardware with Zou Jingyuan winning the men's parallel bars and Tian Hao taking gold in the men's horizontal bar. Qiu Qiyuan also secured a silver in the women's balance beam. Over at the shooting range, Olympic champions Zhang Changhong, Liu Yukun, and Sheng Lihao led China to the men's 50m rifle three positions team title, with Liu also claiming the individual gold. India took the third shooting gold of the day, winning the 10m air pistol mixed team title.
Moreover, China's equestrian team made history by winning the team dressage gold for the first time at the Asian Games. In the men's mountain bike cross-country race, China's Yuan Jinwei staged a brilliant comeback to win in 1:25:15, finishing just three seconds ahead of Japan's Tatsuumi Soejima. In fencing, China won the women's epee team by beating South Korea 45-28, but Hong Kong, China lost to Japan in the men's foil team final.
It was a tale of mixed fortunes for China in team sports. In the women's football quarterfinals, China and Vietnam battled into extra time before Wang Shuang netted a dramatic 109th-minute winner to seal a 1-0 victory. China will advance to face the DPRK in the semifinals, following the latter's 5-1 routing of Chinese Taipei in their quarterfinal clash.
However, on the basketball court, the defending champion Chinese women's team saw their bid for a third straight title dashed after falling to South Korea 85-80 in Thursday's semifinals. Despite dominating the rebounds 52-31 thanks to their height advantage, a scoreless night from three-point range (0-for-13) combined with 18 turnovers left China without enough firepower to close out the win.
In table tennis, China's Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha, and Lin Shidong and Kuai Man, won their respective mixed doubles semifinals Friday at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games to set up an all-Chinese final.
After six days of competition, China led the medal table with 98 gold, 37 silver and 24 bronze medals. Japan was second with 28 gold, 43 silver and 44 bronze medals, followed by South Korea with 13 gold, 17 silver and 34 bronze medals. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Training China's workforce for jobs that barely existed a few years ago
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:49:59 CST
23:49:59 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- A full-size metro carriage has been moved into the National Exhibition and Convention Center in Shanghai, the venue for the 48th WorldSkills Competition -- not for display, but for hands-on competition in rail vehicle technology, one of seven skills making a debut this year.
Competitors in this subject are expected to have the mix of skills required by a modern rail network, including an understanding of high-voltage electrical equipment, braking systems, air conditioning, doors and wheelsets, while diagnosing faults and carrying out maintenance.
Rail vehicle technology is joined by unmanned aerial systems, intelligent security technology, software testing, digital interactive media design, dental prosthetics technology and retail. The seven newcomers, unveiled as 64 competitions got underway in Shanghai this week, span advanced manufacturing, digital industries, healthcare and modern services.
The additions reflect how occupations themselves are changing. The first competition, held in Spain in 1950, focused largely on traditional trades such as construction and manufacturing, while automation, the expansion of the service sector and the rise of the internet later brought new skills onto the competition floor.
"Doing a trade in the 1960s and doing the same trade today are not exactly the same," President of WorldSkills International Francis Hourant told reporters on Tuesday, adding that the competition adjusts its portfolio to stay connected with "the reality of the industry."
China is trying to make its training system move with those changes. In July, the Ministry of Education added 27 programs to the country's vocational education catalogue, targeting areas including the digital economy, low-altitude economy, advanced equipment and emerging services.
The skills behind that shift are already on display at WorldSkills. On Wednesday, pairs of competitors assembled their robots piece by piece. From Thursday, the machines had to prove themselves on the competition floor -- finding their way through maze-like courses, locating objects and completing tasks under the clock.
Zeng Zhiwei, a Chinese coach for autonomous mobile robotics, recalled that earlier versions of the event still involved remote-controlled movement. As LiDAR and autonomous navigation spread, the competition changed too. "The competition follows the industry," he said.
In another hall, competitors in the new software testing event, a key skill in the digital economy, tapped away at their keyboards, searching for bugs and checking whether systems worked as intended. Software testers help ensure products work reliably before they reach users, a role that has grown as software becomes embedded in fields such as transport, finance and education.
Statistics showed that China's digital economy has grown to more than 50 trillion yuan (7.41 trillion U.S. dollars), while the country's digital talent gap remained close to 30 million in 2025.
That gap is already reshaping vocational education. In April, 64 technical colleges in Jiangsu Province added 157 programs, about 42 percent of them related to artificial intelligence. In May, 12 technical colleges in Chongqing announced 23 new programs, among them service robot application and maintenance and intelligent connected vehicle technology.
However, officials still warned of a growing time lag between industrial change and talent development, as training skilled workers can take three to four years, while emerging industries may evolve much faster.
"Technology is changing too fast. If we rush to establish a new program, it may change again very soon," said Zhang Rui, deputy director of the engineering training center at Tianjin University of Technology and Education. "So we start with microprograms."
Rather than enrolling a full cohort, these programs start small, with selected students in experimental classes and pilot training. They allow schools to test new content before deciding whether it is ready to be expanded into a broader program.
Zhang recalled that companies had once turned often to universities for technical expertise. "Now it is the other way around," she said. "We need to send teachers to companies regularly to learn and keep up with new technologies."
At Zhang's university, an industry college works with companies to bring industrial practices into training. Students can work on a smart production-line platform that mirrors an industrial workflow: a customized order placed through an app enters a manufacturing execution system before moving through processes such as material handling, robotic assembly, laser engraving and warehousing.
A similar approach combining industry and education can be found elsewhere. At Jiangxi Software Vocational and Technical University, the campus is integrated with an industrial park, with nearly 100 companies involved in tailored training. Enterprise engineers teach classes, while real commercial projects are brought onto campus.
So far, more than 20 provincial-level regions in China have developed over 300 industry-education-assessment skills networks, with enterprises taking a leading role in training and skills evaluation.
That industry-training link is especially visible in emerging fields such as unmanned aerial systems, where fast-changing commercial applications are creating demand for workers with both hardware and software skills. At the competition in Shanghai, spectators crowd around the arena as competitors piece together drones from roughly 200 components, program them and make final adjustments.
Only after the assembly, programming and testing are complete does the aircraft leave the workbench and rise into the air on its own -- a glimpse of a new kind of skilled work that barely had a name only a few years ago. ■

Namibia halts beef exports due to FMD outbreak
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:49:55 CST
23:49:55 KST

WINDHOEK, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Namibia's beef processing and marketing entity, the Meat Corporation of Namibia (Meatco), has suspended any beef exports due to the foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) outbreak.
The decision follows a national directive from state veterinary authorities under the agriculture ministry ordering an immediate freeze on movements and exports of cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products, to safeguard public health and regional livestock security.
Meatco, in a statement on Thursday evening, confirmed it is in full compliance with the mandated restrictions.
"Our immediate priority is full compliance with the national veterinary response and supporting the authorities in containing the outbreak as quickly as possible. Namibia has built a strong reputation for the integrity of its animal-health and beef-export systems. Meatco will continue to act responsibly and transparently while the authorities undertake the necessary surveillance and control measures," Deputy Chairperson of the Meatco Board Stephanie De Klerk said.
The state-owned entity is reviewing the status of beef shipments that were dispatched, shipped, or in transit before the veterinary directive was confirmed.
"At this stage, Meatco does not wish to speculate on the treatment of individual consignments or whether any product may need to be returned. These matters are governed by veterinary certification, the timing and status of individual consignments and the requirements of the respective importing countries," the statement read.
Regarding the financial implications, the enterprise stated it is too early to assess the complete financial impact.
"The extent of any impact will depend principally on the duration of the control measures, the treatment of consignments already in transit and the time frame within which livestock procurement, slaughter and access to export markets can resume," Meatco concluded. ■

Asian Games | China wins historic Asian Games team dressage gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
22:49:53 CST
23:49:53 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- China's equestrian team made history at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Friday, winning the team dressage gold for the first time in Asian Games history.
The Chinese team, comprising Rao Jiayi, Yu Jiayi, Wu Yue and Gu Zhanzhao, scored 208.148 points to claim the title. South Korea finished second with 205.265 points, while Japan took bronze with 204.117 points.
China had previously won silver in the team dressage at the 2010 Guangzhou and 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, as well as bronze at the 2002 Busan Games. Friday's victory marked China's first Asian Games gold in team dressage.
The gold was also China's second in equestrian at the Aichi-Nagoya Games, further highlighting the country's progress in the sport.
Rao, who anchored the Chinese team as the last rider, said she was delighted with her young teammates, two of whom are 18 years old and one of whom is making her Asian Games debut.
"They've all done very well. They've all performed at least to their normal standard, if not, they rode even better," Rao said.
Rao, who won an individual silver at the previous Asian Games, acknowledged the pressure of being the final rider but said she was pleased with how she handled it.
"I cannot break because other people are relying on me. I'm like the beam in the house. I need to be there," she said.
Reflecting on the historic achievement, Rao emphasized the contribution of generations of Chinese riders and the emergence of a new generation.
"It has been a long journey until what we were able to achieve today. This really reflects the work of older riders (in China). They have encouraged us a lot to achieve this," Rao said.
"Some of my teammates are only 18 and 21 years old, so I am so excited about today's result because we have riders from a new generation who are outstanding, even though they faced a lot of pressure."
China's Olympic rider Alex Hua Tian hailed the victory on social media as a milestone for the country's equestrian sport, saying the young riders represented a new generation and a "historic change" for Chinese equestrian sport.
"They deserve time and patience," Hua said, adding that the next stage would require years of experience and continued support. ■

Bringing together officials, tourism representatives, and business partners from both countries, the Amazing Thailand Mid-Autumn Celebration 2026 featured calligraphy blessings, Thai and Chinese music and dance, and fortune-stick workshops, as well as a tasting of mooncakes, the traditional festival treat.
"Mid-Autumn is rooted in reunion and togetherness," said TAT Governor Thapanee Kiatphaibool, noting that the event aims to turn long-standing ties between the two countries into travel demand.
The event is a centerpiece of the TAT's Nihao Month campaign, now in its third year.
The TAT is also running a cultural and tourism exhibition themed "Under the Same Moon."
From Sept. 26 to 29, 31 Chinese key opinion leaders and social media influencers will travel on four themed trips in Thailand to promote wellness and cultural tourism.
The agency expects around 250,000 Chinese arrivals during the Mid-Autumn and Golden Week holiday period from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, generating approximately 11.5 billion baht (about 344.7 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue. ■

HANGZHOU, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- As the digital economy accelerates, artificial intelligence (AI) has become a new growth driver for China-Africa economic and trade cooperation, driven by expanding practical applications, according to a new report.
Titled China-Africa Economic and Trade Cooperation: Progress and Outlook 2026, the report was unveiled at the ongoing fifth Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, the capital of east China's Zhejiang Province.
The expo, an event dedicated to promoting digital trade and industrial cooperation, is being held from Sept. 23 to 27. This year, the number of its overseas pavilions has already exceeded the combined total of all previous editions.
The application of AI is shifting from a future option to a real agenda in China-Africa cooperation, the report found. This shift is characterized by strong application-scenario drives. Cooperation has expanded into areas such as disaster prevention, healthcare, smart agriculture and urban governance.
"Increasingly, it will require digital infrastructure that enables African businesses to compete in a rapidly changing global economy," said Klaus-Dieter Kaempfer, chief executive of Absa China, noting that digital trade has the potential to lower barriers to entry, connect businesses to new markets and enable entrepreneurs to participate in global commerce regardless of geography.
Alhaji Sarjoh Bah, permanent representative of the African Union to China, called for deeper cooperation in five areas: trade facilitation and cross-border e-commerce; interoperable payments; trusted data governance, cybersecurity and dispute prevention; digital intelligence and industrial parks for value addition; and people-to-people exchanges and digital talent.
Bah called for linking Chinese digital trade industrial parks with African special economic zones and industrial parks, and combining cloud computing, data centers, smart logistics and AI with manufacturing and processing.
"Africa seeks to move from exporting raw minerals to producing processed goods. It seeks equally to move from generating raw data to producing processed intelligence," said Bah, stressing the need for local content, skills development and technology transfer, and building AI systems that reflect African languages and realities.
Concrete cooperation projects are already underway. A highlight of the event was the promotion of the "Mazu" intelligent weather warning system. Designed to meet Africa's needs for meteorological disaster prevention, the system has been deployed in Ethiopia and Djibouti, offering targeted services.
The deepening digital ties mirror the robust growth in China-Africa trade. In 2025, China-Africa trade grew by 17.7 percent year on year to reach 348 billion U.S. dollars. On May 1, China fully implemented a zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations.
China's digitally deliverable service trade value expanded at an average annual rate of 11.2 percent between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global average by 1.8 percentage points. ■
