Russia can restart 80% of Black Sea grain export terminals if attacks stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:47:00 UTC
23:47:00 KST

Russia can restart 80% of Black Sea grain export terminals if attacks stop
MOSCOW, Sept 25 - Russia could quickly restart up to 80% of its grain terminal capacity in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov if diplomatic efforts to halt mutual attacks by Russia and Ukraine result in a ceasefire, a Reuters analysis of industry data showed on Friday.
But three terminals accounting for about 20% of Russia's grain export infrastructure in the area have suffered heavy damage and could take months to repair, the analysis showed.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan is leading an international effort by grain-importing countries to restore Black Sea grain trade, which has been stalled by attacks on ports and vessels in recent months.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Friday that India, Egypt and other Middle Eastern countries were also involved. The Kremlin acknowledged diplomatic contacts but said Russia was finding alternate export routes in the meantime.
Reuters analysed the condition of Russia's nine major grain terminals in the region, as well as smaller facilities in the Sea of Azov and Don river delta, using information from four sources familiar with terminal operations.
The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue. Before the attacks, the route handled up to 70% of Russia's grain exports.
Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, and disruption to shipments has driven up global grain prices and renewed concerns about food security linked to the war in Ukraine.
The analysis found that three of nine major terminals had suffered serious damage in Ukrainian attacks, affecting about one-fifth of grain-loading capacity in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
EXTENT OF DAMAGE
One of Russia's three largest grain terminals, NKHP in the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, suffered serious damage in an August 12 attack. The terminal has annual capacity of 7.1 million metric tons and repairs could take up to six months.
"At NKHP, that conveyor gallery was completely destroyed. It actually collapsed onto the road and was lying across it," one source at Novorossiysk told Reuters.
"The staff were sent home for six months. I don't even know how long the shutdown will last," he said, adding that damage at the other two Novorossiysk terminals, KSK and NZT, was minor and that both were ready to resume operations.
The company said repairs at NKHP could take up to four months.
The other damaged terminals, ZTKT at the Black Sea port of Taman and a terminal in Taganrog on the Azov Sea, have halted operations although the full extent of the damage could not be established. Together, ZTKT and Taganrog have annual capacity of 6.7 million tons.
ZTKT, which has annual capacity of 5.5 million tons, was hit on July 30 and is unable to load grain, another source said, adding that it was unclear when operations could resume.
The analysis showed that terminals with combined capacity of about 53 million tons are currently idle because of security risks but could resume operations. Total grain terminal capacity in the region is about 67 million tons. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Russia's faster Shaheds could rival ballistic missiles this winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:44:30 UTC
23:44:30 KST

Russia's faster Shaheds could rival ballistic missiles this winter
Rescue workers put out a fire at a building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 25, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Oleksiy Moskalenko
Senior Analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center
A few months ago, the only particularly serious threat to Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities came from Russian and North Korean ballistic missiles.
As the Ukrainian mil-tech industry and air defense units perfected their ability to intercept the common "Shahed" drones (now officially called Geran-2, although Ukrainians stick to the original Iranian name), raising the shoot-down rate to 90–95%, a shortage of anti-ballistic interceptor missiles seemed to be the main issue facing Ukraine in the upcoming winter.
However, in this constant arms race, it was Russia's turn to leapfrog, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to new threats while it tested out possible solutions.
August 2026 showed what the new, faster versions of Shahed can do in terms of damage, leaving ground forces' interceptor drone operators — good enough to catch the previous generation of "Shaheds" — without a job. Temporarily.
The new Shaheds are powered by airplane-like jet engines, which allow them to pass through otherwise densely packed air defense zones at speeds of more than 800 km/h (500 mph).
The older generation of attack drones flew at up to 200 km/h (125 mph), requiring the Ukrainian side to master technology that added just 30 km/h (19 mph) to that speed in order to catch up efficiently. Now Ukraine is forced to leap ahead of its current production capacities to build interceptors that can fly at least 450 km/h (280 mph), so the new drones can be taken down when they turn en route or slow down to save fuel.
Whether new interceptors can effectively catch up with jet engine technology is still unknown. We may be heading back to good old missiles as the key means of air defense.
The coming months will give us an answer. Meanwhile, Russia will keep using both old and new drones, as well as ballistic missiles, in an attempt to force Ukrainians to agree to its demands.
As the country braces for another wartime winter, much of the public conversation about Russian air attacks has centered on ballistic missiles and the shortage of Patriot interceptors needed to stop them. But officials and drone crews say that even a cheaper, more numerous threat of new and old Shaheds may end up doing just as much damage.
Over the summer, Russia noticeably scaled back its drone campaign. According to Ukraine's Air Force, the number of older versions of Shahed/Gerbera drones launched fell by a third in June and July compared to a record-setting May.
Yet Moscow has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones, launching nearly 800 of them in just four days in August 2026.
The main reason for this shift, drone unit members say, is that Ukraine has simply gotten better at shooting down the regular, slower drones.
The vast majority of these drones are intercepted by domestically built interceptors flown by dedicated crews stationed across the country. A radar team spots an incoming Shahed, an interceptor crew launches its own drone to locate and pursue the target, and the operator then has to visually acquire the Shahed through the interceptor's onboard camera, close in from behind, and either ram it or detonate nearby, usually knocking off a wing or engine.
For now, the threat from this previous generation of drones seems to have been rendered largely obsolete, but that appearance may be something of an illusion, since the system has one clear weakness: weather.
Strong wind makes the interceptor hard to control, rain can degrade electronics, radar performance, control link, and, crucially, operators still need to see the target through a camera, since radar can guide them to the right area but cannot perform the final identification and targeting itself; low cloud, fog, or rain make that visual search far harder.
It's telling, in this respect, that some interceptor unit command posts reportedly keep a dedicated screen just for tracking weather conditions.
Ukrainian citizens are gradually starting to associate rainy weather with cheaper, slower Shahed drones: "It is likely that today, as on the previous occasion, the adversary will seek to exploit the poor weather to attack areas west of Kyiv using 'conventional' gasoline-powered Shahed drones," said an adviser to the Defense Minister of Ukraine on a rainy evening.
Russian forces appear to be factoring this in already, according to Ukrainian crews, timing launches and routes for stretches when interceptors are least effective.
That is why the summer drop in slower, gasoline Shahed launches shouldn't be read as a lasting decline in the threat.
As fall brings more fog, lower cloud cover, and worse visibility, the conditions that favor Russian drones and hamper Ukrainian interceptors are set to return, giving Moscow an added reason to lean back on its cheapest, slower strike drones.
That, our respondents argue, is the overall conclusion of the current air war.
Each new stage of the technological race doesn't replace the one before it — it adds another layer to a system that has to be sustained with people, hardware, and infrastructure.
Mobile fire groups remain necessary alongside interceptor drones; slower piston-engine Shaheds will keep flying alongside faster jet-powered ones.
Russian forces regularly adapt their tactics and patterns of drone employment in an effort to improve their effectiveness, e.g., they are known to periodically re-test routes they've previously avoided after taking losses, checking whether Ukrainian defenses along that corridor have weakened — which means any capability Ukraine builds now has to be maintained, not shelved, once a newer one arrives.
For now, jet-powered Shaheds are hunted almost exclusively by scarce, expensive fighter jets and surface-to-air missiles, while dedicated faster interceptor drones are still working their way toward serial production.
While this technological gap remains, Ukraine and its partners need to keep investing in developing the skills and the infrastructure of the teams operating in the domain of air defense.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said Friday that Baghdad hopes to make Iraq a global hub for energy production and use the country’s capabilities to strengthen regional and international security and stability.
Addressing the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, Al-Zaidi said Iraq aims to capitalize on its energy potential in a way that supports sustainable security and stability at both the regional and international levels.
He voiced concern, however, over disruptions affecting transportation and maritime navigation and their role in driving up global energy prices.
To contain those risks and their repercussions, Al-Zaidi said Iraq is working to diversify its oil export outlets and develop energy routes linking the country with Türkiye, Jordan, and Syria, with access to global markets.
He said the measures are aimed at contributing to energy security and diversifying supply routes.
Al-Zaidi described economic diversification based on genuine partnerships as a central strategic objective of the government’s economic policy.
He also highlighted Iraq’s Development Road project as a comprehensive vision for regional integration and stability, saying it will serve as a strategic corridor for trade, investment, industry, and energy.
The project is designed to link the Grand Faw Port in southern Iraq with Türkiye and onward to Europe.
Al-Zaidi said Baghdad wants the project to be open to participation by all neighboring and friendly countries, arguing that shared economic interests can help generate prosperity.
He also said that with the end of the international coalition’s mission in Iraq, Baghdad is moving its relationship with strategic partners from military cooperation toward economic and development cooperation serving mutual interests.
On domestic security, Al-Zaidi said the state will continue to retain sole authority over decisions of war and peace and that weapons and instruments of force must remain in the hands of constitutional institutions.

Four suspects held over murder of Dominican singer Julián Oro Duro's wife

14:40:07 UTC
23:40:07 KST

The artist was seriously injured and his wife, 60-year-old Zeneida Socorro Castillo, was killed. According to investigators, she was tortured for six hours in her home in Santo Domingo.
The Dominican Republic's National Police has identified the four suspects in the attack on the home of merengue singer Gilberto Julián Sarante, known as Julián Oro Duro, in which his wife, 60-year-old Zeneida Socorro Castillo, was killed and the singer was seriously injured. All four suspects are already in custody.
Those arrested are Phillips Michael Tejeda Vásquez; Juan Carlos Hernández García, known as Peña; Kevin Dariel Germán Troncoso, known as Yandel, 23; and Lawrence Mark Liranzo Marcos, known as Chiquito, 18. The latter was detained after an active search by the police. According to investigators, all four had working or trusted links with the artist's entourage.
Tejeda Vásquez worked as an air-conditioning technician and carried out private jobs at properties belonging to Julián Oro Duro. The investigation suggests that he may have contacted the other suspects. Liranzo Marcos, for his part, knew the family and worked at a villa the singer was having built in Guerra.
The attack took place on 21 September, when the artist returned to his home in Brisa Oriental VI, in Santo Domingo Este, Dominican Republic, and was ambushed by the assailants after his wife had been held for hours. According to the investigation, Castillo was tortured for several hours before being killed.
The singer suffered traumatic head injuries during the attack and is still recovering. The police and the Public Prosecutor's Office are continuing to gather evidence about the crime. The case has caused widespread shock in the Dominican Republic.

====================================================================================================

Four years after Russia’s wartime exodus began, another wave may be starting. Political scientist Margarita Zavadskaya on what we’ve learned about Russian emigration since 2022.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:39:40 UTC
23:39:40 KST

Four years after Russia’s wartime exodus began, another wave may be starting. Political scientist Margarita Zavadskaya on what we’ve learned about Russian emigration since 2022.
In 2026, Russians are once again leaving the country en masse. For them, the long process of building a new life almost from scratch is only beginning. Meanwhile, many emigrants have already lived in several countries — and still haven’t found a place to settle down. Others have found a genuine new home, while still others have returned to Russia. Meduza spoke with political scientist Margarita Zavadskaya, a senior research fellow at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs and one of the co-founders of the OutRush project, which studies Russian emigration, about adapting to life abroad, the conflict between “those who left” and “those who stayed,” and the differences between the various waves of emigration.
— How do you generally feel about the discourse around “those who left” and “those who stayed”? Sometimes it seems like this conflict exists only on social media.
— This trope is useful to Russian propaganda, which deliberately promotes it: the idea that those who left are traitors. But there’s also resentment in it from people who don’t support the war and the regime but, unlike “those who left,” are forced to stay in Russia or can’t afford to emigrate. It’s quite possible they feel their compatriots abandoned them. Or they want to stay and consider that the right decision.
The Levada Center asked people how they feel about “those who left,” though those questions were specifically about celebrities. For example, they asked how you feel about Alla Pugacheva. And the poll shows there’s some negativity, but it doesn’t reflect the full picture. The number of people in Russia who have someone who left the country is very small, and it’s hard to dislike someone you’ve never met in your life. So I don’t think there’s really a big rift. But the insidious thing is that even by discussing this narrative, by giving it attention, we’re effectively helping it gain traction.
— How are people outside Russia experiencing this disconnect? Do they feel increasingly removed from what’s happening in Russia and from their loved ones there? After all, things are changing very quickly: drone attacks, fuel shortages, and so on.
— Unfortunately, I don’t have data recent enough to assess how the drone attacks and the fuel crisis have affected relationships within families. But if we look further back, since Russia had gone through upheavals before, those who left tend to feel more empathy toward those who stayed than the other way around. It’s a kind of emotional asymmetry. One of the recent studies from 2026, which I worked on and where I interviewed participants, shows there’s no aggression toward those who stayed. On the contrary, people miss them, want to stay in touch, and regularly keep in contact not only with family members but with friends too.
— Based on your data, do emigrants tend to read news from Russia more or less over time?
— There’s a sense that people are getting more irritated and tired. By 2023, even before Alexey Navalny’s death, many were already complaining that they were sick of reading the news. But few decide to step out of the Russian-language media space entirely.
Everyone is tired of depressing news, and the media are responding to that demand. More entertainment-oriented, quasi-political content is appearing, such as [the show on the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain] Drama Queens.
— How many people have you surveyed during your research?
— At the start of the [full-scale] war, several colleagues and I co-founded the OutRush project, which has used questionnaires to survey a total of about 18,000 respondents who left Russia after February 24, 2022.
The sample of respondents isn’t representative, but that’s a problem with all migrant studies, including in countries with advanced statistics and immigrant tracking. That’s because it’s hard to determine where the boundaries of diasporas lie. That is, who counts as part of the Russian-speaking diaspora — in Germany, for example, where there are “late repatriots”, who receive German passports right away but in practice often remain within the Russian-speaking community? All existing studies obviously have sampling biases. Ours skews more liberal, more antiwar.
— Do you distinguish waves in Russian migration after 2022?
— I’d say those are fairly loose categories. Personally, I’m not a fan of dividing people into “Septembrists” [those who left when mobilization began] and “Februarists.” It’s as if there’s a moral hierarchy built into it: we’re the real emigrants, who left before the state wanted to claim our bodies, while those who left in September are somehow defective. That’s the wrong way to frame the question, especially for a researcher. Besides, many people left for ideological reasons after September as well.
— But right now there’s a lot of talk about a “new wave of migration” amid rumors of mobilization. Is that reasoning justified? Will we see a major outflow of people this fall?
— There are indeed grounds to talk about heightened readiness to emigrate right now. But I’d separate a simple rise in the desire to leave from an actual mass outflow that has already occurred. Right now we’re seeing a lot of indirect signs of the former. For example, Kovcheg reports that it received almost eight times more inquiries in August than in May. But there are still no lines at the borders and no shortage of tickets to visa-free countries. So anxiety and readiness to leave have clearly grown, but it’s not yet on the scale of 2022.
Right now we’re dealing with rumors of a possible mobilization, not an announced one. Russian authorities publicly deny having such plans. The conditions for a new wave of emigration have formed, but its scale will depend heavily on whether a new, sharp trigger occurs.
A “wave” isn’t just the moment when everyone on social media starts discussing emigration. For a researcher, several independent indicators need to align. The first is intent: search queries, inquiries to organizations that help with relocation, demand for consultations with migration lawyers, interest in renting housing and working abroad. The second is actual movement: border crossings, the number of Russians entering Armenia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, and other countries, airline ticket sales. And the third is “putting down roots” in the new place: applications for residence permits and other legal statuses, enrolling children in school, registering businesses, employment, long-term rentals. The OECD also recommends combining official statistics with digital and other real-time sources when forecasting migration.
How difficult is it to emigrate in 2026
— How is emigration in 2026 different from emigration in 2022? It feels like the reasons now aren’t quite the same as before. In February 2022, the reasons were primarily ethical, while during the mobilization, it was fear for one’s life. Now it seems more like accumulated fatigue: internet censorship, the gasoline crisis, problems with Wildberries, and new strikes.
— There’s actually a fairly significant difference here. That said, I wouldn’t describe February 2022 too rigidly as purely a “moral” emigration. Even then the reasons were mixed: rejection of the war, fear of political consequences, companies and jobs closing, the breakdown of established professional networks, uncertainty about the future (this is visible in OutRush’s early data from the first months of the [full-scale] war). September 2022, on the other hand, really was a much more unambiguous shock: for a great many men, there was suddenly a direct risk of ending up at war.
By 2026, emigration looks more like one driven by accumulated risk: four and a half years of war, internet restrictions, a worsening economic situation, problems with familiar services, drone attacks, a sense of closing opportunities, and, on top of that, rumors of mobilization. So I wouldn’t say there’s less fear now.
There’s another difference from 2022 as well. Over these years an emigration infrastructure has already emerged: people have friends and relatives abroad, Telegram chats, guides, experience from previous attempts to relocate, and a sense of prices and countries.
— Is it easier for people leaving now than for those who emigrated in 2022?
— Any migration is stressful, but it’s also, to some extent, a story about privilege, if we’re talking about a decision to emigrate on one’s own rather than situations where people were literally evacuated.
First, you need to know that you’re welcome wherever you’re going; second, you need to know how to get the paperwork done; third, you need money for it. You either have a job offer from a company, or the option of getting a residence permit, if we’re talking about the European Union.
Those who left later aren’t necessarily people who have it easier. In many ways, it can be the opposite: harder for them. For example, because of the work of ICE in the United States, migrants’ lives there have become much more unpredictable. Attitudes toward Russians are also changing in the European Union — Germany, for instance, effectively stopped issuing humanitarian visas in 2025, even to those who fear persecution from Russia.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language daily news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
— Do people handle a second or third move more easily, or does each subsequent one wear them down even more?
— Among OutRush’s respondents from 2022–2024, many had already changed their country of residence, and some had even changed countries five or six times. How people handle moving, across the sample as a whole, depends on the person’s age and whether they’re burdened with family and children. But overall we quite rarely come across people who genuinely enjoyed it, though these people did exist too.
I remember an interview from Latin America: the person ended up there after making a huge journey through Asian countries. He deliberately chose not to go to the nearby European Union, because he didn’t want problems stemming from his Russian passport. And he was happy with his choice.
— If the situation in Russia keeps getting worse, but not too drastically, will people keep leaving, or will they get used to it at some point and the outflow will stop?
— Both processes happen at the same time. On one hand, people really do adapt to almost anything. What was perceived as an emergency four years ago is gradually becoming part of everyday life. So the same deterioration in conditions can provoke a much weaker reaction a few years later.
There’s also a self-selection effect. Many of those for whom it was easiest to leave — people with foreign languages, remote jobs, international connections, savings — have already done so. Increasingly, those who remain include people for whom the cost of emigrating is especially high: elderly parents, children, mortgages, a profession that’s hard to transfer to another country, lack of money. So a worsening situation doesn’t automatically translate into a proportional rise in emigration.
But adaptation also has a limit. Gradual deterioration often produces not a smooth curve of emigration but a series of steps: for a while almost nothing happens, then a trigger appears, and we see a spike. There’s another important point: the worse the economic situation gets, the more people may want to leave, but the fewer people can afford to. So rising discontent within the country doesn’t necessarily translate into an equivalent rise in actual emigration.
How Russian emigrants are adapting abroad (spoiler: not badly)
— What do your respondents call themselves? It seems like many, for example, don’t really like the word “emigrant.”
— In April 2027, a book I co-authored with two other researchers is coming out, bringing together the results of all our work over the past several years. One of the chapters, and the beginning of the book, is devoted precisely to how people refer to themselves. We spent a long time thinking about what to call them, because many people find the word “migrants” unpleasant, partly because it echoes migrants within Russia. We often characterize Russians who left after February 2022 as advanced, urbanized people who understand ideas about coloniality within Russia. But many still don’t like calling themselves migrants, because it seems to lower their social status.
Some people like the word “relocant,” because it reflects that you’re in demand, since someone is willing to relocate you. But according to our data, the share of these people is very small. Those whom employers actually hired and relocated, providing them with a package of services including hiring and housing, are an absolute minority. The very term “relocants” is misleading, because it attributes more privilege to the whole group than may actually exist. There’s even a kind of judgment built into the word: the implication that these are people who don’t need and don’t deserve empathy or support, because they can survive on their own.
The way we — researchers, journalists, or states — sort people shapes narratives. And these are dangerous because we build cause-and-effect chains from them, which then translate into specific countries’ political decisions. If Russians are “relocants,” then they’re not entitled to any help. And conversely, you also can’t call everyone refugees, because refugees are, first and foremost, Ukrainians. And then a kind of moral economy kicks in: whose suffering is more important and deserves more attention.
There are other self-designations too: many call themselves a “global citizen,” a “citizen of the world.” In English there’s the word exile and the phrase person in exile. These are the terms we actually use in the book.
— What themes and issues come up most often in the words of the migrants you’ve spoken with?
— In addition to the surveys, we collected 581 interviews with Russians who ended up in more than 60 countries. And at least back in 2023–2024, the country of residence didn’t have that much effect on how people talked about themselves. There was also a lot of dark humor: people often resort to memes and self-deprecation to describe their often difficult situation.
— How successfully are Russians adapting abroad?
— In the first two years of the [full-scale] war, according to our surveys, two-thirds of the people who left in 2022 and had previously worked for Russian companies (including remotely) left those jobs and were able to find new ones. But it’s worth remembering that a fairly large share of Russians who left work in the IT sector, where, at least until the AI boom, things were pretty good. People employed in science and teaching had it hardest of all: finding work abroad is very difficult for them.
— Do emigrants often integrate into local society, or do they more often end up strictly within their own community?
— Based on the material from our 2023 interviews, we can say that people don’t learn the host country’s language well. The first survey data showed that everyone was rushing to learn Georgian, Armenian, or whatever language [of the country] they’d moved to. But over time, most Russians have continued to stay within the Russian-speaking community, even if they think that’s the wrong thing to do.
Yet Russians are often accused of not forming diasporas, even though those who left after 2022 are actually successfully creating groups where they communicate with each other. This community is united by a shared moral shock and by being against the war. And earlier waves of emigration — in the 1990s, for instance — didn’t have that kind of unifying foundation. In this wave of migration we see almost no desire to distance oneself from one’s compatriots, and that’s a very significant shift.
— In one of your papers there’s a concept called discordant privilege, a phenomenon where a migrant’s identity seems to split in two. Can you tell us about this idea?
— This concept comes up in the article about Kyrgyzstan. The thing is, our respondents sometimes “jokingly” mentioned a ranking of countries where you could end up. The coolest ones were, say, Luxembourg, Switzerland, probably the United States. And at the very bottom was Kyrgyzstan. On one hand, you can see an element of disrespect and a colonial attitude toward less economically prosperous countries in this. On the other, this hierarchy reflects internal inequality among those who left themselves. Russia is one of the most unequal countries in the world, and it’s naive to assume that the people who left it are all the same. Not everyone is an IT worker with [a monthly salary of] $5,000. Kyrgyzstan often became the destination for people who, for example, couldn’t move to European Union countries because they lacked connections.
So, we had one interview in Kyrgyzstan where a person who had left Russia quickly found work in healthcare, because Russian-language medicine is in high demand there. He arrived with a sense of “I’m a colonizer, someone who should treat this former Soviet country carefully.” But to his surprise, he was treated with great respect. So discordant privilege is the mismatch between how you’re seen in the host country and how you assume you’ll be seen. You move from one hierarchy into another and have to reconcile your previous position with the positions of the host society.
— It sounds like you’re describing a kind of logic of deservingness and guilt — that you have to prove you hold the “right” antiwar views in order to be accepted in a country. Is that something Russian emigrants experience?
— Yes, many Russians who left retain a sense of guilt in Thomas Mann’s understanding of the term. If we ask respondents in a survey who bears responsibility for the war, most will say: we’re guilty, Russia is guilty. But interestingly, when we start unpacking that emotion in interviews (what exactly should you atone for, and to whom?), a lot of nuance emerges. A person can fully acknowledge that a crime is taking place while denying individual guilt. Many interviewees insist that the host country should judge them only by their individual actions, not by their Russian passport.
Do emigrants believe they’ll ever return home
— How has emigrants’ perception of the war changed over the past year compared to 2022?
— Data comes in very slowly, and I don’t have anything new for 2026. I can point to not-yet-published information from our study in Armenia (though, of course, that can’t give us a complete picture of all emigrants). Overall, attitudes toward the war haven’t changed. It remains a common view that Russia should bear responsibility for rebuilding Ukraine if there’s ever some kind of peace process.
Meanwhile, skepticism toward the West is growing. There’s a study, for example, of Russians in the United States and Poland that confirms disillusionment with democracy in the host countries. The processes underway, especially in America in connection with ICE’s work, are causing many to become disillusioned with European–American democracy. And in Europe we’re also seeing a powerful anti-migration turn. It’s not connected to Russians, but they too are getting swept up in that same vortex and are becoming victims of the rightward shift in European politics.
— It seems like among those who left for political reasons, there are more and more people experiencing apathy and, conversely, withdrawing from politics. How accurate is that?
— Yes, that’s absolutely true. A colleague and I recently published a paper looking at how people demobilize. Among our respondents were people who blossomed after emigrating and became more involved in volunteering: helping the homeless or organizing fundraisers. But more people who had actively participated in political initiatives became demobilized.
The first reason is emotional burnout. My colleagues published a detailed paper on this in 2025, with testimony from Russian emigrants. People burn out in a stream of bad news with no light at the end of it. They’re squeezed on one side by host countries, where they must constantly prove they’re not a security threat or simply maintain their legal status, and on the other by the need to keep thinking about possible threats from their own country. It’s a psychologically unhealthy situation.
The second reason is financial. Activists, media outlets, and human rights advocates lost their sources of support when the largest American donors and many other sponsors withdrew their backing. They’ve had to reinvent themselves in a new reality. The third reason is transnational repression. Many still have relatives and property, some continue traveling to Russia, and these serve as levers of pressure that hold people back.
The Russian diaspora isn’t unique in this respect. If you look at other studies — for example, on the diaspora of people who left Turkey, since Erdogan also triggered several waves of academics and activists leaving the country — you’ll see that the more time passes, the more people demobilize, because they need to see light at the end of the tunnel. If that light isn’t particularly visible yet, people start switching to something else.
But that doesn’t mean no one is engaged in politics anymore. A great many people who left Russia continue to take part in civic initiatives in one way or another, often shifting to less visible forms of activity for safety reasons.
— Compared to 2022, do emigrants more often describe their departure as final? Do many say they won’t return to Russia even if the situation improves significantly? You’ve written that if a person has stayed in emigration for more than two years, the likelihood of returning drops significantly.
— When people are asked why they left and whether they want to return, they can say anything, because they often orient themselves around “correct” and “incorrect” answers. How people will actually behave is a separate, open question. But it really is true: if we understand anything about migration — any migration, not just Russian — the longer people stay abroad, the higher the likelihood they’ll remain there. Two years is more of a rough benchmark. The process can be nonlinear. But it’s roughly the amount of time in which a person can establish themselves in a new place — for example, finding a job and permanent housing.
There are people who left for political reasons who continue to live in Russia in their heads, even though they’re technically not there. For example, offices of many political and civic organizations in exile are located in Vilnius and Berlin. I imagine many people there go to work “in Russia.” Someone out there is surely still living out of a suitcase. There were very few of these people in our interviews, but they existed. One person said: “I still haven’t unpacked my suitcase. If something happens tomorrow, I can just grab it and fly back.” I don’t know if he’s still hasn’t unpacked his suitcase.
— Are there many among your respondents who say they’ve found a genuine new home in emigration?
— That happens, but it’s rare. For most people, the dominant trope is that of the guest, a motif of gratitude and hospitality toward the host country: “We really appreciate that we’re tolerated here.” But the specific sense that this is my new home is rare. Rather, respondents have a sense that they’re gradually getting used to it, which sounds more like resignation.
But the good news is that Russians in emigration have managed to build many communities. And that, I think, is a major breakthrough. I remember when I first flew to the United States as a student in the early 2000s, I met a Soviet migrant who told me: “If you need help, never approach someone who speaks Russian. Better to ask an American for help.” His words, that level of distrust toward what were nominally his own people, really surprised me.
But after 2022, Russians in emigration, united by shared misfortune and shared trauma, displayed forms of civic behavior every bit as strong as those of citizens of any advanced democratic country. For example, they’ve created aid projects like Kovcheg, Emigration for Action, and Idite Lesom [“Get Lost,” an organization assisting Russian deserters]. They cooperate with activists in host countries and open bookstores selling Russian-language books, like Babel in Berlin. Places like these serve as gathering points for the community.
Therefore, when someone says there’s something wrong with our civil society, I want to respond: “We’re fine. The problem isn’t us, or at least, not only us.”

The Prime Minister has supported the concept in various statements over the year

He called it a wonderful effort to blend spirituality with modernity while preserving the sanctity of ‘bhajans’, in his monthly broadcast ‘Mann ki Baat’ that month.Then in July, PM Modi had once again praised the concept of "Bhajan Clubbing" during his visit to Australia, saying the trend reflected how young Indians were finding new ways to connect with faith and spirituality. "You must have heard about the new trend of 'Bhajan Clubbing' in India; it is being driven by our Gen Z. Here in Australia, too, I hear that your weekends are filled with faith and spirituality. Whether it is the Lord Satyanarayan Katha at someone's home, Ardas at the Gurudwara, children performing Bhangra or Bharatanatyam, or a cricket tournament in progress--there is always something happening," he had said at the time.

349 seats for United Russia, Ukrainian attacks on polling stations: CEC statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:37:22 UTC
23:37:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. The State Duma election campaign was held amid unprecedented threats and differed markedly from all previous elections, Central Election Commission (CEC) Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova said at a meeting summing up the results of the State Duma elections.
She noted that voter turnout in the State Duma elections reached 59.8%, with the United Russia party winning 349 seats.
According to Pamfilova, roughly 75 polling station buildings in 11 regions across Russia were damaged as a result of targeted attacks by the Ukrainian military during the recent elections.
TASS has summarized key statements by the CEC chairwoman.
Voter turnout
Voter turnout in the State Duma elections in 2026 was 59.8%, "a total of 67,448,094 people cast their ballots."
In 2021, 51.82% of voters, or 56,484,685 people, cast their ballots, while in 2016, 47.88% of voters, or 52,700,992 people, did so, according to CEC data.
Participants in the special military operation were described as "the most active and engaged voters, who fully understand what they are fighting for and how important stability on the home front is, with elections being an important part of that order."
Results
Following the results of the State Duma elections, the United Russia party secured 349 seats, the Communist Party (CPRF) received 37 seats, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) received 23 seats, the New People party secured 19 seats, A Just Russia received 17 seats, and Rodina received one seat.
As many as four independent candidates also secured seats in the State Duma.
A total of 46 veterans of the special military operation were elected to the State Duma, including 41 from United Russia.
The average age of State Duma deputies has fallen from 57 to 53 following the elections: "The State Duma has gotten a bit younger. It was not old before, but it has gotten younger."
The State Duma has undergone a significant renewal following the elections: "This is a significant renewal. Nearly half of the deputies will be new. But a very strong core, which worked admirably and effectively in the previous Duma, remains."
Remote electronic voting
Remote electronic voting proceeded normally during the elections, with no major disruptions reported.
More than seven million people in 33 regions participated in remote electronic voting: "This year’s remote electronic voting coverage included more than 640 electoral campaigns and over 3,600 types of ballots. The total number of voters who participated in remote electronic voting, including Moscow, exceeded seven million."
United Russia ranked first based on the results of remote electronic voting.
New People came in second, followed by the Communist Party, the Liberal Democratic Party and A Just Russia.
According to the CEC, United Russia received 50.79% of the vote, New People got 13.04%, the CPRF received 11.45%, the LDPR won 8.97% and A Just Russia got 6.34%.
Voting abroad
More than 280,000 people voted at polling stations abroad during the elections: "As planned, 333 polling stations were opened in 152 countries, including seven in the city of Baikonur, Kazakhstan. A total of 280,355 people participated in the elections [abroad]."
United Russia won the vote abroad in the State Duma elections, receiving more than 58% of the ballots cast, with 162,355 people supporting it.
The LDPR was backed by 14,683 people, or 5.2%, the CPRF was supported by 28,970 people, or 10.3%, A Just Russia had 16,027 backers, or 5.7%, while the New People party was supported by 37,122 people, or 13.2%.
Invalid ballots, violations
Despite calls to spoil ballots, these campaigns failed to gain support.
The share of invalid ballots stood at 1.36%.
Among the main reasons for declaring ballots invalid were their improper insertion into the ballot box, damage to seals and stamps and violations of outdoor voting procedures.
As many as 17 precinct election commission members were removed in four regions, with six of them from the Yabloko party.
During the election campaign, the CEC received a total of 6,598 appeals and "only 766 appeals contained information about alleged violations, which is four times fewer than in 2021."
The CEC did everything possible to reduce cases of voter coercion: "I would like to point out significant changes in appeals related to coercion to vote - we carried out enormous preventive work so that no one would dare to force people, so that no one was doing it at gunpoint. And it [the work] paid off - only 31 appeals, which is five times fewer than in 2021."
Observers
Observers representing virtually every continent monitored the elections: "We even broke the record set during the presidential election. There were 1,126 observers and experts from 133 countries - meaning virtually every continent on Earth."
The courage of observers who came from Western countries known for their anti-Russian policies deserves particular respect: "They knew that they were going [to Russia] and putting themselves at risk not in Russia, but at home upon their return. Unfortunately, these facts are being confirmed. That is their freedom of speech and human rights, which they spent years lecturing us about."
No observers from North Korea came to the State Duma elections, but there were observers from South Korea.
A total of 976 people out of more than 41,000 applicants were not allowed to observe the elections: "In 25 regions, 976 people out of 41,610 declared observers were not permitted to monitor [the elections]."
During the voting days, 15 observers from parties were removed from polling stations: "During the voting days, out of 184,106 observers sent by parties, 15 people were removed from polling stations by court decision."
This was "the largest removal compared to previous campaigns," when in 2021 only three observers were removed and in 2024 there were two such cases.
Unprecedented threats
The election campaign was held amid unprecedented threats: "As we have repeatedly said, this campaign differed significantly from all previous ones. And, certainly, from the similar campaign held in peaceful conditions in 2021. Above all, it differed in that it took place amid an escalation of unprecedented, diverse threats."
The 2026 single voting day was the most difficult to organize in post-Soviet Russian history: "The combination of the enormous scale of the campaign, which was truly extensive and multi-level, and its conduct under a complicated operational situation, under sanctions and external pressure, allows us to say that the 2026 single voting day was the most complex election campaign in terms of organization in the history of new Russia."
Ensuring security
The CEC set itself the task of ensuring the security and transparency of the elections, and successfully completed it: "We were faced with an extremely difficult task, which we have successfully accomplished. That is, while ensuring maximum security, we maintained all our fundamental principles of openness and transparency in the electoral process."
Multi-day voting proved to be the key factor in ensuring security: "In this campaign, three-day voting turned out to be one of the most important factors in ensuring security, because it allowed us to spread out citizens and avoid large crowds, given the threats of terrorist attacks and drones that we had anticipated."
Cyberattacks
About 28 million potentially dangerous cyberattacks have been recorded on the CEC’s resources since the start of the election campaign: "From the start of the election campaign through September 22, we recorded approximately 28 million potentially dangerous cyberattacks from the Internet on the Russian CEC’s website, including direct attacks on all our digital resources. Specifically, during the voting and vote-counting days on September 18-22, there were over 14.7 million potentially dangerous attacks from the Internet on the Russian CEC website and our digital resources."
Attackers failed to breach the robust protection systems safeguarding Russia’s digital election services: "I think no country could have withstood attacks of this intensity."
As many as 13 waves of targeted DDoS attacks were recorded, with a total duration of 468 minutes.
Threats to election officials
Election officials faced significant pressure and received constant threats during the campaign: "A constant flow of threats, provocations and mass mailings of fake letters, for example, those sent in the name of the CEC chair demanding that governors stop vote preparations. On the letterhead you can see my signature, you cannot tell it apart."
"Our people are rock-solid. Nothing broke them. I would like to say that, on the contrary, even in the most difficult conditions, they proved themselves incredibly competent, quick and united."
Roughly 75 polling station buildings in 11 regions across Russia were damaged as a result of targeted attacks by the Ukrainian military during the recent elections: "In 11 regions, 75 buildings housing territorial and precinct election commissions were damaged or completely destroyed and were not accidentally affected by fallen debris or anything else. These were targeted attacks."
As many as six election commission members were killed during the campaign as a result of attacks that Russian officials attributed to forces under Vladimir Zelensky.

Diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the Middle East war, launched by the US and Israel with surprise attacks on Iran in late February, have faltered for months.
The June deal aimed to lay the ground for a full peace deal but it quickly unravelled.
There had been optimism that talks might be revived during the UN General Assembly this week, but in a defiant speech to the world body on Wednesday, Pezeshkian said Iran would not "bend at the knee" to the US.
A day later he told Fox News that Iran did "not wish to continue" the war but it was up to Washington to end it.

Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, called on Yemenis on Friday to mobilise and join the armed forces.

Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia hold talks on Houthi attacks
The military chiefs of staff of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have finished a meeting in Riyadh to discuss how to respond to the Houthis' ongoing attacks on the kingdom, Ankara said on Friday.
Turkey's defence ministry earlier said its chief of general staff was travelling to Saudi Arabia on Friday to attend the meeting, with Saudi state media also announcing planned military talks but without providing further details.
Later on Friday, Ankara published photographs of the three military officials in uniform, stating that the meeting had taken place, without disclosing where.
The Iran-backed group has escalated its attacks on the kingdom since July, ending a years-long truce and declaring a maritime blockade, hitting Saudi targets and seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast as they seek to stifle Saudi oil exports.
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.

The United Nations' top official for refugees warned on Friday that conditions for long-displaced people in Western Sahara were getting worse and that their humanitarian needs were starkly underfunded.
Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, has been largely controlled by Morocco since 1975, but the United Nations considers it a non-self-governing territory.

====================================================================================================

For FM Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's diplomatic battlefield is as important as the military one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:34:49 UTC
23:34:49 KST

For nearly two years, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has been pursuing a diplomatic goal that, given the current international climate surrounding Israel, might sound almost unimaginable: persuading foreign governments to move their embassies to Jerusalem.
The campaign is about far more than where diplomats work. It is part of a broader struggle over Israel’s place in the international system – a struggle that Sa’ar increasingly sees as a component of national security alongside the wars being fought on Israel’s borders.
Next month, Colombia is expected to become the 10th country to operate an embassy in Jerusalem. Israel has also reached an understanding with the Democratic Republic of the Congo to open an embassy, although no date has yet been set.
For Sa’ar, the numbers are significant. When he took office less than two years ago, he said, Jerusalem had roughly half the number of foreign embassies it has today.
“I think it is important,” he said. “It is one of the indications that even during this challenging period, we have managed to expand and deepen our diplomatic ties, while at the same time dealing with struggles and blockages in other arenas.”
Progress does not happen on its own
The progress, he stressed, did not happen by itself. Sa’ar made expanding the Foreign Ministry’s diplomatic presence in Jerusalem one of its measurable goals. “I am also working on it. It doesn’t happen by itself.”
For Sa’ar, diplomatic recognition is ultimately a battle over competing narratives – and Israel cannot afford to leave that arena unanswered.
“The struggle for our rights is narrative against narrative,” he said. “Is Jerusalem the ancient capital of the Jewish people, which was never the capital of any other people or state? Or is it something else, which, at best, needs to be divided?”
Moving an embassy to Jerusalem is not an easy decision for a foreign government. Such governments know they may face criticism from the Palestinians, Arab states, and other parts of the international community. That, Sa’ar argued, is why every decision to move an embassy matters.
The conversations, he said, often begin long before a leader takes office. With Colombia, he raised the issue with President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella before the election. He discussed it with Nauru’s vice president during a visit to Fiji and recently raised it with Slovenia’s prime minister.
The circumstances vary from country to country, Sa’ar said, but the principle is the same: Israel has to ask.
“You have to know how to give in places that are important to them, but you also have to know how to demand and put forward the things that are important to you,” he said.
Sa’ar quoted Ze’ev Jabotinsky: “Difficult – that means possible.” “That doesn’t mean it is easy,” he said. “But it is possible in many places.”
Israel-UK relations deteriorate to 'unprecedented low'
IF JERUSALEM represents Sa’ar’s long-term diplomatic campaign, Britain represents the tougher side of his approach.
Relations between Jerusalem and London have deteriorated significantly under the Labour government, particularly following Britain’s decision to impose sanctions related to Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Sa’ar described the relationship as being at an “unprecedented low.”
Israel responded with its own measures, including the closure of the British Consulate in east Jerusalem, restrictions on the activities of British representatives dealing with issues related to the Palestinian Authority and Gaza, and the declaration of several British figures as persona non grata.
Sa’ar rejected the suggestion that such measures are merely diplomatic theater.
“Anyone who acts against Israel with a unilateral, pro-Palestinian and anti-Israel approach, like the Labour government, will lose its effectiveness and relevance in the region,” he said. “As a country, we are not prepared to allow attacks against us to go unanswered.”
He believes the response can also affect other governments’ calculations.
“If we had not acted in this way,” he said, “I have no doubt that other countries would have taken identical steps.”
But Sa’ar is already looking beyond the current Labour government. He pointed to criticism of Labour’s Israel policy from both the Conservatives and Reform UK.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, he said, has indicated that his party would reverse some of the measures if it came to power. For Sa’ar, the episode illustrates a basic reality of diplomacy: governments change.
Iran presents unique challenge to Israeli diplomacy
Iran presents a different challenge. Despite a series of meetings held by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during the UN General Assembly in New York, including meetings with Western foreign ministers, Sa’ar rejected the argument that Tehran emerged from the latest regional upheaval diplomatically strengthened.
“I don’t think Iran has become stronger diplomatically,” he said. “I think it has become weaker.”
He pointed to the international campaign against the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, noting that numerous countries have designated the organization a terrorist group, as well as steps by some governments to reduce diplomatic relations with Tehran. He also cited Iran’s suppression of protests and its regional activities.
Still, Sa’ar did not claim that Iran has become isolated.
“The world is a cynical world,” he said. “Usually, everyone conducts dialogue with everyone, in one way or another.” International politics, he added, is “also a game of interests.”
That pragmatism is particularly relevant to the question of whether Washington and Tehran will return to negotiations. Sa’ar does not currently see an agreement on the horizon. But he also refused to declare diplomacy dead.
“Reality is dynamic,” he said. “It can also change.”
For Israel, however, one issue remains constant: Iran’s nuclear program.
“Our highest commitment is to prevent Iran from having nuclear weapons,” Sa’ar said. “That has not changed.” If necessary, he added, Israel will act.
The same logic applies to the Houthis, although Sa’ar distinguished between confronting a threat and assuming responsibility for every regional crisis. He described the Houthi threat as serious but rejected the idea that Israel should automatically intervene.
“I don’t think there is any country that has contributed more than the State of Israel to harming the Houthis and weakening the Houthis in recent years,” he said.
Israel, he added, cannot solve every problem in the world. “Not even all the problems in the Middle East.”
Instead, Sa’ar said, Jerusalem will continue to maintain discreet channels of dialogue, while acting in line with its national interests.
Latin America open for diplomatic breakthroughs
AGAINST THE backdrop of mounting international pressure, Sa’ar sees Latin America as one of the areas where Israel can still expand its diplomatic reach. He has declared the current year the “Year of Latin America” at the ministry, arguing that the continent offers significant opportunities for diplomatic breakthroughs.
Colombia is the clearest example. In a relatively short period, Israel moved from a highly strained relationship under former president Gustavo Petro to expanding ties with his successor, including the planned move of Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem.
For Sa’ar, the lesson is that Israel cannot simply wait for election results. He began cultivating relationships before politicians reached power.
He recalled meeting de la Espriella nearly a year before the election, when the future president was still relatively low in the polls.
“You build relationships,” Sa’ar said. “You cultivate relationships.”
He pointed to Honduras as another example of the long-term value of such engagement. Israel sends medical teams there, including ophthalmologists who perform surgeries, while other projects focus on water, agriculture, and health.
For Sa’ar, diplomacy is not limited to UN votes or presidential statements. It is also about building relationships between people and companies.
There is a strategic dimension to that work as well. The Trump administration has placed renewed emphasis on the western hemisphere, Sa’ar noted, giving Israeli engagement in Latin America added significance for Washington.
Still, he acknowledged that the picture is far from uniform. Mexico remains challenging, he said, while other countries in the region are moving in different political directions.
“Even in countries where we have made progress, we still have many more steps to take forward,” he said.
Sa’ar is also advocating a more open approach toward some of Europe’s right-wing political parties, while stressing that dialogue does not automatically mean normalization.
Last week, he praised a speech by Austrian Freedom Party leader Herbert Kickl, calling it significant in part because of its reference to Austria’s Nazi past, expression of regret toward Jews, and positive references to Israel.
For decades, Israel kept its distance from the party because of concerns surrounding its ideological history. Those concerns, Sa’ar said, have not suddenly disappeared.
But he believes Kickl’s speech provides a basis for opening a dialogue.
“This is a decision to conduct dialogue,” he emphasized. “It is still not a decision on normalization.”
The distinction is deliberate. Israel, Sa’ar said, will listen, ask questions, and examine commitments. It will not automatically turn a speech into political recognition.
“We will enter this dialogue with an open mind,” he said.
Ultimately, Sa’ar returned to the argument that has come to define his approach: Israel cannot afford to treat diplomacy as secondary to military power.
During his tenure, he said, the ministry’s budget has increased, five Israeli diplomatic missions have been established, and greater resources have been allocated to public diplomacy and the battle over Israel’s international image.
The importance of that campaign has become especially clear during the war. Israel is confronting military threats, but also diplomatic pressure, economic measures, legal proceedings, and an international campaign over its legitimacy.
Sa'ar focuses on broad narrative battle against Israel
Sa’ar rejected the argument that Israel is responding too slowly to cultural events that portray the country negatively. Referring to the film NAZA, which was screened at the Venice Film Festival and which he said portrayed Israel as committing genocide while comparing it to Nazi Germany, Sa’ar dismissed the idea that the government could simply have prevented the screening.
“What could we have done?” he asked. “Go into the editing rooms and change it?”
For Sa’ar, focusing on a single film misses the larger battle.
“This is not a single item,” he said. “It is part of a much broader war.”
That may be the central idea behind Sa’ar’s tenure at the Foreign Ministry. The battlefield can determine what happens on the ground. But the diplomatic battlefield, he argued, determines how much room for maneuver Israel will have once the fighting stops.

The Jerusalem Har Hotzvim Hi-Tech Park, one of the city's key technology and innovation hubs, completed a NIS 44 million redevelopment project, the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA) and the Jerusalem Municipality announced on Wednesday.
According to the JDA, the project included extensive infrastructure and public service improvements throughout the park, took over six years to complete, and added new technological infrastructure to support security systems.
"Our investment in the park goes far beyond roads, sidewalks and public spaces – it is an investment in thousands of employees, leading companies and the next generation of Jerusalem’s high-tech entrepreneurs," said Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion.
The project will host about 15,000 people on a site measuring approximately 450,000 square meters, with further plans to expand the park to about 800,000 square meters.
Projections indicate the site will host over 25,000 employees from Israeli and international companies, including Intel, Mobileye, Medtronic, Medinol, Elbit Systems, Ophir Optronics, Alpha Tau, and Rafael, which inaugurated its campus in the complex last year.
Jerusalem set to open new hi-tech building complex
The JDA also said the renovations focused on new roads and sidewalks, improved parking facilities, the installation of advanced lighting systems, and a comprehensive upgrade of public spaces.
This will also allow for the establishment of food trucks in some areas of the park, which are expected to begin operations in the coming months.
" As the park continues to expand and attract new companies, we are strengthening Jerusalem’s position as a city of innovation, high-quality employment and opportunity for young people," Lion said.
"Investing in the infrastructure of a technology hub of this scale is a direct investment in Jerusalem’s engines of growth – in the companies operating here, their employees and the city’s ability to continue attracting businesses, entrepreneurs and highly skilled talent," added Zachi Namir, CEO of JDA.
An additional improvement included new landscaped seating areas and wooden decks, improved landscaping around the central plaza, and the installation of underground waste systems that replaced conventional waste containers.
"A stronger high-tech sector means more jobs, greater economic activity, and new opportunities for Jerusalem’s residents. Our goal is to see Har Hotzvim continue to grow and remain a major anchor of Jerusalem’s economy for years to come,” Namir said.

23:34:03 KST

The loan portfolio of international financial service NovaPay (NovaPay brand), part of the Nova Group, reached UAH 2.6 billion, compared with UAH 2 billion as of February 18 this year, the company said in a press release posted on its website.
According to the release, credit cards became the most significant lending product by portfolio volume: since February, the portfolio has grown 61.3% to UAH 1 billion, while installment loans increased by just 11% to UAH 925 million.
As for the portfolio under the "Parcel on Credit" service, it declined 29% to UAH 206 million, while the remainder of the portfolio consists of loans to entrepreneurs, including financing for e-commerce and partners of the Nova group of companies.
According to the company, about 50,000 new customers have used its lending products over the past 12 months.
"About 140,000 customers have already used NovaPay lending products over the entire period of their operation. At the same time, 40% of active borrowers use two or more lending products, while about 42% of customers take out loans repeatedly," the press release quoted Bohdan Hryvko, CEO of NovaPay Credit, as saying.
The financial service specified that the average consumer loan amount is UAH 5,000, while the average credit card limit is UAH 27,500, and the average loan amount for individual entrepreneurs in e-commerce is UAH 422,000.
NovaPay was founded in 2001 as an international financial service that is part of the Nova Group (Nova Poshta) and provides financial services online and offline at Nova Poshta branches.
In 2023, the company became the first non-bank financial institution in Ukraine to receive an extended license from the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU), which allowed it to open accounts and issue cards. It was also the first nonbank organization to launch its own financial application with a broad range of financial services at the end of last year.
NovaPay Credit increased net profit 3.2 times in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period of 2025, to UAH 172.01 million, while revenue increased 2.2 times to UAH 586.42 million.
The company's equity at the end of June amounted to UAH 688.5 million, compared with UAH 516.5 million at the beginning of the year, while liabilities stood at UAH 1.69 billion, compared with UAH 1.37 billion.

'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW speaks with Lithuanian premier Mindaugas Sinkevicius
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:34:00 UTC
23:34:00 KST

Lithuanian prime minister urges stronger NATO air defense
September 25, 2026
Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities.
The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.
For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.
"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.
"Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well."
Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond
Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.
Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.
"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."
For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.
National security climbs national agenda
Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.
"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."
But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.
For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.
The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.
Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.
'We will continue to support Ukraine'
Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.
The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.
"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.
Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.
"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."
Edited by: Jess Smee

Reacting to reports that imprisoned Azerbaijani researcher and peace activist Bahruz Samadov harmed himself during a Supreme Court hearing on 25 September, Natalia Nozadze, Amnesty International’s South Caucasus Researcher, said:
“Azerbaijani authorities are obliged to protect and fulfil Bahruz Samadov’s right to health while he remains unjustly imprisoned. While they continue to deny him access to adequate healthcare, including mental health support, his health condition is worsening. The denial of health care, and the restrictions on family contact, may amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, contrary to Azerbaijan’s international human rights obligations.”

The Azerbaijani authorities must release him immediately and unconditionally.”
Background
On 25 September, Bahruz Samadov used a sharp object to cut his right arm several times during a break in a Supreme Court hearing on 25 September, according to his lawyer, Zibeyda Sadigova.
Bahruz Samadov, an Azerbaijani researcher, peace activist and former OC Media contributor, was arrested in Baku on 21 August 2024. He was charged with “high treason” for his contacts with Armenian nationals in relation to his post-conflict and peace activism. On 23 June 2025, he was sentenced to 15 years in prison following an unfair trial. Amnesty International considers the charges against him fabricated and has repeatedly called for his immediate and unconditional release.

German students take to the streets against compulsory military service plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:30:30 UTC
23:30:30 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
More than 45,000 students across Germany walked out of class on Friday to protest proposals for compulsory military service, after hundreds were summoned for medical exams.
The School Strike Against Conscription initiative said demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities after the German Defense Ministry began calling in 18-year-old men for medical screening. Organizers said hundreds of young men who marked 0 out of 10 for interest in military service were also summoned.
Golo Kirsch, an 18-year-old student from Kiel, said a summons arrived even though they had been told it would not come until next year.
“We were told it was about volunteering, that the medical checks would come in 2027,” he said. “But I already had a summons in my mailbox a year early, and the Bundeswehr (armed forces) says the duty already applies now. We won’t let ourselves be forced into a medical check today, and we won’t go into the barracks tomorrow.”
Students who took to the streets on Friday are demanding a halt to forced medical checks, repeal of the new military service law, and an end to what they call a step-by-step return to a military draft.
Germany’s new military service law, which took effect at the start of 2026, requires all men turning 18 to complete a questionnaire assessing their fitness, skills, and interest in joining the armed forces.
While the system currently remains voluntary, protesters say the government aims to bring back conscription in stages, starting with mandatory questionnaires this year.
Medical screening is mandatory for men born in 2008 or later but is being phased in because capacity is limited. Nationwide exams are due as of mid-2027.
The new military service law aims to address chronic personnel shortages in the German armed forces, which currently have about 186,400 active troops.
Amid growing international crises and efforts to meet NATO goals, the Defense Ministry plans to expand the force to more than 260,000 by 2035. That would require 20,000 recruits each year, and many analysts say it would be difficult to reach that target through a voluntary system alone.
If voluntary recruitment falls short, parliament would have to revisit the law and could consider demand-based or even mandatory conscription.

F1 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: the race in Baku
Kyiv • UNN
George Russell won qualifying for the 15th round of the Formula 1 season in Baku. Verstappen will start eighth, and the race will take place on Saturday due to Memorial Day.
On Saturday, September 26, the main race of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix — the 15th round of the 2026 Formula 1 season — will take place on Baku’s street circuit. This time, the event is being held on an unusual schedule due to the country’s Memorial Day. Following qualifying, Mercedes driver George Russell will start from pole position, ahead of Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) and Oscar Piastri (McLaren), while third-practice winner Max Verstappen will start the race only eighth, reports UNN.
F1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: race weekend schedule
From September 24 to 26, the 15th round of the 2026 Formula 1 season — the Azerbaijan Grand Prix — will take place on the city streets of Baku, opening the first triple-header of the championship.
This time, the race weekend will follow an unusual schedule. Because of Azerbaijan’s Memorial Day, observed on September 27, the main race will take place on Saturday rather than Sunday. Free practice was held on Thursday, while the third practice session and qualifying took place on Friday.
After two consecutive victories in Monza and Madrid, Andrea Kimi Antonelli remains the leader of the drivers’ standings. The Mercedes driver has extended his lead over his teammate George Russell to 81 points. Mercedes also leads the constructors’ championship comfortably — after 14 rounds, the team has 503 points. Ferrari is second with 358 points, while McLaren is third with 306.
Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix: qualifying
Today, September 25, the third practice session of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix took place as part of the 2026 Formula 1 season’s latest round.
Red Bull driver Max Verstappen won the session, Mercedes driver George Russell finished second, and Ferrari representative Lewis Hamilton completed the top three.
The Dutchman finished one-tenth ahead of Russell and Lewis Hamilton, setting a time of 1 min 43.922 sec on the streets of Baku during the final hour of practice, as drivers pushed the limits ahead of qualifying, which will take place later on Friday.
As throughout the season, the teams and drivers were reluctant to head out at the start of the third session, as the track surface in Baku was visibly covered with dust and leaves because of strong winds.
Only after 20 minutes did the leading contenders appear on Pirelli soft tires. Hamilton set a time of 1 min 46.168 sec., before being overtaken by Charles Leclerc with a time of 1 min 45.564 sec.
Kimi Antonelli and Russell took third and fourth places after completing their first fastest laps, but both Mercedes drivers began the final practice session on medium-compound tires.
Later, Mercedes driver George Russell finished first in the qualifying session for the 2026 Formula 1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
