Azerbaijan Grand Prix race: the circuit and features of the Baku round
The Baku circuit — the venue for the Formula 1 Grand Prix, which has already established itself as a successful event — is a purely street circuit that offers a highly entertaining spectacle every year.
The circuit, designed by the famous architect of Formula 1 tracks, is more than six kilometers long, making it one of the longest on the world championship calendar. It has 20 corners, while its width varies from 13 meters at its widest point to just 7.6 meters where it passes through the city’s historic center. The race distance is 51 laps (306.049 km).
The Baku street circuit consists of long straights, narrow sections and sharp corners, making it one of the most challenging tracks on the Formula 1 calendar.
The circuit has a unique layout that includes a narrow uphill section, a narrow castle section and a long flat stretch along the waterfront.

EU agrees on €6.6 billion for Ukraine’s defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

EU agrees on €6.6 billion for Ukraine’s defense
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced this on the social media platform X, Ukrinform reports.
“EU Member States have agreed on the terms for releasing €6.6 billion European Peace Facility funds for Ukraine. That’s good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia,” Kallas said.
According to her, the allocation includes €900 million to fund the EU Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine). Another €1 billion will go toward new joint procurement of defense equipment.
The bulk of the package – €4.7 billion – is intended to reimburse member states for military equipment and weapons already provided to Ukraine. Kallas emphasized that some EU countries have already announced their intention to channel the reimbursement shares they receive directly into further support for Ukraine.
The EU’s foreign policy chief also stressed that the Kremlin’s attempts to intimidate Europe through hybrid attacks are producing the opposite effect.
“Moscow’s hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite,” the diplomat concluded.
As reported, the European Peace Facility (EPF) is an off-budget EU instrument established in March 2021 to finance actions under the Common Foreign and Security Policy, including conflict prevention and strengthening international security.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the EU used the fund for the first time in its history to supply lethal weapons and military equipment to a third country under attack.
The fund is financed through contributions from EU member states in proportion to their GDP. The EPF is used both to partially reimburse EU countries for the cost of weapons transferred to Ukraine from their own arsenals and to finance joint procurement and military training missions. Due to prolonged disagreements and the positions of individual countries, the allocation of a significant portion of the fund’s resources had remained blocked for a long time, requiring additional negotiations to agree on the terms of their disbursement.

Kyiv bids farewell to Mykola Karpiuk: former Kremlin political prisoner killed on the Zaporizhzhia front
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:28:54 EEST
23:28:54 KST

Kyiv bids farewell to Mykola Karpiuk: former Kremlin political prisoner killed on the Zaporizhzhia front
Kyiv • UNN
Mykola Karpiuk was killed on September 19 on the Zaporizhzhia front while carrying out a combat mission. On September 25, a farewell ceremony was held for him in Kyiv.
In Kyiv, on September 25, people bid farewell to serviceman, co-founder of the UNA-UNSO, one of the leaders of the "Right Sector," and former Kremlin political prisoner Mykola Karpiuk. The defender, who spent more than five years in Russian detention, was killed while carrying out a combat mission in the Zaporizhzhia sector, UNN reports.
Details
The funeral ceremony and memorial service were held at St. Michael’s Golden-Domed Monastery. Mykola Karpiuk’s relatives, friends, fellow soldiers, and members of the public came to pay their last respects. Afterward, the funeral procession headed to Independence Square, where a citywide farewell ceremony for the activist and defender was planned.
It is known that Mykola Karpiuk will be buried at Baikove Cemetery. His widow, Olena Karpiuk, previously announced this on social media.
How Mykola Karpiuk died
Mykola Karpiuk was killed on September 19, 2026, at the age of 62. It is known that he was carrying out a combat mission in the Zaporizhzhia sector when he came under enemy fire. The injuries he sustained proved fatal.
On September 20, Karpiuk’s death was publicly reported, among others, by former Deputy Head of the Security Service of Ukraine Viktor Yahun, politician Artur Palatnyi, and civic activist Yurii Honcharenko. Yahun remembered him as a principled person who remained devoted to Ukraine despite the trials he had endured. Honcharenko said that he had spoken with Karpiuk about the history of the creation of UNSO less than a month before his death. They had plans to work together in the autumn.
Mykola Karpiuk joined the ranks of Ukraine’s defenders from the very beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
From civic activism to Russian imprisonment: what is known about the life of the fallen defender
Mykola Karpiuk was born on May 21, 1964, in the village of Velykyi Zhytyn in the Rivne region. After finishing school, he worked as a lathe operator at the Gazotron plant in Rivne and completed his compulsory military service. He later worked at enterprises in Rivne and as a journalist for the newspaper "Nasha Sprava." He headed the Rivne branch of the Ukrainian National Assembly and was one of the leaders and co-founders of UNA-UNSO. In 1998 and 2002, he ran for the Verkhovna Rada on the electoral lists of this political force.
In 2000–2001, he took part in the "Ukraine without Kuchma" campaign. In the case concerning the events of March 9, 2001, he was sentenced to four and a half years in prison. In 2015, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that Karpiuk be paid €3,000 in compensation for violations of his rights during the consideration of his case.
Karpiuk also took part in the Revolution of Dignity and was one of the leaders of the "Right Sector."
In March 2014, Mykola Karpiuk was detained upon entering Russia. In 2016, a Russian court sentenced him to 22.5 years in prison on charges related to the First Chechen War. Karpiuk himself denied taking part in hostilities in Chechnya. The human rights organization "Memorial" recognized him and another defendant in the case, Ukrainian national Stanislav Klykh, as political prisoners.
In September 2019, Karpiuk returned to Ukraine as part of a prisoner exchange.

Rare 17th-century wall paintings restored at Lithuania’s Siesikai Castle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Rare 17th-century wall paintings have been restored at Siesikai Castle in central Lithuania, revealing artwork considered unique not only in the country but across the Baltic region.
The two-year restoration project has opened previously inaccessible spaces to visitors, offering a glimpse into the Renaissance artistic and architectural heritage of the historic castle in Ukmergė district.
Among the discoveries is a 17th-century allegorical scene depicting Glory and History, based on an engraving by Hendrick Goltzius, one of Europe’s most prominent artists of the period. Restorers also uncovered additional scenes dating to the 16th and 17th centuries and based on works by renowned European artists.
“The models that were used reveal such a distinctive Renaissance style. The Siesickiai family must have had this in the castle,” restorer Indrė Valkiūnienė said, referring to the family that owned the castle.
Siesikai Castle is often described as a gem of Renaissance architecture, but Valkiūnienė said its surviving wall paintings make it particularly significant.
“We don’t have surviving residential castles with paintings,” she said. “We have some that have been rebuilt or reconstructed, but we don’t have surviving paintings. So these fragments at Siesikai Castle currently have no equivalent in Lithuania.”
Castle administrator Audris Matulaitis said the secular wall paintings were unlike anything else found in Lithuania.
“Sometimes people are quite sceptical because they see scenes they don’t really understand. At first glance, they aren’t particularly vivid,” he said. “But after a few minutes of conversation, the audience usually falls silent and listens very attentively.”
Daiva Tereščenko, director of the Ukmergė Regional Museum, said the restoration allows visitors to see more of the castle’s authentic interior and understand how many stories remain hidden beneath layers of paint and plaster.
She said the discoveries also place Siesikai Castle more firmly on the European cultural heritage map by revealing connections with European art and ancient mythology.
The restoration of the castle’s wall paintings took two years to complete.

Funding increased for Swiss integration measures
The Swiss government intends to increase spending on integration support by the Confederation and the cantons. Between 2028 and 2032, it plans to allocate CHF5.4 million ($6.5 million) more per year than in the current period.
At its meeting on Friday, the government approved a commitment credit totalling CHF334.5 million. This means that, from 2028, the government is expected to spend CHF66.9 million annually on integration measures.
The government justified its plan by stating that the increase was necessary because more people were benefiting from integration support. Justice Minister Beat Jans outlined the details of the decision at a press conference in Bern on Friday.
According to the information provided, CHF37.3 million per year will go to the cantons for their integration programmes. These programmes focus, among other things, on language support and integration into the labour market. The cantons contribute at least as much funding to the programmes as the federal government.

5 ways India is kicking car safety into top gear with Bharat NCAP 2.0: What buyers need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:26:19 UTC
23:26:19 KST

Current Bharat NCAP phase remains valid until Sept 30, 2027, with proposed introduction of Bharat NCAP 2.0 from Oct 2027
Bharat NCAP 2.0, planned for October 2027, will look beyond what happens when a car crashes. The proposed system will examine the entire safety chain: from how a vehicle helps avoid a collision to how well it protects occupants, pedestrians and other vulnerable road users, and what happens after an accident.Union road transport and highways minister Nitin Gadkari announced the proposed timeline at the SIAM Annual Convention in September 2026. The second phase is being planned as the first phase of Bharat New Car Assessment Programme, or Bharat NCAP, approaches the end of its current cycle.According to the ministry of road transport and highways’ draft AIS-197 Revision 1, the first phase of Bharat NCAP began on October 1, 2023 and is valid until September 30, 2027. The draft revision has been prepared as the framework for Bharat NCAP 2.0.The proposed changes could make the safety rating a much broader measure of a car’s performance, not just in a crash, but before, during and after one.
About Bharat NCAP
What is Bharat NCAP?
Bharat NCAP is India’s own vehicle crash-testing and safety-rating programme. It was formally launched by the ministry of road transport and highways in August 2023 and became operational from October 1, 2023.
The programme applies to type-approved passenger vehicles in the M1 category with a gross vehicle weight of less than 3.5 tonnes. It is voluntary, which means manufacturers can offer eligible vehicles for assessment.The programme is anchored by the Central Institute of Road Transport (CIRT), while testing is carried out through designated agencies with the required infrastructure.At its core, Bharat NCAP gives car buyers a common safety benchmark. A vehicle must already meet mandatory regulatory requirements to be sold in India. Bharat NCAP goes a step further by putting eligible vehicles through specified tests and awarding them a rating of between one and five stars.
India's own car safety assessment programme
The idea is fairly simple: instead of looking only at a car’s price, design or features, buyers get an additional reference point to understand how the vehicle performs in standardised safety tests.The government has also positioned the programme as a way to encourage manufacturers to improve vehicle safety and strengthen the safety standards of cars made in India.
How does the current Bharat NCAP system work?
The existing programme broadly assesses three areas:
Adult Occupant Protection (AOP)
Child Occupant Protection (COP)
Safety Assist Technologies (SAT)
Vehicles are subjected to prescribed crash tests and other assessments. Their performance across these parameters is then used to arrive at the overall star rating.The current framework includes a 64 kmph offset frontal impact test, a 50 kmph side movable deformable barrier test and a pole side impact test, among other checks prescribed under AIS-197.The assessment therefore goes beyond simply asking whether the passenger compartment remains intact.Adult Occupant Protection examines the risk of injury to adults in different crash conditions and seating positions. Child Occupant Protection looks at the protection offered to younger passengers, including the use and installation of child restraint systems.Safety Assist Technologies, meanwhile, covers technologies designed to help prevent crashes or reduce their severity.
Quote
Why are adult and child safety assessed separately?
A car may offer different levels of protection to adults and children, so Bharat NCAP evaluates the two separately.The adult assessment focuses on occupant protection during prescribed crash scenarios, while the child assessment considers how effectively younger occupants are protected and how child restraint systems work within the vehicle.This also means that a car’s overall star rating is not simply a score from one crash test. It reflects performance across several safety parameters.For consumers, the individual scores can therefore provide more information than looking at the star rating alone.
Who tests the cars?
Bharat NCAP is anchored by CIRT, with testing carried out through designated testing agencies that have the required facilities.The wider automotive testing ecosystem includes agencies such as the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) and the International Centre for Automotive Technology (ICAT).Manufacturers submit eligible vehicles for assessment under the programme. The existing framework specifies procedures around the variant selected for testing, including provisions concerning the base variant of a model.That distinction matters when reading a Bharat NCAP result. A rating should not automatically be assumed to apply to every variant of a model unless the official assessment covers those variants.
Four assessments of NCAP
Bharat NCAP ratings
Bharat NCAP ratings range from one to five stars. A higher rating indicates stronger performance under the programme’s prescribed assessment criteria.But a five-star rating is not a guarantee that occupants will escape injury in every real-world crash. NCAP testing is conducted under standardised conditions and is intended to provide a basis for comparing vehicle safety performance.It is also important to distinguish Bharat NCAP from the mandatory certification requirements for selling a vehicle in India.Bharat NCAP is voluntary and is designed to provide consumers with additional information beyond the mandatory regulatory framework. A vehicle being tested or rated under Bharat NCAP should therefore not be confused with regulatory approval.Since its launch, Bharat NCAP has increasingly become part of the safety conversation around new car launches. The ratings have also become a factor in how manufacturers present their vehicles to consumers, particularly as safety becomes a more visible consideration in the passenger-vehicle market.
What do the stars represent?
So, what changes with Bharat NCAP 2.0?
This is where the proposed second phase takes a much wider approach.The draft AIS-197 Revision 1 divides Bharat NCAP 2.0 into five safety verticals:
Safe driving
Crash avoidance
Crash protection
Vulnerable road user protection
Post-crash safety
The change is significant because the current system focuses mainly on occupant protection and safety-assist technologies, while the proposed framework looks at the complete safety chain.The draft framework uses a 100-point assessment structure, with Crash Protection accounting for 55% of the assessment. The remaining weightage covers the other safety areas.In other words, the crash itself will still be a major part of the rating, but it will no longer be the only part of the safety story.
Five crash tests in the proposed new framework
Bharat NCAP 2.0 proposes expanding the Crash Protection assessment to five mandatory crash tests:
64 kmph offset frontal impact against a deformable barrier
50 kmph frontal impact against a full-width rigid barrier
50 kmph lateral impact against a mobile deformable barrier
32 kmph oblique side impact against a rigid pole
50 kmph rear impact against a mobile rigid barrier
Adult and child occupant protection will continue to be assessed separately.The addition of full-width frontal and rear-impact tests means the proposed system will examine crash scenarios beyond the core tests in the existing framework.That gives the second phase a wider testing footprint and allows different types of impacts to form part of the overall safety assessment.
Not just about surviving crash
One of the biggest differences in Bharat NCAP 2.0 is that the programme is designed to look at what happens before a crash as well.Crash Avoidance is one of the five proposed verticals. It focuses on technologies and vehicle characteristics that can help prevent a collision or reduce its severity.
Your guide to safer cars
Safe Driving is another proposed category, widening the assessment beyond the vehicle’s passive protection features.Together, these categories shift the focus from simply asking, “How well does this car perform when it crashes?” to a broader question: “How does this vehicle contribute to safety across different stages of a road incident?”Bharat NCAP 2.0 also proposes a separate Vulnerable Road User Protection category. This brings pedestrians and other vulnerable road users more directly into the safety assessment.The proposed framework also asks a different question: what happens once the collision has taken place?Post-Crash Safety is one of the five proposed assessment areas. Minister Gadkari described Bharat NCAP 2.0 as covering the entire safety chain, including post-crash evacuation and care. “We are going to evaluate the entire crash chain,” Gadkari said, adding that new technologies developed globally as well as by startups would be considered under the programme.This means the assessment is intended to extend beyond the instant of impact and examine safety considerations in the period immediately after a crash.It adds another layer to the programme’s approach: avoiding the crash where possible, protecting people during the impact, and addressing safety after the collision.
What does Bharat NCAP mean for car buyers?
For buyers, Bharat NCAP offers an additional way to compare cars beyond mandatory safety requirements.A consumer can look at a vehicle’s overall rating as well as its adult and child protection performance and the safety technologies considered in the assessment.The rating is not meant to replace other factors involved in buying a car. Price, size, fuel efficiency, features, driving requirements and other considerations remain relevant, but the proposed 2.0 framework would expand that information further.Buyers could eventually have a broader picture of how a car performs across crash protection, crash avoidance, safe driving, vulnerable-road-user protection and post-crash safety.Bharat NCAP is one part of a much larger road-safety challenge, focusing on the structure of vehicles. Vehicle design and safety technology can influence the outcome of a crash, but they cannot address every reason why accidents happen.The ministry has identified several factors associated with road crashes, including speeding, mobile-phone use, drunken driving, wrong-side driving, lane indiscipline, jumping red lights and failure to use helmets and seat belts. Vehicle condition, road conditions and weather can also play a role.
Several countries have their own NCAPS
Government data recorded 1,68,491 road accident fatalities in 2022.Bharat NCAP therefore addresses one part of this wider equation: the safety performance of vehicles. Its proposed second phase would broaden that role by looking at what a vehicle can do to help avoid crashes, how it protects people when a crash occurs, how it protects vulnerable road users and what happens afterwards.
The bottom line
The current Bharat NCAP phase remains valid until September 30, 2027. The government has proposed introducing Bharat NCAP 2.0 from October 2027, with the draft AIS-197 Revision 1 serving as the framework for the next phase.The proposed transition would take India’s vehicle safety-rating system from a relatively focused crash and occupant-protection programme to a broader safety assessment.
The familiar one-to-five-star rating would remain the consumer-facing language of vehicle safety, but the assessment behind it is set to become much more comprehensive.The bigger shift is in the question Bharat NCAP is trying to answer. Instead of looking only at how a car performs when it is involved in a crash, the proposed system would examine the vehicle’s safety journey from avoiding a collision to protecting occupants and vulnerable road users, and supporting safety after the crash.That could give Indian car buyers a wider set of safety information to consider when choosing their next vehicle.

Bulgaria’s opposition Democratic Bulgaria party on Friday questioned the government over what it described as conflicting statements by President Iliana Iotova and the Foreign Ministry about whether the country endorsed a UN declaration on Ukraine, Bulgarian news agency BTA reported.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as the EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Kaja Kallas, have said that Bulgaria has joined the UN declaration on Ukraine. President Iliana Iotova says that Bulgaria has not joined it,” Democratic Bulgaria floor leader Nadejda Iordanova told journalists, according to the party.
“This situation is absurd; two institutions in Bulgaria cannot put forward contradictory statements on what exactly the country's position on this issue is,” she said.
Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that the country had endorsed the declaration in support of European unity, while stressing that its national position was not fully reflected in the document. It also said Iotova had presented Bulgaria’s position in her address to the UN General Assembly.
Earlier Friday, the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party rejected two proposals by Democratic Bulgaria to hold a parliamentary hearing involving the foreign minister or a relevant deputy minister over the issue.
Democratic Bulgaria said the conflicting statements “tarnish Bulgaria’s name.”
“We will insist that it be clarified whether President Iotova believes that Kaja Kallas is lying,” Iordanova said, calling the situation “a major scandal and a disgrace for our country.”
Iordanova said countries endorsing such declarations normally have an opportunity to discuss the text before a final version is circulated.
“A country that does not wish to support the document must make an explicit statement to that effect,” she said.
“Clearly, Bulgaria has not made such a statement. So here they are trying to hide the answer to the big question — where does Bulgaria stand on this issue? — behind procedural arguments,” Iordanova said.
Iotova said Thursday that the declaration had not been signed and that Bulgaria had not been given an opportunity to express reservations or seek amendments to the text. She said she did not attend an expanded UN Security Council meeting because of the issue.
In her UN General Assembly address, Iotova said there was “no military solution” to the war in Ukraine and that peace could not be achieved without the participation of both Ukraine and Russia.
The declaration calls on Russia to agree to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire in Ukraine and to begin substantive peace negotiations.
Bulgaria is listed among the countries endorsing the declaration, according to the document cited by BTA.

‘We will get stuff done’: Burnham seeks to banish ghosts of Starmerism at Labour conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:25:25 UTC
23:25:25 KST

Andy Burnham was not even in the audience for the prime minister’s speech at the Labour party conference this time last year. As Keir Starmer made the case for continuity to his restive party, Burnham was spotted slipping out over the bridge towards Liverpool’s Albert Dock.
The then Greater Manchester mayor had been vying for the spotlight throughout the party’s annual gathering, presenting the argument for change. But even he could not have envisaged the schism that would take place in the ensuing 12 months and would put him on the main stage as prime minister at this year’s conference, beginning in Merseyside on Sunday.
At the time, Starmer retained a tentative grip on the party, while Burnham was mocked for leaving Liverpool with his tail between his legs, awkward and abashed, especially over his controversial comments about the government being too “in hock” to the bond markets.
But below the surface, disquiet was starting to take shape in the party. Several cabinet ministers confided privately in Liverpool last year that they believed Burnham would ultimately be seen as the party’s Cassandra: comically ham-fisted, but nonetheless telling hard truths about the party’s problems.
After he succeeded Starmer in the top job in July, Burnham has made “Hope again” his conference slogan, with No 10 strategists pitching this year’s event as a definitive break with the past.
Burnham has been promising to defy the political and economic consensus of the last 40 years since he was elected as MP for Makerfield in a byelection that proved to be the final domino for Starmer’s faltering leadership, and he will use this conference to set out how he aims to do this.
It will also attempt to break old habits in the Labour party’s way of doing business, which has often been hindered by pessimism, fear and factionalism. Cynics in the party will wonder if this effort can withstand current economic pressures, given soaring borrowing costs.
Hayden Munro, Burnham’s new political director, has told cabinet ministers and special advisers they must defy such cynics, and every message they send must be about how there is renewed faith in Britain.
Munro, a former strategist for Jacinda Ardern, who colleagues say is the “in-house hype man”, told them the theme of conference would be how help was coming for ordinary working people.
Burnham’s government would put care of people as the first consideration, he told them, restoring “the right values” – a nod to the widespread fears in Labour about the rise of overt racism across the political sphere.
Ministers have been tasked with announcing policies that deliver immediate breathing room for families, but also long-term plans and investment to make everyday life easier and more affordable, with a particular focus on public control of essential services. Burnham will emphasise again that he intends to deliver the biggest change to Britain in 40 years.
But the other theme of the conference will be courage, that this will finally be a government that will fix problems long been thought to be intractable: rough sleeping, social care, and youth inactivity.
“‘It’s too hard’ will no longer be used as a justification for not acting,” Munro wrote in his note to advisers. “We will get stuff done.”
Addressing the Labour conference in Liverpool is a kind of homecoming for Burnham, even though he is most closely associated with Manchester. He was born in its suburbs, it is where he had his formative political awakening on the Hillsborough injustice, and the area where he returned just a fortnight ago in tragic circumstances, after his father’s death from Alzheimer’s.
Burnham writes all of his own speeches and has spent the last few weeks, in between meetings and travelling by train between London and Manchester, working through his ideas. He told reporters at the UN general assembly in New York this week that his conference speech would be his own political philosophy spelled out in primary colours.
“I keep saying: ‘Nobody won’t know what I’m trying to do.’ People will know, you can make your judgment on whether it’s right or wrong. But people are going to know the direction I want to take this country in,” he said.
This approach marks a definitive break with Starmerism. One Labour strategist said: “If we achieve one thing at this conference, it will be that no one will ever say about Andy Burnham what they said about Keir Starmer. You can never say ‘we don’t know what he stands for’.”
Burnham is the beneficiary of a gentler political landscape than Starmer was a year ago, when Reform and the rapid rise of far-right demonstrations had dominated the summer. Labour had been sinking in the polls even before the scandal-fuelled resignations of Angela Rayner and Peter Mandelson just weeks before the event.
Going into conference now, Labour is in the lead with all pollsters for the first time since October 2024, partly thanks to Burnham’s own bounce but also as a result of declining trust in Reform after a series of scandals.
There is very little appetite for rebellion among the Labour rank and file who have often made it awkward for Labour leaders with votes on the conference floor. “It is going to be very boring,” one senior party figure said. “Everyone is desperate to make it work.”
Activists will be pushing for conference to commit to a commission on electoral reform, which Burnham has said he will put in Labour’s next manifesto but which strategists do not want to make a major topic of his first months in office. At least three dozen local parties have submitted motions on the subject, more than on any single policy issue since conference rules were tightened in 2023, making it likely it will be one of the priority topics for debate.
The only other unwelcome surprise would be an emergency motion on Israel and Palestine. Ministers had hoped Ed Miliband’s announcement of sweeping sanctions against West Bank settlements would be an answer to calls for Labour to take a much more robust position on Israel.
But party staff believe something more could come when emergency motions are tabled this weekend. “There is always another demand, and conference will always vote for almost anything put in front of it on this,” another senior figure said. “The unions have very left policy mandates.”
Most of the exiled former cabinet ministers and Starmer loyalists are swerving conference this year – the exception being Darren Jones, the former chief secretary to the prime minister, who will take part in some keenly watched fringes. But few have his inclination. One ex-minister said he did not feel welcome.
“No one wants a spectre at the feast,” he said. “Any appearance is going to attract some unwelcome attention. I do think more of us will start to speak out, whether on oil and gas, on the economy, maybe on Europe, but frankly doing that at conference is too unhelpful – even if it’s the kind of tactic that Andy himself has been doing for years.”
Many said they saw it as a chance for a break. One former minister close to Starmer compared himself to Arsenal’s Declan Rice, who played more minutes last season than any other English footballer but who will now sit out England’s matches over the international break. “I haven’t had a rest in about six years. I think it makes sense to miss the first Labour conference in about 15 years,” he said.
There will be time for interventions – helpful or otherwise – in the coming months. Conference is the first of four phases that No 10 views as opportunities for Burnham to seize public attention and set direction. After that will be the budget, his 10-year plan expected later in the autumn, and then the spending review next year.
But if conference gives Burnham another poll boost, it will add to the chatter in Westminster that he could decide to call a general election sooner rather than later.
“Conference could be make-or-break for that decision,” one MP said. “If the left looks united, if the polls continue as they are – and if we then beat [the Greens’ Zack] Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras then there will never be a better time.”
Most cabinet ministers are wary. “Why are we here if not to use this majority we have got to improve the country?” one said. “If we are saying we are here to get things done, then let’s do them now.”
For now, Burnham seems to agree. Speaking to broadcasters before the conference, he said he was “not particularly” tempted to call an election. “I see all the speculation and it just races ahead,” he told BBC West’s political editor, Paul Barltrop.
“The time has come: draw a line, get the country looking forward, pulling together, people feeling a bit of hope in their lives again. That’s what I’m trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period rather than putting people back into an election cycle.”

Was Netanyahu's fiery U.N. speech aimed at his own political survival?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:25:21 UTC
23:25:21 KST

Netanyahu lashed Mamdani in fiery U.N. speech, but real aim was his own political survival, analyst says
In a mass visual rebuke for the world to see, hundreds of delegates walked out of the United Nations General Assembly Thursday just as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stepped up to the podium.
He delivered a fiery speech defending the seven-month war on Iran launched jointly by the U.S. and Israel, rejected allegations of genocide in Gaza and attacked New York City's first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani.
"If there are any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall, please do so now," exhorted Netanyahu, as diplomats from more than 70 nations were in the process of walking out.
But one veteran Israeli political analyst told CBS News on Friday that Netanyahu's primary goal in making the speech was shoring up his political position back home, with Israelis being his main intended audience.
Israel is set to hold legislative elections on Oct. 27. Netanyahu and his right-wing coalition government — the most far-right in modern Israeli history — are trailing in the polls.
Yaakov Katz, former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, said Netanyahu's address was very deliberately planned to counter that trend.
"People look at the hostility and they say, 'Oh, Netanyahu is not popular. People are walking out.' Israelis, I think, look at this and they say to themselves: 'The world is against us no matter what, but thank God we have a leader, in this case, Netanyahu, who can stand up to everyone and stick it to them,'" Katz told CBS News.
"That could bring him some votes, or at the very least consolidate the base," he added.
The Israeli leader also used Mamdani as a foil, labeling him antisemitic and claiming "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
"This plays out well, because Israelis look at people like Mamdani and they don't see much of a difference, whether it's Mamdani or it's President Erdogan of Turkey," said Katz, referring to another regular target of Netanyahu's ire, "or it's some other tent encampment or protest on the streets of Sydney or Paris or London. It's one and the same."
Hundreds of people who strongly disagree joined a protest near U.N. headquarters in New York on Thursday. Police arrested dozens of people denouncing both Netanyahu and the U.S. government for continuing to sell weapons to Israel.
Many of the protesters identified as American or Israeli Jews. Some held up signs calling Netanyahu a terrorist, while others repeated the accusation, made by a panel of U.N. experts last year, as well as Mamdani and numerous others, that Israeli actions in Gaza amount to genocide against the Palestinian people.
Since Hamas sparked the Gaza war with its Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killing more than 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage, Israeli operations in Gaza have killed more than 73,000 people, according to the latest U.N. report, citing data compiled by Gaza's health ministry. Israel has always rejected the death toll figures reported by Gazan authorities, but it has not offered its own estimation of the cost of its war in the Palestinian territory in human lives.
"What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? That's a ton for every person," retorted Netanyahu on Thursday, calling the accusation of genocide by Israel "the greatest lie of the century."
There have been periods since Oct. 7, 2023, however, when Israel did restrict supplies of food and other basic goods to Gaza, and in March 2025, Israel enacted a blockade of the densely packed Palestinian territory, freezing shipments of food, fuel, medicine and other goods, that lasted nearly three months.
In August last year, a U.N.-backed global hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, confirmed famine conditions in Gaza for the first time in the Middle East.
Israel's near-total blockade was eventually eased, under international pressure, and Israel started allowing a trickle of supplies into Gaza, which it says has increased steadily.
Responding to Netanyahu's denial that Israel had committed genocide, Mamdani doubled down on the allegation and said Netanyahu had used his U.N. speech to "repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians." The mayor also said no lie could change the fact that Netanyahu remained the subject of an ICC arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Katz told CBS News the Israeli leader's speech may not have done much to move the political needle at home, and he added that Netanyahu's biggest hope is for President Trump to endorse him, which he has not.
"Netanyahu is in the United States, is in New York, tried to get a meeting with President Trump. He would have gone down to D.C. for it, but was not able to get the White House to confirm any time or facetime between the prime minister and the president," he said.
Mr. Trump has, however, recently posted a poll on social media that shows Netanyahu's political fortunes improving slightly.
"So, it still seems that there is that romance that might still remain between these two leaders," said Katz. "Will that lead to a full endorsement? Don't know, but there's still a month left for the Israeli election, and Netanyahu is definitely praying and hoping that Trump comes out more vocally in his support."
Netanyahu did name-check the president in his address, saying that in Israel's "battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump."
The Israeli leader will now be hoping his greatest partner will help keep him in power.

According to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Marat Berdyev, this demonstrates the importance Russia attaches to developing economic ties with its partners in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly China.

Why Hawaii is facing an unprecedented hurricane season
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:24:36 UTC
23:24:36 KST

For the third time this year, Hawaii is under a hurricane watch—that’s never happened before. Hurricane Nolo, currently south of the Big Island, could mark the first time three storms have ever come within 50 miles of the archipelago in a single year. Both firsts are a marker of what an unprecedented hurricane season this has been for the state, brought about by an exceptionally strong El Niño and a dose of bad luck.
As of Friday morning, Nolo is about 200 miles south of the Big Island, moving slowly northward. Because of an area of high pressure developing to the island’s north, it is expected to take a sharp westward turn as a Category 3 storm on Saturday morning. Nolo’s exact track is uncertain, but the storm is expected to avoid a direct landfall. Nevertheless, it will once again bring torrential rains and devastating mudslides—parts of the Big Island could see 35 inches of rain. Many of the areas expected to see the heaviest downpours were already devastated by the 40 inches dumped by Hurricane Lala in August.
The other storm that brushed the islands this season was Hurricane Lowell, which struck Kauai and Niihau, the westernmost islands in the chain, in early September.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Despite its tropical clime, Hawaii rarely sees tropical cyclones (the blanket term for tropical storms, hurricanes and typhoons). For one thing, the ocean waters around it are typically too cold to support the convection that fuels these storms. And any systems that do get close are often torn apart by wind shear, or winds blowing in different directions at different heights in the atmosphere.
But it can happen. And storms are more likely around Hawaii when there’s an El Niño—the cyclical climate event that shifts a pool of warm water in the equatorial Pacific Ocean eastward. That push alters where heat is released into the atmosphere, which causes a cascade of changes to prevailing wind patterns and weather around the world. It tends to lessen shear in the eastern Pacific, which makes the region a hotbed of hurricane activity, as it has been this year (meanwhile the Atlantic has been notably quiet).
But even a strong El Niño isn’t a guarantee that Hawaii will see storms—after all, it’s a small area of land in a vast ocean, so it’s not an easy target to hit. The hurricane season of 2015 was exceptionally active because of a strong El Niño, but it just happened that only one storm came particularly close to the islands.
For Hawaii, only a handful of years have seen multiple close calls with storms. Three hurricanes came within 100 miles of Hawaii in 1957 (another El Niño year), says Phil Klotzbach, citing National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data. Two hurricanes came within that distance in 1959, 2014 and 2016. Nolo is expected to stay about 150 miles south of the Big Island, but if the path changes and it ventures closer, 2026 would be only the second year three such storms have brushed so close to the islands.
Even more remarkably, if it came within 50 miles of the islands, it would be the third to do so this year, which has never happened before, wrote meteorologist Michael Lowry in a blog post. Only six hurricanes have ever come that close to the islands and none within the same year. “This amounts to three decades worth of hurricane threats to Hawaii in one year,” Lowry wrote. But even having had two come that close in one year is remarkable.

Russia changes tactics for deporting Ukrainian children, moving them in smaller groups
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
17:24:00 EEST
23:24:00 KST

Russia changes tactics for deporting Ukrainian children, moving them in smaller groups
Russia continues to remove Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories, but their tactics have changed compared to the first years of the full-scale war.
Source: Maksym Maksymov, the head of Bring Kids Back UA initiative, in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine, a Ukrainian news agency
Details: Instead of large-scale transfers, the Kremlin-appointed occupation authorities are increasingly moving children in smaller groups, sending them to "holiday camps", separating them from their parents during filtration procedures and appointing Russian guardians.
As of 18 September 2026, Ukraine had verified 20,651 cases involving the deportation or forced transfer of Ukrainian children, Bring Kids Back UA reported. However, Ukraine does not know the exact number of children Russia has removed or is holding in occupied territories.
Maksymov said only Russia has the full data, which it does not share, while also changing children's personal details.
Quote: "Verifying a single case is a complex and lengthy process: it requires confirming the child's identity, the circumstances of their transfer, the status of their parents and who their legal representative is in Ukraine.
And this has to be done by comparing several independent sets of data because we receive nothing from Russia. That is why the number of verified cases is increasing slowly."
More details: As of 21 September 2026, Ukraine had brought back 2,616 children, Maksymov said. Of these, 673 had returned since the beginning of this year.
The pace of returns also changed this year: 248 children were brought back by the end of May, while another 425 returned between late May and 21 September.
Ukraine does not release return figures by oblast. Maksymov said this is for security reasons, as details about a particular oblast or return operation could put children, their families and experts working on a case at risk and disrupt operations that are still under way.
How has Russia's approach changed?
Maksymov said that in 2022-2023, one of the main methods involved moving children en masse in a single group, including from boarding schools, children's homes and hospitals.
Now, he said, children are moved in smaller groups, while some do not need to be physically taken out of Russian-occupied territories at all.
Other methods now include:
- sending children to Russian "holiday camps"
- sending them to Russia purportedly for "education"
- separating children from their parents during filtration
- appointing Russian guardians
- subsequently placing children under guardianship, with foster families or for adoption.
Quote: "Some of these transfers are presented as supposedly voluntary. Parents are threatened with losing parental rights or having their child taken away if the child does not attend a Russian school, take part in militarised programmes or go to camps.
"So the parents' formal 'consent' is very often the result of coercion rather than a genuine choice."
More details: Maksymov said another mechanism introduced in 2026 is a new requirement concerning guardianship papers. Under the rules he described, guardianship, custody and adoption documents issued before 30 September 2022 must be reissued by the Kremlin-appointed occupation administration on presentation of a Russian passport. If this requirement is not met, a child may be removed from the family and placed in a Russian boarding school or children's home.
Quote: "The child is placed in the care of whoever the occupation authorities appoint. If the parents have been killed, gone missing, are in captivity, have been separated from the child or deprived of parental rights, the occupation administration appoints a Russian legal representative.
From that point on, all decisions concerning the child are made by whoever is effectively responsible for them. If the child is in an institution, its director may act as that representative and, for example, decide that the child will become a Russian citizen."

Finnish President Urges Musk to Expand Starlink So Ukraine Can Strike Russian Missile Launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:22:19 UTC
23:22:19 KST

- Category
- World
Finnish President Urges Musk to Expand Starlink So Ukraine Can Strike Russian Missile Launchers
Finnish President Alexander Stubb urged Elon Musk on September 24 to expand Starlink coverage over Russian territory so Ukraine can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers, Reuters reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Stubb made the appeal in an interview with Reuters in New York, where world leaders had gathered for the United Nations General Assembly.
He argued that expanded Starlink coverage could help Ukraine locate and target mobile launchers operating from Russian territory before they fire missiles.
According to Reuters, Starlink currently does not operate over Russian territory.
Ukrainian officials believe enabling the service there would allow Ukrainian weapons to strike mobile ballistic missile launchers located within several hundred kilometers of the border.
Stubb said allowing Ukraine to use Starlink in areas where ballistic missile launchers operate, including temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and Russia, could save lives.
He argued that the capability could, “to a certain extent,” serve as a form of air defense by helping Ukraine target launchers before missiles are fired.
The appeal comes as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy and heating infrastructure.
Reuters reported that Russian ballistic missile strikes reached record levels during the summer, while Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptors.
Ukraine’s Patriot systems are currently its only available air-defense capability capable of intercepting such ballistic missiles, Reuters reported.
Interceptor stocks remain severely depleted, while additional supplies are uncertain.
Stubb identified three priorities for Ukraine ahead of winter: strengthening air defenses, protecting energy infrastructure, and securing financing.
He also said Finland was preparing a winter support package, adding that he did not expect the war to end before the season begins.
During the interview, Stubb also discussed possible paths toward ending the war.
He said an unconditional ceasefire would be the simplest starting point, followed by negotiations over security guarantees, territorial issues, reconstruction, and compensation.
Stubb said another possible outcome would be to freeze the war along the current line of contact, with 30-kilometer buffer zones on each side.
He also pointed to a more limited ceasefire that would cover energy- and grain-related targets as another option.
The Finnish president’s appeal follows earlier Ukrainian efforts to secure expanded Starlink access for operations against Russian missile launchers.
In late July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked US President Donald Trump during closed-door White House talks to help secure Musk’s approval for expanded Starlink use, The Atlantic reported at the time.
The proposal was intended to help Ukraine target mobile Russian ballistic missile launchers before winter.
Trump gave no firm commitment during the meeting and said he would consider the request and discuss it with Musk, according to officials cited in the earlier reporting.

Internal Watchdog says Data Leaks and Bribery Push French Police Misconduct Cases to Five-Year High
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:22:00 UTC
23:22:00 KST

Reported by
Offenses involving corruption, influence peddling, and other integrity violations within the French National Police surged by 45 percent between 2024 and 2025, reaching their highest level in five years, according to an internal oversight report released this week.
The annual assessment by the General Inspectorate of the National Police, or IGPN, recorded 341 integrity breaches in 2025, up from 234 the previous year. The infractions encompassed bribery, conflicts of interest, embezzlement of public funds, extortion, breaches of professional secrecy, and the unauthorized handling of sensitive personal data.
The oversight agency reported steep increases across three primary categories: unauthorized queries of police databases, which jumped by 80 percent; corruption offenses, which rose by 33 percent; and breaches of professional secrecy, which increased by 25 percent.
Stéphane Hardouin, the head of the IGPN, acknowledged the sharp rise in misconduct. “There was a significant increase in breaches of integrity,” Hardouin said, pointing specifically to the rise in corruption and database misuse.
The report categorized the motives behind the offenses into three main drivers: financial gain, personal or emotional relationships, and actions carried out under the belief of serving “a just cause.”
In 2025, the watchdog conducted 235 judicial investigations into integrity breaches. These included 88 cases of corruption, five for the misappropriation of public funds, three for influence peddling, and two for extortion by a public official.
However, the degree to which these investigations led to actual punishment remains unclear. In a statement to OCCRP, the communications service of the National Police Directorate noted that while the IGPN conducts extensive inquiries, the oversight body lacks decision-making power, making it impossible to determine how many cases resulted in formal disciplinary action or criminal convictions.

Turkish foreign minister attends informal meeting of his Organization of Turkic States counterparts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:20:42 UTC
23:20:42 KST

Sumeyye Dilara Dincer, Gizem Nisa Demir
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Friday attended an informal meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s current high-level week. 
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, Fidan took part in the informal meeting of the OTS Council of Foreign Ministers in New York. 
The meeting, which marked another high-level contact amid a recent acceleration in engagements within the OTS, was attended by Türkiye, OTS Chair Azerbaijan, as well as other member states Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, observer states the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) and Turkmenistan, and OTS Secretary-General Kubanychbek Omuraliev. 
Preparations for the 13th OTS Summit, which Türkiye is set to host in the capital Ankara on Oct. 29-30, were discussed during the meeting. 
The participants also exchanged views on global and regional issues concerning the Turkic world and discussed ways to develop the organization's institutional cooperation with international organizations. 
In his address, Fidan emphasized the importance of Turkic states acting in close coordination and on the basis of common understanding in the face of global and regional challenges, while outlining Türkiye's vision for boosting the OTS' effectiveness and visibility at the international level. 
A joint statement adopted at the meeting by the OTS Council of Foreign Ministers emphasized, among other issues, the importance of the organization obtaining observer status at the UN General Assembly. 
The statement also included messages aimed at strengthening the OTS' roles internationally and enhancing its capacity to establish institutional relations with international and regional actors. 
The meeting was the fourth informal meeting of the OTS Council of Foreign Ministers held this year, following meetings in Istanbul on March 7, in Antalya on April 18 on the sidelines of Türkiye’s fifth Antalya Diplomacy Forum, and in Turkistan, Kazakhstan, on May 15 on the sidelines of an informal OTS summit. 
OTS membership and next month’s Ankara summit 
The OTS has five members -- Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan -- and four observers: Hungary, Turkmenistan, the TRNC, and the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO). 
The organization was established as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States in 2009 by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan, and changed its name to the Organization of Turkic States at its 2021 summit in Istanbul. 
The OTS' main objectives include strengthening mutual trust among Turkic states, enhancing political solidarity, developing economic and technical cooperation, and preserving and promoting the historical and cultural heritage of the Turkic world. 
The organization's secretariat is based in Istanbul.
The next OTS summit is scheduled to take place in Ankara on Oct. 29-30, with Türkiye hosting. Türkiye is also expected to take over the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan at the summit.
The position of OTS secretary-general is also expected to pass from the current secretary-general, Kubanychbek Omuraliev of Kyrgyzstan, to a candidate designated by Uzbekistan.

Nearly 1.5 million displaced in Haiti as violence spreads, UN says
Sept 25 - Haiti's displacement crisis is spreading beyond the capital, with nearly 1.5 million people uprooted across the country, the International Organization for Migration said in a report published on Friday.
• Nearly 80% of those internally displaced are now located outside the capital of Port-au-Prince, with the sharpest recent displacement increase in Artibonite department, once considered a refuge for families fleeing violence elsewhere, the report said.
• Armed gangs in Haiti have near-total control over Port-au-Prince and have been expanding into rural areas.
• Displacement in Artibonite rose between May and August 2026, as escalating insecurity forced new waves of movement and reduced safe options for the affected population, the IOM said
• Near the capital, recent armed attacks in Kenscoff displaced more than 4,000 people, with reports of homes burned, kidnappings and killings, the report said.
• Hundreds of thousands of displaced people are living in informal settlements, collective sites or other precarious conditions, increasing their vulnerability during the Atlantic hurricane season, the IOM said.
• "For families already displaced by violence, a major storm could trigger another humanitarian emergency," IOM Haiti Senior Emergency Coordinator Elise Verron said in the report. REUTERS

The court upheld Iryna Mudra’s complaint regarding the possible blocking of bail payments. The NBU must check the banks and report within 24 hours.
The investigating judge of the HACC upheld the defense’s complaint regarding the violation of Iryna Mudra’s rights while in custody, so the court ordered the NBU to investigate possible refusals to process payments for posting bail for the former official. This was reported by the High Anti-Corruption Court, as reported by UNN.
Details
According to the information available, the HACC upheld the complaint regarding the violation of the rights of Iryna Mudra, the former deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, who is currently being held in custody.
The court ruled to request from the National Bank of Ukraine and provide the suspect’s defense attorneys, no later than within 24 hours, with information and copies of documents concerning any letters, recommendations, or other communications with banks and payment service providers regarding payments designated as "bail," the HACC’s deposit account concerning the suspect, as well as notifications received by the NBU regarding mass refusals based on the relevant details
In addition, pursuant to the court’s ruling, the NBU must, within the scope of its powers of state regulation and supervision of the payments market, immediately, but no later than within 24 hours of receiving the ruling:
-  verify the facts of categorical blocking of payments to the HACC’s deposit account designated as “bail” for the former deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; 
-  assess whether payment service providers comply with the requirements of the Law of Ukraine “On Payment Services” regarding the possibility of posting bail for the suspect in the criminal proceedings; 
-  take the measures prescribed by law in response if an unjustified refusal to pay bail is identified based solely on the type of payment, the recipient, or the IBAN; 
-  ensure that payment service providers have actually accessible channels for accepting bail for the suspect and for processing duly completed payment instructions from bail providers in the criminal proceedings. 
According to the court’s ruling, the NBU is required to inform the HACC and the defense of the former deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine about the measures taken regarding the submission of the payment instruction and documents, as well as about the results of the investigation, no later than within 24 hours after carrying out this part of the ruling

Suspect in 2022 Paris murder of Argentine rugby star Aramburu begs forgiveness

Paris court convicts two for 2022 murder of Argentine rugby star Aramburu
A Paris court on Friday sentenced the two main suspects in the 2022 murder of Argentine rugby player Federico Martin Aramburu to prison terms. Loik Le Priol, who fired the fatal shots, was sentenced to 26 years while Romain Bouvier, who fired first, was sentenced to 19 years. Both men had links to the far right.
A French court on Friday convicted two far-right activists over the 2022 killing in Paris of former Argentine rugby international Federico Martin Aramburu.
It sentenced Loik Le Priol, a 32-year-old ex-soldier who fired the fatal shots, to 26 years in jail, while the other defendant Romain Bouvier, 35, got 19 years behind bars.
Earlier on Friday, Le Priol asked forgiveness from the victim's family as the trial concluded.
Read morePolice arrest two main suspects in Paris murder of Argentinian rugby star Aramburu
Aramburu was killed at age 42 after a successful career that saw him play 22 times for Argentina and become a firm favourite in France's Basque Country following a stint with local southwestern side Biarritz, where he later lived.
"I am a Christian, just like you," Le Priol told Aramburu's family as the trial concluded. "The pope is in Paris today," he continued, referring to Pope Leo XIV's visit to France. "I don't know if it's a sign, but I hope that one day they will find the strength to forgive me, and that I, too, will find the strength to forgive myself."
He said the requested sentence of 27 years was "staggering – it's the age I was at the time of the incident", he said, adding that "I've come to understand a lot about myself" during the three weeks of proceedings.
'Justice for Fede'
"I will never have the words" to address "the suffering and dignity of Mr Aramburu's family", said Bouvier, his voice choking with emotion as he faced them. Prominent sports figures, such as rugby player Thomas Lievremont and former tennis star and now French Open director Amelie Mauresmo, who lives in the Basque Country, were also present in the courtroom.
The two men, who fired 10 rounds – emptying their magazines – maintained during the proceedings that they had been defending themselves against Aramburu and his friend and former teammate Shaun Hegarty.
While acknowledging their use of deadly weapons, the defence cited childhood trauma in Bouvier’s case and post-traumatic stress disorder for Le Priol, a former marine commando.
Both defendants, former members of the now-dissolved far-right movement GUD (Groupe Union Défense), denied intending to kill Aramburu in their initial statements to the court.
But Hegarty, in his testimony earlier this month, angrily accused the pair of seeking to "evade responsibility" for their actions and said they should stay "in prison for as long as possible".
Aramburu's widow Maria had asked the court for a verdict that would allow their three children "to build their lives as adults".
The trial has also prompted calls for justice in Aramburu's native Argentina, with members of the Pumas wearing black T-shirts bearing the words "Justice for Fede" ahead of a match this month.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Tartu wants to buy 1,000 new rental bikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
14:16:00 UTC
23:16:00 KST

Tartu wants to buy 1,000 new rental bikes
To ensure the long-term success of its bike-share system, Tartu wants to acquire 1,000 new electric bikes compatible with the existing system.
For more than seven years, the city of Tartu has operated its bike-share system with a fleet that now needs renewing to ensure the service can continue over the longer term. The latest procurement for new bikes failed this spring. The city government is now trying again. A tender could be announced later this month under which the city would purchase 1,000 new electric bikes over four years through a framework agreement, Tartu Deputy Mayor Priit Humal said.
"We want to use a single procurement to buy a larger number of bikes so that the quantity the city needs is clear to all potential bidders and gives them confidence to plan their operations and development accordingly. On the other hand, we also want to get a lower price for the city. Until now, bikes have been purchased in smaller quantities and, as a result, the price per bike has been too high," Humal explained.
The city hopes the tender will attract bids for bikes costing less than €2,000 each. The estimated value of the procurement is €1.6 million, Humal added.
"The exact price and decisions will come once we receive the bids in the public procurement."
If the procurement is successful, the first batch of at least 250 new electric bikes could arrive on Tartu's streets as early as next season, said Roman Meeksa, head of Tartu's city transport company.
"The most important thing for us is that the bikes fit into our existing system, both in terms of infrastructure, so they can dock at and charge in our docking stations and, of course, that they are compatible with our software," Meeksa said.
Compatibility with the existing infrastructure has also been one of the main concerns in the past, Humal said.
"Since the current docking system provider ceased operations several years ago, there aren't too many companies on the market offering bikes compatible with this docking system. We see that for suppliers to enter the tender, they have to make additional efforts and incur additional costs to make their bikes compatible with our docking system," the deputy mayor said.
Meeksa added that a market survey was conducted in preparation for the procurement. The survey confirmed that there are enough suppliers on the market capable of producing suitable bikes.
"The main purpose of the market survey was to see whether, in addition to the current suppliers capable of producing bikes for our system — a manufacturer in Tallinn and one in Portugal — there are others that could offer their bikes for our system, increase competition and also bring down the price. There is interest. Whether they actually submit bids is another matter and if they do, what price they offer remains to be seen, but interest has been shown," Meeksa said.
Last year, more than 13,000 people took at least one trip using the bike-share system, which currently has around 6,000 regular users.

Election chief under pressure as protests escalate
Protesters from various groups gathered in Delhi on Friday demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, amid a growing controversy over reported differences within the Election Commission of India (ECI).
The protest followed an investigation published by The Indian Express on September 23, which reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions concerning electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. The report said some of the decisions had been taken without their knowledge.
The Election Commission, however, has rejected the suggestion of an internal breakdown, saying that differences expressed through internal notes are part of the normal decision-making process and that the final decisions of the three-member Commission were unanimous. 
On Thursday, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) gave Gyanesh Kumar 48 hours to resign and warned that it would launch a nationwide agitation, including a second protest at Jantar Mantar, if he did not step down. 
On Friday, CPI(ML) Liberation leader Dipankar Bhattacharya, AISA leader Neha Bora — who had gone on hunger strike during the first Jantar Mantar protest — senior advocate Prashant Bhushan and activist Yogendra Yadav joined the demonstration.
The Delhi Police had heavily barricaded the area around Jantar Mantar and did not allow protesters to enter the designated protest site. Several activists were detained within minutes of arriving at the spot.
Speaking to DW, Neha Bora accused the Election Commission of “stealing votes” and acting against democracy. She demanded Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation and said the protesters would continue their movement.
Dipankar Bhattacharya told DW that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) should be scrapped and that fresh elections should be held in several states.
Police detain protesters at Jantar Mantar rally against election chief
A protest called by left-wing student group All India Students' Association (AISA) and others at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Friday against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was met with a heavy police presence.
Reports said several protesters, including AISA president Neha Bora, were detained.
Earlier, Bora had said the protest would demand the resignation of Kumar and will be "defending our democracy."
Police heavily cordoned off the protest site, preventing people from entering and barring protesters from approaching within about 100 meters, according to a DW correspondent.
Kumar has faced criticism over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists. The Election Commission says the exercise aims to remove deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Critics allege it has also removed eligible voters and benefited the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
US citizen Matthew VanDyke granted bail, allowed to travel back
Self-professed US mercenary Matthew VanDyke and a Ukrainian national were released from Delhi's Tihar jail on Thursday to travel to their respective countries despite being initially booked under India's stringent Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), media reports said.
The two were allowed to travel to their respective countries for a month to meet their families, subject to court conditions, authorities said.
They were among seven foreign nationals arrested by India's National Investigation Agency (NIA) over alleged involvement in a drone-warfare training camp linked to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar.
All seven, including five other Ukrainian nationals, have been granted default bail and allowed to travel to Ukraine and the US.
The NIA had initially charged the group under UAPA, alleging they entered India legally but traveled to the northeast without required permits before crossing into Myanmar.
The agency later dropped terrorism-related UAPA provisions in its chargesheet, saying it lacked direct evidence that the alleged activities harmed India's sovereignty or citizens.
The accused were granted default bail after the NIA failed to complete its investigation within the mandatory 180-day period.
VanDyke describes himself as an international security analyst and founder of Sons of Liberty International. He also directed a film about the war in Syria.

Yet another incident where a minor girl was harassed in public in Bihar has surfaced.

Police are investigating when the incident occurred and trying to identify those seen in the video.

Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few
The Election Commission of India (ECI) introduced a "Mark VIP" feature in an app used by local election officials during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists, the Hindustan Times newspaper reported.
VIP denotes a Very Important Person.
The feature was added to the BLO App on July 30, according to officials in Delhi's chief electoral officer's office, the newspaper reported. Apple's App Store records described the update as "mark VIP elector related changes."
The ECI did not respond to questions about the feature or the legal basis for its introduction, the report said.
A separate investigation by The Reporters' Collective found that election officials had been instructed to mark ministers, judges, bureaucrats, celebrities and other prominent figures as VIPs during the revision. It reported that such voters could receive preferential treatment, including avoiding hearings required of ordinary voters.
In recent days, Delhi's chief electoral officer has issued notices to nearly 3.3 million voters during the SIR exercise, which included Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and Foreign Minister S Jaishankar.
Cockroach party urges opposition to boycott India's 'rigged' elections
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday called on India's opposition parties to stop participating in India's "rigged" elections, as it threatened to launch protests across the country on October 2.
"For opposition: Yes, elections are being rigged," Dipke posted on social media, arguing that if the opposition continues to contest such elections, it legitimizes them and "maintain the illusion that they are free and fair."
"If elections are being rigged, it should matter regardless of the state or which party is affected," Dipke wrote, calling on opposition parties to prioritize democracy over political survival. "You cannot keep saying the game is rigged while continuing to play it. Your participation is the only thing that gives these rigged elections legitimacy."
On Thursday, the CJP accused India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy and demanded his resignation within 48 hours.
CJP alleged that the Election Commission's voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The CJP's demands include:
- Criminal proceedings against Kumar
- All upcoming elections put on hold, freeze Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
- Repeal the 2023 law on the appointment of the Election Commissioners of India
Meanwhile, two petitions were filed in the Bombay High Court on Thursday challenging the SIR process in Maharashtra.
Rahul Gandhi accuses Modi, Shah of being behind election 'rigging'
Both the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and the Cockroach Party political movement called India’s elections "rigged," as the uproar over the Election Commission of India's (ECI) handling of the voter-list revision shows no sign of abating.
On Thursday, Congress Party leader Gandhi alleged that elections in India were being "rigged," and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. It followed a report by Indian Express on objections raised by two election commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists.
The report said that Kumar's fellow Election Commissioners had raised at least 14 objections over 10 months to decisions on voter registrations and electoral data. In one instance, one of the complaints said the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
The three commissioners are overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which the ECI says aims to remove deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Critics say the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters, which has benefitted the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
"If the vote has been destroyed, then our Constitution has been destroyed. It no longer has power," Gandhi said during a press conference.
Gandhi also alleged that Kumar was elevated to Election Commission head by Prime Minster Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, despite his opposition to the appointment. He went on to accuse them of being "at the top of the conspiracy," and called for them to be investigated.
Meanwhile, BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi defended the ECI, saying on Thursday that the SIR process was legally sound and that the commission’s decisions were based on majority consensus. He said the law empowers the ECI to conduct an SIR at its discretion.
India's next general elections are not expected until 2029, but a series of important state elections will take place next year.
