This “rare” autism-linked genetic disorder may be far more common than scientists thought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:32:46 UTC
22:32:46 KST

This “rare” autism-linked genetic disorder may be far more common than scientists thought
A genetic disorder strongly linked to autism may be dramatically more common than scientists thought, with thousands of cases potentially still undiagnosed.
- Date:
- September 25, 2026
- Source:
- CureSHANK
- Summary:
- A major analysis suggests Phelan-McDermid syndrome, a genetic disorder closely linked to autism, may affect about 1 in 7,300 people and more than 45,000 Americans. Researchers warn that thousands of cases may remain hidden because genetic testing is often not performed, even as targeted treatments move into clinical trials.
- Share:
New research led by scientists at the Seaver Autism Center for Research and Treatment at Mount Sinai suggests that Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS) may be much more common than earlier estimates indicated. The findings, published in Autism Research, estimate that the condition affects roughly 1 in 7,300 people.
Phelan-McDermid syndrome is a rare genetic disorder caused by a deletion or mutation involving the SHANK3 gene on chromosome 22. It can lead to a broad range of medical, intellectual, and behavioral challenges. Most people with the syndrome also meet the criteria for autism spectrum disorder, and changes affecting SHANK3 are believed to account for as many as one percent of autism spectrum disorder cases.
Genetic Data Reveal a Much Larger Population
To estimate how common the condition may be, Mount Sinai researchers worked with genetic testing laboratories, academic medical centers, and autism research programs. The team examined data from nearly 180,000 people with autism who had undergone genetic testing.
Their analysis combined information from ten separate sources, including GeneDx, Labcorp, Ambry Genetics, the SPARK research study, the Autism Sequencing Consortium, and several major children's hospitals.
After accounting for undiagnosed cases, limits in genetic testing, and people with Phelan-McDermid syndrome who do not meet the criteria for autism, the researchers estimated a prevalence of 13.7 cases per 100,000 people. That works out to about 1 in 7,300 individuals.
The estimate represents a major change from previous figures and suggests that more than 45,000 people in the United States could be living with Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
"The large gap between known and estimated cases is likely due in large part to the fact that many individuals with developmental disabilities and autism are never offered genetic testing. Families may also face insurance barriers or may receive tests that do not adequately evaluate the SHANK3 gene," said Tess Levy, MSc, Assistant Professor of Psychiatry at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, a certified genetic counselor at the Seaver Autism Center, and first author of the paper.
Why Genetic Testing Could Matter
The researchers say broader access to genetic testing could help identify people who currently have no diagnosis.
"We recommend that every child with autism undergo genetic testing, because knowledge is power. These genetic findings allow researchers to design more targeted clinical trials for potential therapies. I truly believe that within the next five years, we'll see successful examples of new treatments coming from these genetic discoveries," said Joseph D. Buxbaum, PhD, Director of the Seaver Autism Center, co-founder of the Autism Sequencing Consortium, and senior author of the paper.
Supported by CureSHANK and Neuren Pharmaceuticals, the study is described as one of the most comprehensive attempts yet to estimate how many people may have Phelan-McDermid syndrome.
"Neuren Pharmaceuticals initiated this landmark PMS prevalence study in collaboration with the Seaver Autism Center at Mount Sinai and CureSHANK because, with new treatments moving closer to reality, identifying these individuals has become an ethical imperative. Patients cannot benefit from these advances if they never receive a diagnosis," said Rachel Groth, PhD, Head of External Innovation and Patient Advocacy at Neuren Pharmaceuticals.
New Treatments Are Moving Into Clinical Trials
The findings come at an important time for Phelan-McDermid syndrome research. Several clinical trials are now underway, including precision medicine approaches aimed at the biology underlying the disorder.
For people with the condition and their families, receiving a genetic diagnosis can now mean more than simply learning the cause of their symptoms. It may also provide access to specialized medical care, research studies, clinical trials, patient support networks, and potentially disease-modifying treatments.
"This study confirms what many families, clinicians, and advocates have suspected for years," said CureSHANK Board Chair, Geraldine Bliss. "There are likely tens of thousands of individuals with Phelan-McDermid syndrome who have never received a genetic diagnosis. At a time when multiple therapeutics are advancing into clinical trials, finding these individuals has never been more important."
The results also reinforce CureSHANK's push to expand access to genetic testing and support the goals of Start Genetic, a global awareness campaign encouraging patients, families, health care providers, and advocacy groups to think genetic first.
The broader message is that advances in precision medicine can only reach patients who have first been identified and diagnosed.
Story Source:
Materials provided by CureSHANK. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tess Levy, David Lapidus, Kate Friedman, Paige Siper, Larry Glass, Liza Squires, Mary Hames, Joseph D. Buxbaum, Alexander Kolevzon. Prevalence of Phelan McDermid Syndrome Estimated To Be ~1:7300 Using a Multisource Model. Autism Research, 2026; 19 (8) DOI: 10.1002/aur.70297

Afspa extended by six months in 'disturbed areas' of Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:32:17 UTC
22:32:17 KST

NEW DELHI: The Centre has extended the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (Afspa), in specified areas of Nagaland, Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur for another six months from October 1, according to Gazette notifications issued on Friday.The extension follows a review of the law and order situation in the affected areas of the three northeastern states.The Afspa, which grants special powers to the armed forces, will remain in force in these areas for six months from October 1, unless withdrawn earlier, according to the notification.The government order cited Section 3 of the act, which empowers the Centre to declare specified areas as "disturbed areas."
Which are these 'disturbed areas'
In Manipur, the ministry of home affairs has extended the “disturbed area” declaration across the state, excluding areas under the jurisdiction of 13 police stations in five districts.The excluded areas are those under Imphal, Lamphel, City, Singjamei, Patsoi and Wangoi police stations in Imphal West district; Porompat, Heingang and Irilbung police stations in Imphal East; Thoubal police station in Thoubal district; Bishnupur and Nambol police stations in Bishnupur district; and Kakching police station in Kakching district.
In Nagaland, the Afspa has been extended to nine districts — Dimapur, Niuland, Chumoukedima, Mon, Kiphire, Noklak, Phek, Peren and Meluri — which have been declared “disturbed areas” under Section 3 of the Act.The notification also covers areas under the jurisdiction of 21 police stations in five other districts of Nagaland: Kohima, Mokokchung, Longleng, Wokha and Zunheboto.
In Arunachal Pradesh, the Afspa has been extended to Tirap, Changlang and Longding districts.The order also covers areas under the jurisdiction of Namsai, Mahadevpur and Chowkham police stations in Namsai district, bordering Assam.Among the northeastern states, Afspa has been completely withdrawn from Mizoram, Meghalaya, and Tripura, while it remains in force in select areas of Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, and Nagaland.(With PTI inputs)

Unknown

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas (L) attend a joint press-conference following talks in Kyiv on October 13, 2025. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine needs to secure $27 billion to plug a hole in its defense budget in the next two months or risk being unable to buy weapons early next year, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat Friday.
“Most of this money is for our drones, missiles, and supplies for our warriors. About a third of this money, perhaps even a little more, is for drones for January, February, and March. And if we do not order and pay for them in October and November, we will face serious challenges in January and February,” Zelenskyy said.
The president added that covering the deficit was a top topic of his negotiations with European partners: “I am urging the European Commission to provide the second tranche of the €90 billion [loan] sooner. Because, once again, we must have the necessary drones and missiles for January and February.”
Advertisement
Ukraine first announced the budget gap in August. It emerged after Ukraine had to bring forward state defense spending originally planned for the second half of the year, as Hungary delayed the EU’s €90 billion loan to Kyiv. Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June.
The shortfall remains despite €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan.
Zelenskyy said he received a positive and constructive response from the EU during his diplomatic talks this week.
“Everyone understands that covering this deficit is very important. Everyone understands that Ukraine cannot be left on its own and that more must be invested in Ukrainian-made drones and missiles, because most of this deficit is precisely the funding needed for that,” Zelenskyy said.
EU member countries on Friday agreed on the terms for releasing €6.6 billion in European Peace Facility funds for Ukraine, the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said in a statement.
"€900 million are for the EU’s Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine. €1 billion will fund new joint procurement of equipment. And €4.7 billion will reimburse Member States, with some already saying they will channel their share to Ukraine," Kallas said.

China's Zhang wins record seventh Games swimming gold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:30:53 UTC
22:30:53 KST

Chinese teenager Zhang Zhanshuo won a record seventh swimming gold at the Asian Games on Friday and said it had been the "perfect conclusion" to his week in Tokyo.
The 19-year-old wrapped up a scintillating campaign with victory in the 400m freestyle in a Games-record 3min 41.28sec.
No swimmer had previously won seven golds in one Games.
Japan's Rikako Ikee won six in Jakarta in 2018 before China's Zhang Yufei matched her achievement in Hangzhou five years later.
Zhang Zhanshuo went one better and said he was "calmer than I imagined I would be".
"The moment I touched the wall was probably the most exciting," said the towering teenager, who stands 198cm (6ft 6in).
"It was also my final race of the competition. Today feels like a perfect conclusion."
Zhang also won individual golds in the 200m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, as well as three relays.
He was far too hot for the 400m freestyle field to handle, coming home 4.27sec ahead of Japan's silver-medallist Kazushi Imafuku.
He sat on the line divider after the race and slowly counted off all seven medals he had won on his fingers.
Zhang now has the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and world records in his sights.
"I think the most important thing is to stay grounded and focused, because the Asian Games are not my ultimate goal," he said.
"I need to face my shortcomings honestly and recognise the gap between myself and the world's best athletes."
It was another successful night in the pool for the national team, who won five of the day's seven finals.
They topped the overall swimming medal table with 30 golds. Japan were a distant second with seven.
Li Bingjie won her fifth gold of the Games, in the women's 800m freestyle, while Zhang Yufei picked up her fourth in the 50m butterfly. (AFP)

India ‘cannot let the Americans control’ its energy tap – strategic affairs expert (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:30:40 UTC
22:30:40 KST

India ‘cannot let the Americans control’ its energy tap – strategic affairs expert (VIDEO)
India should continue to buy Russian oil and retain control over its energy choices as the US raises the pressure on major buyers, strategic affairs scholar Happymon Jacob told RT.
A recently-passed sanctions bill gives US President Donald Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries, including India, for purchasing Russian energy. New Delhi has maintained that its energy decisions are driven by national requirements and market conditions.
Russian oil should not be removed from the global market and India has no reason to stop buying it, Jacob told RT India in the latest episode of the ‘India, Russia, and the World’ podcast. He is the Delhi-based founder of the Council for Strategic and Defense Research think tank.
“I don’t think the world should take Russian oil off the table. I don’t think India should stop buying Russian oil,” he said. “You cannot let the Americans control your energy tap.”
India needs to keep a broad basket of energy options that include Russia, the Middle East, the US, and South America, along with renewable sources, Jacob said, adding that removing one of these options would reduce India’s flexibility at a time when energy supplies are exposed to geopolitical disruptions.
Russia is now India’s top supplier of crude oil, with September shipments tracking at around 1.9 million barrels per day, preliminary data from Kpler shows.
India is dependent on several external partners across key sectors, Jacob said. For energy, New Delhi relies heavily on Russia and the Gulf, while its technology links are concentrated in the US and allied countries. He argued that these dependencies mean India has to weigh the costs of resisting pressure from larger powers. 
Jacob called the threat of US sanctions on India as “unfair and unjust,” adding that New Delhi will need to manage its relationship with Washington through diplomacy and other channels. 
India has limited room to push back, he argued, pointing to New Delhi’s earlier decision to halt Iranian oil purchases, and its subsequent reduction in Russian oil imports following US pressure. He noted that India’s actions have often been more cautious than its public responses. Maintaining access to multiple suppliers, including Russia, is crucial to India’s energy security, Jacob said.

Evan Gershkovich says his arrest in Russia was carefully planned FSB sting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:26:57 UTC
22:26:57 KST

US reporter Evan Gershkovich says his arrest in Russia was carefully planned FSB sting
- US reporter Evan Gershkovich reveals his 2023 arrest in Russia was a planned FSB sting during his reporting on military production in Yekaterinburg.
- He was detained after receiving secret documents from a source, sentenced to 16 years, then freed in a prisoner swap in 2024.
- Gershkovich believes the FSB aimed to convince Putin he was a spy, a claim denied by him, his newspaper, and the US government.
AI generated
LONDON - US reporter Evan Gershkovich, in his first detailed published account of his arrest in Russia in 2023, says he was the victim of an elaborate sting operation by the FSB security service.
In an extract from his book, This Cursed Beautiful Land, Gershkovich says that while working on a story for the Wall Street Journal about Russian military production, he held two meetings with the union boss of a factory in Yekaterinburg, a major defence-industry hub.
At their second encounter, in a steakhouse, the source produced papers with hand-copied tables of figures, telling the reporter that they related to the production of tanks.
As he jotted down notes, Gershkovich said, he heard the sound of marching feet and looked up to see a group of masked men approaching their table.
“A pang of guilt ripped through me: Had I compromised a source? But panic immediately replaced that thought. Instinct took over, my hands moving to hide the papers in the gap between the bench and the wall,” he wrote in the book extract, published by the Journal on Sept 25.
“The men quickly descended on us. An arm was yanking my neck, pulling me off the couch... Someone shouted: ‘You are under arrest by the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation.’”
A long sentence, then a prisoner swop
Gershkovich, then 31, became the first US reporter arrested on espionage charges in Russia since the Cold War. He was later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being freed in an East-West prisoner swop in August 2024.
He writes that he and his editors had considered the risks of the reporting trip and agreed that the source should not bring any documents to the meeting; if he did so, Gershkovich should not accept anything from him.
But at the meeting, the source had “thrust the papers into my hands”.
Although he had reported on the arrests of other Americans in Russia, and on the targeting and even murder of Russian journalists, Gershkovich writes that the “unspoken rule” was that foreign correspondents enjoyed a degree of immunity: they might be expelled, but not arrested.
Reeling with shock, he was handcuffed, had a black sack placed over his head and was whisked into a van where he was placed in a chokehold and punched in the abdomen while being questioned, he writes.
FSB ‘backup plan’
Gershkovich said that since his release he had learned of evidence that the FSB had a “backup plan” to arrest him on another of his planned reporting trips, to Siberia, if the Yekaterinburg operation had failed.
He said he believes the two meetings with the source in Yekaterinburg were designed to help the FSB persuade President Vladimir Putin that he was a spy and secure approval for his arrest at the second meeting.
“Putin, it seems to me, fully bought into this narrative,” he said.
The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Putin said in a February 2024 interview with US television host Tucker Carlson that Gershkovich had been “caught red-handed” while collecting confidential information.
The journalist, his newspaper and the US government all strongly deny the allegation that Gershkovich was a spy. REUTERS

Pakistan's Sharif rails against India, praises Trump at UNGA

Iran says it gave US 7-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
Iran has given the US a seven-day plan that would involve reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday.
Speaking to reporters at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, Araghchi said the plan was delivered via Qatar and the choice now rests with Washington to meet the conditions Tehran has laid out.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure," he said.
Sharif blames India for 2025 clashes, calls for 'just and fair' Kashmir resolution
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also took aim at India in his speech as he discussed the limited military clashes between the uneasy neighbors last year.
"A year ago, Pakistan faced external aggression from India under a false pretext," the prime minister alleged. "Pakistan exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations charter."
He praised the country's military saying, "They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attack, and taught it a lesson it shall never ever forget," as the UN's TV feed cut to an Indian observer in the assembly shaking his head as he listened.
Pakistan considers Indian missile strikes on May 7 to be the start of the low-level conflict, that ran for less than a week, while India contends that the strikes were retalliation for an attack in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir in late April. New Delhi had accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, which Islambad denied.
Sharif praised US President Donald Trump's "resolute and visionary leadership," crediting it with saving "hundreds of millions of lives in South Asia" by intervening and helping to broker a truce "when two nuclear neighbors stood at the brink of all-out war."
Sharif asked "who knows the extent of devastation that could have taken place" without Trump's "clarity of thought and action" at a critical moment.
He said it was necessary to ensure that South Asia "never reaches this precipice again," and said that doing so would require "a just and fair resolution of the Kashmir dispute."
He said Kashmiri people had been waiting eight decades for the UN to "fulfill its solemn commitment of a free and impartial plebiscite under its auspices." He also criticized recent "attempts to alter the legal status of Jammu and Kashmir through demographic reengineering and other illegal measures."
He also criticized India for its decision to hold a treat on the Indus River System in abeyance, saying this move had "no legal basis whatsoever."
Pakistan's Sharif: Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb are 'arteries of global economy' and 'must remain open'
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif touted his country's efforts to mediate in the war between the US and Iran since February, particularly in reaching the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding that brought an uneasy calm to hostilities for a few weeks earlier this year — albeit without resolving many of the wider issues in the conflict.
"Regrettably, Mr. President, recently we have witnessed a dangerous surge of hostilties," Sharif said. "Yet amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger."
"The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are arteries of the global economy," Sharif said, also referring to the western entry to the Red Sea coming under increasing pressure from the Iran-aligned Houthis. "They must remain open, connecting nations, not becoming the chokepoints of confrontation."
Sharif said these waters "must carry the promise of prosperity, not the perils of war."
He said Pakistan condemned recent "deplorable" Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia "in the strongest possible terms," not least the reported attempted drone attack on the holy city of Mecca, which he said had "outraged Muslims across the globe."
Albania's Rama tells of 'Flamingo Revolution,' warning not of a rogue AI, but one following rogue orders
Prime Minister Edi Rama told the chamber that while Albania was not a developer of "frontier models" in AI, "we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating," given how outside actors had tried out the technology's darker capabilites on its citizens.
Rama said he felt he owed the chamber a "simple message," if not necessarily the one most commonly discussed during the week.
"The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity. The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly," he said.
"The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators," Rama said. "But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts, they multiply ours. They have no ambition of their own, they serve the ambition of others. They carry no flag, but they can be deployed by a state. They tell no lie for their own benefit, but they can tell a billion lies on others' behalf."
Rama mentioned how Albania had become the first government to launch an AI minister. He said this showed his government's belief that "inside an accountable state," the technology could be used to "reduced the distance between citizens and public services."
But he said Albania had also learned how "artificial intelligence outside accountability can be used to eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind."
He relayed the story of the so-called "Flamingo Revolution," a "fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast."
This entirely fictional invasion "was manufactured, was personalized and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted." Rama explained how the details of the overarching story were personalized to maximize their impact with the individuals reading them.
"Different fabriactions entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie," he said. "The consequences were real. Citizens had their own reasons to protest — don't take me wrong. But suddenly, they started to protest also against a phantom enemy. Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse for the first time ever."
Rama said that amid the AI disinformation drive, "fear became anger, anger became mobilization and fabrication became political reality."
"And this was not a laboratory experiment. I'm not talking to you about a science fiction movie. It was a Tuesday, in Tirana, our capital city."
Rama said it wasn't an algorithm that invented the objective, but rather a human actor. The algorithm didn't develop hatred, but "it discovered how to activate ours."
He called this particular use case "systematic fraud as a service," and warned its potential for use in scenarios like elections were just as real as in trying to amplify animosity to war in the Middle East.
St. Lucia urges assembly not to forget Haiti in war-torn world
Prime Minister Philip Pierre from the Caribbean island of Saint Lucia said his country "laments the continued conflicts and human suffering across the globe," listing some of the most notable wars in Ukraine, Gaza, the wider Middle East and Sudan.
He said his country of around 184,000 people called for the establishment of a Palestinian state with full UN membership.
Pierre then turned to a Caribbean conflict that has featured rather less this week in New York, Haiti.
"Member states of this organization must act in a manner that will restore the trust of the people of Haiti in the United Nations," Pierre said. "Some member states have failed to meet the commitments and pledges to the gang suppression force in Haiti, whose one-year mandate ends this month."
He urged the Security Council to renew the force's mandate, and called on member states to provide it with sufficient "resources to operation effectively and successfully."
He said that while gang violence was "the main factor to be resolved," the crisis in the country was "multidimensional."
"The international response must include long-term socio-economic assistance that will help restore an acceptable quality of life for the people of Haiti," he said.
Pacific archipelago Tuvalu appeals for climate finance, Taiwanese UN membership
Tuvalu's Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski told the assembly that climate change "is and remains the single, greatest existential threat to Tuvalu's survival, security and sustainable development."
He said the low-lying archipelago of some 10,000 people acknowledged global efforts to contain the climate crisis but said the "pace and scale of global actions remain insufficient."
Mickoscki called for a "fast, fair, just and orderly transition away from fossil fuels."
He called for moves to provide climate financing "as grants" to allow countries like his to better prepare and adapt for coming changes.
He said his country was keenly anticipating the pre-COP meetings this October, prior to the main UN COP31 summit in Turkey in November.
"Tuvalu may have only 26 square kilometers of land," he said, "but we are custodians of some 750,000 square kilometers of ocean, which makes Tuvalu a large ocean state."
Tuvalu joins Palau in appealing for Taiwanese membership
Tuvalu is also known as one of just 12 countries in the world to retain full diplomatic relations with Taiwan, rather than having formal ties to China.
Mickoscki said that the UN "must also uphold the principles of dignity, inclusion and equality" for everyone.
"Yet, too many communities remain outside the structures designed to serve all humanity," he said. "Tuvalu therefore calls for arrangements that enable the meaningful participation of the 23.3 million people of Taiwan in the United Nations and its specialized agencies and mechanisms."
He said that Taipei had consistently demonstrated that it was an "able, trustworthy and constructive partner," saying its UN exclusion "undermines both the spirit and effectiveness of multilateral cooperation."
The People's Republic of China took over the Chinese seat at the UN — and the Security Council veto that came with it — in 1971, more than two decades after the Chinese Communist revolution. Since then, Taiwan has been excluded from the UN for more than half a century since then, with no clear route towards membership, given that it is only possible with Beijing's blessing.
Not far away, during his state visit to Washington DC to speak with President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping on Thursday appealed to Trump to change the US stance on Taiwanese independence from not "supporting" it to openly "opposing" it.
Lebanese prime minister says 'the problem is not the absence of rules'
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told the UN that "without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among states, nor can competition among them flourish."
He said that the UN was founded, more than 80 years ago, on "the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force."
But Salam said that wars and conflicts still plague a world that spends more on armaments than on development.
"The problem is not the absence of rules," Salam said. "It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application."
He did not mention Israel by name in his preamble but did later in his speech.
Salam said his government had three commitments to fulfil, and argued that all three were interconnected:
- Restoring trust and credibility in Lebanese authorities after the economic collapse and vast port explosion in Beirut of August 4, 2020
- Ensuring that only the Lebanese government held weapons and made decisions of war for the country — comments seemingly aimed at the pro-Iranian Hezbollah group, which he did not name
- Reclaiming occupied Lebanese territory from Israel under the terms of UN Resolution 1701 adopted to end the Second Lebanon War between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006
"Our position on the war has been clear from the outset," Salam said. "We want it to end. We want the ceasefire consolidated. We want Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognized borders, in accordance with the 1949 General Armistice Agreement and as affirmed by Resolution 1701. We want the release of all our detainees, the safe and dignified return of our people to their villages and towns, and a reconstruction of what the war destroyed."
Under the tense ceasefire deal between Lebanon and Israel, brokered by the US, Israel is supposed to withdraw its forces from a self-declared "buffer zone" in southern Lebanon. In turn, Lebanon's government is supposed to move its military fores into these areas and stop Hezbollah from using them to launch attacks into northern Israel. The current goal is to create so-called pilot zones where the Lebanese army moves in and Israel's troops move out.
The process is making only gradual progress, as both sides accuse the other of failing to meet their obligations.
Lebanon PM calls for peacekeeping troops after UNIFIL mandate ends
Lebanon Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called for the UN to keep its UNIFIL (UN Interim Force in Lebanon) peacekeeping troops in place after their mandate expires at year's end.
"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," he said.
The UN's troops, currently numbering 7,500 from 46 different countries, have been in Lebanon since 1978.
Last year, however, the US pushed the UN Security Council to terminate the mandate when it ran out.
UNIFIL's expected departure comes as Israel maintains troops in its own self-declared "security zone" extending some 10 kilometers (6 miles) into south Lebanon.

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's young prime minister stood at the podium of the UN General Assembly to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.
"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," said Balendra Shah as he began his address to the UNGA on Thursday.
Nepal's leader calls for international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas
The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.
"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a "Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism," which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.
Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.
Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
Shah noted that his country only contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he wasn not blaming any nation or continent.
"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.
Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery
The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of "Responsibility, Reparation and Resilience" as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.
Shah said that vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'
Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Tawakecolati Lalabalavu addressed the chamber on behalf of one of the low-lying island nations at severe risk from climate change on Thursday.

Lalabalavu said these funds paid for school fees, rebuilt homes after cyclones and sustained families between harvests.

Lalabalavu also alluded to Fiji recently declaring a national HIV emergency and said that organized crime and drug trafficking was exacerbating this problem. He said that as a small impoverished country, Fiji had three requests for the international community:
"That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. That the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resources at a level that does not force triage between regions, and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is."

Gadi Eisenkot and the Palestinian economy: What could really change if he leads Israel? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:24:01 UTC
22:24:01 KST

If Gadi Eisenkot leads Israel’s next government, what could Palestinians realistically expect from him economically?
The answer should not begin with the assumption that an Israeli prime minister can, on his own, solve the Palestinian economy’s problems. Palestinian reforms, investment, the private sector, international support, and internal governance all matter.
But the Palestinian economy is not an independent economy with full control over its monetary, trade, and sovereign policies. It is deeply linked to Israel through the framework created by the 1994 Paris Economic Protocol and through the everyday movement of workers, goods, revenues, and money.
The Israeli shekel is the dominant currency in Palestinian transactions. Clearance revenues are a major source of Palestinian public income. Much Palestinian trade moves through crossings and ports subject to Israeli procedures. Many Palestinian households depend on work in Israel, while Palestinian banks rely on correspondent relationships with Israeli banks.
The result is an interconnected economic system. Restrictions on workers affect household income. Restrictions on movement affect businesses. Problems with clearance revenues affect public salaries and consumption. Banking restrictions affect trade and liquidity.
This is why Eisenkot’s approach to the Palestinian Authority matters economically as well as politically.
In 2022, Eisenkot publicly warned against dismantling the Palestinian Authority and annexing the West Bank. That statement should not be treated as a detailed economic program for 2026. But it did indicate that, in his thinking at the time, preventing the collapse of Palestinian institutions was connected to Israeli security interests.
The practical question is therefore straightforward: if preventing the PA’s collapse remains part of his strategic outlook, can that objective be separated from the economy that enables the PA and Palestinian society to function?
The first test: Palestinian workers
The clearest indication so far comes from Eisenkot’s position on Palestinian workers.
In an interview published by Israel Hayom on August 27, Eisenkot argued that the broad ban on Palestinian workers entering Israel had not prevented unauthorized entry. He said it could make more sense to allow Palestinian family breadwinners to work in Israel after security screening and under Shin Bet supervision.
His argument was primarily about security, not economic development.
That distinction matters.
Eisenkot did not promise a full reopening of the Israeli labor market. He did not specify how many workers would return or when. But the policy he described could have significant economic consequences.
For a Palestinian worker, returning to work means more than employment. It can mean income returning to a household, bills being paid, debt being reduced, food and medicine becoming more affordable, and purchasing power returning to the local economy.
PCPO polling reflects the scale of these concerns. In our surveys, 59.9% identified restrictions on Palestinian employment in Israel and the decline in permits as a major economic challenge. Some 79.3% pointed to unemployment and limited job opportunities, while 70.2% cited declining income and weakened purchasing power.
These are perceptions, not official unemployment statistics. But they show how closely Palestinians connect access to work with economic security.
Workers cannot help the economy if they cannot move
Permits alone are not enough.
A worker needs to reach the workplace predictably. A business needs employees and materials to arrive on time. A trader must know when goods can move. A factory must know whether deliveries will arrive today or tomorrow.
That makes checkpoints and road gates an economic issue as well as a security issue.
In April 2026, OCHA reported 925 movement obstacles across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, based on a December 2025 survey. These included 89 checkpoints operating around the clock, 218 partial checkpoints and 232 road gates. OCHA also found that 459 obstacles hindered access between Palestinian communities and major roads.
For businesses, uncertainty itself becomes a cost.
A delayed worker, a truck forced onto a longer route, or raw materials arriving unpredictably can affect contracts, prices, production, and investment.
In PCPO polling, 62.8% identified restrictions on movement and mobility as a major economic challenge. Some 70.6% selected facilitating freedom of movement as an important economic measure, while 69.9% supported removing or reducing military checkpoints inside the West Bank.
Yet respondents did not necessarily see mobility and security as opposites: 68.3% said freedom of movement and security and stability were equally important.
That finding is particularly relevant when considering Eisenkot, whose career was shaped within Israel’s security establishment.
The question is not whether security considerations disappear. It is whether they can be managed in ways that also reduce unnecessary economic uncertainty.
Clearance revenues: the financial test
The same logic applies to Palestinian public finances.
According to a 2026 analysis by Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, clearance revenues actually transferred to the Palestinian Authority after deductions fell from about NIS 8.8 billion in 2022 to NIS 7.9 billion in 2023, then to approximately NIS 4.4 billion in 2024 and around NIS 2 billion in 2025. More than NIS 4 billion was withheld in 2025.
Foreign assistance helped offset part of the decline, which is an important qualification. The PA’s fiscal crisis cannot be attributed to clearance revenues alone.
But the effects are not confined to a government balance sheet.
Behind every public budget is a household budget.
In a PCPO survey of 503 Palestinians conducted between June 24 and July 5, 2026, 83.5% said delayed or reduced salaries had changed their household spending. The impact extended to food, health care, education, utilities, loans, and debt.
Eisenkot has not announced a specific policy on clearance revenues. There is therefore no basis for claiming that he would release withheld funds or end existing deductions.
But the question remains: if the objective is to prevent institutional collapse, how sustainable is that objective when the PA’s principal source of revenue remains unstable?
Banks and the movement of money
There is another part of the same economic chain: correspondent banking.
Reuters reported on September 1 that Israel Discount Bank and Bank Hapoalim would continue correspondent banking services with Palestinian banks through the end of 2026. Around NIS 51 billion in transactions pass through these relationships annually, while approximately 90% of Palestinian trade depends on access to Israel’s financial system. Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Andrew Abir said the next Israeli government would need to find a long-term solution.
For Palestinians, this is not merely a technical banking dispute.
These channels help process payments for trade, imports, fuel, medicine, and essential goods.
Closely connected is the accumulation of surplus shekels in Palestinian banks. When cash cannot be transferred regularly, liquidity pressures rise. Electronic payments can reduce dependence on cash, but they cannot replace correspondent banking or solve the underlying fiscal problems.
This is why workers, checkpoints, clearance revenues, correspondent banking, and surplus shekels should not be viewed as separate crises.
They form one economic cycle.
When revenues fall, salaries are affected. When salaries are delayed, households cut spending. When demand weakens, businesses lose sales. When workers and goods cannot move predictably, costs rise. When money cannot move normally through the banking system, pressure accumulates elsewhere.
The real test of change
This brings us back to Eisenkot.
There is currently no evidence that he has committed himself to resolving all of these issues.
His clearest published position concerns Palestinian workers. On clearance revenues, correspondent banking, surplus shekels, checkpoints, and crossings, there is no comprehensive public program from him so far.
Nor would implementation depend on a prime minister alone. Coalition partners, government ministries, Israeli security institutions, the Bank of Israel, Palestinian institutions, and international actors would all matter.
But these issues provide measurable tests for any future government.
If preventing the collapse of the Palestinian Authority remains part of Eisenkot’s strategic thinking, the test cannot be limited to preventing the final moment of collapse.
It must also include whether Palestinian institutions and the economy around them can function before reaching that point.
Economic stability is not a substitute for political rights, nor can it replace a political settlement. But economic instability can make an already difficult political and security environment more fragile.
In PCPO polling, 83.8% said Palestinian economic stability could contribute to greater political and security stability in the region.
For Palestinians, however, the meaning of economic change is ultimately much more concrete.
It means a worker being able to reach his job, a public employee being able to rely on a salary, a trader being able to move goods and transfer money, a bank being able to settle payments, and a young person being able to plan for tomorrow with less fear that another economic bottleneck will suddenly close the road ahead.
The writer is the founder and president of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion (PCPO).

Joni Lamb, late Daystar co-founder, named Israel's top Christian ally for 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:23:59 UTC
22:23:59 KST

The late Christian broadcaster Joni Lamb has been named Israel's leading Christian ally for 2026, topping the Israel Allies Foundation's annual list of 50 Christian leaders recognized for their support of the Jewish state.
Lamb, the co-founder and former president of Daystar Television Network, was placed first on this year's list posthumously following her death in May.
The annual ranking, released to coincide with Sukkot, or the Feast of Tabernacles, recognizes pastors, ministry leaders, broadcasters and other public figures whose advocacy, humanitarian work and faith-based activity have contributed to support for Israel around the world.
Lamb had been a prominent supporter of Israel for years, using Daystar's international Christian broadcasting network to advocate for the Jewish state and mobilize its audience on Israel's behalf.
Her work extended beyond advocacy. Through Daystar's House of Hope Israel initiative, Lamb supported Holocaust survivors and other humanitarian projects in the country.
Israel Allies Award winner for support of the country following October 7
In 2024, the Israel Allies Foundation presented Lamb with its Israel Allies Award in recognition of her support for Israel following the October 7 massacre.
Taking second place this year is Paula White-Cain, the longtime spiritual adviser to US President Donald Trump and head of the White House Faith Office.
White-Cain topped the list last year and is the only person to have been ranked No. 1 more than once since the Israel Allies Foundation began publishing the annual ranking in 2020.
Her relationship with Israel and the Jewish community stretches back years. The Florida pastor has repeatedly emphasized Jerusalem's place in the Judeo-Christian tradition and, through the National Faith Advisory Board, has helped mobilize tens of thousands of American faith leaders.
List includes wide range of Christian leaders
The 2026 list also includes figures from well beyond the traditional world of pastors and Christian ministries, among them Pastor Larry Huch, political commentator Scott Jennings, Erika Kirk and Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi.
"In a time when support for Israel is often tested, these Christian leaders have chosen clarity, courage, and conviction," Israel Allies Foundation President Josh Reinstein said.
"They lead not just in words alone, but by faithful action. Their example strengthens the bridge between our communities and advances the cause of faith-based diplomacy."
The list has become an annual Sukkot tradition for the organization and reflects the particular significance that many evangelical and other Bible-believing Christians attach to the Jewish festival.
Christian interest in Sukkot draws in part from the biblical Book of Zechariah, which describes a future in which people from the nations of the world travel to Jerusalem to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.
That connection has for decades brought Christian pilgrims to Jerusalem during the holiday and has also provided the backdrop for the Israel Allies Foundation's annual recognition of prominent Christian supporters of Israel.
Type of people on the list has changed over time
The composition of the list has changed considerably over the years.
Former US secretary of state Mike Pompeo topped the ranking in 2023, followed by former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro and pastors Larry and Tiz Huch. In 2024, Franklin Graham, president of the international humanitarian organization Samaritan's Purse and son of evangelist Billy Graham, took first place.
White-Cain headed the 2025 list, with the late Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk ranked second posthumously.
The foundation's selection also reflects the broader network it has spent nearly two decades building around what Reinstein describes as "faith-based diplomacy."
Founded in 2007, the Israel Allies Foundation works with pro-Israel parliamentary caucuses around the world, seeking to translate support for Israel among Christian communities into political and diplomatic cooperation.
Christian political support impacts Israel's diplomatic achievements
The organization says its network has now grown to 66 parliamentary caucuses representing more than 1,700 legislators worldwide.
The network includes the Knesset Christian Allies Caucus and its counterparts in legislatures across Europe, Africa, Latin America and elsewhere.
The foundation has argued that Christian political support has played a significant role in a number of Israel's diplomatic achievements over the years, from the recognition of Jerusalem to legislation combating the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement and antisemitism.
This year's list comes at a time when Israel's relationship with Christian communities abroad has assumed renewed importance amid the diplomatic and political fallout of the wars and upheavals that have followed October 7.
For the Israel Allies Foundation, the 50 names are intended to highlight the individuals who have continued to translate that support into public advocacy and practical action.
"The consistent voice of Christian supporters remains one of Israel's most important strategic, diplomatic and moral assets," the foundation said.

EXPLAINER- How panda diplomacy became part of US-China ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:23:50 UTC
22:23:50 KST

- Chinese President Xi Jinping says 2 pandas will arrive in Atlanta ‘in a few days,’ continuing a diplomatic tradition closely associated with Nixon’s 1972 China visit
- Once goodwill gifts, pandas now travel under conservation agreements that support research, breeding and habitat protection
-  Atlanta’s incoming pair will bring US giant panda population to 6, as renewed loans offer a sign of cooperation amid wider tensions
Two giant pandas heading from China to Atlanta will join a diplomatic tradition that has linked American zoos and Chinese leaders for more than eight decades.
“In a few days, two pandas – Ping Ping and Fu Shuang – will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people,” Chinese President Xi Jinping announced Thursday before talks with US President Donald Trump at the White House.
"The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans," he added, giving a familiar symbol of cooperation a place alongside much-anticipated discussions of trade, geopolitics and technology competition.
The pandas’ destination was already known. Zoo Atlanta announced the agreement in April, identifying Ping Ping as a male and Fu Shuang as a female, both born at China’s Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
Xi’s remarks supplied the arrival timeframe.
But how did these furry, bamboo-eating bears become symbols of US-China diplomacy? 
How it started
China’s use of pandas as diplomatic gifts predates the establishment of the People’s Republic in 1949.
Some accounts trace panda diplomacy back to the seventh century, when Empress Wu Zetian reportedly sent pandas to Japan during the Tang dynasty.
The practice reemerged in the 20th century.
In 1941, two young pandas, Pan-dee and Pan-dah, arrived at New York’s Bronx Zoo as gifts from Madame Chiang Kai-shek, China’s first lady, thanking Americans for aid to China during its war with Japan, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society’s archives.
The animals were initially thought to be a breeding pair, but both turned out to be female.
In the following decades, the People’s Republic sent pandas to friendly countries, including the Soviet Union and North Korea.
The animals offered China an unusual diplomatic advantage in that wild giant pandas live only in China, making access to them a distinctive gesture of goodwill.
Their appeal also extended beyond government officials. A panda could draw crowds to a zoo and generate public interest in a country that many visitors knew little about. 
The 1972 breakthrough
The best-known episode in US-China panda diplomacy followed President Richard Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972.
The visit helped end more than two decades of estrangement between Washington and Beijing, although formal diplomatic relations were not established until 1979.
During the visit, Nixon’s wife, first lady Pat, mentioned that she liked pandas after seeing them at a Beijing zoo.
Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai responded by offering two pandas to the American people.
Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing arrived at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington and were an instant sensation. More than 20,000 people came on the first day, and the following Sunday about 75,000 visitors formed a line a quarter-mile long.
The US reciprocated with a pair of musk oxen, Milton and Matilda.
The musk oxen had a rougher start. Time magazine reported they suffered "culture shock," with runny noses and hair loss, though they eventually recovered. 
From gifts to conservation loans
China moved away from giving pandas outright in the 1980s, turning instead to loans. Over time, long-term conservation and research agreements became the basis for overseas placements.
Such arrangements commonly run for about 10 years and can involve annual payments of around $1 million per pair. Under modern loan agreements, the pandas and their offspring remain Chinese property.
The shift to loans gave panda diplomacy a stronger conservation focus, with zoos contributing funding and expertise to breeding, research and habitat protection.
The US Fish and Wildlife Service listed the species as endangered in 1984 and adopted a conservation-focused panda permit policy in 1998, requiring all panda imports to directly benefit the conservation of pandas in the wild rather than serving short-term commercial exhibition.
The arrangement has been productive. US zoos have successfully raised 17 giant panda cubs – six in San Diego, four in Washington and seven in Atlanta – according to Chinese state media.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature reclassified giant pandas from endangered to vulnerable in 2016, citing a 17% population increase over the decade to 2014, when a nationwide census counted 1,864 in the wild in China, according to the World Wildlife Fund. 
What do panda movements tell us?
Panda arrivals and departures often attract attention far beyond the zoos involved.
As US-China relations deteriorated in recent years, the departure of pandas from American zoos became a particularly visible symbol of the tensions.
In November 2023, the Smithsonian’s National Zoo returned its three pandas to China as their loan agreement expired, leaving Zoo Atlanta as the only US zoo housing giant pandas.
Later that month, after meeting then-President Joe Biden in California, Xi said China was ready to continue panda conservation cooperation with the US – a gesture of goodwill amid efforts to stabilize relations.
A new pair arrived in San Diego in June 2024, before Atlanta’s four pandas departed that October. Another pair arrived in Washington later the same month.
Four giant pandas are currently in the US. Atlanta’s incoming pair would bring the total to six, compared with a historical peak of 15 reported by CNN. 
Atlanta’s next chapter
Zoo Atlanta’s original panda partnership began in 1999 and lasted 25 years. Its pandas produced seven cubs during that period.
The return of its four remaining bears in October 2024 closed that chapter, but the new agreement announced in April opened another.
For Atlanta, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will restore a major attraction and renew a research partnership. For Beijing, their arrival offers another opportunity to present cooperation with the US through animals that have long drawn American crowds.
Their arrival will not settle disputes over tariffs or AI regulation. But the two bears will offer an adorable reminder that Washington and Beijing still have room for friendship.

The women who should enter Israel’s sukkah this Sukkot - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:23:47 UTC
22:23:47 KST

Seven women will enter the sukkah, and at the end it will remain open — inviting us to build together a world of greater opportunity and possibility for all.
The following women will enter the sukkah:
Who are the women ushpizin?
On the first evening, we will welcome the woman who built the sukkah.
In 1971, Naomi Shemer wrote the song “Shlomit Builds a Sukkah,” dedicating it to the daughter of her neighbors. These were days when women could dream not only of building a sukkah of peace, but also of leading the nation — as Golda Meir was doing at the time as Israel’s prime minister.
But since then, there has been no other Golda, and decisions about our national sukkah are still made primarily by men. In fact, if current polls are borne out, the next Knesset may have only 31 women — approximately 26% of its members.
Five decades after the song was written, Shlomit knows: the time has come for everyone to truly have a place.
On the second evening, we will welcome the woman who was left one step behind.
She did not encounter a glass ceiling; she encountered a broken rung.
She is good at her job and highly regarded, but when she went on maternity leave, someone else was promoted to the first management position. Later, because he already had the experience, he was preferred for the next promotion as well.
There is a name for this phenomenon: “the broken rung.”
A 2025 Women in the Workplace study found that for every 100 men promoted into their first management position, only 93 women were promoted.
A seemingly small gap at the bottom of the ladder becomes far more significant the higher we climb.
On the third evening, we will welcome the woman who did not put herself forward.
When the position was advertised, she thought she did not meet all the requirements. When she was encouraged to apply, she said she wasn't sure it was for her. When the list was drawn up, she waited for someone to think of her — but no one did.
We like to say that the door is open to women. Sometimes, that is even true.
But an open door is not enough if, for years, boys have been taught to walk toward it with confidence, while girls are still waiting to be invited.
You are invited. Come in.
On the fourth evening, we will welcome the woman who did everything right.
She studied, worked, excelled, raised a family, picked up the children from kindergarten and answered emails at night.
And yet, there are still very few women around her.
According to the Israel Innovation Authority’s 2025 report, women make up only 17.6% of senior management positions in privately held high-tech companies and just 10.6% of start-up CEOs in Israel.
And the gap is not only in management; it exists in pay as well. Men earn approximately 44% more than women.
She does not understand why this is still happening.
On the fifth evening, we will welcome the woman who made it.
She is a manager, an entrepreneur, an elected public official, a researcher and a commander.
But she is alone.
Women make up 64% of the civil service, yet at the very highest levels, only 9% are women.
In hi-tech, too, women make up more than 30% of entry-level and middle-management positions, but only 17.6% of senior management.
She is waiting for more women to join her.
On the sixth evening, we will welcome a girl.
She does not yet know what she wants to be when she grows up.
When she enters the sukkah, she will look around and see women of different backgrounds, different ages and different walks of life. They will smile at her and introduce her to the other girls.
She will see many chairs and many opportunities, and she will know that everything is open to her.
On the seventh evening, no one will be invited — but the sukkah will be full.
Sarah and Miriam will be there, as will Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah, and Esther.
Henrietta Szold, Naomi Shemer, Golda Meir, and Ada Yonath will be chatting together.
Because this is the real story of the ushpizin.
It is not about who receives a ceremonial invitation to enter for one evening, but about what kind of sukkah we build in the first place.
The first step in correcting injustices that have persisted for years is to recognize the challenges, bring them into the public conversation, and promote clear policies to change the situation.
The second step is to create broad partnerships — between women and men, between organizations, and between different sectors of society.
Only when all women's voices are heard — and answered — can we ensure a truly equal society.
The writer is chair of Emunah — the Religious Zionist Women’s Movement.

US Senate rejects resolution curbing Trump's Iran war powers

The US Senate on Thursday narrowly rejected a Democratic-led resolution aiming to stop the Iran war until hostilities are authorized by Congress.
The Senate voted 50 to 49 to reject the resolution, which had passed the House of Representatives in July. The vote was largely along party lines, with most of US President Donald Trump's Republicans rejecting the measure and almost every Democrat voting for it.
Seven Republicans back Iran war powers resolution, widening GOP split with Trump
Earlier in September, in the House of Representatives, seven Republicans joined Democrats in backing a similar resolution directing Trump to remove American forces from hostilities against Iran unless Congress formally authorizes the war.
The resolution invokes Section 5(c) of the 1973 War Powers Resolution and directs Trump to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran unless Congress declares war or specifically authorizes the use of military force. It preserves Trump's ability to maintain the forces necessary to defend the US or an ally against an imminent attack, subject to the law's reporting requirements.
The legal force of such congressional efforts has long been disputed, and previous resolutions have not changed the course of US military operations. The Senate would also have to act for Congress to present a unified challenge to the administration.
Maya Zanger-Shamir and Idan Kweller contributed to this report.

EU countries agree conditions for allocating €6.6bn to Ukraine from Peace Facility

Source: Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Kallas stressed that this was "good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia".
She said €900 million would be allocated to the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine.
Another €1 billion will go towards financing new joint purchases of equipment.
The remaining €4.7 billion will be used to reimburse member states for their costs, with some of them having already said they would redirect their share towards Ukraine's needs, the EU foreign policy chief said.
"Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite," Kallas concluded.
The final decision is to be taken by the defence ministers of EU member states at a Council of the EU meeting on Monday.
Meanwhile, the distribution of the €4.7 billion among member states remains unresolved, as does how much of this amount will be transferred to Ukraine.
Background:
- Kallas previously said she was working with EU member state governments on allocating another €1 billion from the European Peace Facility for Ukraine's military needs.
- Germany previously said that the €6.6 billion from the Peace Facility, unblocked by Hungary, should be fully transferred to Ukraine, but not all EU countries support this.
- Hungary has lifted its veto on the €6.6 billion from the European Peace Facility, and EU defence ministers have already discussed how the funds could be used to benefit Ukraine.

Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international population evacuation plan

Unknown Publisher

Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international population evacuation plan
Kyiv • UNN
Lithuania and Poland are assessing the logistics and infrastructure for evacuating residents of the Baltic countries. Particular attention will be paid to the Suwałki Corridor.
Lithuania, together with Poland, is developing an international evacuation plan that will be used if it becomes necessary to evacuate some residents of Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia across the border. Delfi reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the director of the National Crisis Management Center (NCMC), Vilmantas Vitkauskas, procedures, logistical and infrastructure capabilities are currently being assessed jointly with Polish colleagues, and the plan itself is to be prepared after coordination between the two countries.
"We also have an international aspect of evacuation: what will happen if it becomes necessary to evacuate across the border a certain number of residents of Lithuania as well as neighboring Latvia and Estonia. In such situations, when there is a threat of war that is gradually approaching in the exercise scenario, the border regime usually changes. Border control is introduced to ensure mobilization and prevent people holding certain important positions from leaving the country, so that they remain here and perform their duties," Vitkauskas said.
According to him, in such a case, a large flow of evacuees could accumulate near the border, so it is necessary to assess in advance, together with Polish colleagues, how to manage such a situation.
"We will examine all procedural shortcomings, document them, and then a plan will emerge, to be prepared jointly by agreement between the two countries," the head of the NCMC noted.
He emphasized that, while preparing the plan, it is also necessary to assess traffic flows, transport connections, and the condition of the infrastructure. As Vitkauskas noted, it is important to anticipate how the flows of people leaving and arriving will be organized, as well as to assess the need to reinforce bridges and other infrastructure requirements.
Vitkauskas pointed out that the Suwałki Corridor is of particular importance in this process, as it is important both from a military and a logistical perspective.
"Therefore, the participation of Polish colleagues is of great importance, and we are extremely grateful to them for joining us and showing great interest… Poland's participation takes us to another level," he added.

====================================================================================================

Trump-Xi Summit: Heavy of Vibes, Light on Substance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:22:00 UTC
22:22:00 KST

When Chinese President Xi Jinping held a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump on September 24, Trump made sure Xi knew how he felt. The U.S. leader expressed no fewer than three times in the first minute of their joint remarks that it was his “honor” – or even “great honor” – to host Xi.
The “honor,” apparently was all Trump’s. Xi made no similar expression of feeling “honored” to be hosted by the U.S. president, simply saying he was “glad” to be in Washington.
That set the tone for a meeting that was long on symbolism but short on substance. Trump was eager to impress; Xi was all business.
Trump was reportedly keen to match the lavish hosting he received during his visit to Beijing in May. As Xi pointed out at the state dinner in Washington, it’s “unprecedented” for the Chinese and American presidents to exchange state visits in such a short period of time.
“Today, President Trump and I had sincere and in-depth exchanges and reached common understanding on many issues,” Xi said. “This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, and provided new strategic guidance for China-U.S. relations.”
“The constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability” is Beijing’s new mantra for the relationship – and the first that China has successfully gotten Washington to buy into. The basic gist is that China and the United States will continue to compete – something Beijing has finally admitted is happening, after years of studiously denying any rivalry – but keep their competition “within bounds.”
Other than agreeing, in principle, not to let their competition spill into conflict, though, it wasn’t immediately clear what “common understandings” were reached at the summit. No major breakthroughs were expected, and that turned out to be accurate.
The biggest deliverable was an agreement – actually reached before the summit, during China-U.S. economic talks on September 20 – to extend their trade truce through January 10. The original deal, reached at the first Trump-Xi summit in Busan, South Korea in October 2025, saw the U.S. lower tariffs on Chinese goods, while Chinese agreed to pause enforcement of export controls on certain critical minerals. The deal was only good for a year initially, and was set to expire in November.
Many experts had predicted an extension was in the offing – if that hadn’t been the case, it was suggested that there wouldn’t have been much reason for Trump and Xi to meet at all. But the short length of the extension – just two extra months – was a bit of a surprise. Bessent mentioned that China needed to make good on its promises, suggesting that the deal could be extended again if Washington is satisfied with what it sees. Or it could be eventually scrapped.
China, meanwhile, hasn’t confirmed even that limited extension. The official readout from the Chinese Foreign Ministry said a “new joint arrangement” had been reached in economic and trade discussions, but did not elaborate on what that deal was.
To recap: the biggest practical impact of the Trump-Xi summit was a possible agreement to slightly extend a pause – not a cancellation – on the worst of the trade war. Oh, and two more pandas for the Atlanta Zoo. That about sums up the fruits of the fragile truce currently in place between China and the United States.
If the outcome on trade was a mixed bag, other areas were even murkier. There was much focus on artificial intelligence (AI) prior to the summit, especially as U.S. AI companies themselves have begun raising safety concerns. There had been suggestions that the U.S. and China could unveil an “AI safety mechanism” that would see both sides notify the other of concerning incidents.
Trump, however, has consistently rejected any calls for additional oversight of AI – precisely because he wants the United States to go full speed ahead in the race against China. In a Truth Social post, prior to the summit, Trump stated that AI (which he has started referring to as “super intelligence”) “will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.”
Xi, however, was more cautious on AI, referencing the need to “jointly prevented the misuse and abuse of AI,” and emphasizing that “AI must be kept under human control.” But, like Trump, his primary concern was the AI race and preventing the U.S. from “guarding against” China’s AI development through export controls and other restrictions. As James Wang noted in a recent analysis for The Diplomat, Beijing is well aware of Washington’s tendency to frame restrictions on Chinese technology as safety measures.
As expected, Xi also brought up Taiwan. He explicitly asked “the U.S. side” to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence.’” Much reporting ahead of the summit held that Xi was hoping to get Trump to explicitly say that the U.S. “opposes Taiwan independence.” The usual phrasing is that the U.S. “does not support Taiwan independence.” For China, an outright expression of opposition would be a key win – especially because Beijing purposefully conflates Taiwan’s ruling party and president with “Taiwan independence forces.”
Beijing is also hoping to extend the current “pause” on U.S. arms sales to Taiwan to a de facto moratorium – something it’s tried to do in the past, but without success. Whenever a U.S. administration signals openness to scaling back arms sales to please China, Beijing ups the pressure.
Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, called the current period the “fourth Taiwan arms sale freeze,” following “two under former President George W. Bush from 2005-2007 and 2007-2008, and one under former President Barack Obama from 2011-2015.” In all these cases, Hammond-Chambers argued, the “freeze” did nothing more than embolden Beijing.
“The Trump Administration has let the fox in the henhouse. Telegraphing sensitivity to the Chinese position on Taiwan this past spring, Trump has empowered China to affect his decisions [on arms sales],” Hammond-Chambers wrote in a media release.
There’s been no movement on the arms sale, which has been on hold since before the May summit.
As with the Trump-Xi summit in May, this time there was another brief reference to an exchange of views “on major international and regional issues including the situation in the Middle East, the Ukraine crisis and the Korean Peninsula.” There was, however, no suggestion of any agreement or alignment on those issues – unlike after the May summit, when Trump got Xi to say that China opposes Iran’s development of nuclear weapons and supports “the free flow of energy” through the Strait of Hormuz.
If the actual substance showed little sign of convergence, you’d never know it from the optics. Trump lauded his “truly great friendship” with Xi and showed special deference to the Chinese president, including personally meeting him on the tarmac upon Xi’s arrival in the United States. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump also arranged an opulent welcome ceremony, featuring musical performances and drills by 479 military personnel and ending with a flyover by a B-2 stealth bomber and four F-22 fighter jets.
After the summit proper came the state dinner attended by a who’s who list of top American businesspeople: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Google’s Sundar Pichai, and Elon Musk of Tesla, X, and SpaceX.
Notably, though, Xi did not bring his own entourage of business leaders – a marked contrast with Trump’s visit to Beijing, when he included top CEOs in his delegation. Speaking to the New York Times, Emily Kilcrease of the Center for a New American Security called the absence of Chinese business leaders “a rather depressing marks of how bad the relationship has gotten.”
Overall, the summit left the impression of a stable, positive relationship, but there was little to back up that sentiment. Trump claimed that he and Xi had “made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries” – including the “unbelievably successful” Board of Trade, which hasn’t actually even launched yet – but as always, there were no specifics.
Xi’s positive comments, meanwhile, were mostly forward-looking. “[T]hrough candid, in-depth, and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” he said – an aspiration, not an accomplishment.
Xi also emphasize the parallels between the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” and Trump’s “make America great again” slogan, which he argued can “be mutually reinforcing.” Xi continued: “Our competition should be a healthy one and should be kept within bounds. It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses.”
It was a somewhat odd way of trying to cast competition as “win-win.” I don’t know what races Xi has been watching, but generally those have a winner as well – and multiple losers.
Given the shallow nature of the current era of good feelings in China-U.S. relations, it’s telling that the trade truce was extended only until January 10 – just long enough to keep relations steady through the APEC summit (to be held in Shenzhen, China from November 18-19) and the G20 summit (Miami, the United States, December 14-15). Assuming Trump and Xi attend both events, that could set up two additional summits, for a total of four in 2026 alone.
After that, all bets are off.
