NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Thitaphat Preechayan left the table tennis venue with a backpack slung over his shoulders, smiling as he walked away after losing to world No. 1 Wang Chuqin at the Asian Games.
The Thai high school student had spent the previous several days testing himself against some of the world's best table tennis players.
Three days earlier, the 16-year-old, ranked 275th in the world, stunned world No. 8 Lin Shidong 3-2 in the men's team quarterfinals.
Before that match, Preechayan repeatedly watched videos of Lin on social media, studying his opponent before stepping onto the court.
"I was very excited to play against them," Preechayan said. "I thought I couldn't lose. I just played point by point, and finally I won."
On Friday, the teenager took the opening game 11-3 against Wang in the men's singles round of 32 before the Chinese star settled into the match and won 4-2.
"I was fully focused during the match," Preechayan said. "I knew I was going to play against a world-class player, but I wasn't afraid."
"We had never played against each other before, and his ability to beat Lin was beyond what many people expected," Wang admitted. "I attached great importance to this match. I tried to make every point count and played very tightly."
"I feel very happy because I was able to take two games from him," Preechayan said. "But I think I still have to work harder."
Preechayan was born in Bangkok in 2010. He first picked up a table tennis racket at the age of seven after becoming fascinated in the sport by watching his older brother's practice.
His talent became apparent soon. His family decided to homeschool him between the ages of seven and 12, giving him more time to train before he returned to traditional schooling.
It was not long before Sanon Wongkaew, who was then coaching Preechayan's older brother and later joined the Thai national team's coaching staff, took notice and invited the teenager for a tryout.
Preechayan was able to hit topspin on his first attempt. Wongkaew encouraged him to train regularly and enter more competitions, where he soon found himself beating older players.
At 12, he earned a place on Thailand's under-13 national team.
"At that time, I didn't even know what it meant to be on the national team. I just knew I'd been selected," Preechayan said. "The more I competed, the more fun it became, and I loved table tennis even more."
His progress sped up in 2025. He won the U15 mixed doubles title at the ITTF World Youth Championships with Thai teammate Kulapassr Vijitviriyagul, becoming the first Thai to win gold at the event. He also won the U15 boys' singles title at the WTT Youth Contender San Francisco.
Thailand is not traditionally regarded as a table tennis powerhouse, but its national program has placed greater emphasis on developing young players and providing more opportunities for them to train overseas.
Preechayan normally trains at the Thai national team's base at a university. Ahead of the Asian Games, he also spent time training in Jinan, capital of China's Shandong province, gaining first-hand experience of training in the sport's leading nation.
His favorite player is another Chinese player, Fan Zhendong, an Olympic champion known for tenacity.
"I like his style of play," Preechayan said. "His mental strength is very strong."
For now, his ambition is simple but significant: to make his name known to Thai fans and build a career that can leave a mark for Thailand in the years ahead.
"I want to go to the Olympics," he said. "Maybe I can win a medal." ■

A Weekend in Riga Beyond the Sightseeing Checklist  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:08:24 UTC
22:08:24 KST

Riga is easy to approach as a list of landmarks: walk through the Old Town, photograph the best-known buildings and move on. But a short visit becomes more rewarding when there is time to notice how the city fits together. The market, the river, residential streets and evening venues offer a fuller picture than a hurried route between attractions.
Begin on Foot, but Leave Time to Wander
The Old Town is a practical starting point for a first visit. Its compact streets make it possible to explore without a strict itinerary. A short walk can take you from a quiet courtyard to a busy square, then towards the Daugava for a different view of the city.
Rather than trying to see every building in one morning, choose a few places that genuinely interest you. Leave time for a café stop or an unexpected detour. A flexible route is especially useful when the weather changes or a place turns out to deserve more time than planned.
Make the Central Market Part of the Day
Riga Central Market is close to the Old Town and the central transport stations, so it can be part of a walk rather than a separate excursion. It is a working market as well as a visitor attraction: people come to shop for ordinary meals, not only to show travellers local products.
Browse beyond the first stalls you see and pay attention to what is in season. Buying a small snack can make the visit more memorable than treating the market only as a place to photograph. Check current opening hours before setting out, and be considerate of traders and shoppers if you want to take pictures.
Explore a Different Side of Riga’s Architecture
Riga’s Art Nouveau district offers a change of pace from the Old Town. Alberta iela is known for its decorated façades, but the pleasure of the neighbourhood lies in looking closely. Entrances, windows and individual details are easy to miss when you are focused on reaching the next landmark.
A weekend also leaves space for a museum, a concert or a neighbourhood café. Check programmes and opening hours directly with the venue, particularly around public holidays. Having one indoor option in mind is useful if the weather does not cooperate.
Choose an Evening That Suits You
After dark, visitors might keep things simple with dinner and a walk, attend a performance or explore a venue that matches their interests and budget. Nightlife need not be a required part of a city break. The best choice is one you can enjoy without rushing or spending more than planned.
Some travellers also consider gambling among their entertainment options. If that interests you, distinguish between visiting a physical venue and using a website: rules and availability can differ. An online casino comparison can help readers identify questions to ask about licences, payment methods and terms before choosing an operator. It does not replace checking the operator’s current legal status and conditions.
It is also worth distinguishing locally licensed services from foreign online casinos. A licence issued abroad does not automatically mean an operator is authorised in Latvia or available to every visitor. Check the applicable rules and your eligibility, set a spending limit in advance, and never treat gambling as a way to pay for a trip.
Riga works well as a weekend destination because a visitor does not need to do everything. A market visit, two neighbourhood walks and one well-chosen evening activity can leave a clearer impression than an overfilled schedule. Keep some of the trip unscripted and give the city time to be more than a checklist.

Microsoft abandons personal AI chatbot race with Copilot reboot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:08:00 UTC
22:08:00 KST

Microsoft abandons personal AI chatbot race with Copilot reboot
- Microsoft has merged its consumer and workplace Copilot AI assistants into one product focused on corporate customers, exiting the personal chatbot market dominated by OpenAI, Google, and Meta.
- The new Copilot app improves workplace productivity by allowing editing in Word and Excel, includes a coding assistant, and rebrands the Scout assistant as Autopilot.
- Microsoft’s shift reflects user demand for AI tools that enhance work tasks, with over 30 million subscriptions already and plans to integrate personal Copilot features into enterprise use.
AI generated
Microsoft is merging the consumer and workplace versions of its Copilot AI assistant into one product aimed at corporate customers, ceding the crowded market for personal chatbots to OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google and, now, Meta Platforms.
At an event in Seattle earlier this week, Microsoft executives gave a few dozen business and technology leaders a preview of what they are calling the new Copilot. The result of a six-month engineering effort, the latest iteration of the assistant has absorbed the separate version for home use, adopting some of its slick design features, and casting aside the marketing that sought to position the company as a builder of personal AI.
People have high expectations for workplace software, informed by their experience with smartphone apps, Jacob Andreou, who leads product development of the unified Copilot app, told the audience of corporate customers on Sept 23. Importing some user experience features from the consumer app “made Copilot so much better in just the last few months”, he said.
Microsoft’s individual users, Andreou added, tend to be people who like to poke around in PowerPoint and Excel, and are more interested in “the full power that we offer to enterprise users” than a simplified chat app.
The updated software, announced on Sept 25, gives users the ability to edit Word or Excel documents within a Copilot app or browser tab, addressing a common gripe that Microsoft’s assistant had only limited reach into the company’s own productivity software.
There is also a tab for a coding assistant to enable regular users to put together dashboards or automate tasks. Microsoft’s Scout, an always-on assistant that co-workers can summon, is joining the Copilot package too, rebranded as Autopilot.
The new Copilot, which will roll out in the coming weeks, brings to a close one of Microsoft’s biggest bets of the AI era. Two years ago, executives formed separate teams to build two assistants – one for the workplace and one for home. Having helped OpenAI bring ChatGPT to the world, Microsoft bet that its own consumer assistant could win over a new set of customers and tapped AI industry veteran Mustafa Suleyman to lead the effort.
It quickly became an uphill battle when ChatGPT sprinted to a billion users and Google deployed its Gemini personal assistant to the vast Android ecosystem. Comparatively few people took Microsoft up on its offer of a personal chatbot. Suleyman in March ceded his Copilot product development responsibilities to Andreou, a former Snap executive.
Microsoft’s retreat coincides with the arrival of Meta’s Muse, a personal assistant that can act on users’ behalf and has raced to the top of the app download charts.
In interviews this week, Andreou and Charles Lamanna, an executive who oversees Microsoft teams working on some of Copilot’s core workplace features, said Muse’s success proved people were receptive to AI automation. Microsoft’s opportunity, they said, is to bring similar capabilities to office workers.
“We’re not going to build a Copilot that’s like your personal companion,” Lamanna said. (In April 2025, Suleyman had laid out Microsoft’s ambitions for Copilot in those very terms, standing in front of an enormous video screen introducing “Your AI Companion”.)
“That’s just not what people want from Microsoft,” Lamanna said. “We help you get stuff done.”
Andreou said many of the features of the personal Copilot, including specialised tools for health questions, studying or surfacing news and information, were incorporated into the rebuilt product. “In this unified Copilot, you actually still have all of these amazing consumer verticals and all of these kind of bespoke experiences,” he said.
Some other features included in the personal Copilot, including custom podcasts and an animated blob of an avatar that popped up during conversations, have been retired. Anthropomorphic touches live on in the new Autopilot bots, which appear as smiling shapes when they are invoked in a Teams chat or e-mail.
Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella compared the shift in office work brought about by automated AI services to the personal computer’s displacement of inter-office memos and faxes. “That was not just about our new digital tools,” he said at this week’s event. “It was a complete, new way to conceptualise how that business process trajectory worked. That’s what’s happening around Copilot.”
Companies were paying for more than 30 million Copilot subscriptions as at the end of June. And while individual users are free to use limited versions of Copilot’s chat experience, its most powerful tools are reserved for subscribers to the company’s M365 apps bundle, which has about 90 million paying users.
David McLaren, who leads data and AI work at GHD, a Canadian engineering and professional services firm that is part of a Microsoft programme for early adopters of AI tools, said employees were turning to Copilot for summaries of conference calls and help managing e-mail, as well as work putting together pitches and analysis for clients. “It will get you off the white, blank page,” he said.
GHD started using Copilot in late 2023 with a 300-person trial, and has since rolled out the tool to all of its 12,000 employees.
“I’m amazed by the use cases,” McLaren said. “They’re all over the place.” BLOOMBERG

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto, and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global.
A source close to Healey said: “Having Rav join John’s team as an experienced heavyweight economist at the Treasury ahead of this budget will be invaluable. His political nous will add to the special adviser team, providing John with guidance and counsel to the chancellor.”
Burnham flatly denied that he planned to call an early election on Friday. Asked by ITV Calendar whether the next general election would be in 2029, he said, “well, yes, that’s when the next election will be. All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead.”
Nevertheless, Athwal’s presence on Healey’s team could be seen as a strength if the prime minister did decide to draw up a fresh manifesto.
Athwal’s arrival is also likely to increase concerns among some in Labour that the Treasury’s instinctive caution is fuelling a “continuity Starmer” approach to economics.
The pledge at the heart of the manifesto not to increase income tax, national insurance or VAT was seen by Starmer’s team as key to Labour’s landslide victory two years ago. But it is widely agreed that it has restricted the party’s room for manoeuvre once in power.
People with knowledge of Athwal’s thinking suggest he has learned from the travails of Labour’s early months in office, however. One left-of-centre economist said: “I’d say he was at the more interesting and curious end of the Starmerite project.”
Before joining Labour, Athwal was a Treasury civil servant, rising to be head of growth strategy. One former colleague described him as “nice and clever – a good combination”.
After taking over at the Treasury in July, Healey hired Will Straw, who played a leading role in the remain campaign during the Brexit referendum, to be his chief of staff; some of Rachel Reeves’s economic advisers, including Spencer Thompson, stayed on.
Reeves’s chief economic adviser, the former Clean Bandit violinist Neil Amin-Smith, who was closely involved in her plans to devolve more tax revenue to local leaders, has moved across to Burnham’s No 10.
Athwal is expected to arrive in post next week, a month before Healey’s first budget.
With inflation and borrowing costs expected to have wiped out at least half of the headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules, Healey faces a series of tough decisions.
He has promised to maintain a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly smaller than the £24bn in the spring forecast.
Depending on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, restoring the cushion in full would be likely to require large tax rises or spending cuts. But government sources say Healey wants this to be a “focused” budget, after Reeves used her two budgets as chancellor to increase taxes by £70bn a year.
Key decisions about future tax and spending appear likely to be delayed until a Treasury spending review next year, which will come after Burnham has set out his long-term priorities in a 10-year plan, expected after the budget.
Healey has made clear he does not intend to set a timetable for when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence at the budget, for example – a target he insisted, when he resigned from Starmer’s government in June, must be met by 2030.
However, hopes of a low-key budget are under pressure from persistently high global oil and gas prices, which make it likely that the energy price cap, which determines UK consumer bills, will rise sharply in January.
Treasury sources have said officials are working “at pace” on options for consumer support, though help is expected to fall far short of the costly universal approach taken by Liz Truss in 2022.
Flint Global was approached for comment.

Indian Medical Parliamentarians’ Forum organises National Policy Summit on ‘Swasth bharat se saksham bharat’ to reimagine MedTech access in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:04:56 UTC
22:04:56 KST

The Indian Medical Parliamentarians’ Forum (IMPF) convened the National Policy Summit on MedTech Access on September 22
India’s healthcare landscape is evolving rapidly, with medical technology playing an increasingly important role in improving diagnosis, treatment and patient outcomes. Against this backdrop, and as the country works towards expanding access to quality and affordable healthcare, the Indian Medical Parliamentarians’ Forum (IMPF) convened the National Policy Summit on MedTech Access on September 22 at Meril Academy, Vapi, under the theme ‘Swasth Bharat Se Saksham Bharat | Reimagining MedTech Access in India.’ The summit brought together Members of Parliament, senior government officials, healthcare institutions, clinical experts and industry stakeholders to discuss strengthening India’s medical technology ecosystem and expanding access to quality, advanced and affordable healthcare technologies.Established in 2006, IMPF is a non-partisan platform for Members of Parliament from the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha with backgrounds in medicine and healthcare. The forum promotes evidence-based dialogue on public health priorities and connects parliamentary leadership with government, clinical experts, civil society, academia and industry to support national health policy discussions.The summit was chaired byDr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha and Chairperson, IMPF. Senior representatives from the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Department of Health Research, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Health Authority (NHA), AIIMS Nagpur and the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC) participated.The summit featured two panel discussions bringing together policymakers, healthcare experts, academic leaders and industry representatives to examine the development of India’s MedTech ecosystem and pathways to wider patient access.The first panel, ‘Building a sustainable and globally competitive MedTech ecosystem,’ examined the ecosystem required to support indigenous medical technology development and global competitiveness. Discussions covered research and innovation, regulatory and quality frameworks, industry-academia collaboration, domestic manufacturing, supply-chain resilience and clinical requirements. The panel was chaired by Dr Shivaji Bandappa Kalge, with Shri Manoj Joshi as Co-Chair. Dr Vibhav Garg, Meril, moderated the discussion, with Prof. (Dr.) Prashant P. Joshi and Dr Neha Dumka participating as panellists.The second panel, ‘Expanding access to quality care through MedTech innovation,’ focused on translating medical innovation into meaningful patient access. Discussions covered clinical evidence, health technology assessment, financing and reimbursement, technology adoption, healthcare workforce capabilities and extending advanced technologies across different levels of the health system. The panel was chaired by Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar and moderated by Dr Sharmila Sarkar, with Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan, Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav and Dr Suchita Markan as panellists.Speaking at the summit, Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde said, “Innovation without access has limited impact, and access without evidence cannot be sustained. For India to build a globally competitive medical technology ecosystem, we need stronger indigenous research and development, credible clinical evidence, appropriate health technology assessment and sustainable reimbursement mechanisms. Manufacturing must be supported by the right clinical skills, infrastructure and technical ecosystem. Our ultimate objective must be Indian innovation, global-quality technology and affordable access for every patient who needs it.”Manoj Kumar Joshi, Co-Chair and Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, said, “For India to become self-reliant in medical devices, we need a strong ecosystem built around quality, evidence and credibility. Our regulatory system must evolve to ensure products developed in India meet globally credible standards. We also need to strengthen domestic supply chains, engineering capabilities and component manufacturing. This will support healthcare access while contributing to employment and the country’s prosperity.”Highlighting the role of healthcare institutions, Dr Prashant P. Joshi said, “Medical institutions should not be limited to validating technologies developed elsewhere; they should identify unmet clinical needs and work with engineers, researchers and innovators to develop solutions. Stronger collaboration between medical and engineering institutions through joint research, academic programmes, fellowships and training can significantly strengthen India’s medical technology ecosystem.”On clinical adoption and capacity building, Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan said, “Access to medical technology is not simply about making a device available. Meaningful impact is possible only when healthcare professionals can use it safely, confidently and effectively. We need to move from an equipment-centric approach to a technology adoption model supported by competency-based training for healthcare professionals.”Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav, IAS, Joint Director, National Health Authority, highlighted the importance of financing and reimbursement. He said, “For medical technology to reach patients, clinical effectiveness must be supported by appropriate financing and reimbursement pathways. Under Ayushman Bharat, newer interventions require credible clinical and economic evidence before incorporation into health benefit packages. We must also consider the total cost of care rather than only the upfront cost of a device.”Emphasising health-system requirements, Dr Neha Dumka said, “Technology has an important role in strengthening primary healthcare. However, innovation must be assessed for technical capabilities as well as ease of use, cost-effectiveness, scalability and sustainability. Technologies must be capable of effective adoption at different levels of care and ultimately reach the beneficiaries who need them.”Speaking on grassroots healthcare delivery, Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar said, “To take medical technology from innovation to meaningful patient access, we need to identify bottlenecks in the existing system and strengthen the capabilities of healthcare professionals at the grassroots, particularly at CHCs and sub-district centres. Technologies should be introduced systematically and evaluated through comparative, data-based studies.”Highlighting the potential of domestic manufacturers, Dr Shivaji Kalge said, “Indian medical device companies are increasingly capable of developing technologies that meet international standards while remaining affordable for Indian patients. Continued investment in research, quality and innovation can help these technologies gain wider acceptance globally while improving access to quality healthcare.”
The summit also included representatives from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), National Health Authority, government medical institutions, clinical experts and industry associations.The discussions underscored the need for a coordinated approach spanning indigenous innovation, evidence generation, regulatory quality, clinical education, health technology assessment, financing, reimbursement and institutional adoption, while connecting MedTech innovation with the needs of healthcare providers and patients, particularly in underserved areas.Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.

Small businesses in rural France bears the brunt of energy crisis triggered by Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:03:25 UTC
22:03:25 KST

In the Oise department, soaring energy prices driven by the war in Iran are hitting rural businesses hard, as they face rocketing bills for heating oil and diesel.
France's rural communities are feeling the full force of the global energy crisis sparked by the war in Iran. Almost 21 million people — nearly a third of the French population — live in the countryside, which covers around 90% of the country's landmass.
In Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, a town of around 6,000 people in the northern Oise department, rising energy prices are being felt even in the local bakery.
Kevin Luce bakes his bread in two heating oil-fired ovens — a fuel that was once cost-effective but has become increasingly expensive. "At the outset it was a good deal: an oil-fired oven was cheaper to run than an electric one, until the price went up by 50%," he said.
His last delivery, two days ago, came to 2,200 euros for 1,200 litres. Six months earlier, he had paid 2,100 euros for 2,000 litres. The difference is being absorbed directly by the business.
"All this excessive spending on energy is money we are losing. It's wages we can't take, pay rises we can't give our employees, investments we can't make," Luce said.
Small businesses forced to cut back
Food truck owner Martial Realland has taken a different approach — he has stopped refilling his oil tank altogether. "Last year I had 1,500 litres delivered. It cost me 1,600 euros. Now, at 1.80 or 1.90 euros a litre, it's almost double. So I'm not getting any delivered," he said.
Realland has also begun turning down jobs that involve long distances. "Ever since I was born there have always been crises. But this is no longer bearable," he said.
The surge in energy costs is reviving memories of the gilets jaunes movement, which erupted in autumn 2018 after a rise in fuel taxes. The protest gained its strongest momentum in rural and outer-suburban areas — the same communities now bearing the heaviest burden of the current crisis.

What are the Lib Dems for? They must champion localism to stay relevant in an age of single-issue politics | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:02:14 UTC
22:02:14 KST

September is the cruellest month for political commentators because it is when something has to be said about the Liberal Democrats. They are a play without a plot, a chorus line of seemingly endless “don’t knows”. Their leader, Ed Davey, recently warned that “we’re in the fight of our lives” to defend the values of liberty and equality. Really? How can this be when Davey is becoming about as relevant as Count Binface?
The Lib Dems’ central predicament has remained unchanged for a century, ever since the decline of David Lloyd George and the rise of the Labour party. There is simply no space in Britain for a centrist party when so little divides the big parties and they broadly stick to the prevailing ecomomic orthodoxy.
But there is now a ray of hope. One of the newer developments in British politics is the rise of single-issue parties. In Scotland and Wales, the Scottish National party and Plaid Cymru demand independence from the UK, while in England the Reform party has dedicated itself to curbing immigration.
A lack of a clarifying message could partly explain why the Lib Dems have suffered heavy defeats at recent byelections, and slipped to fourth or fifth place in many national opinion polls, regularly trailing the Greens and Reform.
In order to improve their electoral fortunes, the Lib Dems need an equally straightforward cause, one that should have broad appeal and identify an area neglected by the other parties. That cause is now glaring: the devolution of government authority.
Time and again in national league tables, England ranks as having one of the most concentrated central governments in Europe, and by some measures in the world. English citizens’ ability to participate in local democracy is extremely weak compared to other countries such as France, Germany and those in Scandinavia.
Welfare comparisons show the UK’s local services fare poorly and inequitably compared with those, for instance, in localised Scandinavia. The authority of Britain’s central executive over local government is overbearing, with ever more disappointing outcomes for citizens.
Localism is the issue and one that has featured prominently in political debate for decades. New Labour even proposed a “new localism”. The result was just 12 elected mayors in England and Wales between 2001 and 2005.
In 2010, David Cameron pledged a “radical shift in power from central government to neighbourhoods”. He then did the opposite through enforced housing targets and a fierce programme of austerity. Similarly, in 2024 Keir Starmer promised to “deepen democracy by … devolving power to communities”. Yet one of his first moves was to overrule local discretion in planning approvals, describing councils as “blockers and nimbys”.
Over the years, the phrase “shifting power locally” became an almost ritualistic election chant, clearly based on polling data. No government really meant it. Ever since Margaret Thatcher, the centre has taken ever more control of local taxation, education, housing, care services and planning. The job of a British local council today is in effect to do what the centre tells it. It has not much money nor power for anything else. It is therefore no wonder that local democracy is subject to ridicule: see, for instance, the recent “independence” vote in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington.
Unquestionably the most headline-grabbing of Westminster’s pseudo-localists is Andy Burnham. Does he mean it? His innovation of a cohort of metro mayors – introduced under the Conservatives – inserts a new level of regional bureaucracy between central and local government. Their role will primarily be to enforce national targets of housebuilding and energy investment, and presumably to override decisions of local councils beneath them.
Burnham’s announcement that mayors in England will be able to keep a share of income tax and business rates was cited as proof of his commitment to his so-called devolution agenda. But the extent to which mayors will be able to wield these powers remains to be seen.
The prime minister’s moving of parts of the No 10 operation to Manchester hardly reduces the power of the centre. It merely relocates it, temporarily. Here, surely, is a Liberal Democrat cause.
Significantly, the one area in which the Lib Dems have flourished is local government. At last May’s local elections, the party took their control of councils up to 76, establishing them as a major political force across local government. This was a major achievement. There are now more Liberal Democrat council leaders in Britain than the 71 Lib Dem MPs. As such, their impact on the actual government of the country is substantial.
This cries out for revolution and the Lib Dems have every reason to be its champions. The party should go flat out for democratic, truly local self-government. Models of appropriate tiers and functions can be found across Europe. The cause is now aided by mountainous evidence that Britain’s centrist model – the famous “Rolls-Royce” of Whitehall – is now a clapped out jalopy. Every week the headlines cry that nothing seems to work.
This is the all-consuming challenge for the Lib Dems to make their own. Propose a major constitutional reform. The party’s 76 local councils can list the powers they want restored to them. It is these council leaders who must stand on stage at their conference, not Westminster’s indolent parliamentarians. Liberal Democrats should become the party of local Britain and restore the government of the people to the people.
- 
  Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

YEREVAN, September 25. /TASS/. Nearly 60% of Armenian citizens surveyed favor holding a referendum on the country's membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), according to a poll presented by Gallup International.
"Some 38.9% stated that a referendum should definitely be held, while 20.3% said it likely should be. This means approximately 60% of citizens believe a referendum is necessary. Meanwhile, 9.3% of respondents felt a referendum likely should not be held, 25.1% stated it is definitely not needed, and 6.9% were undecided," Aram Navasardyan, head of Gallup International's Armenian branch, said during the presentation of the poll results.
He also noted that when choosing between Armenia's membership in the EAEU or the European Union, supporters of both paths were almost evenly split: 29.4% of citizens said the country should remain in the EAEU, while 35.1% favored moving toward EU membership. "Another 24.7% stated they would not vote, and 10.9% found it difficult to answer," Navasardyan reported.
The telephone poll of 1,001 respondents was conducted from September 22 to 24, with a margin of error of ±3%.
On March 26, 2025, the Armenian parliament passed a law initiating the process of the republic's accession to the EU. Russian President Vladimir Putin previously noted that EU integration would automatically terminate Armenia's cooperation with the EAEU and lead to the loss of all associated preferences. At the EAEU summit in Astana on May 29, the leaders of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan issued a joint statement backing a nationwide referendum in Armenia on whether to join the EU or remain in the EAEU.
On August 11, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told TASS that Armenia
needed to hold a nationwide referendum before December of this year, when potential steps regarding Yerevan will be discussed at a meeting of EAEU heads of state.
On August 24, Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Chairman of the Russian Security Council, told TASS that Yerevan would never become an EU member but would instead severely damage its long-term relations with the EAEU and Moscow.

CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:01:20 UTC
22:01:20 KST

CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
- Date:
- September 25, 2026
- Source:
- CERN
- Summary:
- CERN has started replacing some of the Large Hadron Collider’s most important magnets as part of its High-Luminosity upgrade. The new superconducting magnets will produce fields about 40% stronger, allowing particle beams to be squeezed more tightly before they collide. That should create far more collisions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments to analyze, giving physicists a much larger window into the fundamental workings of the universe.
- Share:
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) stretches 27 km around and relies on thousands of magnets of different types - dipoles, quadrupoles, sextupoles, octupoles, decapoles, etc. - to steer and control its particle beams. Each type performs a specialized task.
Some of the most important are known as inner triplets. These groups of three quadrupole magnets (hence the name) sit on both sides of the LHC's four main experiments. Their job is to focus the particle beams as tightly as possible just before the particles collide inside the detectors.
The tighter the beams are "compressed," the greater the chance that particles will collide. That makes the inner triplets essential for increasing the LHC's luminosity, i.e. the number of collisions that occur in a given period of time. More luminosity means more collisions, giving researchers more data to analyze.
Preparing the LHC for a New Era
A major part of the future High-Luminosity LHC (HiLumi LHC) project involves replacing the existing inner triplets with a much more powerful generation of magnets.
The work is taking place during the third long shutdown (LS3). Reently, crews cut the first magnet interconnection, formally beginning the replacement operation. CERN Director-General Mark Thomson also visited LHC Point 1 (the ATLAS experiment) to mark the milestone.
"The replacement of these magnets with the new HiLumi LHC inner triplets is crucial for the coming high-luminosity years. The first quadrupole of the new triplets should arrive in the tunnel at the start of 2029. In total, 16 cryostats and 28 cryo-assemblies will be installed - a major undertaking," explains Jean-Philippe Tock, Head of the LS3 Coordination Team.
Magnets About 40% Stronger
The new inner triplets are the product of years of research and development. They represent a major technological advance over the niobium-titanium magnets currently operating inside the LHC.
Instead of niobium-titanium, the upgraded magnets use niobium-tin superconducting coils. This allows them to generate magnetic fields reaching 11.3 tesla, about 40% stronger than the fields produced by the current magnets.
The new equipment will be installed around the ATLAS and CMS experiments, where the increased collision rate will be especially important.
ALICE and LHCb operate differently and pursue different physics programs, so they do not need the same increase in instantaneous luminosity. Their existing inner triplets can therefore remain in place. However, those magnets will still be upgraded so that both experiments can benefit from the overall increase in luminosity.
Removing 28 Superconducting Magnets
Since September 7, CERN teams have been dismantling sections of the collider on either side of ATLAS and CMS. The goal is to remove 28 superconducting magnets (including the inner triplets) that are scheduled to be replaced.
The operation marks the end of an era for hardware that has been part of the LHC since its construction.
"Today's event is a major milestone for CERN, especially for the HiLumi LHC project team. The current inner triplets date back to the LHC construction phase and were installed in the machine between 2005 and 2007. After nearly twenty years of operation, they will give way to a new generation of even more powerful magnets. It's truly remarkable to witness such a handover from one generation of innovation to the next," says Markus Zerlauth, the HiLumi LHC Project Leader.
Story Source:

Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:00:55 UTC
22:00:55 KST

Danish intelligence officials have warned that Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, on Thursday identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it wrote in a report.
"The purpose would be to redirect European resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response."
The DDIS added that it saw no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a NATO country, although it said it could not rule this out.
Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops, possibly without national insignia, into NATO countries on its border, the DDIS said. However, it said that such a buildup would be difficult to conceal and take several months to prepare.
The new threat assessment joins a chorus of Russia warnings from top European security officials and lawmakers in recent days.
NATO members that border Russia are Finland, Norway and Poland as well as the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Poland's government on Thursday said a blaze at a Starlink ground station in the country was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.
Poland's deputy prime minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, said it had not yet been established who was responsible for the fire, but "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new doctrine of attack," according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Russia's embassy in London was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC. The Kremlin has previously denied involvement in similar incidents.
Denmark's intelligence service also warned that Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more attacks against the West and NATO, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past."
These could include major cyberattacks that seriously damage vital societal functions as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, the DDIS said.

From Croatia without waste: “truly circular” process offers hazardous chemicals a second life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:00:17 UTC
22:00:17 KST

A clean-tech company in Croatia claims to recycle around three million kilograms of polluted solvents annually – without any waste. An “efficient, safe and economically valuable” recycling process of hazardous chemicals… made in Europe.
Equipped with air-filtering masks, workers at a recycling plant in Ivanić-Grad, Croatia, recycle ethanol, benzene or acetones, and thinners to dilute paints. These and other used solvents come from the food packaging, pharmaceutical or automotive industries. They are full of hazardous substances.
A complex process removes all their residues and turns contaminated solvents into clean ones, ready to be re-used.
“This is the contaminated solvent that we are taking from the machine and into the distillator. We are distilling it, and for the result we are getting the clean solvent that is used to further production. Clean as a whistle”, explains Mario Želježnjak, Production Supervisor at Premifab Ltd as he shows us the different technologies at an unassuming plant recently inaugurated.
Along with water and other impurities, the resulting waste is basically sludge that is used to produce energy that feeds the recycling facilities. “Everything is burned inside a rotary kiln and turned into harmless ash,” explains Mario. This ash can subsequently be used as a construction material.
Partially funded by the European Union, the clean-tech company claims to recycle around three million kilograms of used solvents annually—a 90% recycling rate for the contaminated raw material sent by its clients. Facing stiff competition from other major industry players in Germany, France, Spain, and Italy, the company must offer efficiency and versatility, explains its business development director, Igor Podravac.
“We have a lot of high demanding customers from pharmaceutical, automotive, paint industry,food packaging industry also. After they pollute a material and it is no longer usable for a second treatment, they send this material to us,” he explains while showing us the work done workers. “We are accepting the material, analysing the material, purifying the material and after all the parameters are checked, we return that material into the same production line to get a closed loop circular economy in real life.”
The first step starts at the company´s laboratory. Samples of used solvents are here first analysed to determine if and how they can safely and effectively be recycled. Very different parameters, including temperature, pressure or energy balance must be considered. “Maybe the distillation yield is too low, so it's not really feasible, both material-wise and financial-wise. And on the other hand, if we have lots of distillation residue remaining, that we cannot do anything about it, we opt not to use that material at all,.”, explains Silvija Petković, Quality Control Director & Laboratory Manager. “The specificity within the solvents is their flammability. So they're all flammable liquids, and we need to take all the precautionary measures in order not to burn anything, not to light anything up,” she adds.
After the distillation, and prior to sending the now clean solvents back to the clients, quality control checks are enforced again.
“This one does not conform because of the precipitation, so this one cannot go to the customer. So, this sample is going to stay here, and we need to do further filtration,” Silvija, explains to our camera while holding one sample. “This one is okay, no precipitation, whatsoever. It can be closed and sealed and put into the truck,”after checking a second, much transparent sample.
The approved recovered solvents are shipped to the clients in special containers. We follow one such delivery with Nikola Gojavić, a driver at the company. “This cargo is unique because it’s in a liquid state and is highly explosive. Great care is required during loading and transport, so specialised drivers are needed—it’s quite a challenging job,” he tells us while driving.
“The driver must be a specialist because, in the event of an accident or any incident, they must remain composed and be trained to carry out the necessary procedures.”
The cargo we follow brings back recovered solvents to a family business called Rotoplast. Each year, it manufactures approximately 5,000 tonnes of packaging and labelling for the food, energy and pet product industries. Solvents are used here to dissolve inks in the printing processes.
“It is important to us that our products, along with being highly effective from a production point of view, are also environmentally sustainable,” says Production Director Antun Čengić. “In cooperation with Premifab, we collect all our waste in a safe way, we transport it to their location, so that they can process it and return it to us as a new resource. With this, we reduce the costs of production.”
The company was founded in 1975 and currently employs 260 staff. Solvents are among the many recycled products that are reused here, claims the CEO, Blaženko Marić.
“80% of materials, it's possible to use like this. We would like to move to mono materials. For all materials, for all customers. This is the plan for the next few years, to be completely phase out materials which are unrecyclable,” he explains.
Igor Podravac, its business development director, says their turnover has grown “approximately 20 to 25% per year” since they started operations, in December 2014. The company claims that, compared to primary production, recovered solvents generate up to 10 times less CO2 emissions.

People with excessive smartphone habits show distinct neural responses to social exclusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:00:11 UTC
22:00:11 KST

Individuals who exhibit excessive smartphone use display distinct brain activity patterns when experiencing social exclusion. A small study published in Computers in Human Behavior indicates that this heightened neural sensitivity could play a role in the persistence of screen-related behavioral addictions. The research highlights specific emotional and cognitive vulnerabilities that accompany heavy smartphone reliance.
The psychological boundaries between habit and addiction are a subject of ongoing debate among mental health professionals. Behavioral addictions often arise from a combination of underlying personal traits, heightened responses to external cues, and impaired cognitive control. Researchers refer to these intersecting factors to understand how people develop compulsive routines over time. In the context of smartphones, many applications are designed specifically to facilitate digital social interaction and constant connectivity.
When a person feels left out of these digital interactions, they may experience a form of emotional distress that resembles physical pain. Social exclusion is a recognized psychological stressor that triggers strong biobehavioral responses. People who struggle with emotional regulation might rely on their devices to manage this distress or to maintain a false sense of belonging. The fear of missing out, or FOMO, is a related concept that describes the persistent anxiety of being absent from rewarding social events.
A research team led by psychiatrist Robert C. Wolf at Heidelberg University in Germany set out to observe the brain activity of people who use their phones excessively. The investigators focused on the socio-cognitive aspects of smartphone habits, an area that receives less attention than reward-seeking behaviors. They wanted to see how the brains of frequent users react to being socially excluded compared to people with average phone habits.
The investigators recruited 41 young adults between the ages of 18 and 30 for this small study. To divide the participants into two groups, the researchers administered a standardized questionnaire that measures excessive smartphone use. This diagnostic tool assesses behaviors like withdrawal symptoms, building a tolerance to screen time, and how much phone habits interfere with daily life. Based on the scores, 23 participants were placed in the excessive use group, and 18 were assigned to the control group.
Before brain scanning, all participants completed additional surveys to measure their levels of depression, social phobia, and fear of missing out. The researchers then used functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, to observe blood flow in the participants’ brains. This advanced imaging technique allows scientists to see which areas of the brain are most active during specific cognitive tasks.
While inside the scanner, the participants played a virtual ball-tossing game called Cyberball. The researchers told the participants that they were playing online with two other real human volunteers. To make the scenario more convincing, the game started with a loading screen stating a network connection was being established. The interface also displayed artificial intelligence-generated portrait photos of the supposed co-players.
In reality, the other players were controlled by a computer program designed to manipulate the participant’s social experience. The game was divided into different structured phases. During the inclusion phase, the computer-controlled players threw the ball to the human participant regularly. During the exclusion phase, the computer players only passed the ball back and forth to each other, leaving the human participant out of the game entirely.
The brain scans revealed marked differences between the two groups during these simulated social interactions. When comparing the exclusion phase to the inclusion phase, the excessive smartphone use group showed heightened activity in the right middle cingulate cortex. This region of the brain is known to be heavily involved in processing pain, including the emotional sting of social rejection. The heightened activation suggests that people who use their phones excessively might have an altered threshold for social pain.
This brain activation also extended into the right superior frontal cortex. This area is traditionally associated with complex cognitive functions, executive control, and decision-making. The simultaneous activation of these areas implies an intense emotional and cognitive reaction to being left out of the group activity.
Conversely, the control group displayed increased activity in a different part of the brain during the exclusion phase. These individuals showed higher activation in the left superior parietal cortex. This specific brain region helps manage working memory and integrates various streams of sensory information. The findings indicate that average smartphone users process social exclusion using different neural pathways than heavy users.
The behavioral survey results aligned closely with the brain imaging data. Participants in the excessive use group scored substantially higher on the fear of missing out scale than those in the control group. The excessive use group also reported higher levels of functional impairment in their daily routines due to their screen habits.
The researchers then looked for mathematical relationships between the survey scores and the localized brain scan data. In the excessive use group, the level of activity in the left superior parietal cortex positively correlated with their functional impairment scores. The investigators also mapped the overall brain activity patterns to known neurotransmitter networks to see which chemical messengers were at work.
They found that dopamine and serotonin pathways were highly active during the social exclusion phase for both groups. These specific chemicals help regulate mood, reward processing, and pain perception in the human nervous system. The involvement of these neurotransmitters confirms that the virtual game successfully induced a genuine feeling of social distress across the entire study sample.
Because this was an observational cross-sectional study, causality cannot be firmly established. It is not possible to say whether excessive smartphone use causes heightened sensitivity to social exclusion, or if a pre-existing emotional sensitivity drives people to use their phones more often. The sample size was also limited, which means the results should be treated as preliminary until replicated in larger populations.
The experimental setup itself presented some methodological limitations. Several participants suspected that they were playing against a computer program rather than real people. This awareness might have dampened the emotional impact of the social exclusion exercise for those specific individuals. Additionally, screening for underlying psychiatric conditions relied entirely on self-reported surveys rather than in-depth clinical evaluations by a mental health professional.
Future investigations will need to track participants over longer periods of time to see how smartphone habits and social sensitivities develop sequentially. Experimental designs that involve periods of enforced smartphone restriction could help clarify how social pain and digital habits influence one another. These longitudinal approaches could provide a better understanding of how people use digital networks to manage their basic human need for connection and belonging.
The study, “Neural correlates of social exclusion in individuals with excessive smartphone use,” was authored by Gudrun M. Henemann, Mike M. Schmitgen, Sophie H. Haage, Jakob P. Rosero, Patrick Bach, Nadine D. Wolf, Julian Koenig, and Robert C. Wolf.

See the secret to DNA hookups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

See the secret to DNA hookups
How DNA strands meet to divvy up chromosomes was a longtime mystery
DNA needs a little help to zip up its genes.
In a first, scientists have visualized how pieces of DNA pair up. Computer simulations further reveal that charged metal ions help twin double helices align, researchers report September 9 in Nucleic Acids Research.
The work adds insight to the process in which cells pair up chromosomes before divvying DNA into eggs or sperm. Matching the chromosomes allows them to exchange information and keeps them from going astray, much like how folding socks keeps pairs together.
But it’s not so easy to bring two DNA double helices together. The strands have a negative electrical charge and repel each other. Researchers previously hypothesized that positively charged ions could facilitate zipping the twisting strands of DNA together.
Scientists at the University of Sheffield in England used atomic force microscopy to visualize short strands of DNA pairing up. The specialized microscope technique works like a record player, says microscopist Thomas Catley. A very sharp-tipped needle is dragged across a surface containing molecules the researchers want to examine. “We detect how that tip moves, and we turn that into an image signal, basically the same way that you get sound from a record player,” he says.
The zipped DNA strands look like twisted pieces of yarn with their grooves nestling together.
DNA pairing revealed
An atomic force microscope image shows identical DNA double helices pairing up. A zoomed in look (box, upper left) shows two double strands of DNA nestling together. Pink stars and green triangles indicate the alternating arrangement of grooves where the attraction between positively charged metal ions and negatively charged DNA holds the helices together.
Agnes Noy, a computational biophysicist at the University of York in England, was so taken with the images that she and colleagues did computer simulations to explain the mechanism. Positively charged metal ions nestle in the grooves of the DNA’s spiral staircases. That’s where information-carrying bases sit. The ions form bridges with the negatively charged ridges of the DNA backbone.
The DNA strands are staggered so that positive and negative charges alternate, the simulations suggest. The opposite charges attract the strands to each other. Together the images and simulations confirm the DNA zipper model, the researchers say.
This knowledge may help bioengineers make better folds in DNA origami structures used to deliver drugs and give a better understanding of biological processes, including what goes wrong in some cancers.

Details: The UAVs have also been given a function which allows several drones to remain on standby and respond quickly when a target appears.
According to Ptashka Drones, an unlimited number of drones can be connected to a single ground station while in standby mode. However, the manufacturer has not publicly disclosed the technical details of how the new function works, providing them to unit representatives during consultations.
As Ukrainian military media outlet Militarnyi reports, the microphone is highly sensitive and allows potential targets to be detected at a considerable distance from the ambush site.
"At a distance of 200 m, you can clearly hear a car moving along the road through the microphone," a Ptashka Drones representative said.
The amount of time a drone can remain in standby mode depends on its modification, battery capacity and distance from the operator. For example, the Ptashka 15-O-30km can remain in ambush mode for up to five hours after landing 25 km from the operator.
"You can control one selected drone and listen to what is happening through headphones, while the others display a light indicator showing the sound level," the company explained.
Ptashka Drones manufactures radio-controlled and fibre-optic FPV drones. Its range includes 10-, 15- and 17-inch UAVs. The company also develops counter-UAV systems, including handheld and drone-mounted net guns.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported on tests of Ukrainian systems for detecting FPV drones, including acoustic detectors. One of the developers said that, depending on the size of such a system, it can detect a drone by sound at a distance of up to several hundred metres.

Hungary dramatically cuts EU defence loan request under new government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:59:38 UTC
21:59:38 KST

The administration of Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has significantly reduced its requested EU defence loan, from €16.4 billion to €5.4 billion, Brussels announced on Friday.
Hungarian authorities have informed Brussels that they intend to limit their request for an EU defence loan to €5.4 billion under the EU’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) programme, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed on Friday.
The latest figure is less than half the €16.4 billion originally requested by former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
The original proposal was contested by Orbán’s successor, Péter Magyar, who took office in April. It is understood that Magyar wanted to reassess the original proposal over alleged corruption risks linked to the previous government.
“We were always very clear with the new incoming Hungarian authorities and government that they would be able to take stock of the current situation, and they have now decided to take less than what we initially allocated to Hungary,” Regnier added.
Meanwhile, the size of Italy’s SAFE defence loan was also confirmed on Friday, with Regnier stating that Italy has formally requested €8 billion under the programme.
This is also roughly half of the €14.9 billion originally anticipated by the government of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
The announcement comes after terse negotiations between Brussels and Rome over the allocation, which was never formally finalised but nevertheless caused consternation between the two capitals.
The SAFE low-interest loan scheme was launched by Brussels last year to strengthen defence industries and military readiness across the bloc in response to the threat posed by Russia.
The programme has a total funding envelope of €150 billion, which is to be distributed among 19 member states.
SAFE forms part of the Commission’s Readiness 2030 plan, which aims to mobilise up to €800 billion in additional defence spending by the end of the decade. It places a particular focus on boosting the procurement of priority defence products.
Under the programme, at least 65% of the value of the weapon system being acquired must be sourced from an EU member state, Ukraine, or a country belonging to the European Economic Area or European Free Trade Association.
The remaining 35% may be sourced from any third country.

What’s Behind Australia’s New $42 Million in Assistance to Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:59:00 UTC
21:59:00 KST

Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York this week. Out of that meeting came a new bilateral security agreement, unlocking a further US$42 million in Australian assistance to Ukraine – split between Australian Defense Force (ADF) equipment, Ukraine’s Energy Support Fund, and humanitarian assistance. This brings Australia’s total contribution to almost US$1.4 billion.
Ukraine is obviously far away from Australia’s immediate security concerns in the Indo-Pacific, but Canberra’s support for the country is driven principally by its interest in preventing territorial conquest from becoming an accepted instrument of international relations. As a geographically isolated country with considerable economic interests beyond its immediate region, Australia depends on international rules that constrain the use of force. Canberra understands that allowing this principle to be undermined in Europe would weaken its application elsewhere, including in the Indo-Pacific. Alongside this is the position that smaller and middle-sized countries should retain the freedom to make their own security and diplomatic decisions.
Alongside its assistance package, Australia will also join the United Kingdom and Norway-led Maritime Capability Coalition which is helping Ukraine develop its naval capabilities. Yet what is most interesting about the new security agreement with Ukraine is not so much the assistance that Australia can provide Ukraine, but what Australia can learn from Ukraine.
Over the past four years, Ukraine has been forced into one of the more consequential live experiments in modern warfare. It has had to develop systems and capabilities that can counter a larger and more well-equipped military force with cunning and creativity. The most visible product of this has been in unmanned systems. Ukraine’s naval drone program, epitomized by the Magura platform, has proved to be a relatively inexpensive, but high impact weapons program adaptable to multiple roles, from attacking warships and aircraft, to striking the industrial infrastructure inside Russia that funds its invading force.
What makes this experience important and valuable to Australia is not just the technology itself, but what it can learn from how quickly Ukraine has been able to develop and adapt its capabilities. Ukraine has significantly shortened the gap between identifying a battlefield need, developing a solution, and putting it into action. Its defense-tech sector operates more like a startup than a traditional defense industry, as it is constantly adapting and replacing systems as Russia responds. The key lesson is that in a rapidly changing battlefield, the ability to adapt faster than the enemy can be more important than having the most advanced individual systems.
Australia still relies heavily on a small number of highly capable and expensive defense platforms. Yet it is coming to the realization that in a modern warfare scenario, these may not be as impactful as necessary. It is this realization that has driven an element of the new security agreement with Ukraine to deepen cooperation on uncrewed systems. Albanese and Zelenskyy committed the two countries to explore joint production of drones and similar defense technologies.
Of course, Australia’s own desire to develop autonomous systems predates this week’s agreement. Australia’s flagship Ghost Shark autonomous undersea vehicle is considered one of the more advanced technologies in the maritime space. Australia is not a novice here, but what it is trying to do is fuse the systems it has been working on with the capabilities that Ukraine has developed within an ever-evolving combat zone. The technology has to match the real world practicalities to be useful.
The Indo-Pacific relevance is what concerns Australia the most. China has been closely observing how Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has unfolded and how Ukraine’s defense of itself could be replicated by Taiwan. The potential for conflict over Taiwan remains the most pressing concern in Australia’s defense planning. Australia is heavily reliant on the sea lines of communication to northeast Asia, making deterrence a vital national interest. Ukraine’s innovative resistance may prove to be a powerful deterrence to any Chinese invasion plans.
Yet it would be wrong to read this new security agreement with Ukraine purely as one of Australia’s strategic self-interest. Canberra’s support for Ukraine also comes from a straightforward belief that Russia’s invasion is wrong, and helping Ukraine is the right thing to do. Australia’s desire to learn from Ukraine is a sign of enormous respect, and that cooperation in advancing peace is central to any good friendship.

What’s behind the US decision not to invite OSCE election observers
Ahead of its mid-term elections, the US has done something more typically associated with Russia: it has not invited any observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE)
The non-invitation for November’s mid-term votes is the first in 25 years: since 2002, OSCE election observers have been present at 12 federal elections in the US, including six mid-terms. Pere Joan Pons, President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, said the US decision represents “a significant departure from established democratic practice”.
Switzerland also regrets the lack of an invitation
Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis, who currently holds the role of OSCE Chairperson-in-Office, has not yet commented on the matter. However, it is understood that Switzerland had called on US authorities in bilateral discussions to allow the OSCE election observation mission to proceed as usual.
In a statement, Nicolas Bideau, the head of communications at the Swiss foreign ministry, expressed the regret of the Swiss OSCE Chairmanship at the failure by the US to issue an invite.
“Support for election observation missions is a priority for the Swiss OSCE Chairmanship,” Bideau wrote, adding “it would be regrettable if the United States were not to invite the ODIHR [Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights] to observe the forthcoming elections”.
According to Fredy Gsteiger, the diplomatic correspondent at Swiss public broadcaster SRF, the failure to issue an invitation comes as no surprise. “Behind the scenes, the US spent months trying to persuade the OSCE to withdraw its report on the 2020 elections, when Joe Biden was elected president,” he says.
“Donald Trump still claims to this day that Biden was not elected at all. However, the OSCE came to the clear conclusion that the election was conducted correctly – and that does not sit well with Trump and his supporters,” adds Gsteiger.
More
When is a democracy no longer a democracy?
For the time being, there has been no explanation from the US for the non-invitation – neither from Washington nor from the US embassy to the OSCE in Vienna. “The embassy’s website still says the US is committed to the OSCE. After much hesitation, they have now also re-accredited an ambassador there,” says Gsteiger.
Although the US has been putting financial pressure on the OSCE for some time, it has continued to cooperate with the organisation even under President Trump.
According to Gsteiger, it is not implausible to think that the Trump administration wants to use the exclusion of OSCE observers to clear the way for actually manipulating the election results.
“If the Republicans lose, they could also claim that the elections were not conducted properly,” says Gsteiger – something which would be much more difficult if the OSCE confirmed the election had been conducted fairly.
“After all, OSCE election observation is regarded as the gold standard,” says Gsteiger. “Not least, the vast majority of the media rely on its reports.”
Long experience, high regard
The OSCE sees itself as a platform bringing together East and West to resolve conflicts and defend democracy and human rights. As part of its mission, the organisation has developed experience observing elections and in conflict zones. Decisions on OSCE missions need the approval of all 57 member statesExternal link.
According to Gsteiger, other bodies or organisations can also carry out election observation missions: for example, political parties themselves, university institutes or NGOs. “But no one has as much experience or enjoys such high standing in this field as the OSCE,” he says.
Up to now, it has tended to be other countries that have refused to admit OSCE observers – and not democratic ones, explains Gsteiger. For instance, Russia excluded OSCE observers for the third time ahead of and during the Duma elections last weekend.
Belarus also recently kept the OSCE waiting a long time and only sent an invitation at the last moment. “That came too late for the OSCE – too late to prepare professionally for the observation and, above all, too late to monitor the election campaign,” says the SRF correspondent.
More

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Primetime' - Robert Pattinson needs to catch his predator (and ratings)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
12:52:33 UTC
21:52:33 KST

Lance Oppenheim’s narrative debut features a masterful turn from Robert Pattinson in a dark media satire about blurring the lines between journalism and exploitation. Primetime will fascinate and occasionally frustrate as a surface-level mood piece.
Robert Pattinson has been having one hell of a year on screen, with critically acclaimed turns in the excellent The Drama and Christopher Nolan’s box office juggernaut The Odyssey. Before heading to Arrakis in the concluding chapter of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, he stars in what might be his most provocative outing of 2026.
He plays American TV journalist Chris Hansen, the former host of the show To Catch a Predator, in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime. And while the film may perplex audiences, there’s no denying that Pattinson should by all rights be on his way to an Oscar nomination.
Inspired by the true story of Hansen and the show which ran as part of Dateline NBC from 2004 to 2007, Primetime shows how To Catch A Predator hired decoys to lure grown men to suburban homes where they expected to have sex with minors. Instead, they found Hansen, who was there with a full camera crew to confront them with their sordid online chat transcripts. Essentially, a series of staged sting operations which would conclude with the police arresting the would-be paedophiles.
Ratings for the show are huge, which leads Hansen to be summoned to the office of NBC, where a skeptical network president (Jeff Zucker, playing himself) bumps Hansen’s time slot to put the show in direct competition with the hit series Lost. Only promotion comes with expectation: the network demands that Hansen must deliver something big.
For his first narrative feature, Oppenheim – previously a documentary director – delivers a dark and surreal media satire which exposes the disturbingly fragile line between journalism and entertainment. This is embodied through Hansen, who sees himself as a righteous crusader. But he’s no saint. He’s a serial adulterer and can barely manage not to let his mask slip. A mask that hides deep-rooted insecurity (he’s clearly intimidated by Stone Phillips, the co-anchor of Dateline NBC) but also one which reveals that Hansen has a messiah complex, as he’s fooling himself into believing he’s “cleansing the world of an ancient evil”.
Pattinson excels here, being both suave and smarmy, a man convinced he’s a journalist but is in fact a self-obsessed TV star who is fixated on chasing ratings. The actor never goes full moustache-twirling villain, but effortlessly slips in an out of a psyche that is outwardly convinced that his show pursuing justice but inwardly, cripplingly fame addicted.
His performance (with spot-on mannerisms and vocal inflections) is buttressed by some brilliant performances, specifically from Merritt Wever as the show’s ruthless producer Andie Bender and Skyler Gisondo, who plays Dan Plum – a babyfaced and struggling actor whose lane is described as “hairless, nubile, boy-man." The Rent-loving wannabe-thesp is hired by the show as a decoy, alongside Del (singer Phoebe Bridgers), who sees her role as a decoy as “a form of activism”. It’s Dan’s job to lure the predators into the house, and he accepts his bait role as his big break, a desperate means to get his Screen Actors’ Guild card.
“It’s more than acting – you're saving children,” Chris tells Dan, who ends up playing a prominent role in attempting to lure “a whale” - a high profile target which ends up being a Texas district attorney. What follows – and shan’t be spoiled here – is a loose reenactment of actual events that took place during the filming of the show’s final episode, which eventually led to To Catch A Predator being cancelled.
As a cautionary tale on ambition and a damning portrait of American greed disguising itself behind layers of toxic sanctimony and corrupted righteousness, Primetime is thought-provoking. On top of that, it successfully sustains an uneasy, almost hypnotic atmosphere. Kudos here to DoP David Bolen, who creates an ominous aesthetic which combines hyper-stylised lighting and grainy digital cinematography that heightens the period and hallucinatory mood. However, Primetime never quite escapes being a queasy mood piece, with Ajon Singh’s screenplay never completely delivering on the promise of the material and ending up feeling a bit hollow – especially in the rushed third act.
To the film's credit, it never holds the audience’s hand through spelled-out discussions on crossing ethical lines and dealing with moral ramifications. For that and a more detailed history of To Catch A Predator, seek out David Osit’s 2025 documentary Predators. As for Primetime, it doesn’t always delve as deep as it could have in terms of the characters or feel as immediately compelling as some of its genre neighbours – most memorably the Jake Gyllenhaal-led Nightcrawler, which also focused on the actions of a charismatic hustler who exposes his narcissism while blurring the lines between journalism and exploitation.
Thankfully, Primetime does get by on its fascinating performances, especially Pattinson’s. His take on Hansen highlights how To Catch A Predator was never about saving children; it was about ratings and performative justice. As frustrating as parts of the film may be, it does stand as another useful reminder to be mistrustful of the morally corrupt who claim to want to do good for the people but in reality perform for money, ratings, and to feed their own narcissism. Remind you of a hustler-turned-TV entertainer currently cosplaying as a moral crusader for the good old American way?
Primetime is out in cinemas now.
