Has China’s Panda Diplomacy Lost Its Charm? It’s Not So Black-and-White
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:35:57 UTC
19:35:57 KST

“This move is a diplomatic all-timer,” Santi Ruiz, a policy-focused writer for the Institute for Progress and editorial team member at AI company Anthropic, posted on X. “It's like Messi cutting inside. You know it’s coming. It doesn’t matter how many times they run it. You’re getting those pandas, and you’ll like it.”
The tried-and-tested offering came once again on Thursday as Chinese President Xi Jinping announced during his state visit to the U.S. that Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, two giant pandas from a research base in Chengdu, would be lent to Zoo Atlanta in the state of Georgia—but whether this so-called panda diplomacy remains as welcome as it has over the decades is less clear, eliciting mixed reactions in 2026.
The practice gained traction after the National Zoo received giant pandas from Beijing in the wake of President Richard Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon’s historic trip to China in 1972, which marked a new, positive chapter in U.S.-China relations.
China claims ownership of nearly all the giant pandas in the world, even their offspring, and controls who receives them. Beijing eventually shifted from gifting giant pandas to leasing them to other countries in 1984 as the animal’s population dwindled, but the practice continued and spread to other nations like Austria, Canada, and Malaysia. China regularly considers loaning pandas an act of goodwill—even when the host nation typically foots the bill of about $1 million annually for a pair.
A giant panda’s presence or absence in a country tends to represent ebbs and flows of its relationship with China. For instance, amid tensions with Japan over Taiwan, Tokyo returned two giant pandas to Sichuan on loan in January, marking the first time Japan does not have a giant panda since 1972, when China-Japan ties first normalized. In 2010, two U.S.-born panda cubs returned to China, days after Chinese officials warned then-President Barack Obama against meeting the Dalai Lama, whom Beijing considers a separatist.
“No other animal has been turned into a symbol to the extent that pandas have been,” says Czeslaw Tubilewicz, a senior lecturer at Adelaide University.
It’s also no coincidence that Zoo Atlanta received the giant pandas, Tubilewicz says, as the gift represented Beijing’s appreciation of Georgia’s historical economic partnership with China on several aspects: “When most southern states, especially Republican states, turned very negative on China, Georgia continued its pro-China policy consistently. So when it comes to those pandas, and in [Zoo Atlanta], in a way, Xi Jinping is trying to kill two birds with two pandas.”
But China’s transformation from a developing economy to one of the world’s superpowers has also raised questions about whether the gesture of sending giant pandas still works. China is massively different from how it used to be in the 1970s, and is currently embroiled in a wide range of issues, not only with the U.S., but also with other countries, which makes categorizing it neatly as a friend or foe less easy.
Ja Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, tells TIME that “the image of the pandas as soft, friendly, and cuddly—they don’t work today because a lot of [China’s aggressive] actions now are a lot more visible and fresh in people’s minds.”
“No one cares about pandas when national security or geostrategic interests come into play,” Tubilewicz added.
Falling for pandas
A 2022 peer-reviewed study at the University of Connecticut found that U.S. students who viewed panda videos that were not sourced from the government were likely to have a positive attitude toward Chinese culture and, in turn, Chinese people.
But while China’s practice of leasing pandas gives some people warm feelings, it makes others hot with anger. Conservationists and animal advocates have argued against using pandas as geopolitical pawns. Following the South Korea-China Summit earlier this year, the countries’ respective environmental officials discussed additional giant panda loans. But a Korean animal rights group slammed the move, saying that the creatures “are not beings born for human entertainment or interstate friendship.”
And many others are also starting to look past the panda diplomacy and demand other measures. A 2026 survey of U.S. adults conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago found that 28% of respondents said sending pandas to American zoos would improve their view of China, but much higher percentages said that more concrete actions like Chinese cooperation on curbing fentanyl precursors or easing trade restrictions would improve their view of China.
“The symbolism was still dominant in the 1970s,” Chong said. “It’s just that, given the lack of information, given the environment of that time, the symbolism probably got a lot more traction before than today.”
While surveys show many Americans are warming to China, Chong says “deep reservoirs of reservations remain,” particularly among Trump’s MAGA base: a July survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says that 63% of MAGA Republicans favor limiting the growth of Chinese power.
“Affection for pandas does not automatically translate into support for Chinese government policies,” Yu Tao, associate professor in Chinese Studies at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “Its more realistic contribution is to sustain public goodwill and opportunities for cooperation. The strongest case for panda diplomacy is that it gives people something they want to preserve in a relationship otherwise defined pretty much by disputes.”

London home renovation by Polysmiths uses "light as the primary material"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:30:03 UTC
19:30:03 KST

London home renovation by Polysmiths uses "light as the primary material"
Lime-plastered brickwork, timber boards and cork panels were used to help capture the changing light at Pine House, a terraced home in London renovated by local architecture studio Polysmiths.
Located in Peckham, the project set out to tackle what Polysmiths founder Charles Wu described as the "well-known limitations" of London's ubiquitous Victorian terraces.
This included opening up the home's narrow plan by carving out an expansive double-height void at its centre.
"The problems of the Victorian terrace typology became the generative brief: long, narrow proportions, a compressed rear extension, and poor daylight penetration," Wu told Dezeen.
"The project is built around designing light itself as the primary material, to reinterpret the terrace into an open, generous home," he added.
"The guiding principle is that light needs shadow to exist. Textures and shadows are what give a space its atmosphere."
Key to creating a feeling of spaciousness in Pine House was establishing a single axis through its ground floor, connecting a reception room with a large bay window at the front to an angular glazed garden room sheltered by timber slats at the rear.
In between, the central kitchen and dining area sits at the base of the newly-created double-height void, illuminated by a row of windows to the south and overlooked by a small mezzanine library to the north.
"Rather than a conventional rear extension or side-return, we removed a mid-floor over the rear outrigger to create a double-height void, letting south-facing upper-level light fall through to the kitchen and living room," Wu told Dezeen.
"The rear elevation faces south-east, which we treated as an opportunity by angling the garden room glazing further south to soften that corner and pull in more light," he added.
The central space combines all the elements in Pine House's material palette, with lime-washed brick walls above, timber-lined walls and storage surrounding the kitchen, and cork boards used for the ceilings and garden room's walls.
On the first and second floors, across which four bedrooms and two bathrooms are organised, lime-washed brick walls are complemented by plastered surfaces, timber floors and tiled bathrooms.
"Interior walls were stripped to brick and given only a thin lime-plaster wash, creating a textured surface that catches changing shadow through the day," Wu explained.
"Solid Radiata Pine boards line the main living spaces for a warm, honey-toned glow; the garden room is lined in dark expanded cork boards, chosen so southern sunlight would create strong texture and shadow contrast," he added.
Facing the street, the home's facade has been kept the same, save for a slatted timber fence and storage area topped with planting.
Polysmiths was founded by Wu in 2017. Previous projects by the studio include the renovation of a home in Wanstead informed by Mediterranean villas and the redesign of a basement flat in Tufnell Park to feel like a "cabin in the woods".
The photography is by Lorenzo Zandri.

====================================================================================================

Warsh's regime change at the Fed pushes ahead – and meets resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:30:01 UTC
19:30:01 KST

Chairman Kevin Warsh likes to measure his tenure as Federal Reserve chairman in days, and 127 days in, his promise of regime change is taking shape. He's moving fast on some easy and very visible items directly in his control but is constrained from making bigger changes by the state of the economy and by his colleagues on the Fed.
Warsh has quickly put his stamp on the way the Fed communicates. Some changes appear cosmetic, such as shortening the news conference that occurs after meetings of the Fed's rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee and changing the seating arrangements for reporters to be alphabetical by news organization. But those cosmetic changes hide a more profound shift: the way Warsh thinks about and communicates his views on monetary policy represents a sharp break from his predecessors.
Warsh hasn't been able to act yet on one of his key priorities, cutting the Fed's balance sheet, in part because inflation is a more pressing concern. And he constrained himself on other priorities by appointing five task forces to examine Fed practices. They are supposed to report back early next year.
Last week's unanimous quarter-point interest rate increase and any ones that follow will likely be the highlights of Warsh's early tenure in a move that answered his critics' concern about his independence from President Donald Trump. Based on how he has explained his way of thinking about markets and the economy, Warsh seems likely to support additional hikes if inflation remains a problem. Last week's increase was the first since 2023.
For a Fed chairman who prides himself on taking signals from the market, Wall Street is sending a strong one. The 2-year Treasury yield traded nearly a full percentage point above the effective federal funds rate on Wednesday, indicating traders expect more rate increases. It's the largest spread of the 2-year over the funds rate since 2023. Inflation is running at 3.7% as measured by the Fed's preferred personal consumption expenditures indicator in July, the most recent reading. It has been above the central bank's 2% target for more than 5½ years.
Fed chairs for years described the funds rate as either accommodative, neutral or restrictive. But asked at his Sept. 16 news conference where the Fed was relative to neutral, Warsh dismissed the very premise. He responded that the concept is "useful academically" but had no bearing on the decision to hike.
The comments caused consternation among some in the central banking world who had been accustomed to thinking of the funds rate in those terms.
"What is odd is that Warsh framed the decision as 'removing a dose of accommodation' and then distanced himself from the concept that defines accommodation,'' wrote economist Claudia Sahm. "But now that the Fed has hiked, how will he judge whether to hike again, and when to stop?"
Warsh's critics argued after his vague performance in July that he lacked credibility because he hadn't articulated a consistent theory for how to set interest rates. Yet a careful look at Warsh's public comments suggests a new regime for determining policy is being gradually articulated.
That regime encompasses a broad array of financial and market indicators. Three times in his Jackson Hole, Wyoming, speech and three more times in his most recent news conference, Warsh highlighted "financial conditions" as a key to his thinking. He said a review of market conditions indicated to him that conditions were not restrictive.
He pointed in Jackson Hole to "the level and change in asset prices across sectors ... the prices and trading volumes of Treasury securities ... the foreign exchange value of the dollar ... the cost and availability of credit ... and the price of a broad set of commodities." Warsh went on to say: "These and other indicators should inform the Fed's near-term outlook on economic activity and inflation throughout the business cycle. They should also reveal the state of broader financial conditions ... and the risks and uncertainties in the financial cycle.''
That logic may strike some as circular, since expectations for the Fed form a large part of financial conditions. So the feedback can amount to the market telling the Fed what it expects the central bank to do.
But taken at face value, the comments indicate scope for further hikes. The stock market remains buoyant; the labor market is robust; most financial conditions indicators continue to show little restraint, either in lending or borrowing. Growth looks to be strong.
The market is sending the same message with the probability of a follow-on hike in October at 70%, and as many as two more priced in from now until March.
Warsh's focus on sometimes arcane market indicators is more intense than previous chairs and somewhat reminiscent of former Fed Chair Alan Greenspan, who was famous for digging deeply into everything from company capital expenditures plans to scrap metal prices.
In his Jackson Hole speech, Warsh said he was watching a suite of indicators for monetary expansion including credit spreads, the Fed's Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, which gauges the willingness of banks to lend, and credit availability and demand. His conclusion? Money is easy.
"That helps explain the growth we've seen this year in those loans," he said. "Credit and loan markets are showing few signs of policy restraint." Easy credit conditions would not necessarily require rate hikes. In Warsh's formulation, the central bank could need to lean against a private credit system making credit too easy when inflation is running above target.
"We should pay attention to money created by the central bank and money that comes from the banking and financial systems," Warsh said at Jackson Hole. Continuing loose credit conditions clear the way for further rate increases in Warsh's framework. But hikes will be likely only if inflation remains high along with oil and diesel prices.
"The recent rise in overall commodity prices also bears watching," Warsh said at Jackson Hole. The Bloomberg Commodity Index, a broad measure of commodity prices, is up more than 30% this year. Some energy products are faring worse: diesel has risen 83%.
A slower pace for other Fed officials
It's unclear if other members of the FOMC have cast off the neutral framework and adopted one more closely aligned with Warsh's broad concept of financial conditions. While those conditions have always been part of the way Fed officials have evaluated policy, few speak about them now as much more than just a part of their decision-making. Former Fed Chair Jerome Powell often noted how difficult it was to determine the neutral rate, but still often described rates as "modestly restrictive."
So far, Warsh has been virtually alone in refusing to forecast the outlook for the funds rate in the Summary of Economic Projections, the so-called dot plot. And many board members also continue to offer their outlooks for the economy and rates in speeches and interviews, a practice Warsh has rejected.
That reluctance highlights the slower parts of regime change so far. Warsh inherited his committee and the economy he has to steward, both of which work together to slow the reforms Warsh wants to put in place.
Reform has arguably been slowest on what may be Warsh's longest-standing policy priority. Since at least 2011, Warsh said the Fed should reverse the growth in its balance sheet, now at $6.7 trillion. He hasn't committed to a plan for making that happen, which could mean selling securities the Fed already owns or allowing bonds to mature without replacing them. He quit his first stint on the Fed's board that year because he was uncomfortable with the growth in the balance sheet, though he said he voted for expanding it out of loyalty to the institution.
Now, back and in control of the Fed's agenda, Warsh finds himself unable to quickly follow through on his plans for balance sheet cuts, even though that could in theory have taken more accommodation out of the economy. The FOMC's minutes for July show other voters were reluctant to move quickly toward cutting the balance sheet, preferring to wait for Warsh's task forces to report back.
The state of the economy and the markets also may have complicated Warsh's plans. With inflation above the Fed's target and oil surging, the committee had an immediate need to address prices, making it the wrong time to experiment with whether Warsh was right that cutting the balance sheet would meaningfully restrain the economy.
Meanwhile, the yield on the 10-year Treasury has risen above 5%, pulling up rates on mortgages and other consumer debt with it. That makes this a particularly inopportune time for the Fed to start asking the market to take on additional supply of mortgages and Treasury notes if the Fed were to reduce the balance sheet.

How to Record Your Screen on Any Phone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

There are numerous reasons why you might want to record what’s happening on your phone. Maybe you’re having a problem with an app and you want to share what’s going wrong with a tech-savvy friend; or maybe you're the tech-savvy friend, and you want to show someone else how to fix a bug.
Perhaps you’re starting up a YouTube channel of smartphone tutorials. Or it could be that you want to capture evidence of a new high score in a mobile game—not just a screenshot of it, but the actual act of you achieving it.
For these reasons and more, screen recordings are useful, and they’re not difficult to capture no matter what the make and model of your handset. You’ll find instructions below for the two most well-known Android phone brands, and the iPhone.
Record Your Screen on a Google Pixel
If your phone of choice is the Google Pixel, unlock your handset then swipe down from the top of the screen with two fingers to bring up the full Quick Settings selection. You should see a widget for Screen recorder—if you can’t see it, try swiping left or right. If you still can’t see it, tap the pen icon (lower right) to add it to the Quick Settings menu.
Next you’ll see a panel of toggle switches: These options let you choose whether or not the screen touches are visible in the recording, and whether you want the selfie camera feed to be visible as an overlay (handy if you’re narrating or reacting to what’s on screen). You can also opt to include audio from your phone’s apps or from the microphone.
The drop-down menu at the top lets you decide between recording the entire screen or just a single app. When you’re happy, tap Start. You’ll see a short countdown, then the recording begins. To end the recording, tap the red recording timer in the status bar at the top, then Stop. The video will be saved to Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on a Samsung Galaxy
On Samsung Galaxy phones, the process is similar but not quite identical to screen recording on a Pixel. With your phone unlocked, swipe down from the top of the display, then swipe down again on the central pane (with icons for features including Wi-Fi and the flashlight) to reveal the Screen recorder icon.
This brings up a settings panel. You can choose between Full screen and Partial screen for your recording, and there are three options for audio: None, Media (whatever your phone is playing), and Media and mic (whatever your phone is playing plus the microphone input). There’s also a toggle switch for showing taps and touches on screen.
When you’re good to go, tap Start recording. You get a short countdown, and then the recording begins—up in the corner of the screen you’ll see a widget overlay for adding annotations or a selfie camera overlay, and for pausing or stopping the recording. When you tap the stop button, the video is saved in Samsung Gallery and (if you’ve got it installed) Google Photos.
Record Your Screen on an iPhone
For iOS, the screen recorder is launched by swiping down from the top right corner of the display, then tapping the screen recorder button (it’s a circle with another circle outside it). If the icon has been removed from the Control Center somehow, tap the + (plus) button in the top left corner to add it back.
You can either tap the record button once to start the countdown and launch the recording, or press and hold the record button to choose a different app for the recording besides the default Photos option—so you can use this to broadcast your recording to Facebook or WhatsApp for example.
Pressing and holding on the record button also lets you choose whether or not to include the iPhone mic audio. (The iPhone’s native output audio is always included.) To stop the recording, tap the recording indicator at the top of the screen, then the red stop button. You’ll find your saved video stored in the Photos app.
Third-Party Screen Recording Apps
It’s worth noting that iOS restricts what third-party apps can do in terms of screen recordings, for security and privacy reasons. Most apps in this category in the Apple App Store simply tap into the iPhone’s own recording capabilities, though Record It! is worth a look if you want to add commentaries and selfie cam reactions—you just need to add these after the main recording. Clips over three minutes require the $6 Pro purchase.
On Android, there are fewer limits on what apps can do. AZ Recorder has been a popular choice for years, giving you one-tap recording options, a choice of video quality settings, and some basic editing options included as well. To remove the ads in the app and the watermarks on your exported videos, you can pay $4.49 a month for the Pro version.
Mobizen Screen Recorder is another of the leading screen recorders on Android, and comes with a similar set of features as AZ Recorder: A widget overlay for instantly starting recordings, editing tools, and a few options for video quality (both resolution and refresh rate). Again, payment is required to remove the ads and watermarks—that will set you back $3.35 a month.

Finland and Sweden Jointly Intercept Russian Aircraft Over Gulf of Finland for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:28:57 UTC
19:28:57 KST

On September 24, Finnish and Swedish fighter jets carried out their first joint mission to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft over the Gulf of Finland.
The Swedish Armed Forces announced the operation.
The mission involved Finnish F/A-18 Hornet and Swedish JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets from the countries’ Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) forces. The aircraft operated under the command of the Finnish Air Force’s Air Operations Centre.
The fighter jets intercepted three Russian military aircraft flying in international airspace: a Tu-134 transport plane, a MiG-31 interceptor, and a Su-30 multirole fighter.
Finnish and Swedish fighter jets normally carry out Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) missions from their own national air bases. However, when needed, they can also operate from air bases in the neighboring country. The deployment of the aircraft and their response times are adjusted based on the operational situation.
Militarnyi previously reported that in July 2024, Sweden and Finland simultaneously scrambled fighter jets to escort Russian aircraft over the Baltic Sea. In April 2026, Swedish JAS 39 Gripen fighters, together with Danish aircraft, also intercepted Russian Tu-22M3 bombers and their escort fighters over the Baltic Sea.
Such missions are important for continuously monitoring the airspace and responding quickly to possible airspace violations. This is particularly relevant given that a Russian military aircraft violated Finnish airspace earlier this year, after which the incident was investigated by the Finnish Border Guard.

Ethiopia faces return to war as fighting spreads
Unknown

Ethiopia faces return to war as fighting spreads
Fighting has escalated between Ethiopian troops and Tigrayan forces, triggering the suspension of flights to the holy town of Lalibela amid fears of a return to full-scale war in the north of the country.
Ethiopia’s federal army said it repelled attacks in Amhara’s North Wollo Zone and killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 others in a counteroffensive. Northeast army commander Lieutenant General Assefa Chekol said fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and allied groups attempted to break through at several locations.
“The army is carrying out the crucial task of clearing the occupied zone of the enemy by conducting targeted counter-attacks from key military positions it holds,” Chekol said in a statement on Thursday.
The suspension of flights to Lalibela, home to UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches, came a day after TPLF-linked forces seized airports in Mekelle, Axum, and Shire. Ethiopian Airlines also halted flights to these three cities in Tigray.
The two sides give conflicting accounts of how the fighting began. On Wednesday, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed accused the TPLF of launching an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Amhara and Afar. Tigray’s regional authorities said their troops entered a “defensive battle” after federal forces attacked them with aircraft, drones, and artillery on Tuesday.
“We are in the situation of full-blown war now,” TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa told AFP on Thursday.
The TPLF dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018. A power struggle between his government and Tigray’s leaders erupted into war in November 2020. Eritrean troops and Amhara forces fought alongside the federal army against Tigrayan forces. Hundreds of thousands died before an African Union-mediated peace agreement was signed in 2022. The agreement ended the large-scale war, but disputes over territory, the return of displaced people, and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces remain unresolved.
In May, the TPLF restored Tigray’s prewar regional council and elected party leader Debretsion Gebremichael as president following a dispute over the region’s leadership.
The latest escalation follows Sunday’s announcement of an alliance between the TPLF and six other groups, including its former Amhara adversaries, seeking to remove Abiy’s government.
The African Union has condemned the violence, warning that “the formation of new political and military alliances” risks further destabilizing the region and “reversing the gains made to silencing the guns, since 2020.” It said the airport seizures and detention of federal personnel violate the 2022 peace agreement, asking AU mediator and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo to reengage with the parties. The UN has called for civilian protection and humanitarian access.

UK kept Israel arms flowing despite Gaza evidence: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:28:15 UTC
19:28:15 KST

Breadcrumb
UK ignored Gaza legal warnings to keep Israel arms flowing: report
Internal UK government documents reveal that ministers continued to approve arms exports to Israel despite receiving assessments warning that its conduct in Gaza could breach international humanitarian law, according to a new investigation.
Hundreds of pages of Foreign Office assessments obtained by Channel 4's Dispatches show how the British government examined alleged Israeli attacks on civilians, aid workers and humanitarian sites as it considered whether Israel was complying with international law.
The documents informed decisions on whether Britain could legally continue licensing arms exports to Israel during its war on Gaza.
The investigation found that officials examined hundreds of graphic videos and reports documenting civilian deaths, but the government concluded in the overwhelming majority of cases that there was insufficient information to determine that Israel had breached international humanitarian law, because Israel itself had not provided "sufficient evidence" on incidents examined.
Ramita Navai, the reporter and a producer on the investigation, told The New Arab: "Something has gone deeply wrong with the way both the Conservative and Labour governments have dealt with allegations of and evidence for Israeli war crimes."
"The apparent bias towards Israel means our government may have breached international law," she said, adding, "Our institutions should never be bent for any ally, and there needs to be accountability, especially when it is about genocide."
Legal experts interviewed by Dispatches questioned the methodology behind the assessments, saying the process made it extremely difficult to reach a finding against Israel when the Israeli military did not provide sufficient information about its targets or military objectives.
Professor William Schabas, an expert in international human rights and criminal law who reviewed the assessments, said the methodology appeared to be structured in a way that produced findings that violations had not taken place.
"My impression from looking at all this material is that the British government has adopted what looks like a methodology, but one designed to produce a result that no violations are taking place," he told the programme.
Israel has previously accused Schabas of bias against it, an allegation he rejects.
Cameron received warnings over humanitarian aid
The documents also shed new light on what former Foreign Secretary David Cameron knew about concerns over Israel's conduct.
In January 2024, Cameron was repeatedly questioned by parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee over whether he had received legal advice suggesting Israel was violating international humanitarian law.
He declined to give a direct answer, saying he could not recall every document he had received.
But Dispatches says Cameron had received two assessments only weeks earlier concluding that Israel's restrictions on humanitarian relief could potentially breach international humanitarian law.
An email obtained by the programme recorded that Cameron had "carefully considered all the information" contained in one assessment.
Despite the warnings, Cameron determined that Israel remained committed to complying with international humanitarian law overall and arms exports continued.
The investigation also reveals that Cameron later concluded Israel had not been committed to complying with international humanitarian law regarding humanitarian relief during a period between December 2023 and January 2024.
However, he said that finding did not require existing arms licences to be suspended.
In a letter obtained by Dispatches, Cameron also noted that suspending licences would have a "significant impact on UK interests".
Civilian deaths deemed 'inconclusive'
Among the incidents examined by officials was an Israeli strike on a compound in Al-Mawasi housing four British doctors working with Medical Aid for Palestinians and the International Rescue Committee.
The compound was located inside an Israeli-designated humanitarian zone and its location had been coordinated with the Israeli military.
Despite receiving what Dispatches described as inconsistent explanations from Israeli officials, the government's assessment concluded there was insufficient information to determine whether the strike represented a possible breach of international law.
Other cases included an attack on Al-Fakhoura school in Jabalia refugee camp, where at least 24 Palestinians were reported killed, and the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab, an incident that gained widespread public notoriety as being emblematic of Israel's conduct in Gaza.
Rajab was trapped in a car with members of her family and pleaded for help by telephone before she was later found dead.
The assessments did not reach conclusions on whether international law had been breached in those cases because officials said they lacked sufficient information from Israel about the military objectives involved.
The Israeli military initially denied that its forces were present in the area in the immediate aftermath of Hind Rajab's killing, and later admitted in August 2026 that its soldiers had fired on the car.
The programme also examines the Israeli strike on a World Central Kitchen convoy in April 2024 that killed seven aid workers, including three British veterans.
Israel acknowledged responsibility for the attack, calling it a "grave mistake", and dismissed two officers.
Two days after the attack, while Cameron was publicly demanding answers from Israel, his office approved a decision not to suspend existing arms export licences, according to the investigation.
Officials warned 'system is broken'
The investigation also details concerns within the Foreign Office over Britain's handling of the war.
Several senior officials told Dispatches that tensions between civil servants and ministers over Gaza were deeper than during any previous conflict.
They said officials had been instructed not to use terms including "ethnic cleansing" and "genocide" in reports, while hundreds of civil servants raised concerns about the risk of British complicity in alleged war crimes.
Former diplomat Mark Smith, who had previously worked on assessments of British arms sales during the Saudi-led war in Yemen, resigned from the Foreign Office in August 2024 over the government's refusal to halt arms sales to Israel.
"The nature of the assessment is such that you can kind of make it say whatever you want. And that is why the system is broken," Smith told Dispatches.
UK assessment examined genocide allegations
A June 2024 government assessment obtained by the programme also stated that it was "uncontentious" that the physical components of genocide were present in Gaza, while concluding that genocidal intent on Israel's part had not been established.
The UK government's position under both Conservative and Labour governments has been that determinations of genocide should be made by competent courts following full judicial processes.
Israel rejects allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza or deliberately targeting women and children.
After Labour came to power in July 2024, Foreign Secretary David Lammy suspended around 30 arms export licences to Israel after the government found a "clear risk" that some British-supplied equipment could be used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law.
The suspension did not cover British-made components entering the international supply chain for F-35 fighter jets.
A spokesperson for Lammy rejected suggestions made by the programme concerning the timing of legal advice he received, saying the relevant advice was dated nearly six weeks before his decision to suspend licences and that "many events unfolded" during that period.
The Foreign Office defended its procedures, saying Britain's processes for assessing international humanitarian law risks and arms exports were "among the most robust and rigorous in the world".
"Officials provide impartial, evidence-based advice and ministers take decisions on that basis. Any suggestion that assessments were not conducted professionally and rigorously is wrong," it said.
The Israeli military claims it operates "solely based on military necessity and in strict accordance with international law" and reportedly takes precautionary measures to reduce harm to civilians.
Chris Doyle, Director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, told The New Arab that the investigation is "just continued evidence that previous governments ignored, deliberately or through negligence, all the evidence that Israel was systematically violating international law in Gaza."
Doyle said that the position of the UK government towards Israel's conduct in Gaza contrasted with its position in other conflicts, including in Syria and Ukraine, and he welcomed the recent changes brought about by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
"Israel has to be held accountable for its actions, but also those in the United Kingdom and elsewhere who facilitated or enabled this also have to answer for what they have done or not done," he added.

Leonardo gets U.S. Army deal for powerful diode lasers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:26:54 UTC
19:26:54 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Leonardo Electronics US a $30.1 million modification to research single-beam output from phase-locked semiconductor diode laser arrays.
- Work will take place in Tucson, Arizona, through March 29, 2029, funded entirely with fiscal 2026 Army research money.
The U.S. Army has awarded Leonardo Electronics US $30.1 million to keep developing a way to combine the light from many small semiconductor lasers into a single, more powerful beam, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The modification to an existing research contract covers work to develop, study and scale up the power emitted in one beam from a phase-locked semiconductor diode laser array. Leonardo will do the work at its laser plant in Tucson, Arizona, and is scheduled to finish by March 29, 2029. The Army obligated the full amount at award from fiscal 2026 research and development funds. Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, is managing the contract.
The announcement did not say what power level the Army is aiming for or what weapon or sensor the technology is meant to feed.
A laser diode is a chip-sized semiconductor laser, the same basic technology found in fiber-optic links and laser pointers, scaled up for industrial and military use. A single diode puts out limited power. Engineers can stack many emitters together, but their light normally adds up as a wide, messy glow that is hard to focus at long range.
Phase-locking tackles that problem. When every emitter in an array is forced to fire in step, their light waves line up and combine into one tight beam. That would let diodes produce a usable high-power beam on their own. Today, high-energy military lasers typically use diodes only as a “pump,” feeding energy into a separate fiber or crystal laser that shapes the final beam.
Leonardo Electronics US, a subsidiary of Italy’s Leonardo, was formerly known as Lasertel. It makes semiconductor wafers, laser diode packages and beam-shaping optics in Tucson, and says it is the leading supplier of pump diodes for military targeting systems. The company supplies laser systems for U.S. platforms including the AH-64 Apache helicopter and the F-35 fighter. Its Tucson diodes cover wavelengths from 760 to 1,700 nanometers, with peak power of up to several kilowatts.
Leonardo has worked on directed energy research for the U.S. military before. In 2017, it won a Phase I contract of just over $1 million under the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s Efficient Ultra-Compact Laser Integrated Devices program, known as EUCLID, to build lighter diode pump sources for fiber lasers used in laser weapons.
The contract number shows the original award dates to fiscal 2024.

Desolate Arctic outpost likely to host US troops under new Greenland deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:22:42 UTC
19:22:42 KST

Desolate Arctic outpost likely to host US troops under new Greenland deal
COPENHAGEN, Sept 25 - At a windswept gravel airstrip in eastern Greenland, a small Danish military detachment has quietly kept watch for decades.
Now, under a new US defence agreement signed this week, the outpost at Mestersvig could soon become a key American military foothold in the Arctic.
Mestersvig sits 240 kilometres (149 miles) from the nearest settlement (population 330), at the edge of an uninhabited national park larger than Germany and France combined. The place is covered in darkness during winter, with average temperatures of around minus 10 degrees Celsius (14 degrees Fahrenheit).
"This is as remote, as cold, and as extreme as you can find in the world. You have to go to Antarctica to find similar conditions," said Anders Ibsen, a former officer with Denmark's Sirius dog sled patrol, an elite unit that uses Mestersvig to resupply.
STRATEGIC CHOKEPOINT
It oversees the stretch of ocean between Greenland, Iceland and Britain — known as the GIUK gap — that Russia's Northern Fleet must cross to reach the Atlantic. For NATO, controlling this chokepoint is critical to containing Russian naval power.
Local member of parliament Justus Hansen welcomed the expansion, saying: "In east Greenland, we really need that new money."
Under the defence agreement, Washington will be allowed to establish a new base at Mestersvig and Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, potentially marking the first US military expansion on the vast, semi-autonomous Arctic island in decades.
Currently, only three soldiers maintain the facility, which was built in the 1960s and includes barracks to house 150 soldiers.
The US has made no public announcement about its plans for the base.
A HISTORY OF OUTSIDE INTEREST
During World War Two, this stretch of the Arctic island's coast became a front line in the "weather war", a race between Germany and the Allies to read Greenland's weather, which shaped conditions over the North Atlantic and Europe days later.
Germany secretly built manned stations here, but Danish dog sled patrols tracked them down, and Allied forces drove them out.
Nearby, an EU-backed project aims to mine molybdenum — a critical metal for aerospace and defence — some 20 kilometres (12 miles) away. A Texas oil company plans to drill for oil this winter at an untested basin just south of Mestersvig, although it still lacks a permit to do so.
The previous owner, ARCO, spent heavily on seismic work in the 1970s but never drilled.
"Any infrastructural improvements in Greenland would be very welcome," said Robert Price, CEO of Greenland Energy, the oil company.
The 1.8-km (1.1-mile) airstrip — long enough for military transport planes to land — can collect up to 5 meters of snow a year. "When it's snowing, you're basically removing snow 24/7," said Ibsen, the former dog sled patrol officer who spent a year at Mestersvig.
"You have plenty to do just staying alive." REUTERS

Rising sea destroys homes, erases beaches in California. Is worse to come?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:22:26 UTC
19:22:26 KST

Rising sea destroys homes, erases beaches in California. Is worse to come?
CARLSBAD, California, Sept 25 - In Malibu, the Pacific Ocean opened a sinkhole near the home of movie star Nicolas Cage and wreaked havoc on beachfront property. Along Beach Road in the city of Dana Point, waves destroyed one home and forced the city to vacate or restrict occupancy to 16 others.
Such damage up and down Southern California this summer was provoked by a series of Eastern Pacific cyclones and hurricanes, enhanced by the weather phenomenon known as El Niño. Although the hurricanes did not make landfall in California, they generated swells that slammed into the coast, denuding beaches of sand and transforming a coastline that is as much a part of California's identity as Hollywood or Silicon Valley.
Experts say even more ferocious waves could arrive in the coming months, when naturally occurring weather cycles, supercharged by climate change, could coincide with the highest of high tides.
"Things are definitely lining up for this to be a pretty epic winter in terms of potential hazards," said Patrick Barnard, research director of the Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at the University of California, Santa Cruz. "Everything's amplified by climate change."
California this week preemptively declared a state of emergency to help mobilize disaster relief and first responders in preparation for more turmoil from El Niño, which emerged in June. The phenomenon is expected to demonstrate its greatest effects through year end and into early 2027.
On Friday, another hurricane, Polo, churned off the Mexican Pacific coast. It could send more waves northward. Officials canceled the inaugural Ocean Way Festival set for this weekend in Santa Monica, after storm surf and runoff from Hurricane Marie over Labor Day weekend eroded much of the concert site just south of the pier.
El Niño occurs every few years, when surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, altering atmospheric circulation and weather around the world.
The Southern California sea level has risen 8 to 12 inches (20 cm to 30 cm) over the past century. A strong El Niño could temporarily increase the sea level another 6 to 12 inches (15 to 30 cm).
KELVIN WAVE AND KING TIDES
Related to El Niño is the underwater Kelvin wave, which could temporarily add another 6 to 12 inches in sea level. The first major Kelvin wave of the current El Niño is expected to reach California in early October, according to Michael Jacox, an oceanographer at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
The effects could coincide with seasonally extreme king tides occurring during the tide-amplifying phase of the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle. El Niño could also produce massive rainstorms known as atmospheric rivers that often flood coastal areas and erode beach bluffs.
California's generally steep coastline has until now largely spared residents the chronic inundation seen in low-lying coastal areas elsewhere in the world.
In Carlsbad, a city of 112,000 about 35 miles (56 km) north of San Diego, the sand disappeared almost overnight from Tamarack beach, the jewel for a city that raises 14% of its operating budget from hotel room taxes.
Adam Young, a coastal geomorphologist from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography, visited Tamarack recently, climbing over cobblestones where there used to be sandy beach. Just to the south, the ocean swallowed the beach completely, cascading into a parking lot that once allowed visitors to park just a few steps from the sand.
Young said state and local government can attempt to harden properties, add sand to the beach, or form dunes out of the cobblestones, mimicking nature.
"There often isn't one solution that works for everyone," Young said. "It's important to remember that erosion on the coastline has been going on for thousands of years. It's a natural process. The problem is really that we build stuff in the way and on the beaches and in these hazardous areas, and that's caused the problem."
Surfers still flock to Tamarack. But a beach typically populated with tourists and locals now has only a few visitors who stake out a patch of what little sand remains.
"Hopefully they can figure out a solution because honestly, I think Mother Nature is going to take everything back until they stop it, right?" said surfer Alex Stott after a morning session. "It's showing it can take the entire beach if it wants to pretty quickly." REUTERS

AI, Cryptocurrency, and Shell Companies: How A7 Procures Components for Russian Defense Industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:19:57 UTC
19:19:57 KST

Russian financial company A7 has developed an extensive network of shell companies that allows Russia to circumvent Western sanctions and procure goods for its defense industry.
The New York Times reported this, citing leaked internal company documents and an analysis of its software.
A7 was established in 2024 by Moldovan-Israeli oligarch Ilan Shor together with the sanctioned Russian Promsvyazbank PJSC. According to Western intelligence agencies, Shor oversees these activities under the direct command of the Russian presidential administration.
Kyrgyzstan served as the main financial hub for A7’s schemes for a long time. More than $100 million in U.S. dollars and Chinese yuan flowed through the bank accounts of local shell companies.
To evade international scrutiny, A7 developed a dedicated AI-powered system that automatically forged invoices and customs documents. Instead of dual-use electronics, the documents listed civilian goods such as car mats or light boxes.
In the first four months of 2025 alone, the company processed more than $500 million in prohibited transactions. More than $130 million of that went toward procuring products for Russia’s defense industry.
Among the purchased goods was steelmaking equipment from China’s Xi’an Heavy Equipment, which is used in the production of shells and armor. Payments were also made for Nvidia servers for AI development and video components for Walksnail drones.
A7 obtained foreign currency for international transactions by transferring Gazprom’s revenues from gas sales in the UAE. The funds were converted into U.S. dollars, euros, and the Tether stablecoin.
Overall, the company claims to handle one-fifth of Russia’s annual foreign trade turnover, amounting to approximately $130 billion.
After Kyrgyz authorities closed the accounts of several shell companies under Western pressure, A7 quickly shifted its operations to other jurisdictions. Journalists identified at least 71 affiliated companies in the UAE, Bahrain, Nigeria, Qatar, and Mongolia.
Despite the imposition of sanctions on Shor and affiliated entities, the scheme remains highly flexible and continues to operate through the constant creation of new legal entities.
It is worth noting that Chinese state-owned company Jilin Chemical Fiber Group supplied raw materials to Russia’s defense industry for the production of strike drones.

BERLIN, September 25. /TASS/. Key questions over who carried out the sabotage of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, who ordered it, and who ultimately benefited remain unanswered, Russia’s ambassador to Germany, Sergey Nechayev, said on the fourth anniversary of the attacks. "The topic is being pushed out of the public eye," Nechayev said.
The ambassador pointed out that German authorities, "quick to pass judgment on Russia, are displaying surprising restraint regarding the proven terrorist attacks on the Nord Stream pipelines."
"It is as if this were not a matter of a global man-made disaster that resulted - beyond multi-billion-dollar investor losses, the destruction of completed gas pipelines, and the effective lifting of the taboo against attacking critical civilian infrastructure - in the largest methane release in history, causing colossal environmental damage," the diplomat stated. "The angry outcries over this issue and the promises not to let such a flagrant crime go unpunished have been forgotten," he added.
He noted that German authorities were "far more concerned about an abandoned, malfunctioning drone found at Leipzig Airport," adding that any alleged link to Russia, as in other similar cases, was based on nothing more than "highly likely" speculation.
Nevertheless, the ambassador said, the German government had deemed this sufficient to close the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, while expelling more than 150 Russian employees and their family members from the country.
"These utterly inappropriate measures have been described as a ‘measured and proportionate response’ to Russian ‘hybrid attacks.’ It takes quite an imagination to envision what a ‘proportionate’ response from Berlin would look like in the event of proven involvement by the Kiev regime - and the ‘string-pullers’ behind it - in the terrorist attacks on the Nord Stream pipelines, which primarily harmed Germany and its citizens," Nechayev emphasized.
Meanwhile, he remarked, "multi-billion-euro financial flows from European state budgets and borrowed funds continue to line the pockets of corrupt officials in Kiev, heads of military-industrial conglomerates, and numerous lobbyists and middlemen."
"Abandoning Russian energy supplies has been hailed as one of the key achievements of Germany's policy of a 'turning point' (Zeitenwende)," the ambassador noted.
Four years ago
On September 26, 2022, unprecedented damage was recorded on three lines of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas carriers. As a result, only one line of Nord Stream 2 remained intact and could theoretically be put into operation. Following the damage to the pipelines, the Russian Prosecutor General's Office initiated proceedings regarding an act of international terrorism. It is currently impossible to determine a timeframe for restoring the pipelines to operational status.

Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:15:05 UTC
19:15:05 KST

Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent
Meta is creating a tiny, portable Muse Charm device for carrying around the company's AI agent, chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has announced.
Produced by Meta's new design team, led by former Apple design chief Alan Dye, the device resembles an Apple Watch but with a small lanyard instead of a strap.
A customisable cartoon character occupies the entire two-inch screen, prompting comparisons to an AI-powered Tamagotchi.
This avatar acts as the cutesy embodiment of the Muse AI agent the company launched earlier this month, billed as a "personal assistant" that can automate daily admin such as writing emails and booking appointments, rather than just answering questions.
The Muse Charm features a fingerprint sensor in the corner that users can tap to start talking to the AI, with a built-in 5G modem for Wi-Fi-less internet access. There also appears to be a small camera, allowing the agent to take in information about the user's surroundings.
Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg teased the product, set to go on sale ahead of the Christmas holidays, during the company's annual Meta Connect showcase, which also saw the launch of two new smart glasses.
"We've packed a lot of technology into this little guy," Zuckerberg said in his keynote. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what's going on around you."
The avatar can be set to a menagerie of characters, from a Muse mascot known as "Jolly" to an anthropomorphic mango, a labradoodle and a piece of toast wearing sunglasses.
Combined with playing into Gen Z's love for bag charms and Labubu-style plushies, the device seems to be pitched at a younger demographic, who are already more likely to see AI bots as companions rather than mere helpers.
Meta's Muse AI has been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since its launch in early September, according to Sensor Tower data, and is set to be added to Meta smart glasses over the coming months.
The company does not have the best track record when it comes to handling private and sensitive information.
Meta Glasses have faced backlash for being used to film people – especially women – without their consent, and for sharing private videos captured by users with subcontractors in Kenya as part of training Muse AI.
These issues may be compounded by adding an AI agent into the mix and giving it eyes and ears. In the two weeks since its launch, Muse AI has already been accused of reading users' private messages, attempting to hack their Gmail and nudging them to share their passport information and bank account details.
Using cuteness as a way to encourage users to adopt a product they might otherwise be sceptical of is not new. Robotics companies have been following a similar playbook in recent years, with launches including fluffy robots that clip onto a handbag and emotionally intelligent AI pets.

‘Flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food’ – Nepal PM mocks world system
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah has slammed the current global system, saying it allows weapons to be moved efficiently but leaves poorer countries struggling to secure food, fuel, and other essentials for their populations. 
“We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food,” Shah told the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday. 
The rapper-turned-politician pointed to the shortages his country has faced amid conflicts and geopolitical tensions disrupting supply chains, saying farmers have struggled to obtain fertilizer, road projects lacked bitumen, and families faced shortages of cooking fuel. 
“Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline,” Shah, who was elected to Nepal’s top job earlier this year following ‘Gen Z’ protests against corruption, told the assembled world leaders. “But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.”

He argued that the problem extends beyond his country, specifically pointing to India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, the Maldives, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka as regional states facing pressures from climate shocks and conflicts.
Nepal is recovering from catastrophic flash floods that were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Tibetan border on August 26. The wall of water, mud, and rock tore through mountain communities, killing at least 1,400 people and leaving more than 6,000 missing. Nepal estimates its physical recovery needs at around 10% of its gross domestic product.
The prime minister described the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster as a “warning to the world,” saying a warming climate is destabilizing the Himalayan ecology and increasing the risks of avalanches, floods, and landslides. The devastation affected both sides of the Nepal-China border before floodwaters continued downstream toward India.
Shah also proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India, and China. The initiative would involve sharing satellite data and technical expertise, monitoring dangerous glacial lakes, strengthening joint early-warning systems, and coordinating assistance when disasters cross borders.
India and China were among the countries Shah thanked for providing what he called “prompt and generous assistance” after the floods.
The Nepalese leader also called for greater grant-based support for countries rebuilding after climate disasters, arguing that recovery should not force poorer states to take on additional debt. He said Nepal is not seeking to blame individual countries, but wants greater international responsibility and a more equitable global system

Child malnutrition rises in Yemen as fighting intensifies, says UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:12:01 UTC
19:12:01 KST

Child malnutrition rises in Yemen as fighting intensifies, says UNICEF
GENEVA, Sept 25 - The United Nations children's agency reported on Friday a rise in acute malnutrition among children in Yemen, including in the most severe cases, as fighting disrupts access to healthcare and treatment centres.
“We're very concerned about a very visible increase in acute malnutrition among children,” UNICEF’s Country Representative in Yemen, Akhil Iyer, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Aden.
More than a quarter of the nearly 2,900 children screened in recent weeks by UNICEF mobile nutrition teams in accessible areas were acutely malnourished, Iyer said, with 200 of those considered severe, the worst category.
Yemen's civil war between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis has sharply escalated after it had largely been frozen in a 2022 truce.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around the southwestern city of Taiz, as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 133,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
Over the past three weeks, around 71,000 children have been forced from their homes due to the conflict, UNICEF said.
Every day, UNICEF is recording more cases of child malnutrition in areas it can access where internally displaced people have recently arrived.
However, UNICEF said this was only a snapshot of the situation unfolding across the country, where 2.2 million children under five are projected to be acutely malnourished this year, with over half a million projected to be suffering from severe acute malnutrition. REUTERS

Man appears in London court accused of providing Russian intelligence with drone factory details
LONDON, Sept 25 - A British man will go on trial next year accused of providing information about factories which manufacture drones and offering to sabotage them on behalf of Russian intelligence, a London court was told on Friday.
Joshua Cammidge, 31, is charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparing an act of sabotage after contact with the GRU Volunteer Corps, which prosecutors said was controlled by Russia's GRU military intelligence agency.
Prosecutor Sarah Przybylska told London's Old Bailey court that Cammidge, from Swindon, west England, had exchanged messages with a British national who had gone to Russia to fight against Ukraine, in which Cammidge was tasked with locating drone manufacturing sites.
"They discussed sabotaging a site and the defendant volunteered to carry out such sabotage," she said. "It was clear all of this was to assist the Russian war effort."
Prosecutors have also accused him of conducting research about a Wi-Fi jamming device and undertaking reconnaissance.
Cammidge was not asked to enter pleas, but his lawyer John Oliver told the court he intended to deny the accusations.
Oliver said there was "no intention to cause or take part in sabotage" and the communications between the men were "not to be taken seriously".
Russia's embassy in London has not commented on the case. Cammidge was remanded in custody and will appear again in court to enter a plea in January, with the trial due to take place at Winchester Crown Court in April. REUTERS

Voronezhsynthezkauchuk Petrochemical Plant Hit in Voronezh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:09:36 UTC
19:09:36 KST

Drones attacked the Voronezhsynthezkauchuk plant in Voronezh, Russia, overnight on September 25.
The OSINT outlet Exilenova+ reported the incident.
The attack began on the evening of September 24 and continued overnight. Local residents reported a series of explosions, while an air raid alert was issued several times in the city.
Voronezhsynthezkauchuk is a major Russian petrochemical plant specializing in the production of synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. The plant is wholly owned by the Russian petrochemical company SIBUR.
The plant produces butadiene and styrene-butadiene rubbers, as well as thermoplastic elastomers used in tire manufacturing, road construction, and roofing materials. The facility has a total annual production capacity of 226,000 tonnes of rubber and 135,000 tonnes of SBS polymers. In 2023, the plant employed around 1,500 people.
Such products have dual-use applications and can be utilised, among other things, in the production of tires and rubber components for various types of equipment. In addition, at the Voronezhsynthezkauchuk site SIBUR is building a large n-Butyllithium production facility, a component required for manufacturing the products.
A combined heat and power (CHP) plant is also located near the facility. According to an OSINT analysis by ASTRA, a Pantsir SPAAGM system position is located less than two kilometers from the facility, while a position of S-300/S-400 systems may be nearby.

Explainer-Why the court fight over the White House media ban isn't over

Explainer-Why the court fight over the White House media ban isn't over
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 - US President Donald Trump's administration complied on Thursday with a judge's order to restore White House access to three media outlets he had banned last week — CNN, Politico, and MS NOW — but litigation over the ban is not over yet.
Here is what to know about the next steps in the lawsuit filed by the three media outlets.
DID THE JUDGE ISSUE A FINAL RULING?
No. The judge assigned to the case, US District Judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, issued a temporary order that reinstated the outlets’ access for 14 days while their legal challenge proceeded.
In his ruling, Kelly said legal precedents make clear that once White House press credentials are issued to journalists, they have a right to "notice and an opportunity to be heard" before those credentials are revoked.
Kelly, a Trump-appointed judge, said the news outlets were likely to succeed on their claim that this constitutional right to due process was violated.
But Kelly did not reach a primary issue in the case: a claim by the news outlets that the ban violated the rights to freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the US Constitution's First Amendment.
Kelly said it was not necessary to resolve that issue, since the due process claim was sufficient grounds to grant a temporary restraining order halting Trump's ban.
Kelly set a September 28 deadline for the outlets to request a follow-up ruling, known as a preliminary injunction, which would extend his block on Trump's ban for the duration of the case.
CAN THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION APPEAL?
If Kelly converts his initial order to an injunction, which seems likely, the administration could ask a federal appeals court in Washington to lift the injunction.
Trump, anticipating a loss before Kelly, vowed an appeal on Monday, before the judge had even ruled.
Trump announced the ban on Friday on his social media platform, saying the three news organizations "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States."
In a filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security with their coverage, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump's White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention.
Kelly handled a similar case in 2018 when Trump, during his first term, revoked the White House press credentials of former CNN journalist Jim Acosta.
After Kelly issued a preliminary decision in Acosta's favor, the White House sent the journalist a letter saying it had made a "final determination" to restore his press pass, leading him to voluntarily drop his case.
COULD THE WHITE HOUSE TRY AGAIN TO REVOKE THE OUTLETS' WHITE HOUSE ACCESS?
Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for the three outlets, warned of this possibility during a court hearing on Wednesday.
Boutrous had urged Kelly to rule on both the due process and First Amendment issues. By focusing exclusively on due process, Boutrous said during the court hearing, the judge was opening the door for the Trump administration to try again to bar the outlets in a more formal but preordained process.
Boutrous drew a parallel to the case of Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook. Trump last month renewed his push to remove her from the central bank, following a Supreme Court ruling earlier in the summer that blocked a previous attempt due to a lack of due process.
"I'm very concerned that even if the court grants a TRO [temporary restraining order] on due process grounds, the shenanigans will continue," Boutrous said.
In an interview with MS NOW on Thursday, Boutrous said his clients' First Amendment arguments "will come front and center" in the coming weeks.
"I imagine the government will somehow try to justify and shore up this baseless national security argument they came up with after the fact," Boutrous added. REUTERS

Germany’s rejection of Russian gas drives fivefold price surge over 5 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:05:29 UTC
19:05:29 KST

MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Berlin’s politically motivated rejection of Russian gas has led to a fivefold increase in gas prices over the past five years, Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexey Shevtsov said in a commentary.
"In the context of diversification, the first thing that comes to mind is Europe, particularly the former powerhouse of its economy, Germany. Berlin’s politically motivated rejection of Russian gas has led to a fivefold increase in gas prices over the past five years. As a result, we are seeing economic stagnation turning into recession, a sharp decline in industrial production, and a reduction in the number of jobs," he said.
"At the same time, it should be kept in mind that Germany, unlike Armenia, has developed infrastructure that allows it to receive pipeline and liquefied gas from various sources, although the use of LNG adds the costs of liquefaction, tanker freight, and regasification to the price of every cubic meter," Shevtsov added.

Drone Attack Halts Operations at Russia’s Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
10:01:49 UTC
19:01:49 KST

The Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia’s Rostov region.
The region’s governor, Yury Slyusar, confirmed that the refinery was damaged in the attack. The OSINT community Exilenova+ also published video footage showing explosions at the facility.
According to Slyusar, Russian air defenses shot down 50 Ukrainian drones over the region. Despite this, the refinery was damaged and has temporarily suspended operations.
“Following the drone attack, the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery was damaged. The facility has temporarily suspended operations,” Slyusar said.
The Novoshakhtinsk refinery has a designed processing capacity of around 7.5 million tonnes of crude oil per year, equivalent to approximately 112,000–115,000 barrels per day. However, some sources cite a capacity of 5.6–7.5 million tonnes, depending on the estimate.
The refinery began operations in 2009. It was one of the first major oil refineries to be built in Russia in a long period.

People who are easily disgusted tend to hold more conservative political views, but a new study indicates that this connection depends heavily on how well individuals tune into their own bodily sensations. The research suggests that the link between feeling disgust and identifying as a conservative is strongest in those who are less aware of their internal physical states. The findings were published in Politics and the Life Sciences.
To understand these findings, it helps to look at two psychological concepts: disgust sensitivity and interoceptive sensibility. Disgust sensitivity refers to how intensely and easily a person experiences disgust in response to things like germs, taboo sexual acts, or moral violations like lying. Interoceptive sensibility is a person’s conscious awareness of their internal bodily signals. For instance, it involves noticing a racing heartbeat, a tense stomach, or shallow breathing during an emotional moment.
Early studies in political psychology suggested that visceral reactions to threat and disgust drive conservative political beliefs. A 2008 study reported that people with stronger involuntary physical reactions to startling or disturbing images leaned more politically conservative. Following this line of thought, research covered by PsyPost in 2019 found a psychological association in which higher self-reported disgust sensitivity predicted higher endorsement of conservative political beliefs.
Later large-scale replications challenged the biological aspect of this narrative, failing to find a dependable link between physical reactions and political ideology. A 2019 replication study found no evidence that conservatives and liberals actually differ in their automatic physiological responses to threats. Three studies covered by PsyPost in 2020 also failed to reproduce the idea that conservatives exhibit stronger physical threat responses.
This created a puzzle in the field of political psychology. Why do self-reported feelings of disgust consistently predict political ideology, even when automatic bodily reactions do not? The study was conducted by Mariana von Mohr, now a lecturer in social and affective neuroscience at the University of Kent, and Manos Tsakiris at the Centre for the Politics of Feelings. The researchers sought to address this stalemate by testing whether a person’s conscious awareness of their internal bodily signals explains why the connection appears in some people but not others.
“There is a long-standing idea that political attitudes are linked to emotional responses such as disgust, but this relationship has been surprisingly inconsistent across studies,” von Mohr told PsyPost. “We wondered whether interoception might help explain why.”
To explore this, the researchers recruited 632 adults from the United States through an online survey platform. The sample was evenly split by design, featuring 321 participants who identified as Democrats and 311 who identified as Republicans. The participants completed a series of questionnaires designed to measure their bodily awareness, their disgust triggers, and their political leanings.
To measure interoceptive sensibility, participants answered questions about how often they notice changes in their body, whether they trust their physical sensations, and how they use bodily cues to regulate their emotions. To measure disgust sensitivity, the researchers used a scale that divides disgust into three domains. These domains included pathogen disgust (like stepping on dog waste), sexual disgust (like hearing strangers engage in sexual acts), and moral disgust (like deceiving a friend).
Finally, the participants reported their political ideology on a seven-point scale ranging from very liberal to very conservative. They also confirmed their political party affiliation. The researchers then used statistical models to see how disgust sensitivity, bodily awareness, and political ideology interacted with one another.
Overall, the results confirmed past findings: higher overall disgust sensitivity was associated with a greater likelihood of identifying as a Republican and holding a conservative ideology. However, the researchers found that interoceptive sensibility changed the strength of this relationship. The connection between disgust and conservatism was most prominent among individuals who reported low awareness of their bodily sensations.
Among people with low interoceptive sensibility, those who were highly sensitive to disgust were highly likely to identify as Republicans. Statistical estimates showed that a person with high disgust sensitivity and low bodily awareness had a 64.1% probability of identifying as a Republican. They also scored on the more conservative end of the ideology scale.
In contrast, this relationship weakened among people who were highly attuned to their bodily signals. For individuals with high interoceptive sensibility, having high disgust sensitivity resulted in only a 55.4% probability of identifying as a Republican. For this group, the link between feeling easily disgusted and holding conservative views was not statistically significant after certain data corrections were applied.
When the researchers looked at the three specific domains of disgust, they found that moral disgust was the primary driver of these results. Pathogen disgust and sexual disgust did not show the same interaction with bodily awareness. The tendency for low bodily awareness to strengthen the link between disgust and conservatism was specific to situations involving moral violations and broken social norms.
“The main takeaway is that the relationship between disgust and political orientation may be more conditional than is often assumed,” von Mohr noted. “More broadly, our findings suggest that understanding the link between emotions and political attitudes may require looking not only at what people feel, but also at how much they attend to the bodily signals accompanying those feelings.”
The authors suggest that when people are less tuned into their actual physical sensations, they might rely more on socially acquired meanings to interpret their feelings. Disgust is a complex emotion shaped by culture, and conservative political frameworks often place a heavy emphasis on moral purity.
“One possibility is that people who pay less attention to their internal bodily signals may rely more on socially learned expectations to interpret what they are feeling, including ideas about what is disgusting, inappropriate, or morally wrong,” von Mohr explained. “In other words, when bodily cues are less salient, contextual and socially learned information may play a greater role in shaping how an emotion is interpreted.”
If a person is not closely monitoring their internal physical state, they might lean on these cultural scripts to make sense of what they are feeling. On the other hand, individuals who are highly attuned to their internal signals might ground their emotional experiences more in their actual biology. Because they rely more on their direct physical sensations to figure out how they feel, social and political framing might play a smaller role in their emotional interpretations. This could explain why their feelings of disgust do not map as strongly onto their political party or ideology.
There are a few things to keep in mind about this research. The data is based entirely on self-reported surveys at a single point in time, which means the study cannot determine whether feeling disgusted causes someone to become conservative, or vice versa.
“It is important not to interpret these findings as showing that bodily processes determine someone’s political beliefs, or that people with one political orientation are simply more or less ‘in touch’ with their bodies,” von Mohr clarified. She emphasized that the idea that people with lower interoceptive sensibility may rely more on socially learned interpretations is just one possible explanation for the pattern they observed, rather than something they directly tested.
The researchers also note that the direction of this relationship might depend heavily on the specific culture being studied. In a different society where liberals moralize a different set of disgust triggers, the ideological pattern might look different. Additionally, the study did not measure actual physiological responses, such as heart rate or skin conductance. The researchers measured how aware people thought they were of their bodies, rather than their objective ability to detect physical changes.
“The next step is to test the mechanism more directly,” von Mohr said. “A particularly important direction is to incorporate physiological measures, for example by examining autonomic responses such as heart rate or skin conductance while people are exposed to disgust-evoking stimuli.”
“This would allow us to distinguish more clearly between the bodily response itself, how accurately or strongly people perceive that response, and how they subsequently interpret it,” she added. “Ultimately, the broader goal is to understand how physiological responses, awareness of those responses, and socially learned meanings interact in shaping political attitudes, rather than treating emotion, physiology, and ideology as separate influences.”
The study, “The embodied roots of ideology: Interoceptive sensibility moderates the link between disgust sensitivity and political orientation,” was authored by Mariana Von Mohr and Manos Tsakiris.
