The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.

Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.

“But it is not as though they have to pay ground rent,” he added.
Løkke said the “further terms” for the two new US military bases in Greenland still need to be agreed upon.
The bases must also take the environment and Greenlandic lifestyle and culture into account, he said.
“These are important things that strengthen Greenland in relation to the 1951 agreement,” Løkke said.
He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.
“That is, after all, completely obvious,” he said.
Pituffik Space Base was previously known as Thule Air Base and has around 150 US military personnel stationed there.
Under the new security and defense agreement, the US has been granted permission to establish new bases in the settlement of Narsarsuaq and in Mestersvig.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a written response that the new agreement between the three countries “does not concern financing”.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.

There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.
Shares in several companies operating in Greenland rose sharply after reports that Denmark, Greenland and the United States are close to an agreement concerning the Arctic territory, TV 2 reports.
Greenland Energy, which extracts oil and gas, rose 135 percent in US trading. Greenland Mines gained 148 percent.
Both companies had lost more than 80 percent of their market value before Monday’s increases.
Critical Metals Corp., which extracts rare earth minerals in Greenland, rose 34 percent.
The increases followed indications that Greenland, Denmark and the United States had reached or were close to reaching an agreement. Its details have not been made public.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates have traveled to the United States.
They are expected to take part in the signing of an agreement involving Denmark, Greenland and the United States during the week.
The three governments have said the planned agreement is intended to strengthen security cooperation in Greenland, the Arctic and the North Atlantic.
Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.

Destroyed Storage Tanks, Pumping Station and Pipelines: Aftermath of Strikes on Kuibyshev Refinery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:36:34 UTC
18:36:34 KST

Following the September 22 attack, the Kuibyshev Refinery likely halted operations completely.
The OSINT project Absolutely Reliable Source reported on this, publishing satellite imagery with the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes on the facility.
Three oil storage tanks were destroyed, while another one was likely damaged.
The pumping station and pipelines leading to the AVT-4 and AVT-5 primary oil refining units also suffered damage.
Damage to the transport infrastructure and storage tanks disrupted the stable supply of feedstock, forcing the refinery to halt production.
At the same time, no direct signs of damage were observed on the primary and secondary oil refining units themselves.
The Kuibyshev Refinery is one of the leading refineries in the Volga region. The facility is located in Samara and is part of Rosneft’s vertically integrated structure.
Together with the Novokuibyshev and Syzran oil refineries, it forms Rosneft’s Samara group of refineries. The facilities in this refining cluster process crude oil produced by the company, including in Western Siberia and the Samara region.
The Kuibyshev Refinery has a design capacity of about 7 million tonnes of crude oil per year. However, actual processing volumes have remained lower in recent years. In 2024, the refinery processed 4.7 million tonnes of crude oil, or about 94,400 barrels per day.
During that period, the refinery produced about 800,000 tonnes of gasoline, 1.4 million tonnes of diesel fuel, and 1.3 million tonnes of fuel oil.
The attack caused fires at both of the facility’s primary oil refining units, and restoring operations could take several weeks.

Türkiye are a very good team, will cause France problems: Zidane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:33:52 UTC
18:33:52 KST

Kadir Yildiz, Sahin Oktay
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
France head coach Zinedine Zidane praised Türkiye ahead of his first match in charge of the national team, warning that the hosts would pose a difficult challenge in their UEFA Nations League opener.
“Türkiye are a very good team. They competed at the most recent World Cup, and in my opinion, their elimination in the first round was unexpected,” Zidane told a news conference Thursday at Kocaeli Stadium.
“They are not where they deserve to be. Tomorrow will be a very difficult match, and they will cause us problems.”
Türkiye and France will meet Friday in the opening match of Group 1 in League A of the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League. The game will mark Zidane’s coaching debut with Les Bleus.
Zidane succeeded his former France teammate Didier Deschamps following the 2026 World Cup, ending Deschamps’ 14-year tenure.
Reflecting on his return to the national team 32 years after making his international debut as a player, Zidane said he continued to feel the same excitement and wanted to lead France to more trophies.
The former Real Madrid coach said France had completed three training sessions under his leadership and would enter the game with the sole aim of winning.
Zidane, whose appointment has attracted significant attention, said he was comfortable with the spotlight but stressed that the team’s performance would matter most.
“It does not bother me. It is something very natural,” he said. “But today I am a coach. My players know what they have to do, and everyone knows their role.”
Asked about the six uncapped players selected for his first squad, Zidane said the national team remained open to anyone who earned an opportunity.
“I am very happy to be the first national team coach to call them up, and I trust them,” he said. “They will get their chance to wear the shirt, and when they do, I believe they can help take France to a better place.”
Zidane also praised Türkiye and Real Madrid midfielder Arda Guler.
“Arda is a very, very good player. I like him, and I am happy that he plays for Real Madrid,” he said.
 
Rabiot expects passionate atmosphere
France midfielder Adrien Rabiot said the team’s objective was to begin Zidane’s tenure with a victory and ultimately finish first in their Nations League group.
Rabiot said he had not seen a major change in France’s overall system, although Zidane was expected to ask the full-backs to contribute more in attack.
Describing Zidane as a football legend, Rabiot said the coach paid close attention to his players and helped them through his presence and communication.
Asked about the atmosphere awaiting France in Kocaeli, Rabiot said the players were familiar with the passion surrounding football in Türkiye.
“We know Turkish clubs and the Turkish national team. There is a very passionate football environment here, and we have spoken about it among ourselves,” he said.
“We are professional players, and our aim is to play our game with composure. I hope people will watch a good match.”
Rabiot also said he would be pleased to face Türkiye defender Merih Demiral, his former Juventus teammate, on the pitch.

The push to reunify Libya: Why it matters to Türkiye and the region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:33:47 UTC
18:33:47 KST

Libya, an energy-rich North African country with Africa’s largest oil reserves, descended into a bloody civil war in 2014 between rival western and eastern factions, three years after the violent overthrow and killing of longtime leader Muammar Gaddafi.
Despite intermittent fighting between the rival forces, the internationally recognised government in Tripoli has largely retained its legitimacy, signing significant agreements with countries such as Türkiye.
In recent years, however, political dialogue between the rival administrations has gained momentum, with Türkiye promoting its "One Libya" policy and supporting rapprochement between the two sides to unify the fractured country under a single central government.
In April, the rival eastern and western factions agreed on a centralised national budget to share the country's substantial oil revenues, marking a step towards reunification.
In August, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan made a significant visit to Libya, holding talks not only in Tripoli, the seat of the internationally recognised government in the west, but also in Benghazi, the stronghold of the eastern administration led by Khalifa Haftar, General Commander of the Libyan National Army.
"It is essential that our Libyan brothers and sisters build their own future freely, securely, and prosperously. In line with the vision set out by our President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, we will continue to support dialogue and cooperation between Libya's west and east and to contribute to Libya's peace, stability, and prosperity," he said after his Libya consultations.
‘One Libya’ policy
Two weeks after Fidan’s meetings in Libya, the UN announced a roadmap outlining a two-year timeline for presidential and parliamentary elections, institutional unification, and the restructuring of the electoral commission, marking another step towards reunifying the country.
“That Türkiye is now able to engage with actors on both sides of Libya’s divide is very beneficial,” Salah Bakkoush, a Libyan political analyst, tells TRT World.
“Türkiye's leverage will be most consequential when engagement with both sides translates into institutional unification rather than accommodation of permanent parallel structures,” Bakkoush, also a former advisor to the High Council of the Libyan state, says.
Bakkoush observes a growing willingness among Libya’s rival political factions to reach a compromise.
However, he cautions that unifying competing centres of power under a single state authority will be difficult because “institutional authority remains unresolved” between the two sides.
Following Fidan’s visit, diplomatic contacts between Libya and Türkiye have intensified. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Libya’s acting defence minister, Abdussalam Zubi, in Istanbul on Saturday to discuss ongoing efforts towards institutional unification.
On Tuesday, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan also met Mohamed Menfi, chairman of Libya’s Presidential Council, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, emphasising the importance of national dialogue and reconciliation.
"A fragmented Libya exports insecurity; a sovereign Libya can contain it," says Bakkoush. "The more Libya restores unified control over its institutions, borders and security forces" the better the country will prevent illegal trafficking networks and help regional stability, adds the Libyan analyst.
Ankara-Benghazi channels
Türkiye's efforts to unify Libya have taken shape particularly since the October 2020 ceasefire agreement between the UN-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar’s eastern-based Libyan National Army (LNA), which ended large-scale fighting in the country's civil war.
Before the ceasefire, Türkiye had already established important ties with Libya, signing a landmark maritime agreement with the Tripoli government in 2019 that delineated their respective maritime jurisdictions in the gas-rich Eastern Mediterranean. Following the ceasefire, Ankara increasingly turned its attention towards Libya's east.
“Since the 2020 ceasefire, Türkiye’s engagement with eastern Libya has evolved beyond humanitarian assistance and reconstruction to include greater political, economic, and defence-related cooperation,” Ferhat Polat, a senior researcher and analyst specialising in North African geopolitics and security, tells TRT World.
Saddam Haftar, the youngest son of Khalifa Haftar, who was appointed deputy general commander of eastern forces in August 2025, has been “an important figure in this rapprochement, visiting Türkiye several times and meeting with senior Turkish officials,” Polat says.
According to Polat, Haftar's visits, alongside growing institutional contacts between Ankara and eastern Libya, have opened new channels of communication between the two sides, contributing to the ongoing national dialogue between the rival western and eastern administrations.
He also points to Türkiye's growing defence capabilities and military ties with Libya as factors that could help the North African country establish a unified security structure across its vast territory.
In August 2025, the Turkish naval vessel TCG Kinaliada made a significant port call in Benghazi, where Turkish and eastern Libyan military officials discussed cooperation under the framework of a “One Libya, One Army” objective.
“Once security is firmly established across the country, the broader stabilization process can progress more smoothly. In this context, bringing Libya’s military institutions under a unified command structure is crucial,” Polat tells TRT World.
“Türkiye has provided training and other support to strengthen the professionalism and institutional capacity of the Libyan army.”

Splitting cells informs Shanghai research campus' interconnected buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:33:17 UTC
18:33:17 KST

Splitting cells informs Shanghai research campus' interconnected buildings
Architecture studio BDP has unveiled a pharmaceutical research campus in Shanghai, China, comprised of interconnected buildings that evoke the movement of cell division.
Located within Hongqiao International Central Business District in west Shanghai, the 186,000-square-metre research and development headquarters was developed for Chia Tai Tianqing Pharmaceutical Group (CTTQ), one of China's leading pharmaceutical companies.
BDP's design was informed by the structure of cells, with two pairs of interconnected buildings on the site.
Both pairs were designed to resemble cells splitting with glass covered bridges connecting them.
The cores of the two research buildings are split between either end of the buildings, allowing large and flexible floor plates for changing laboratory requirements.
One of the research buildings was connected to a smaller block containing staff accommodation, while the other one was connected to a taller administrative building.
The administrative building is the highest on the site, with the aim of creating a vocal point for the new headquarters. A conference centre is connected to this building.
"This is a place for research within a campus that doesn't turn its back on the city or the people using it," said BDP director Tianyi Gu.
"The central heart opens the site up to the public, while the buildings are planned to make research, collaboration and everyday life work together."
A raised sky bridge curves around the site to connect all the buildings on the campus as well as providing a series of indoor and outdoor spaces for people to meet and interact.
Cafes, a canteen and gym are located at the lower levels of the buildings, supporting the wellbeing of the staff and work-life balance.
According to BDP, the arrangement of the four blocks was designed to break down the scale of the campus into a series of destinations.
"We've paid close attention to the things that make a difference to people's working day – access to daylight and fresh air, places to meet, eat and exercise, and spaces to step away from the laboratory," said Gu.
"For CTTQ, this is a research campus built for change, but also a place for people, a place with a strong sense of identity and an identifiable connection to Shanghai."
Passive design strategies were applied across the campus, including natural ventilation, facade solar shading, as well as customised facade designs responding to different orientations and functions.
Low-E glass was used to improve energy performance, while a large array of photovoltaic panels were installed on the roof, creating a unique pattern that add to the identity of the campus.
Elsewhere in China, KPF designed a tech campus in Shenzhen wrapped by a one-kilometer-long "landscape ribbon", while RSHP has completed a mixed-use skyscraper in Shanghai, informed by the city's historical laneway network.
The photography is courtesy of BDP.

Türkiye puts forward UN FAO leader candidate with global food security vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
09:30:39 UTC
18:30:39 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gokkoyun, Dilara Zengin Okay and Emir Yildirim
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Türkiye’s nominee for director-general of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Mehdi Eker, is accelerating his diplomatic campaign to share Ankara’s vision to resolve the world’s deepening food security issues.
Eker told Anadolu that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan sought support for Türkiye’s candidacy during various meetings, securing direct talks and support pledges from around 100 of the 193 UN member states.
“Some 645 million people are going hungry worldwide, while 1.4 billion are obese, and 2.3 billion do not have enough food on their plates,” he said, noting that the world produces enough food for 11 billion people.
“There’s something wrong here — the issue of food security is one of global security, and ensuring global security will be very difficult so long as this is not resolved,” he added.
Eker stated that food shortages can lead to population displacement and migration, while Türkiye’s approach is based on safeguarding food as a fundamental human right.
“Food is weaponized against people in Gaza, against children — this brutality, this oppression, must somehow come to an end, and the right to food must not be violated,” he said.
“Türkiye’s perspective, approach, understanding of humanity, and vision of civilization will be reflected in the governance of this organization,” he added.
Eker noted that mitigating these humanitarian crises requires stabilizing vulnerable agricultural supply routes across the Black Sea Basin, the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden.
He stated that the UN FAO has three core functions, starting with strengthening global agricultural standards via the international Food Codex and expanding the organization’s statistical network.
The second core function is providing technical assistance and advisory services to developing countries, while Eker’s agenda for the organization focuses on providing these gains through projects to reduce food waste and combat animal diseases threatening human health.
The third function is combating global hunger, where the UN FAO plays an active role. Eker said fulfilling this role is linked to the organization’s sound management.
“This is a matter of humanity, the future of humanity — it’s impossible for the world to function and move forward amid such oppression, darkness, and brutality, when food is weaponized against vulnerable populations like children, women, and the elderly, who are dying of hunger,” he noted.
“As Türkiye, we believe the UN FAO, like all other UN agencies, will be engaged in more effective, efficient, and beneficial work for humanity,” he added.
UN FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu’s second term will expire in 2027.
Angola, Italy, Spain, and Ireland put forward their candidates for this position.
The new director-general will be elected in Rome next summer to serve the organization from 2027 to 2031.

18:30:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s government-recognized tourism factories attracted 21.36 million visitors last year, generating NT$6.69 billion (US$211 million) in output, Sinotrade reported Friday.
The tourism factory program was launched in 2003 to help revitalize existing manufacturing sites as industries moved overseas. As of the end of August, Taiwan had 150 factories that had passed the government’s evaluation process.
Taiwan Cement Corp.’s open-ecology factory in Hualien attracted the most visitors last year. The site offers a rare glimpse into a 20-year-old industrial complex bringing together a cement plant, power plant, and industrial port, according to Tourism Factory.
Tainan’s Arwin Therapy Garden ranked second. Covering nearly 50,000 square meters, the site features large pinecone-shaped installations, vibrant colors, the sounds of nature, and the scents of plants and flowers, according to Travel Tainan.
The third most popular site was Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corp.’s Puli Winery in Nantou. The winery offers visitors a chance to learn about the production of rice wine, according to GreenMobile.
The country's tourism factories span 18 industries, with food manufacturing accounting for the largest share at 69 sites, or 46% of the total. Beverage manufacturing ranked second with 18 facilities, while other industries included textiles, metal products, machinery, and furniture.

ReSKU 2.0 fabric by Camira
Dezeen Showroom: recycled wool and renewable flax come together in a warm melange of colour in British textile brand Camira's ReSKU 2.0 fabric.
ReSKU 2.0 was launched to celebrate Camira's 50th anniversary in 2024 and inspired by the brand's original 1998 ReSKU fabric, made from recycled army jumpers.
For ReSKU 2.0, the brand combined recycled wool and polyamide generated from its own manufacturing waste with harvested flax, a renewable, low-carbon crop that grows with little water.
The process is conducted through Camira's textile recycling arm, iinouiio, which makes use of advanced textile reprocessing techniques, and the fabric it yields has a rich, tweedy look that showcases the natural colour variation of recycled materials.
ReSKU 2.0 is available in a choice of 24 shades. Camira says it is suitable for applications such as seating, curtains and panels, in settings including modern workplaces and hospitality venues.
"More than a fabric, ReSKU 2.0 represents a commitment to circular thinking and responsible manufacturing," said Camira.
"By turning production waste into a valuable resource, it demonstrates how heritage, innovation and sustainability can work together to create a textile that is recycled, renewable and ready for the future."

Voyage apostolique du Pape Léon XIV en France.

Le Président de la République a accueilli Sa Sainteté le Pape Léon XIV au Palais de l'Élysée ce vendredi 25 septembre 2026, dans le cadre de son voyage apostolique en France.
Cette visite fait suite à la première rencontre entre le chef de l’État et le Pape Léon XIV au Vatican en avril dernier.
Elle s'inscrit dans le cadre des relations traditionnelles entre la France et le Saint-Siège, et témoigne de la profondeur d'un dialogue fondé sur des valeurs et des engagements partagés.
Revoir l'accueil à l'aéroport :
 
            Le Président de la République et Madame Brigitte Macron ont ensuite accueilli le Saint-Père au Palais de l'Élysée.
Revoir l'accueil :
Les échanges entre le Président de la République et le Saint-Père ont permis d’aborder les aspects clés de la relation bilatérale, ainsi que les principaux défis globaux qui mobilisent conjointement la France et le Saint-Siège, au premier rang desquels le climat et l'intelligence artificielle.
À cette occasion ont également été abordés les grands enjeux internationaux, la guerre en Ukraine, la paix et la stabilité au Proche-Orient, les partenariats avec l’Afrique, sur la base d’une volonté conjointe d’œuvrer pour la paix et le dialogue.
Revoir les allocutions :
25 septembre 2026 - Seul le prononcé fait foi
Discours du Président de la République - Voyage apostolique de Sa Sainteté le Pape Léon XIV en France
Emmanuel MACRON
Très Saint-Père, Mesdames et Messieurs en vos grades et qualités,
C'est pour la République française un grand honneur et aussi une grande joie que de vous accueillir aujourd'hui sur notre sol. Un grand honneur et une grande joie en ce que, confrontés souvent au spectacle des misères du monde, beaucoup de nos compatriotes ressentent, avec votre visite en France, une espérance.
Oui, comme il est dit dans l'Ecclésiaste, il ne faut pas s'attrister comme ceux qui n'ont pas d'espérance, et c'est un sentiment, je le sais, que vous partagez. Vous voici, 18 mois après le commencement de votre pontificat. Et vous voici pour un temps long que vous nous offrez et qui nous touche. C'est ici que débute ce chemin de foi, si j'ose dire, qui va vous mener du cœur de Paris à Notre-Dame, de l'Elysée à l'UNESCO, de la place de la Concorde à Saint-Denis, du Stade de France à la Maison Bakhita, de Lourdes, ville de Bernadette Soubirous, à Metz, carrefour des mémoires chrétiennes de notre Europe. Autant d'étapes qui disent votre lien personnel avec notre pays. Très Saint-Père, nous sommes fiers de vos racines normandes. Et vous verrez que nous avons même trouvé des racines béarnaises et bigourdanes.
Autant d'étapes comme autant d'épisodes qui racontent aussi cette histoire si particulière qui lie le christianisme à notre pays. Histoire deux fois millénaire, dont témoignent ces paysages de France, parsemés de cathédrales, basiliques, églises, monuments venus du fond des âges, inestimables dons de ceux qui nous ont précédés et qui se faisaient de notre pays une certaine idée. Il fut long. Ce temps où la religion chrétienne, ambitieuse d'être l'architecte de l'universel, guidait nos ancêtres à tailler la pierre, afin de laisser inscrite dans la chaîne des temps la trace visible de leur idéal. Croire, c'est créer. Et c'est au nom de cet héritage que nous avons œuvré, après le terrible incendie de Notre-Dame de Paris, pour qu'elle puisse être rebâtie en cinq ans et rendue non seulement aux catholiques, mais à tous les Français et au-delà encore au monde entier, et tant de talents, d'artisans, d'apprentis, de bénévoles, s'y sont donnés avec cette espérance chevillée au cœur.
Car Notre-Dame est une part de nous, un emblème de cette volonté si française d'offrir au monde toutes les beautés que peut engendrer l'esprit humain dès lors qu'il est mu par un idéal de fraternité universelle. Oui, cette histoire deux fois millénaire a créé un lien singulier entre la France et l'Église catholique. Et lorsque la République décida, il y a un peu plus de 120 ans, de la séparation entre l'Église et l'État, elle donna forme à une laïcité française qui n'est nullement la négation de la religion. La République se fait un devoir de permettre à chacune et à chacun en conscience de penser et d'exprimer son point de vue dans toutes les sphères de son existence, de croire ou de ne pas croire, dans l'intimité comme dans la sphère publique, à condition d'en respecter les lois. C'est dans ce cadre, très Saint-Père, que vous solliciterez la conscience de tous les Français qui s'associent en pensée et en action à ce que vous représentez, à eux, à tous ceux qui, en France comme ailleurs, sont attentifs à ce que vous avez à dire au monde, et je m'en réjouis.
La République veille aussi. Depuis 15 ans, les actes commis à l'encontre de personnes ou de biens en raison de leur religion ont malheureusement connu une recrudescence. Et ces insupportables démonstrations d'intolérance frappent la religion chrétienne au cœur. Les communautés juives et musulmanes en sont aussi victimes. Et c'est un combat essentiel que nous menons et mènerons pour protéger les lieux de culte, continuer de former les esprits à la tolérance, en même temps que nous encourageons le dialogue interreligieux si vivant dans notre pays.
La quête de la paix sur tous les fronts est une nécessité existentielle. Et il n'est pas un catholique qui ne puisse être sensible à ce combat pour le bien commun. Et j'ajouterai, pas un juif, pas un musulman, pas un protestant, ni un orthodoxe ou un bouddhiste. Il n'est personne en France, croyant ou non, qui puisse refuser de faire sienne cette quête. La paix est aussi cet horizon pour lequel nous œuvrons ensemble. Vous avez placé les premiers mois de votre pontificat sous le signe d'une paix désarmée et désarmante. Exigence qui prend une force particulière alors que la guerre meurtrit notre continent et que partout tensions et conflits ressurgissent. Exigence qui rappelle aussi que la paix est davantage que le silence des armes et qu'elle suppose justice, sécurité, respect des droits de l'homme, souveraineté des nations, et droit des peuples à disposer d'eux-mêmes. Et plus fondamentalement la capacité à reconnaître l'autre pour ce qu'il entend être.
La France se tient du côté de la paix, du multilatéralisme d'action, du respect du droit international et de la charte des Nations Unies. Et nous nous y tenons partout, sans double standard, avec cohérence et constance, car une vie vaut une vie et tous les peuples sont à défendre.
Ce combat pour la paix est inséparable de celui pour la dignité humaine et la lutte contre les injustices. Partout, ce sont toujours les plus fragiles qui paient le prix des crises et des conflits, qui contraignent tant de femmes et d'hommes à fuir leur pays. A la maison Bakhita, vous rencontrerez celles et ceux qui accueillent les exilés, les plus pauvres, les plus isolés. Là encore, la République et l'Église croisent souvent les mêmes visages. Le visage de ceux qu'il nous faut voir en face, le visage de ceux dont la voix peine à porter, de ceux qui nous rappellent l'exigence de fraternité, celle-là même qui fait de l'autre son frère en République, cette attention que nous devons aux plus fragiles.
Et je veux saluer ici l'engagement quotidien de tant de Français, de bénévoles, d'associations et notamment chrétiennes qui servent quotidiennement leurs prochains. Leur dévouement, leur solidarité disent un formidable élan d'espoir. Comme je veux saluer l'engagement de tous ceux qui contribuent à l'éducation de nos enfants, qu'il s'agisse de l'enseignement public ou de l'enseignement privé dans notre pays. Tous sont aussi au service de la défense du bien commun que nous partageons par-delà les frontières, notre planète et le vivant.
C'est pour cela que la France a porté l'Accord de Paris il y a 11 ans et s'est battue pour obtenir l'Accord sur les océans l'année dernière. C'est pour cela aussi que nous continuons de défendre le pacte de Paris pour les peuples et la planète, afin que nul pays n'ait à retarder sa transition faute de moyens, ni à choisir entre son développement et la préservation de la planète et du vivant. Climat et biodiversité irriguent les choix de notre siècle. L'Église catholique, avec le pape François, puis avec vous-même, l'a toujours rappelé sans ambiguïté. Nous vous en rendons grâce. Ce n'est pas seulement affaire de technologie ou d'ajustement. Cela révèle notre manière d'habiter le monde, d'y produire, de consommer, de concevoir ensemble la voie du progrès humain. Telle est notre responsabilité commune. Et elle ne s'arrête pas là.
Les ruptures technologiques de notre époque risquent d'engendrer des ruptures anthropologiques inédites. L'être humain ne doit pas être lié par le numérique, mais libéré. Question vertigineuse pour notre génération, parce qu'elle touche non seulement à ce que nous faisons, mais plus encore à l'essentiel, à ce que nous sommes.
L'intelligence artificielle bouleverse déjà le travail, la création, la recherche, l'éducation, l'information, le lien social. Elle décuple nos capacités mais substitue la prédiction au jugement, la performance à la conscience et nous conduit à déléguer une part de notre liberté.
Dès les premiers mois de votre pontificat, vous lui avez consacré l’encyclique Magnifica Humanitas. Et ce message est essentiel. Face à la puissance de la machinerie numérique, l'être humain doit garder la place qui est la sienne. L'intelligence artificielle doit être un serviteur et non un maître. La révolution numérique doit entraîner et non enchaîner. La responsabilité nous revient donc de ne pas permettre que les modèles les plus performants ne se retrouvent entre quelques mains qui auraient à décider pour toute l'humanité, ni que ces avancées les plus exponentielles ne nous conduisent à perdre le contrôle.
C'est pour cela que nous devons trouver la voie d'une organisation internationale réconciliant progrès technologique, justice et humanisme. De la même manière, comme nous sommes en train de le faire pour les réseaux sociaux, il nous faut protéger nos enfants et accompagner nos adolescents. Leur développement affectif et cognitif suppose en effet de les protéger pour pouvoir transmettre et les préparer à la vie.
La lecture, l'apprentissage, les arts et la culture, le sport et le temps avec les autres sont des trésors à leur donner et à protéger des écrans, des algorithmes, comme des chat-box. Protéger nos enfants, accompagner notre jeunesse dans ses interrogations et accueillir son besoin de sens et son engagement sont nos plus beaux devoirs.
La veillée des jeunes que vous présiderez au Stade de France aura une force toute particulière. Des milliers de jeunes y seront en demande d'une parole de responsabilité et de lucide espérance. Leur soif d'engagement dit toute leur vitalité. Ils ne demandent pas qu'on leur promette un monde facile, ils demandent à pouvoir bâtir un monde meilleur.
Très Saint-Père, lors de votre visite, vous allez rencontrer la France, pays de la diversité, comme le disait l'un de nos plus grands historiens, Fernand Braudel. Et c'est précisément parce qu'elle est patrie de liberté et d'esprit que la France est diverse, Nation qui nourrit une passion particulière pour le débat permanent. Ainsi faut-il la considérer pour bien l'aimer. Les grands débats sociaux et sociétaux de ces dernières années en attestent. L'éthique est l'un de nos grands sujets français. Où est la frontière entre le bien et le mal ? Comment concilier les progrès technologiques, notre conscience, notre attachement à la dignité humaine ? Ainsi sommes-nous attentifs toujours à toutes les réponses qui peuvent être apportées à ces questions fondamentales.
Et soyez assuré, très Saint-Père, que tous les Français, moi le premier, vous écouteront avec le plus grand intérêt. Je veux vous redire mon attachement à cette écoute qui a pour vocation de nourrir un dialogue exigeant avec l'Eglise catholique, comme avec tous les autres cultes, avec les croyants, comme avec les non-croyants, avec toutes les traditions philosophiques et humanistes qui font notre pays. Parce que la République ne craint pas les consciences libres, parce que notre Nation est forte du dialogue nécessaire entre toutes les opinions, en demeurant fidèle à notre humanisme, notre attachement à la dignité humaine, en fondant nos décisions sur la science, tout en veillant aux plus fragiles.
Très Saint-Père, je forme le vœu que ces quelques jours vous permettent de rencontrer la France dans toute sa vérité, ses forces, sa diversité, ses débats. Une France empreinte de spiritualité et cherchant toujours l'universel. Une France émancipée, attachée à son projet de liberté, d'égalité et de fraternité, diverse et unie. Une France engagée, sensible à votre présence et dont vous sentirez la ferveur. Très Saint-Père, c'est cette France qui vous reçoit aujourd'hui avec beaucoup d'humilité, avec beaucoup d'honneur et une très grande joie. Soyez le bienvenu.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet plans to push about 40 priority bills and seek quick approval of key government budgets in the new legislative session, CNA reported Friday.
The new legislative session begins Tuesday, with both pending and new bills on the Cabinet’s priority list, per Money Weekly. Officials also want lawmakers to quickly review funding for weapons purchases, price and electricity stabilization, and other government programs.
The Cabinet-approved 2027 central government budget sets revenue and spending at NT$3.93 trillion (US$123.7 billion), with no new borrowing planned. Defense spending totals NT$1.12 trillion, exceeding NT$1 trillion for the first time and accounting for more than 3% of GDP.
The budget includes NT$235.7 billion for planned cash payments and NT$39.2 billion for pay adjustments for military personnel, civil servants, and teachers. A separate 2026 supplementary budget of NT$607.63 billion covers price and electricity stabilization, welfare payments, military pay increases, and weapons purchases.
Eight bills supporting families with children are also among the Cabinet’s priorities. They cover workplace gender equality, employment insurance, housing and land taxes, and benefits for military personnel, per Liberty Times.
The Cabinet also plans changes to laws supporting small- and medium-sized businesses and startups. The proposals include NT$100 billion in investment over eight years, per CTEE.
Another proposal would extend securities transaction tax exemptions for corporate bonds, financial bonds, and certain bond exchange-traded funds through the end of 2036, per Economic Daily News.

A cyberattack on a Polish healthcare software provider compromised the confidentiality of patients’ personal data, a treatment center said, weeks after a separate breach reportedly exposed records belonging to nearly 19 million people, local media reported on Friday.
The latest attack targeted Qbusoft, the company behind Medyc software used by healthcare providers to manage patient records, Polish broadcaster TVP World reported.
The Rehabilitation and Psychiatric Treatment Center in Inowroclaw said Thursday that patients’ contact details and national identification numbers may have been affected. It did not specify how many patients were involved.
Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the Central Office for Combating Cybercrime was examining the incident as part of a broader investigation. He said the government had issued new security recommendations to companies supplying software to the healthcare sector.
“In the event of a breach of any security procedure by a private company, strict consequences will be imposed,” Gawkowski said.
The incident follows an August breach involving MyDr, a system used by about 12,000 healthcare providers. Data belonging to almost 19 million people, including information on medicines and prescriptions, was reportedly exposed in that attack.

Necva Tastan Sevinc
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Finnish and Swedish fighter jets carried out their first joint operational identification flight Thursday, identifying Russian military aircraft in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, the Finnish Air Force said in a statement Friday.
The mission involved Finnish F/A-18 Hornet and Swedish JAS 39 Gripen fighters, which identified a Russian Tu-134 transport aircraft, as well as MiG-31 and Su-30 fighters, the statement said.
The flight was led by Finland’s Air Operations Center as part of bilateral cooperation between the two countries to monitor and protect their airspace.
“The deeper cooperation that began this autumn enables joint operational reconnaissance flights and the use of standby fighters at the other country's bases,” said Col. Vesa Mantyla, the Finnish Air Force’s chief of operations.
Swedish Air Force Commander Maj. Gen. Jonas Wikman said years of cooperation had enabled the two forces to operate together.
“This is what close cooperation looks like in practice. Thanks to years of cooperation built on trust and strong personal relationships, we can now operate seamlessly together – as air forces, nations and allies,” he said.
The Finnish Air Force said fighters normally remain on alert at bases in their own countries but can use bases across the border when operational needs require it. The two air forces have also conducted cross-border training flights almost weekly for years, it added.

Elsewhere in Asia, Japan defeated Uruguay 3-1, while South Korea recorded an impressive 3-0 victory over Ecuador.

Putin casts doubt on resuming Ukraine talks, citing mass drone attack during Russian election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
