5th Global Digital Trade Expo opens in Hangzhou, highlighting AI-empowered future
The 5th Global Digital Trade Expo (GDTE) kicks off today in east China's Hangzhou City. As China's sole national-level international professional exhibition themed on digital trade, the five-day-long expo puts artificial intelligence center-stage under the theme "Meet the AI Future at GDTE."
Across its 170,000-square-metre exhibition halls, the event links technological innovation, business matchmaking and international cooperation, mirroring the robust global expansion momentum of Hangzhou's AI industry.
Stepping into the sprawling venue, visitors are greeted with a strong sense of the future. The specially built Token Zone lays out a full-fledged innovation chain covering computing-power infrastructure, large language models, and industry-specific real-world applications. More than 200 AI large models are on collective display. Cutting-edge achievements such as brain-computer interfaces and embodied intelligence, once confined to research papers, are now demonstrated live for the general public.
Attendees may stop to observe how brain-computer devices rebuild bridges for people with disabilities to perceive the world. They can sit through simulated consultations powered by a traditional Chinese medicine large-model system, or get hands-on experience with service robots and smart wearable devices to see how technology transforms daily life. The Global Open-source AI Challenge and the Global Digital Trade Innovation Competition, which focuses on embodied intelligence robots, run concurrently. Developers from across the globe compete and exchange ideas, turning conceptual creativity into practical, real-world solutions.
Openness and connectivity lie at the very heart of the GDTE. Malaysia and Hungary serve as this edition's Guest Countries of Honour, with overseas exhibition groups larger than in previous years. Representatives from 121 countries and regions as well as 29 international organizations gather at the event.
Signature sessions including the Silk Road E-Commerce Day, the BRICS Special Economic Zones Hangzhou Dialogue and Africa Digital Trade Day are held successively. Participants sit together to exchange insights and advance pragmatic collaboration on Silk-Road-themed e-commerce, cross-border data flows and green digital trade.
Working together with five leading international authoritative institutions, the expo compiles and releases its flagship report, Global Digital Trade Development Report 2026, alongside several high-profile industry publications. These documents deliver valuable observations and reflections for the fast-evolving global digital-trade landscape.
Nearly 40,000 professional buyers and sellers take part in the grand gathering, among whom over 12,000 are overseas delegates. More than 1,300 business-matching sessions are held in orderly fashion, with AI assistants facilitating precise matchmaking for business opportunities.
Beyond the short-term offline exhibition, the upgraded Digital Trade Online platform creates a "never-ending digital-trade expo." It connects online cross-border-e-commerce platforms with offline specialized markets, extending trade engagement throughout the full pre-, during- and post-event cycle. Ticket interoperability has been realized between the GDTE, the APSARA Conference and the West Lake Conference, enabling mutual empowerment and amplifying the event's outreach.
Coinciding with the Mid-Autumn Festival, the expo also transforms into a lively digital carnival steeped in everyday charm. One hundred AI application scenarios, 100 premium digital-trade products and 100 consumer-experience spots are scattered across the venue.
An 800-meter-long bazaar brims with a rich array of exotic goods from around the world. Supporting services such as streamlined entry procedures and one-stop tax-refund processing for departing visitors are fully available. Guests from afar can fully immerse themselves in cutting-edge technology while strolling at leisure to savor the vivid delights of digital consumption.
The expo's vibrancy is rooted in Hangzhou's long-term industrial accumulation. The city is now home to 938 core-sector AI enterprises. In the first half of 2026, local core-AI-industry revenue reached 270.5 billion yuan, representing a year-on-year increase of 26%. Home-grown tech innovators are going global: dexterous humanoid robots are shipped worldwide, and rehabilitation exoskeletons cross oceans to help patients suffering from muscle weakness stand again. Cold hardware carries the warmth of human-centered care.
From January to July this year, exports by Hangzhou-based AI enterprises surged 156?% year-on-year. AI-related deals account for half of the intended-order agreements signed during this expo. The China headquarters of the Arab Federation for Digital Economy will settle in Hangzhou, building a collaborative platform for Chinese and foreign enterprises to pursue joint-technology research and co-create products, so digital innovations originating in the East can benefit broader global markets.
As the Qiantang River's mighty tides roll onward, digital trade has become an undeniable force driving global-economic growth. At this expo, AI is far more than eye-catching technology. It acts as a bond linking enterprises, connecting markets and benefiting ordinary people. Drawing participants worldwide to Hangzhou, the expo fosters technical exchanges and business negotiations to jointly explore an open, inclusive, win-win development path for the digital age.

At the Launching Ceremony of the Fifth Global Digital Trade Expo

“We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:19:34 UTC
12:19:34 KST

“We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- ESO
- Summary:
- A dead white dwarf with no detectable disk has somehow produced a powerful shock wave that appears to have persisted for at least 1,000 years. Its magnetic field may be partly responsible, but astronomers say an unexplained “mystery engine” may also be at work.
- Share:
Stars can produce powerful shock waves when gas and dust streaming away from them collide with material in the surrounding space. Astronomers have now captured a striking example around the dead star RXJ0528+2838 using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT).
The discovery is puzzling because, based on known mechanisms, this small stellar remnant should not be capable of producing the structure seen around it. The unexpected finding challenges current ideas about how dead stars exchange matter and energy with their surroundings.
"We found something never seen before and, more importantly, entirely unexpected," says Simone Scaringi, associate professor at Durham University, UK and co-lead author of the study published in Nature Astronomy.
"Our observations reveal a powerful outflow that, according to our current understanding, shouldn't be there," says Krystian Ilkiewicz, a postdoctoral researcher at the Nicolaus Copernicus Astronomical Center in Warsaw, Poland and study co-lead.
Astronomers use the term 'outflow' to describe material expelled from an object in space.
A Shock Wave Around a Dead Star
RXJ0528+2838 lies about 730 light-years from Earth. Like the Sun and other stars, it travels around the center of the Milky Way. As it moves through space, it encounters gas between the stars, producing a type of shock wave known as a bow shock.
Noel Castro Segura, research fellow at the University of Warwick in the UK and collaborator in this study, describes it as "a curved arc of material, similar to the wave that builds up in front of a ship."
Bow shocks are typically produced when material flowing away from a star slams into its surroundings. In the case of RXJ0528+2838, however, astronomers cannot identify any known process that fully accounts for what they observed.
A White Dwarf With No Disk
RXJ0528+2838 is a white dwarf, the leftover core of a dying low-mass star, and it is orbited by a Sun-like companion.
In binary systems like this one, material can be pulled away from the companion and transferred onto the white dwarf. That material often forms a disc around the dead star. The disc feeds the white dwarf, while some matter can also be thrown back into space in powerful outflows.
RXJ0528+2838 is different. Astronomers see no evidence of such a disc, leaving them without the usual explanation for the outflow and the surrounding nebula.
"The surprise that a supposedly quiet, discless system could drive such a spectacular nebula was one of those rare 'wow' moments," says Scaringi.
VLT Observations Confirm the Source
The unusual structure was first noticed in images taken with the Isaac Newton Telescope in Spain. Its strange appearance prompted the researchers to investigate it more closely using the MUSE instrument on ESO's VLT.
"Observations with the ESO MUSE instrument allowed us to map the bow shock in detail and analyse its composition. This was crucial to confirm that the structure really originates from the binary system and not from an unrelated nebula or interstellar cloud," Ilkiewicz explains.
The bow shock's size and shape suggest that RXJ0528+2838 has been producing a powerful outflow for at least 1000 years.
That creates another problem. Scientists do not yet know how a dead star without a disc could sustain such an outflow for so long, although the system's magnetic field may provide an important clue.
A Magnetic Field May Hold Part of the Answer
RXJ0528+2838 is known to possess a strong magnetic field, something the MUSE observations also confirmed.
Instead of allowing material from the companion star to settle into a disc, the magnetic field appears to guide that matter directly onto the white dwarf.
"Our finding shows that even without a disc, these systems can drive powerful outflows, revealing a mechanism we do not yet understand. This discovery challenges the standard picture of how matter moves and interacts in these extreme binary systems," Ilkiewicz explains.
The researchers suspect that the magnetic field could be connected to a hidden source of energy, which Scaringi describes as a 'mystery engine.' But the explanation remains incomplete.
According to the observations, the white dwarf's present-day magnetic field could sustain a bow shock for only a few hundred years. The structure appears to have existed for at least 1000 years, meaning the magnetic field alone cannot yet explain the full phenomenon.
Searching for the "Mystery Engine"
Astronomers will need to investigate many more binary systems to determine how these powerful outflows can form without discs.
ESO's upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) could play an important role by allowing scientists to study both known systems and much fainter examples in greater detail.
Scaringi expects the telescope "to map more of these systems as well as fainter ones and detect similar systems in detail, ultimately helping in understanding the mysterious energy source that remains unexplained."
Story Source:
Materials provided by ESO. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Krystian Iłkiewicz, Simone Scaringi, Domitilla de Martino, Christian Knigge, Sara E. Motta, Nanda Rea, David Buckley, Noel Castro Segura, Paul J. Groot, Anna F. McLeod, Luke T. Parker, Martina Veresvarska. A persistent bow shock in a diskless magnetized accreting white dwarf. Nature Astronomy, 2026; 10 (3): 391 DOI: 10.1038/s41550-025-02748-8

Editor’s Notes: I believed in Israel’s third bloc until pollsters proved me wrong - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:17:24 UTC
12:17:24 KST

I was wrong about Israel’s third bloc. I also wanted it to succeed.
I wanted a political force strong enough to make the moderate parties of the Center-Right and Center-Left form a broad unity government. Enough seats to force politicians who could find endless reasons to avoid each other to discover reasons to sit together.
After the October 7 massacre and the war, I thought that was possible. I wrote columns explaining why.
The polling has forced me to reconsider. The independent camp I expected has failed to take shape. We are back to Bibi or no Bibi.
Wanting a broad government seems to me a perfectly reasonable position. Forecasting the emergence of a bloc that could force one into existence required evidence. I gave the possibility more weight than the campaign has justified, and I have to ask how much wanting that outcome influenced my judgment.
In August, I wrote about conversations around me in Gush Etzion, south of Jerusalem: at the kiddush after going to the synagogue, in the supermarket, at the park. People who had voted the same way for years were reconsidering their choices. They remained on the Right. Some were moving further Right. Their attachment to particular politicians had weakened.
My own thinking had changed, too. For years, I had argued that persuading haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men to serve in the military would achieve more than coercion. During the war, I came to support financial consequences for avoiding service. I knew how far I had moved on a question I had written about repeatedly.
I thought enough changes like these could produce a new political alignment. In that August column, I wrote: “Israel is going through the same thing with the lights on and pollsters in the room, failing to measure it.”
I was confident enough to suggest that the pollsters were missing something. Their numbers have since given me reason to question my own reading.
There was a leap in the argument. Dissatisfied voters still have to agree on where to go. Two reservists can agree about the unfairness of the burden they carry and disagree completely about who should be prime minister. A voter can lose faith in one right-wing politician and choose another who intends to join the same coalition. Changed loyalties can move seats around inside an existing camp.
The third bloc I imagined also had to do something quite demanding with those seats. It had to remain together, make a broad government a condition of its support, and leave the larger parties dependent on that support. Each step could fail. Even a respectable election result would have been only the beginning.
Those promising unity struggled to unite
Instead, some of the people promising unity struggled to unite with one another.
On September 4, Gilad Erdan withdrew his Unity party from the election, citing insufficient support and unsuccessful efforts to join forces with other parties. An N12 poll had put a potential combination of Unity and Benny Gantz’s Blue and White at 2.6%, below the 3.25% threshold for entering the Knesset.
Erdan said voters were primarily looking for an answer to “the question of who will be prime minister.” That was a fairly direct assessment from someone whose political offer had depended on voters giving a different question priority.
The negotiations also exposed a familiar problem. Asked by Walla why he insisted on leading a merged list, Gantz answered: “Because I need to lead this path.”
A project that asks parties across the political spectrum to compromise needs leaders capable of doing so themselves. The order of names on a list is a useful place to start. Those failed talks give us reason to examine the politicians’ decisions alongside the voters’ choices.
Some new lists remain. In the September 18 Maariv poll conducted by Lazar Research, Yoaz Hendel, and Yaron Zelekha’s joint list received four seats, as did Ofer Winter’s People of Israel. Both were narrowly above the electoral threshold. Winter’s seats were counted in the Netanyahu camp.
Four seats can matter enormously in a parliament of 120, where a majority requires 61. Those lists may yet affect who can form a government. The substantial independent camp I expected has nevertheless failed to emerge.
I also underestimated what the Netanyahu question would mean after October 7.
I had expected the scale of the catastrophe and the demands of the war to create pressure for a broad government. They could also make the choice of prime minister feel more consequential. A voter who holds Netanyahu responsible has a powerful reason to insist on his departure. A voter who trusts him most on security has a powerful reason to insist that he stay. The same war can deepen both convictions.
Mere calls for unity can not resolve disagreement
Calling for unity does very little to resolve that disagreement. Any party seeking to force a broad government has to explain whether it would serve under Netanyahu, what conditions it would set, and what it would do if those conditions were rejected. The answer could cost precisely the voters it was trying to bring together.
That is a harder problem than getting people to agree that the country needs unity. I gave too much weight to the apparent demand for a broad government, and too little to the compromises people would have to accept to produce one.
The election is still ahead. Polls can change, and small parties can cross the threshold or fall below it. But the weak numbers and failed attempts to build a common political vehicle are evidence I have to take seriously now. A columnist cannot keep extending the deadline for his own argument until it comes true.
I still want a broad government of the moderate Center-Right and Center-Left. I think it would give Israel a better chance of making decisions on military service, rebuilding, and responsibility for October 7 that could survive beyond one coalition.
The route I expected to get us there has failed in this campaign. A third bloc may have another chance in another election.
I would need to see leaders able to work together, voters prepared to accept the necessary compromises, and a credible way to turn their votes into a broad government. I owe readers that evidence before making the prediction again.

Pray for Leiter: The importance of supporting soldiers who protect Israeli life - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
03:17:11 UTC
12:17:11 KST

IDF reservist Neria Leiter was seriously wounded Wednesday when a Palestinian attacker rammed a vehicle into him at a checkpoint near Beit Horon on Route 443.
After hours of surgery at Jerusalem’s Shaare Zedek Medical Center, doctors said his condition had stabilized, but his life remained in danger. His family has asked the public to pray for Neria Dov ben Chana.
His father, Israel’s ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, flew home from New York. At the hospital on Thursday, he spoke about a previous journey through grief. In November 2023, his eldest son, Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidya Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza.
“He died instantly,” Yechiel said. This time, he said, the family could gather at Neria’s bedside while doctors worked to save him, and they could pray together and ask others to join them. “His life is still in danger,” he told reporters.
There are many ways to describe this family. Yechiel Leiter left the United States for Israel at 18, making a deliberate choice about where to build his life. His children grew up here and made their own choices about service.
Neria returned to reserve duty after his brother's death
Moshe served for years, became a father of six, and was studying medicine when war called him back. After Moshe’s death, Neria returned to reserve duty.
Their father has spoken about other sons and sons-in-law who served on the front lines, of a son in a support role, and of another son who has Down syndrome, living through the war with the family. Each has a life beyond this accounting of service.
Neria described the decision to go back in a post this year. “As a bereaved brother,” he wrote, returning to the reserves “was not simple at all.” Losing Moshe had torn at him.
He also had opinions and criticisms about how the war and the country were being run. The question he posed, in translation, was: “What do I need to do? What is in my control?”
He could not sit at home while his friends reported for one reserve stint after another. His team included religious and secular men, husbands and fathers, alongside single men, from Israel’s center and its periphery. By then, the rounds of duty were too numerous to count. His closing words were about the privilege of defending home.
Israel's reservists carry an enormous weight for their country
Read the whole account, and its honesty becomes clear. A person can believe in his duty and feel the strain of carrying it.
He can disagree with those making the decisions and still answer the call. No country should mistake that resolve for an inexhaustible supply of time, health, or courage.
Israel has needed its reservists across multiple fronts since the October 7 massacre. Their families have lived with repeated departures, interrupted work, and the fear that accompanies every call.
The Leiter family’s name is known because Yechiel represents Israel in Washington. Countless families whose names never reach a newspaper have carried comparable burdens. They, too, deserve to be seen while they are serving and long after they return.
'Choosing life' means caring for the soldiers who protect it
Yechiel wrote after the attack that he believes prayer and national unity can bring miracles. “Neria needs a miracle,” he said, adding: “They choose death – we choose life.”
A father whose son is fighting for his life is entitled to speak with that force. For the rest of us, choosing life must also mean tending to those who protect it: giving wounded service members and their families sustained care, making repeated reserve service bearable, examining attacks seriously, and sharing the demands of defense as fairly as possible.
That requires support for families and employers long after the headlines have moved on. Officials must hear reservists who voice criticism, even when those same reservists continue to serve.
At Shaare Zedek, Yechiel’s daughter gave birth after visiting her brother. A new life began in one part of the hospital while doctors worked to save Neria in another. Nothing about that proximity tells us how Neria’s story will end. For now, the only ending to seek is his recovery.
The family has asked us to pray. We join that prayer. We should also listen to what Neria wrote when he was well enough to explain why he kept going – and make sure Israel lives up to the people who do.

The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye have discussed arrangements for an urgent meeting of the three countries' chiefs of staff to consider ways to support Saudi Arabia under the Mecca defence agreement, the Saudi Gazette reported.
Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Ishaq Dar and Hakan Fidan held consultations at the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's permanent mission to the UN in New York.
The ministers reviewed ongoing preparations for the chiefs of staff meeting, which will examine mechanisms for supporting Saudi Arabia in line with commitments under the defence pact.

During the meeting, the ministers "strongly condemned" attacks attempting to target Mecca as well as civilian and economic facilities in Saudi Arabia.
They discussed the latest regional developments and stressed the importance of upholding international law, good-neighbourly relations, mutual respect for state sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs.
They also underlined the importance of ensuring the security and freedom of maritime navigation.
The ministers renewed their commitment to working toward sustainable peace and stability in the region, supporting efforts to de-escalate tensions and advancing peaceful solutions to ongoing crises.

Newest AIM-9X Missiles Not Meeting Operational Availability Goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:54:25 UTC
11:54:25 KST

One of the Air Force and Navy’s most common air-to-air missiles is falling short of a key readiness metric, and the services are ramping up stocks of a vital air-to-ground missile, according to recent Pentagon reports.
The Modernized Selected Acquisition Reports on the AIM-9 and the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile, cleared for publication in July, lay out progress and shortfalls and provide a snapshot for the health of these key munitions.
According to the reports, the AIM-9X Sidewinder Block II is facing operational availability shortages. The Warfighting Acquisition University defines operational availability as “the degree … to which one can expect a piece of equipment or weapon system to work properly when it is required.” The Air Force is at 58 percent operational availability for the latest version of the Sidewinder, and the Navy is at 78 percent—the requirement is 86 percent, the report says.
That shortage is forcing squadrons to face lower training asset availability, preventing fighter pilots from having the requisite number of Captive Air Training Missiles. Those CATMs have live seekers and guidance units that pilots use on regular training sorties to practice locking onto targets, tracking high off-boresight angles, and simulating missile shots.
When enough training pods are nonoperational, aircrews don’t have enough rounds to fly daily air-to-air tactical training with realistic seekers.
The Air Force and Navy plan to buy more than 11,000 AIM-9X Block II missiles, which are infrared-guided, short-range, supersonic air-to-air weapons.
But reliability problems with integrating a new circuit processor into the latest configuration, the AIM-9X-4, have “impacted missile reliability and halted testing.”
As a result, a software update called Operational Flight Software 10.4, meant to integrate the advanced guidance control unit and inertial measurement unit hardware upgrades, will not be fielded.
Report authors note that the follow-on software that will fix the problem won’t be ready until September 2027.
AIM-9X maker RTX declined to comment on the report.
JASSM and LRASM Work
As the two services work out the air-to-air missile problem, both are seeking to expand their plans for the Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles and its cousin, the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile.
Another shared munition between USAF and the Navy, the JASSM is a linchpin munition with multiple variants fielded and in production.
The AGM-158A JASSM is a 14-foot-long missile that strikes beyond 200 miles and has been a staple of U.S. aircraft use since 2001. The B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry it and its variants, and the F-35A Lightning II and B-21 Raider are planned to integrate it.
The AGM-158B JASSM-Extended Range can hit targets at more than twice the distance, with public reports showing ranges of more than 500 miles.
The AGM-158C LRASM has a range closer to the baseline JASSM but is equipped with radio-frequency seekers designed to strike large, moving targets such as ships.
According to the recent selected acquisition report, the joint program office between the two services had delivered 5,348 JASSM variants to the Pentagon as of April, according to the report.
Current production capacity sits at about 600 JASSMs annually, with near-term plans to reach 860 missiles a year.
More mid-term plans call for ramping up that production to 1,280 missiles annually by fiscal year 2030 and 1,880 by fiscal 2032, according to the report.
A March $52 million contract modification to LRASM will raise the missile’s production from 240 per year to 320 per year beginning in fiscal 2029, according to the report.
Lockheed announced a new JAASM option at AFA’s Air, Space, & Cyber conference earlier this month, the AGM-158 FLEX.
The company sees FLEX, a modular, designed munition which has swappable nose and launch options, as another way to offer a variety of strike options in the JASSM form factor.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The stockpile plus-up, however, will use current factory space via expansion efforts, the Eglin spokesperson wrote, and “will not require a new facility construction.”
Lockheed’s investment strategy includes $8 to $9 million through 2030 to meet heightened munitions demand.
“We are expanding production and building and modernizing more than 20 facilities in Arkansas, Alabama, Florida, Massachusetts, and Texas,” Lockheed spokesman Scott Swofford told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “This includes upgrading existing facilities and incorporating advanced manufacturing techniques, production lines, tooling, and plant layouts to meet urgent production demand.”
Software, Paint, and Engines
Like the AIM-9X, the JASSM also faced software integration problems, specifically with its 54.0.02 flight software update. But an Eglin spokesperson said the software had received fielding approval since data for the selected acquisition report was gathered in April, and that “there are no impacts to combat readiness.”
The Air Force is also pressing to accelerate the integration of the Universal Armament Interface, a software architecture to standardize aircraft mission systems-weapons interface, but this has introduced “added software risk,” according to the report.
But the Eglin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the UAI program has “made no changes to the delivery schedule” of the JASSMs.
“Integration activities remain on track to deliver planned capabilities as scheduled. Software risk is being actively managed through early software-in-the-loop integration, resource prioritization, and agile contract actions,” the spokesperson said.
Separately, the report noted that in an inspection of 1,356 JASSMs, inspectors flagged 49 missiles for depot-level maintenance and overhaul, mostly due to stealth coating defects. The report says that issue won’t be resolved until 2029.
Lockheed switched from the flat gray paint scheme to a semi-gloss black coating to reduce radar and visual signatures. The new coating can absorb and deflect electromagnetic energy more easily during longer flight times used by the new, extended-range variants.
The shift began in 2021 with the Lot 19 contract award for the AGM-158B-2 variant.
The Eglin spokesperson said that both the program office and Lockheed Martin are “exploring contracting actions to increase repair capacity and return serviceable missiles to the field more efficiently.”
Beyond software updates, the Air Force also spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 to procure and mature a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ERs.
“Investing in a second engine source for the AGM-158 is essential to securing our supply chain and ramping up production of critical long-range strike weapons,” the Eglin spokesperson said. “By establishing a second production line, we eliminate manufacturing bottlenecks, drive competition, and secure deliveries of JASSM and LRASM to the warfighter.”

US tech titans attend Trump-Xi dinner. Who wasn’t invited?
Virtually all of America’s most powerful technology executives joined US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a lavish White House state dinner on Thursday, as AI emerged as a major theme of the Chinese leader’s visit.
The black-tie dinner in the White House East Room brought together more than 130 guests, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
Apple chairman Tim Cook, AMD chief Lisa Su, Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, Zoom CEO Eric Yuan, and Dell Technologies chief Michael Dell were also among those invited. Major finance and industrial executives, including JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, and Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg, attended as well.
One notable Silicon Valley name was missing, however. Anthropic – the developer of the Claude AI models and one of OpenAI’s biggest US rivals – had no representative. CEO Dario Amodei has been among the industry’s more vocal advocates of tighter safeguards around increasingly powerful AI systems.
Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel was also absent, though he was in Berlin that evening receiving the 2026 Axel Springer Award. His CIA-seeded data-mining giant has grown into one of Silicon Valley’s biggest defense-tech players, supplying AI and analytics software to all six branches of the US military, as well as the FBI, NSA, and DIA. Its technology is also used by NATO and the Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, while the company has faced sustained criticism over its expanding role in surveillance and AI-enabled warfare.
Intel, IBM, and Oracle were also absent from the guest list, which otherwise featured most of America’s biggest technology and AI companies.
There was also a conspicuous absence on the other side of the table: No Chinese corporate executives were listed, despite earlier expectations that business leaders could accompany Xi. Instead, his delegation at the dinner was composed of senior Chinese officials.
The concentration of American tech executives came as Trump and Xi discussed the increasingly intense US-China competition in AI and advanced semiconductors.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi said both countries have a responsibility to ensure AI remains “under human control” and is developed for the benefit of people.
Trump said AI – which he has increasingly referred to as “superintelligence” – was high on the agenda of the summit, while reiterating his opposition to slowing development through extensive regulation. Washington has also proposed establishing a mechanism allowing the two countries to notify each other about serious AI-related incidents, an idea discussed by senior economic officials ahead of the summit.
The dinner followed around 90 minutes of talks between Trump and Xi at the White House, where the two sides also addressed trade, Taiwan, and the ongoing conflict involving Iran. Washington and Beijing agreed earlier this week to extend their existing trade truce by two months while negotiations continue.
Trump emphasized cooperation despite the rivalry, saying the two leaders represent “different systems” but can continue building a relationship promoting prosperity and security.

Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
Ancient meteorite grains reveal that powerful magnetism may have helped shape the solar system from its very beginning.
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- Ancient grains inside one of the oldest known meteorites reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed during the solar system’s first 200,000 years. The discovery suggests magnetism worked alongside gravity to help transform a vast cloud of gas and dust into the sun and planetary disk.
- Share:
About 4.6 billion years ago, the solar system began as an enormous cloud of gas and dust. Over the next several million years, this "solar nebula" changed dramatically. The cloud collapsed and flattened into a disk, eventually giving rise to the sun at its center and the planets that formed around it.
Gravity has long been considered the main force behind this transformation. New research from MIT, however, suggests that magnetism may also have been an important part of the process.
Scientists found evidence of ancient magnetic fields preserved in some of the oldest meteorite material ever identified. The researchers studied microscopic grains inside a meteorite discovered in Antarctica in 2008. Known as calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions, or CAIs, these grains formed during the solar system's first 200,000 years and represent the oldest known material from that period.
Their magnetic signatures indicate that a substantial magnetic field was already present during the solar nebula stage. The researchers estimate that this field was stronger than Earth's magnetic field today and may have helped move primordial material inward as the young sun formed.
"This transition, from a spherical cloud to a protoplanetary disk, is one of the most significant events in all of solar system history," says Benjamin Weiss, the Robert R. Shrock Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences at MIT. "It has long been theorized that gravity caused this, but our measurements show magnetism likely played a role."
The findings were reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Along with Weiss, the study's MIT co-authors are first author Cauê Borlina PhD '22, Elias Mansbach PhD '24, and Nilanjan Chatterjee. Other collaborators include Xue-Ning Bai of Tsinghua University, Po-Yen Tung and Richard Harrison of Cambridge University, François Tissot of Caltech, and Kevin McKeegan of the University of California at Los Angeles.
How Early Solar Magnetism Could Have Worked
Magnetic fields arise when electrically charged matter moves. During the earliest stage of solar system formation, the collapsing cloud of gas and dust may have generated a plasma containing charged particles. As those particles circulated through the developing disk, they could have created and maintained a magnetic field.
If a magnetic field was present, Weiss and his colleagues reasoned, it should have left a lasting imprint on some of the material forming within the disk. As that material condensed, tiny magnetic minerals could have recorded the strength of the surrounding field. If those minerals survived for billions of years and eventually reached Earth, their "remanent magnetization" could provide evidence that magnetism existed in the young solar system and influenced its development.
The researchers had already found evidence of magnetism from about 2 million years after the solar system began forming. By that point, scientists believe the sun had already formed and the planets were beginning to assemble. That earlier work suggested magnetic fields may have contributed to planet formation.
"Nowadays people don't debate whether magnetism is present when planets are forming. But the debate is around the very early solar system, before planets are forming, when there's just a disk," says Borlina, who led the new study as an MIT graduate student and is now an assistant professor at Purdue University. "That's where the debate still resides, and that's where we're operating now."
A Meteorite With an Unusually Pristine Record
The latest study pushed the search even farther back in time, focusing on whether magnetism was present while the sun itself was still coming together.
The researchers examined samples from DOM 08006, a meteorite found in 2008 in Dominion Range, a mountain range along the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. Since its discovery, the meteorite has been studied extensively because of its unusually primitive composition.
DOM 08006 contains mineral grains from the earliest stages of solar system formation, possibly dating to before the sun had fully formed. Remarkably, the meteorite has retained much of its original mineral makeup despite surviving billions of years of solar system history.
"Other meteorites went through many different processes over this 4.5 billion year history," Weiss says. "They were formed in the solar nebula, then added to bodies with water, then got destroyed, moved to the asteroid belt, and then landed here. But somehow, DOM has experienced less alteration than any other meteorite."
That unusual preservation made DOM 08006 an especially promising place to search for evidence of magnetic fields from the earliest solar system.
If such a field existed, its signature might still be preserved in some of the meteorite's CAIs.
"We know they are the oldest things we have of the early solar system," Borlina says. "But CAI's are very complex and are not all the same, even within a 1-millimeter piece of the meteorite. So we have to carefully identify what types they are."
A Magnetic Field Stronger Than Earth's
Using small pieces of the original meteorite, the team separated tiny mineral grains and identified several CAIs containing naturally magnetic minerals, including iron. The researchers then carried out a series of tests to determine whether those grains still preserved ancient magnetism.
They found traces of a magnetic field recorded inside the minerals. From those measurements, the team estimates that the early solar system had a magnetic field measuring roughly 150 to 600 microteslas. That is about three to 12 times stronger than Earth's magnetic field today.
The result suggests that magnetism may have played a meaningful role in controlling how material moved through the protoplanetary disk as the sun was forming.
"We think these kinds of magnetic fields were helping to move gas from the protoplanetary disk, in toward this central star, the sun," Borlina says. "Gravity is also playing a role. But we are now showing that, if you want to fully understand how the sun and planets formed, you should include magnetic fields in the ingredients that make them."
This research was supported, in part, by NASA.

Paleomagnetic evidence for a nebular magnetic field from calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (36) DOI: 10.1073/PNAS.2521660123

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked two Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and five official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Thursday and 6 a.m. on Friday.

Nepal’s prime minister calls for climate justice, proposes Himalayan resilience mechanism at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:24:57 UTC
11:24:57 KST

Faisal Mahmud
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah called for climate justice and proposed a new regional mechanism involving Nepal, India and China to confront growing climate risks across the Himalayas during his address to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday.
Addressing the 81st session of the General Assembly, Shah said last month’s catastrophic disaster involving a tsunami-like flash flood triggered by a massive high-altitude glacier collapse demonstrated how climate change was destabilizing Himalayan ecology through melting permafrost, unstable mountain slopes and growing risks of ice-rock avalanches, floods and landslides.
“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” he said, noting that Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
The Aug. 26 disaster killed more than 1,400 people, while thousands remain missing, according to Nepali authorities. Recent assessments have put economic losses and physical damage at billions of dollars.
Shah proposed establishing a “Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism” led by Nepal, India and China to share satellite data and scientific expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, strengthen cross-border early-warning systems and coordinate disaster assistance.
“Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation rather than a frontier of fragmented information,” he said.
Shah also urged richer countries to provide greater grant-based climate financing, arguing that mechanisms such as the Loss and Damage Fund and Global Environment Facility remain inadequate.
“Climate justice cannot remain a beautiful phrase in United Nations documents,” he said.
Nepal has increasingly pushed climate justice to the center of its international diplomacy following the disaster, which devastated homes, roads, schools and hydropower infrastructure across several districts.
Shah said the international response should be built around six principles: “relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction” as well as “responsibility, reparation and resilience.”

Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Rahman said Bangladesh has been hosting more than 1.2 million forcibly displaced Rohingya for over nine years, putting pressure on the country's resources, environment, security and host communities.
“The origin and source of the Rohingya crisis is in Myanmar. Therefore, its solution also lies there,” he said in his maiden address to the General Assembly.

He also reiterated Bangladesh's support for Palestinians' right to self-determination and an independent state while calling for conflicts worldwide to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.
Rahman said Bangladesh was rebuilding after more than 15 years of what he called “fascist rule” following the 2024 mass uprising and the Feb. 12 national election.
He paid tribute to those killed and injured during the July-August 2024 uprising, describing it as a movement against “fascism,” as well as those who sacrificed their lives in earlier struggles for democracy, justice and human rights.
Rahman said his government was pursuing a “3-R” strategy — Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction — as Bangladesh returned to the democratic path.
On climate change, he said Bangladesh remained among the countries most vulnerable to its effects, despite contributing little to global carbon emissions, and called for stronger international action on climate justice, financing and adaptation.
He said his government plans to plant 250 million trees over five years, expand clean and solar energy, and excavate 20,000 kilometers (12,427 miles) of canals to address flooding and drought.
Rahman also called for greater technology transfer and affordable access to emerging technologies for developing countries, warning that today's digital divide should not become tomorrow's “artificial intelligence divide.”

He was addressing a long march organized by the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI)-led 11-party opposition alliance to press a seven-point demand, including implementation of the February referendum verdict, action on rising prices, the energy and fertilizer crisis, deteriorating law and order, and corruption. JI chief Shafiqur Rahman spoke at the same gathering.
This has become a familiar picture in Bangladesh, where NCP routinely joins JI in long marches, alliance meetings and parliamentary protests.
The NCP emerged from the student protests that brought down the Awami League government in August 2024. For a party that entered politics promising a new political alternative, this raises a basic question. What still separates NCP from JI?
NCP says the relationship is strategic, not ideological. But less than two years after emerging from the student-led uprising, the party is struggling to show voters what still makes it politically distinct.
When NCP was launched in February 2025, it carried a heavy political promise. Its leaders had come directly from the student movement that helped bring down Sheikh Hasina’s authoritarian rule. Many were young, had never held party office, and spoke about building a political system different from the one Bangladesh had known for decades.
At its launch, NCP called for a new constitution and a “Second Republic.” It promised democratic institutions, an end to corruption and nepotism, and politics based on equality and representation. Thousands attended the launch in Dhaka. The party presented itself as a centrist force and an alternative to the older parties that had dominated Bangladesh.
Less than two years later, NCP is in parliament. But how it arrived there has created a more difficult question. Can it still convince voters that it represents something genuinely new?
The turning point came before the February 2026 national election, when NCP joined an electoral alliance led by JI.
For a new party without a strong nationwide organization, the calculation was understandable. Elections in Bangladesh require candidates, polling agents, local networks, money and organization across hundreds of constituencies. NCP had enthusiasm and recognizable leaders, but it did not have the machinery of an established party.
JI did.
But JI’s history made the NCP’s choice contentious. The party had sided with Pakistan against Bangladesh’s independence in 1971, and some of its leaders and members had collaborated with Pakistani forces during the genocide. So, the deal came with a political cost.
Before coming to an agreement with JI, the NCP held seat-sharing talks with the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), while also considering a separate third alliance. NCP reportedly sought at least 20 seats from the BNP, but the party was willing to offer it only around six or seven, with some NCP leaders saying the final number could fall to three.
JI, meanwhile, was prepared to offer around 30 constituencies. For a new party still struggling to build a nationwide organization, the JI deal offered a much clearer path into parliament.
However, in the JI-led alliance, JI received by far the largest share. According to media reports, the decision caused serious resistance inside the NCP. At least 30 senior members either resigned or publicly opposed the alliance. Tasnim Jara, one of the party’s best known figures, left the NCP before the election.
By the NCP’s first anniversary in February, at least 60 leaders and activists had resigned from the party during its first year. Not all left over JI, but the electoral alliance became the clearest public sign of an internal disagreement over what NCP was supposed to become.
NCP leaders have consistently rejected the idea that this means ideological integration with JI. In a March 2026 interview with The Diplomat, Chief Coordinator of NCP Nasiruddin Patwary said NCP had wanted to work with the BNP. But disagreements over reform and electoral realities pushed the party toward JI. He said JI’s religious ideology was not NCP’s position and argued that if the two parties believed in the same politics, NCP would have simply joined JI.
In the February election, NCP won only six parliamentary seats. JI won 68 while the 11-party coalition won a total of 77 seats among 300.
For a party less than a year old, six MPs cannot simply be dismissed as failure.
But the numbers also show the limits of NCP’s rise. It had emerged from a national uprising and once hoped to compete across Bangladesh. Instead, it entered parliament after contesting in only a small part of the country under a seat-sharing arrangement dominated by JI.
Some young Bangladeshis saw the alliance as a retreat from the politics NCP had originally promised. The party also faced more basic problems. It lacked the resources, organization and local structure enjoyed by older parties.
The bigger challenge is what happened after the election. The partnership with JI did not end when voting ended. JI chief Shafiqur Rahman became leader of the opposition. NCP convener Nahid Islam became opposition chief whip. The two parties remained together in the opposition bloc.
Their cooperation has continued well beyond parliament.
This creates challenges for its political identity. NCP says it is a separate party. That is true institutionally. But voters do not judge political identity only through party constitutions or official statements. They also see who shares platforms, who coordinates parliamentary action and who campaigns together on the streets.
The more NCP operates within the JI-led bloc, the harder it may become to explain what makes NCP politically distinct from the alliance around it.
Other controversies have also hurt the NCP’s image. Spokesperson Asif Mahmud Shojib Bhuyain, a former interim government adviser, is under investigation by the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) over allegations, including abuse of power and accumulation of illegal wealth. The ACC has said the allegations are not yet proven, while Asif has rejected them.
NCP’s student wing Jatiya Chhatra Shakti (JCS) has also faced scrutiny. In March, a Dhaka University student accused JCS activists of beating him. In August, its activists were involved in a clash with Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, BNP’s student wing, and Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir, JI’s student wing, at Jagannath University in Dhaka that left at least 70 people injured.
NCP had promised a different kind of politics. Incidents like these raise questions about how different it really is.
NCP has also struggled to show what is genuinely new about its politics. Much of its agenda still centers on constitutional reform, criticism of India, and street programs that often take place alongside JI. The two parties frequently use similar language about sovereignty, foreign influence, and reform.
The NCP has offered fewer detailed answers on problems such as jobs, inflation, energy shortages, and the wider economic pressures facing ordinary Bangladeshis.
The contrast was visible after Bangladesh signed its trade agreement with the United States on February 9, just three days before the national election. Economists and civil society figures soon raised questions over its timing, lack of transparency, and possible impact on Bangladesh’s economic and strategic independence.
NCP, however, did not make the agreement a major political issue in the immediate aftermath of its signing. Its criticism became clearer only later, when party leaders called for revisions and raised concerns directly with the U.S. ambassador. That raises a question about consistency. If sovereignty and foreign influence are central to NCP’s criticism of Delhi, why did an agreement with Washington receive much less attention at the beginning?
With all its shortcomings, it would still be premature to write off the NCP.
The NCP still has six lawmakers, while Nahid Islam serves as opposition chief whip. The party also plans to contest the upcoming local government elections independently rather than as part of an electoral arrangement with JI.
Those elections could provide a clearer picture of NCP’s own political strength. The national election showed that an alliance with JI could help the party enter parliament. Contesting separately will show how much support NCP can attract under its own name.
NCP has secured a place in parliament. However, for now, its future depends entirely on whether it can step out of the shadows and prove it is an independent force, rather than just a junior partner in a JI-led coalition.

Brain structure changes appear seven years before Alzheimer’s plaques are detected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:00:08 UTC
11:00:08 KST

Structural changes in the brain’s outer layer can be detected years before amyloid-beta proteins reach high levels on brain scans. This discovery suggests that physical alterations to brain tissue might be an earlier sign of Alzheimer’s disease than previously thought. The findings were published in Nature Neuroscience.
Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurological condition that destroys memory and other important mental functions. One of the main biological hallmarks of the disease is the accumulation of amyloid-beta, a protein that clumps together to form plaques between nerve cells in the brain. Historically, the standard model of Alzheimer’s assumed that these amyloid plaques build up first and trigger brain shrinkage later. A 2010 study proposed exactly this timeline, arguing that amyloid buildup is the very first event in the disease process, with brain volume loss occurring only as a later consequence.
Earlier research showed that elevated amyloid-beta levels accelerate brain volume loss. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that people with high amyloid levels exhibited faster brain volume loss even before cognitive symptoms appeared. However, hints emerged that brain tissue might paradoxically swell and change well before amyloid scans turn positive. A 2020 review noted that the outer layer of the brain temporarily thickens or swells in the earliest stages of genetic Alzheimer’s before it begins to waste away.
The new study directly tracks people over time to confirm that these cortical changes can be detected years before amyloid buildup crosses the threshold of detection on brain scans. The cerebral cortex is the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, playing a major role in memory, thinking, and reasoning. The thickness of this layer typically decreases as people age, a process known as cortical thinning. The research, led by James M. Roe and Yunpeng Wang of the University of Oslo, aimed to see if changes in this thinning process happen before a person registers as positive for amyloid-beta.
To investigate this timeline, the researchers analyzed data from three large, long-term studies of cognitive aging. They focused on individuals who were cognitively healthy, meaning they did not show signs of dementia or cognitive impairment. The researchers used magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, which is a technique that uses magnetic fields to create detailed images of brain structure. This allowed them to measure the thickness of the cerebral cortex over time. They also used positron emission tomography, or PET scans, which use a mildly radioactive tracer to reveal the presence and quantity of amyloid-beta plaques in the brain.
The final sample included 4,570 MRI scans from 1,051 individuals. Among these participants, 691 also had amyloid-beta PET scans available. The research team used the PET scan data to divide the participants into two distinct groups. The first group consisted of 77 converters, which were people who initially had low levels of amyloid-beta but later crossed the threshold into high, positive levels during the study. The second group consisted of 412 individuals who remained negative for high amyloid-beta across all of their available PET scans.
The scientists then looked back at the MRI data. For the converters, they artificially cut off the timeline, excluding any MRI scans taken near or after the time the person tested positive for amyloid-beta. Instead, they focused purely on brain scans taken between one and ten years before the individual’s first positive PET scan. By doing this, they could compare the early brain structures of people who would eventually develop high amyloid-beta to those who never did. In their analyses, the researchers controlled for variables like biological sex, average age, overall brain size, and the specific type of MRI scanner used.
The results provided evidence that individuals who later developed high amyloid levels showed a thicker cerebral cortex compared to those who remained amyloid-negative. These individuals also exhibited a slower rate of age-related cortical thinning over time. Essentially, the expected rate of brain shrinkage was reduced in the years leading up to a positive amyloid scan. These physical differences were detectable in MRI scans taken at least seven years before the participants reached amyloid levels high enough to be classified as positive.
These structural differences were especially prominent in the frontal regions of the brain. The researchers wanted to know if these differences were simply a byproduct of slowly rising amyloid levels that had not yet crossed the positive threshold. When they adjusted their statistical models to account for the exact, continuous levels of amyloid buildup measured in the early PET scans, many of the cortical thickness differences persisted. This indicates that the structural changes to the cortex are at least partly independent of early amyloid accumulation.
The researchers also found a spatial relationship between the brain changes and amyloid buildup. The geographic pattern of cortical thickening closely mapped onto the regions of the brain where amyloid-beta tends to accumulate. In addition, the timing of these structural changes paralleled the spread of the plaques. Brain regions that experienced earlier structural changes tended to be the exact regions where amyloid began to deposit first.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The time cutoffs used in the study were based on when an individual was first observed to have high amyloid-beta, not the exact biological moment they crossed the threshold. Because PET scans were taken at intervals, some people might have developed undetected amyloid buildup earlier than their first positive scan recorded. To address this, the researchers used statistical predictions to estimate the exact age of positivity, and the results remained consistent, though this approach relies on mathematical assumptions.
Another detail to consider is that the study only included cognitively healthy older adults. Participants who volunteer for long-term aging studies often represent a particularly healthy and high-performing demographic, which might not completely reflect the general population. It is also important to note that the study did not include measures of tau, another key protein involved in Alzheimer’s disease that strongly affects brain shrinkage. The researchers pointed out that because tau typically accumulates after amyloid-beta, it is unlikely to be driving the structural changes seen seven years prior to amyloid positivity.
Future research will need to explore what exactly causes this early increase in cortical thickness. An apparent increase in thickness on an MRI scan could reflect several different biological processes, such as an inflammatory response to early amyloid deposits, or changes in the supporting cells of the brain, rather than the addition of new neurons. Tracking these changes alongside other biological markers will help clarify whether this early swelling is a protective mechanism or the first step in the neurodegenerative process.
The study, “Cortical thickness changes precede high levels of amyloid by at least 7 years,” was authored by James M. Roe, William J. Jagust, Susan M. Landau, Theresa M. Harrison, Håkon Grydeland, Maksim Slivka, José-Luis Alatorre-Warren, Pablo F. Garrido, Øystein Sørensen, Edvard O. S. Grødem, Tyler J. Ward, Esten H. Leonardsen, Alice Murphy, JiaQie Lee, Tormod Fladby, Atle Bjørnerud, Kristine B. Walhovd, Anders M. Fjell, Didac Vidal-Piñeiro, and Yunpeng Wang.

Scientists discover an “impossible” cellular survival pathway that could help fight cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
01:55:32 UTC
10:55:32 KST

Scientists discover an “impossible” cellular survival pathway that could help fight cancer
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Montana State University
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered a surprising backup system that lets mammalian cells make the essential amino acid cysteine even when the pathways once considered indispensable are disabled. The same survival mechanism may help cancer cells resist treatment, raising the possibility that shutting it down could make tumors easier to kill.
- Share:
A molecular geneticist at Montana State University has uncovered a previously unknown survival mechanism that allows mammalian cells to produce the amino acid cysteine even when the cellular systems normally responsible for supplying it stop working. Scientists once thought this kind of survival was impossible.
The finding, published in Nature Chemical Biology, could eventually point researchers toward new ways to make some cancers more vulnerable to treatment.
"All cells need a constant supply of an amino acid called cysteine in order to stay alive," said the paper's lead author Ed Schmidt, a professor of genetics and development in the Department of Microbiology and Cell Biology in MSU's College of Agriculture. "Yet cysteine is not available outside of the cells."
Why Cells Depend on Cysteine
Cysteine performs several essential jobs inside cells. It is used to make proteins, helps cells protect themselves from damage and contributes to the formation of disulfide bonds. These bonds help stabilize proteins and maintain their three dimensional structures.
For decades, researchers believed that cells could not simply obtain cysteine from their surroundings. Instead, they must generate it internally by breaking apart cystine, an oxidized form of cysteine.
Cells normally accomplish this through what is known as a disulfide reductase system. Scientists had long assumed that having at least one functioning version of this system was essential for cellular life.
"Scientists long believed this process was absolutely essential for all living cells," Schmidt said. "However, we have discovered a previously unknown system in mammalian cells that can take over when the main systems fail."
Mice Survived When They Should Not Have
The discovery unfolded in three stages over nine years.
Schmidt said the first major clue appeared in 2014, when a colony of genetically engineered mice survived under conditions that, according to scientific understanding at the time, should have been fatal. The mice lacked any known mechanism for converting cystine into the cysteine their cells required.
"This was supposed to be impossible," he said. "No living organism or cell had ever been found that could live without having a functioning disulfide reductase system."
The finding was not the result of an accidental observation. Schmidt had previously engineered mice whose liver cells separately lacked one or the other of the two main disulfide reductases.
The behavior of those animals made him question whether the prevailing assumption about cell survival was correct.
"Some of the physiological responses we were seeing in the livers of each of those mouse lines suggested to me that the belief that no cell could live without having at least one of these two reductases might not be correct," he said. "I wanted to test this."
A Hidden Backup Pathway
Finding the explanation took another seven years.
Schmidt's team worked with collaborator Peter Nagy and his group at the Hungarian National Institute of Oncology in Budapest. Nagy's team contributed analytical capabilities that helped the researchers determine how the cells were still obtaining cysteine from cystine despite lacking a working disulfide reductase system.
They found that mammalian cells possess an alternative chemical route.
When the usual disulfide reductase pathway is unavailable, this backup mechanism breaks an adjacent carbon sulfur bond within cystine. That reaction ultimately frees cysteine that the cell can use.
The pathway provides cells with another way to obtain a molecule that is essential for survival, even after their better known machinery has failed.
An Ancient Defense Against Toxins
Schmidt said this backup system may originally have evolved as a defense against electrophilic toxins.
Many such toxins are organic molecules produced by organisms as chemical weapons against predators or competing organisms. By giving cells another way to survive chemical stress, the newly identified pathway may have provided an evolutionary advantage to early multicellular organisms.
"The ability of our cells to survive, at least for a time, without disulfide reductases, likely evolved in our earliest multicellular ancestors as a mechanism that allowed these organisms to resist being killed by electrophilic toxins made by the things they ate or the things found in their environment," Schmidt said.
A Possible Weakness in Cancer Cells
The same mechanism that protects healthy cells could also have a less helpful consequence.
Researchers suspect that some cancer cells may use this backup pathway to survive chemotherapy, radiation therapy or immune therapy. Those treatments are designed to damage or destroy cancer cells, but cellular defense systems can sometimes help tumors endure the stress.
"This same pathway that protects our cells from oxidants or toxins also likely protects cancer cells from therapies," Schmidt said. "Now that we know they have this defense mechanism, we might be able to precisely disable it in cancers, making them more susceptible to cancer therapies, as well."
If scientists can learn how to selectively interfere with the pathway in tumors, the discovery could eventually provide another way to increase the effectiveness of existing cancer treatments.
Students Helped Drive the Discovery
Several Montana State University students contributed to the research, including some who have since graduated.
Zoe Seaford and Sydney Austad served as co-first authors and conducted their work as undergraduate students in Schmidt's laboratory. Martina Serrano Alvarez and Reed Noyd also participated while they were undergraduates, and Colin Miller contributed as a doctoral student.
Scientists and trainees from several other institutions also collaborated on portions of the work.
"This scientific breakthrough underscores the power of research to redefine what we thought was possible and advance new approaches to cancer treatment," said Sreekala Bajwa, dean of the agricultural college. "I congratulate Dr. Schmidt and his team for their exceptional achievement and for engaging students as true partners in research that delivers global impact."
Schmidt joined Montana State University in 1999. His research spans gene regulation, cell and organismal physiology, mouse genetics, embryology, biochemistry, metabolism and laboratory mice whose DNA have been genetically altered by inserting one or more genes from another organism into the mouse genome.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Montana State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Edward E. Schmidt, Eszter Petra Jurányi, Colin G. Miller, Sydney A. Austad, Tamás Ditrói, Zoe M. Seaford, Sang Jun Yoon, Reed C. Noyd, Yun Pyo Kang, Justin R. Prigge, Vivien Csikós, Martina Serrano Alvarez, Katalin Erdélyi, Dóra Kővári, Gina M. DeNicola, Peter Nagy. Cystine C–S bond cleavage fuels cysteine production under disulfide reductase deficiency. Nature Chemical Biology, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41589-026-02213-1

Tesla opened its first factory for high-volume production of the Semi, a heavy-duty electric truck, in Sparks, Nevada, on Thursday, as CEO Elon Musk aims to push into big rigs.
The company first unveiled its Semi in 2017, and started selling the trucks in very limited quantities to early customers, including anchor client PepsiCo., in 2022. A livestream of the ribbon-cutting event aired Thursday evening.
Musk wasn't at the opening, but he showed up by video recording for the audience, and called the Semi a "breakthrough product for heavy shipping."
"It's almost like a sports car in truck form," said Musk, who is attending a state dinner in Washington, D.C., with President Donald Trump and Chinese Leader Xi Jinping.

Tesla has struggled to gain much traction with its angular steel Cybertruck, a pickup that it first delivered to customers in 2023.
Tesla's stock price is down 16% this year, underperforming all of its megacap tech peers.

Priestley said the company plans to produce 50,000 Semi trucks per year there, or about 1,000 per week, and to bring "more than 3,000 jobs during that ramp period" to Nevada.
On Tesla's last earnings call in July, Musk told investors that the company's automated driving systems (known as FSD, or Full Self-Driving) would be available for the Semi in the near future, but he declined to give a specific date. Musk said at the time that he sees driverless systems as essential for the trucking industry.
"There just aren't enough people around who want to drive trucks, which are crucial for transport throughout America," Musk said. "An autonomous Semi is actually going to be very important to address the shortage of truck drivers."
Musk, who has a long history of missing his stated deadlines when it comes to driverless vehicles, added that the company expects "to get self-driving working on the Tesla Semi probably around the end of this year or early next year."
Meanwhile, competitors Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI are already conducting driverless testing with their trucks and hauling cargo for partners.
For now, Tesla's primary selling point for the Semi is its battery range and charging network. A long-range version of the Tesla Semi can travel an estimated 500 miles on a full battery, while its standard variant gets an estimated 325 miles, the company says.
Priestley said Thursday that Semi trucks in fleet operations have demonstrated 98% uptime, and rarely needed to spend time out of service for unscheduled maintenance. The company said it's setting up a bespoke service network for Semi owners, and will be sending mobile service technicians for repairs when possible.
According to ICCT, trucks and buses represent less than 10% of road vehicles globally yet account for nearly half of transport-related air pollution. Switching to efficient zero-emission commercial vehicles can reduce pollution levels and bring "savings to fleet operators through lower costs," the group said in a 2025 report.
Tesla also plans to bring the Semi to Europe, where rivals like Volvo and Daimler Truck already sell battery-powered models.

“I was born a Jew. I didn’t pick it, and I’ve never hidden it,” she wrote. “And this week a whole lot of people decided what I believe without asking me, without checking a single thing I’ve ever said or done, because a repost and the word ‘Jew’ were apparently enough to fill in the rest.”
In her post, Pink wrote that she does not “speak for Israel, or for any government,” and that “Palestinians deserve a future that honors their humanity and their aspirations.” She lamented the use of the word “‘Zionist,’ spat like it’s a slur.”
She also wrote that she did not call for Macklemore to be dropped from the tour, which some critics did.

Petition gains thousands of signatures to oust Pink
The petition calling for Pink’s ouster was published the same day that she posted her statement, and has since gained nearly 200,000 signatures. Her comments, the petition writes, have “fueled ongoing conflict and struggles for visibility and empathy,” and removing her “would reaffirm UNICEF’s commitment to impartiality and its dedication to all children, irrespective of nationality or heritage.”
Bardem and his wife, actress Penelope Cruz, faced threats of a boycott in 2014 after they joined an open letter condemning Israel for its conduct in its war that year with Hamas. Bardem particularly stirred outrage with a separate statement at the time in which he said: “I cannot understand this barbarism, even more brutal and incomprehensible considering all of the horrible things the Jewish people have gone through in the past.” He and Cruz soon walked back their comments.
Pink was first named a US national ambassador for UNICEF in 2015. UNICEF’s website also says that Pink is passionate about ending global malnutrition and that she has used QR codes in her merchandise booths that link to UNICEF donation pages.
UN officials have previously defended the right of UNICEF ambassadors to express political views in their personal capacity.
The Pakistani government called for UNICEF to drop Indian actor Priyanka Chopra as one of its ambassadors in 2019, saying that her “support for war” and for India’s government amid heightened conflict in the disputed region of Kashmir made a “mockery” of the role.
“When UNICEF Goodwill Ambassadors speak in their personal capacity, they retain the right to speak about issues that interest or concern them,” Stephane Dujarric, a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General António Guterres, said at the time, adding that their “personal views or actions do not necessarily reflect those of UNICEF.”
UNICEF has, however, removed an ambassador over political conduct. In 1987, it terminated its association with goodwill ambassador Boris Becker after the tennis player declined to commit to not returning to apartheid-era South Africa.
