Prominent scholars, legal experts among 6,000 signatories to letter rejecting Gaza genocide charge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
01:48:23 UTC
10:48:23 KST

Prominent academics, legal experts, and historians are among more than 6,000 signatories of an open letter released earlier this month rejecting as a “blood libel” the accusation that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
The letter, which launched with more than 5,000 signatories and later surpassed 6,000, argues that the accusation of genocide is contradicted by Israel’s actual conduct in the war and has been weaponized as a pretext to exclude and attack Jews around the world.
The letter was released by Creative Community for Peace in partnership with its authors: Yossi Klein Halevi, Rabbi Yitz Greenberg, Rabbi Micha Odenheimer, and Binghamton University historian Jonathan Karp.
Open letter: 'We must unite in repudiating the lie of genocide'
“There is a vigorous debate within the Jewish community over aspects of how this war was fought, and that is a sign of moral health. So is our pain over every innocent life lost. But we must unite in repudiating the lie of genocide,” the letter states.
It goes on to address the “unprecedented combat conditions” in Gaza, including Hamas’s use of “hundreds of kilometers of tunnels, thousands of boobytrapped homes [and] the conflating of combatants with ‘journalists’ and ‘human rights workers.’”
It also addresses the civilian-to-combatant casualty ratio, which it says is “considered low for asymmetrical urban warfare.”
Taking the Gaza Health Ministry’s current death toll, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants, alongside INSS’s May estimate of more than 23,000 terrorists killed, the implied civilian-to-combatant ratio would be roughly 2:1.
The letter also cites “the absence of mass starvation despite repeated claims of imminent catastrophe” and “the warnings given to civilians before attack,” and asserts that “All these factors were erased in the eagerness to indict Israel for genocide.”
Meanwhile, the letter argues that Israel went to war after October 7 to break what it calls an “Iranian-led siege of terror enclaves” on its borders, while noting that anti-Zionists were already leveling accusations of genocide against Israel the following day.
Letter: In 'bitter irony,' Israel is only country to face 'sustained war of attempted genocide'
“The bitter irony is that Israel, home to half the world’s Jews, is the only country to face a sustained war of attempted genocide – from its inception in 1948 until today,” the letter states.
Prominent scholars who signed the letter include Harvard professor and public intellectual Steven Pinker. Other Harvard-affiliated signatories include Harvard Law professor Jesse Fried and visiting scholar Anat Alon-Beck, a professor of law at Case Western Reserve University.
Other notable scholars who signed on include historian Niall Ferguson, Israeli historian Benny Morris, Holocaust historian and former US Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism Deborah Lipstadt, Tel Aviv University professor emerita and former Yad Vashem chief historian Dina Porat, historian and author Simon Sebag Montefiore, UCLA professor Judea Pearl, and Brandeis University professor emeritus Jonathan Sarna.
The signatories also include John Spencer, chair of Urban Warfare Studies at the Modern War Institute at West Point.
Prominent legal figures include former Canadian justice minister and attorney general Irwin Cotler, Cornell Law professor Robert Hockett, Jeffrey Mausner, a former prosecutor with the US Justice Department’s Nazi War Crimes Unit, and Eugene Kontorovich, a professor of law at George Mason University’s Scalia Law School and director of its Center for the Middle East and International Law.
“The genocide libel is a case study in the longstanding – and intensified post-October 7th – historical, moral, legal and normative inversions of fact, law and history,” Cotler said in a statement cited by CCFP.
Political signatories include former UK prime minister Boris Johnson, Iraqi-born former UK cabinet minister Nadhim Zahawi, and former US secretary of veterans affairs Robert Wilkie, among others.

Trump administration asks US Supreme Court to intervene to allow third-country deportations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
01:40:00 UTC
10:40:00 KST

Trump administration asks US Supreme Court to intervene to allow third-country deportations
- The Trump administration asked the US Supreme Court to allow continued deportations of migrants to third countries without hearings, challenging a lower court ruling that deemed this policy unlawful.
- Since 2025, over 25,000 migrants were deported to 29 countries under this policy, including unstable nations like South Sudan, raising concerns about their safety and legal protections.
- Immigrant groups sued to stop these removals, citing due process violations and risks of abuse; courts have issued conflicting rulings, and the case remains highly contested with significant legal and diplomatic implications.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump’s administration asked the US Supreme Court on Sept 24 to allow it to continue to deport migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face – a key tool in his immigration crackdown.
The administration in an emergency filing asked Supreme Court justices to put on hold Boston-based US District Judge Brian Murphy’s ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful, while it appeals to the Supreme Court.
The dispute escalated quickly after the Boston-based Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, which upheld Murphy’s decision on Sept 18, put that decision into effect late on Sept 23.
More than 25,000 migrants have been deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented in 2025, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico.
The Supreme Court previously sided with the administration, lifting a preliminary order that Murphy issued earlier in the case halting the removals.
The policy is one of a number of measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump’s goal of mass deportation. The Republican President has enforced a sweeping crackdown on immigration – among his top priorities – since returning to office in 2025.
The administration has carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan, which the US State Department urges Americans to avoid due to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Liberia, the Central African Republic and other nations.
In its filing on Sept 24, the Justice Department told the Supreme Court that the rulings by the lower courts disrupt “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens”.
The department said the administration has already cancelled flights or plans for removals to various countries and warned of harms to diplomatic arrangements and US foreign policy.
“While certain aliens may benefit from stalling their removal, the nation does not,” the filing stated.
Trina Realmuto, a lawyer from the National Immigration Litigation Alliance who represents the plaintiffs, said in an interview that the fact that the administration opted to take the case to the Supreme Court was not surprising, as it has “repeatedly and publicly stated an intention to do so”.
She said the First Circuit’s order at night on Sept 23 “makes crystal clear no flights or buses should carry out third-country removals”.
Stepping up deportations
The case began in 2025 after the Department of Homeland Security moved to step up deportations of migrants who cannot be returned to any country listed on their deportation orders.
Immigrant rights groups filed a class-action lawsuit on behalf of a group of migrants, seeking to prevent their removal to such third countries without notice and a chance to assert the harms they could face.
The policy provided that migrants could be swiftly removed to third countries that have provided credible diplomatic assurance that they will not persecute or torture the individuals.
For countries that have not provided such assurance, deportees would be notified of their destination, and the US authorities would assess the likelihood of persecution or torture only if the individuals raise such fears on their own.
In February, Murphy ruled that the policy violates immigration law procedures and due process protections under the US Constitution’s Fifth Amendment. Due process generally requires the government to provide notice and an opportunity for a hearing before taking certain adverse actions.
The administration has said these deportations are needed to expel migrants who commit crimes and are considered “some of the worst of the worst illegal aliens in this country” because their countries of origin are often unwilling to take them back.
But both Murphy and critics of the administration said the policy is also targeting migrants who had been granted legal protection from being sent back to their home countries.
The policy has resulted in deportees being unlawfully transferred by third countries back to their home countries, while others have been abused, detained or have disappeared, the plaintiffs said in a court filing.
The First Circuit upheld most of the judge’s ruling on Sept 18. On Sept 23, at the behest of the plaintiffs, the First Circuit dissolved a pause it had placed on Murphy’s ruling during the Justice Department’s appeal.
The First Circuit acted after the challengers to the policy reported that the government had planned to fly a group of migrants to several countries in Africa on Sept 24.
The case has been hotly contested since it began and included findings by Murphy that the government “repeatedly violated, or attempted to violate” his orders.
Murphy in 2025 found that the administration had violated his order requiring additional steps before attempting to send a group of migrants to South Sudan. REUTERS

For so long an underdog, front-running Freo ready to claim first flag

2026-09-25

Thu, 3 Sept, 8:10 pm, Final score, Dockers 40, Hawks 72
analysis
Fremantle prepared for AFL grand final stage after years of being underdog
Football fans unite in glory, but the bonds of fandom are often forged in failure.
It is fair to say that Fremantle fans have suffered more than most since their club's entry to the AFL. It's also fair to say that, as a result, Dockers fans are some of the most passionate and dedicated in the league. It's why something like Wharfie Time is endearing instead of cheesy. The Purple Army is something to believe in.
The Fremantle experience has often been one of struggle. Struggling against the bigger brother in blue and yellow. Struggling against the tyranny of distance in a league based on the other side of the continent. Struggling against the weight of its own history.
The anchor is sometimes less a motif of their moniker and instead a weight tethering their expectations.
But this year everything seems different. This year Fremantle has led from the front, often without looking back.
Even as the pack came for the Dockers, they didn't fold under the pressure. Instead, they buckled down and somehow got better.
"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained last week.
"So we all know what's on the line, but we've just got to make sure that we give our best at each moment, and the next moment's the most important one."
The Dockers showed a resilience often only attached to the best of teams. It's also one baked into the identity of their side.
Fremantle aren't just stocked with high-draft picks. The Dockers are also filled with players overlooked and discarded by others. Almost half of the side that will run out on Saturday fits into those categories, with a few rookies to boot. If these players had given up at the first rejection, they wouldn't be in the league.
More pertinently, Fremantle wouldn't be in the big dance without many of these names.
If Fremantle's fandom and side are somewhat unconventional, its success on the field is anything but. Like many successful teams of years' past, they have been built on a solid defensive base, with enough star power to shine through when needed. Like many great teams, they are more than the sum of their parts.
Like many great teams, they play their best footy when it matters most. Last week, Fremantle put together arguably the best quarter of its season to make the grand final.
"We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us … I'm just so proud of everyone," captain Alex Pearce said in the immediate wake of last week's victory.
Thirteen years after their first grand final, the Dockers finally seem primed to break their premiership drought. In their way stands a side featuring the only remaining Fremantle player from that 2013 loss: Lachie Neale.
Strength in defence
Often the leaders of a side dictate the identity and style of a side.
Led ably by captain and All-Australian Alex Pearce, Fremantle's backline may not be as star-studded as other defensive units around the league, but it is as sturdy as any. They scramble, hustle and fight through all four quarters. Regularly through the year teams fell away as the Dockers held strong.
The Dockers have had the league's most consistently good defence across all facets of the game. Some backlines drop their heads when the tide starts to turn — not Fremantle.
Fremantle excels at defending before danger begins. Its midfield works hard to prevent clean exits from stoppages and contests around the ground. Although the Dockers don't have the best clearance differential or ability to win ground balls in the mid-arc, they are exceptional at preventing opposition teams from scoring from these sources.
When they lose possession in their front half, the Dockers stay eager to get the ball in their hands. They are the best side in the league at winning the ball back in the middle third of the ground.
If the ball does end up inside their defensive 50, no side is better at repelling opposition forwards. Miserly is an understatement about how Fremantle defends. It is the biggest reason that the Dockers are still alive in season 2026.
When they win the ball back, they can turn on the jets and blow opposition sides away.
The cherry on top
Few fans turn up to the footy for stout defence. It's the action at the other end that hypnotises.
Despite their defensive DNA, Freo are not lacking for weapons of their own. They turn defence into attack at the drop of a hat thanks to a plethora of creative players.
Fremantle can put on a show like few others when everything is firing, possessing the ability to pile goal after goal on the scoreboard. While their defence is often understated, their attack is anything but.
Few players generate more highlights than Shai Bolton, with the former Mark of the Year winner routinely getting Purple fans off the edge of their seats. Bolton isn't alone however.
The Dockers side is stocked with players that use the ball well.
Murphy Reid has quickly cemented himself as an attacking line breaker, while Caleb Serong, Jordan Clark and Corey Wagner gain ground with ease.
Luke Jackson also proves a challenge for any opponent as the most capable ruck at ground level in the league. Jackson has the most score involvements of any ruck this year.
The Dockers often attack in straight lines, and use the tallest timber in the league to their advantage.
But when sides like Sydney take those avenues away, Fremantle doesn't shy away from changing angles of attack and look laterally as well.
That ability to win aerial contests has another benefit. It tends to encourage opposition players to fly more often than they should, leaving Fremantle with an outnumber at ground level. That allows even more room for the ground gang to work in.
Up forward, the Dockers can beat you in any number of ways. The likes of Hye Amiss, Patrick Voss and Josh Treacy can take clunks and convert them into sure scores. At ground level, Michael Frederick, Isaiah Dudley and Shai Bolton regularly hit the scoreboard and strike fear into the hearts of opposition small defenders.
Their big men love a bomb from the top of the arc, but Freo don't tend to score a lot from out wide. That makes Hayden Young's preliminary final heroics all the more notable.
Perhaps Fremantle's biggest strength is their evenness across the board. Against Hawthorn it wasn't just the stars like Bolton and Luke Jackson that stood up late, but also players like Judd McVee and Frederick. It is clear that there's belief in this team, and dedication to a united cause.
The Final Challenge
Although Fremantle has been the best side across the year, it isn't coming into the grand final at the peak of its mid-season powers. The Dockers have won just three quarters in their three finals so far — a feat no other team has achieved before.
The Dockers have struggled late in the year when the ball has hit the deck against good sides, and some of the best midfields have overwhelmed their attacking midfield unit. These may sound like minor issues, but to win a grand final against the two-time defending champions, everything has to be on point.
But the Lions are a side that the Dockers have vanquished through the year. In round 12, the Dockers eased to a 25-point win in one of their most impressive wins of the year. The Dockers absorbed the Lions' clearance dominance while preventing them from getting the upper hand in the marking battle. Fremantle worked out a way to penetrate the Lions' whole ground defence, scoring a massive 52 points from their defensive half.
But it was also a Brisbane side that Longmuir acknowledged wasn't at their best coming into the game.
"We felt like there were some opportunities there. You know, Fages [Lions coach Chris Fagan] would come in here and say they're not in the greatest form," he said.
"I just don't want to be disrespectful with that because they've been in the last three grand finals."
Longmuir and Fagan both know that premierships aren't won in May. The early season Lions are vastly different to the side that Fremantle has to beat in the grand final.
But there's hope in the West that the result will be the same and that the Dockers three-decade drought will be over.

Iran offers Trump deal before US election

2026-09-25
01:36:50 UTC
10:36:50 KST

Iran offers Trump deal before US election
Iran has offered the US a new deal aimed at ending the months-long conflict before the midterm election in November, directly challenging President Donald Trump’s claim that Tehran is deliberately waiting until after the election to reach an agreement.
Trump claimed in a speech at the UN on Tuesday that Iran is deliberately stalling the talks to see how Republicans perform in the November 3 midterm election, and predicted that Tehran would make a deal “right after” the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if negotiations fail.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday. “We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” he said, referring to the memorandum of understanding reached by the US and Iran in June.
“We did reach an agreement with your president… The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialogue, descended into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway,” Pezeshkian said in an interview with Fox News. “We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war… It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has submitted a proposal in which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within around a week and negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program rapidly resumed. The proposal was sent through mediators during talks in New York this week.
Under the plan, Tehran would restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its economic blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also seeking an end to hostilities on other fronts, including Israel’s combat operations in Lebanon.
US and Iranian negotiators are discussing a phased arrangement in which the blockade and restrictions on Hormuz would be addressed first, Reuters reported, citing Iranian, regional, and Western diplomatic sources.
Tehran has not abandoned its claim to regulate Hormuz, with Iranian officials continuing to insist that the waterway should be managed by Iran and Oman and that fees should be charged for services provided to passing vessels.
Araghchi said the proposal largely follows the terms of the June memorandum rather than introducing new demands, adding that Iran is waiting for a response.
Araghchi has also held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts in New York, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Moscow has said there is “no alternative” to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the “illegal actions” of the US and Israel.
The renewed diplomatic push comes amid mounting pressure on both sides. The US blockade has sharply restricted Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran’s controls over Hormuz have disrupted one of the world’s most important energy corridors and helped push oil prices above $100 a barrel and US diesel prices to historic highs.
Pezeshkian, who is the first foreign head of state to speak at the UN while his country is at war with the US, told the chamber on Wednesday that Tehran is prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but will not negotiate under threats of force and “will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

Commander rejected plans to rebase before deadly drone strike, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
01:01:00 UTC
10:01:00 KST

Commander rejected plans to rebase farther from Iran before deadly drone strike, sources say
The dozens of U.S. troops bombarded by Iranian drones at a small Kuwaiti port in the opening days of the Iran war could have relocated to safer positions in western Saudi Arabia, multiple sources told CBS News, but those plans were rejected by the unit's commanding general despite intelligence warning of a potential attack on their post.
About one week before the launch of Operation Epic Fury, most American soldiers and Air Force personnel stationed in Kuwait were moved to Jordan and Saudi Arabia — farther away from Iranian missile range. At least two options were scouted, planned and presented to the leadership of the 103rd Sustainment Command, the Army Reserve unit that ran logistics for U.S. Central Command: one was Logistical Support Area (LSA) Jenkins, a U.S. military base near the southwest port city of Yanbu, and another was Prince Sultan Air Force Base, just southeast of the Saudi capital city Riyadh.
A third option, supported by the commander, Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, was to follow the playbook from the unit that was previously deployed to Kuwait before the 103rd arrived in September 2025. During the 12-day war between Israel and Iran that July, the active unit briefly moved from their home base at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait to Port of Shuaiba, roughly 30 miles south of Kuwait City and just 65 miles southwest of Iran.
"That was a totally different scenario," one service member, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak with the media, told CBS News. "Missiles and drones were flying overhead between Iran and Israel and we were more worried about one of them being intercepted and falling out of the sky."
The U.S., Israel and other allies joined in shooting down dozens of the Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Israel that summer, but Iran never directly targeted U.S. positions in the Mideast.
By late fall 2025, however, Army intelligence began to map out potential Iranian retaliation scenarios in the event the U.S. became more engaged in military activity against the Iranian regime.
In January, the sources said Army intelligence began briefing Barnes that Port of Shuaiba was a potential target, but in the days before the launch of Operation Epic Fury, he nonetheless chose to move the unit there instead of Saudi Arabia.
"Shuaiba was the easy button," another service member said.
The Army on Thursday declined comment. CBS News has also reached out to Barnes but has not received a response.
The revelations are the latest in a series of whistleblower accounts made by active and reserve service members regarding the decision-making process leading up to and following the deadliest attack of the war. Six U.S. troops were killed in the strike on March 1, and more than 20 were wounded.
Notably, Prince Sultan Air Force Base, one of the other options for the unit's relocation, was also attacked by Iranian fire. Pictures obtained exclusively by CBS News showed damage to a large Air Force jet, though there were no reported deaths as a result of the strikes on PSAB.
U.S. Army Central and Third Army this summer ordered a Pentagon probe "to determine the facts and circumstances" of the Iranian attack at Port of Shuaiba, but before the review was underway, a CBS News investigation began shedding light on what several survivors of the attack described as "strategic failures" ahead of, during and after the strike.
One day after the deadly strike, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the Iranian drone as a "squirter" — suggesting that the drone managed to slip past the defenses of a fortified unit inside Kuwait. In April, one of the injured soldiers told CBS News that "painting a picture that 'one squeaked through'" was not accurate. The soldier said the unit was "unprepared to provide any defense for itself. It was not a fortified position."
Jim and Stacey Khork, the Gold Star parents of Maj. Cody Khork, told CBS News in an exclusive interview that their son, as one of the unit's force protection officers, was among the key soldiers warning Barnes of the site's vulnerability.
"My son died unnecessarily," Stacey Khork lamented. "Yes, he died for my country. Yes, he was a patriot. Yes, he was a hero. I hate to use the word murder because it's strong, but if a loved one of yours was murdered, our justice system is built to have accountability and to have atonement for that and for the grief of the family."
CBS News spoke with other survivors of the blast who detailed requests to leadership for more resources ahead of the strike. Those requests focused on the number of medical personnel as well as the availability and accessibility of medical supplies.
"This was a failure," Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom said in an interview with CBS News in May, adding he believed Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, another of the six soldiers killed, could have survived her wounds had there been a doctor, a fixed aid station or more than one ambulance at the post. The soldiers, according to witnesses, instead triaged themselves with makeshift bandages, braces and tourniquets. They commandeered civilian vehicles to drive the wounded to two local Kuwaiti hospitals.
The Pentagon has repeatedly pushed back on claims that the Army tried to downplay the incident. In a post on X in March addressing prior CBS News reporting on the strike, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said "every possible measure has been taken to safeguard our troops — at every level" and that "[t]he secure facility was fortified with 6-foot walls."
Earlier this month, an Army spokesperson confirmed to the Khorks and CBS News that its probe into the deadly Iranian attack was completed in early July, but officials have yet to release it. In a statement to CBS News, an Army spokesperson asked for "patience" and said the Pentagon "will not comment on specific details, individual accounts, or leaked portions of the report at this time."
A spokesperson for the Iowa-based 103rd Sustainment Command declined comment, while multiple requests to Brig. Gen. Barnes have gone unanswered.
Congressional Democrats urge committee hearings
As families like the Khorks await findings from the Army, more than 20 congressional Democrats from both chambers are urging the House and Senate Armed Services Committees to hold investigative hearings on the deadly strike.
A new letter sent this week to GOP Sen. Roger Wicker of Kansas and Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama, the chairmen of their respective committees, cited multiple CBS News reports on the attack. Lawmakers who signed the letter include military veterans Rep. Pat Ryan of New York and Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado. Signatories also include Senators Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith of Minnesota, the home state of Master Sgt. Nicole Amor.
"It is critical that Congress gets answers on the failures that led to the attacks, and on the subsequent mistreatment of survivors and families of those killed," the letter reads. "We urge you to hold public hearings to determine why [the Department of Defense] was not properly prepared for this attack and why it has failed to ensure that injured service members get access to the care they need. As the administration continues to ask Congress for more resources for this war, we can no longer afford to wait for DoD to deign when they are going to answer these questions."
The chairmen's respective offices did not respond to inquiries from CBS News about the letter.
The Senate on Thursday again rejected a resolution aimed at limiting President Trump's war powers in Iran, though the Democrat-led effort picked up one new GOP supporter.
In a 49-50 vote, four Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Rand Paul of Kentucky and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — joined Democrats in voting to advance the measure. Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania was the sole Democrat to oppose.
The resolution would have directed the president to "remove the use of United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran or any part of its government or military, including potential ground forces in a combat role or used for occupation, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or specific authorization for use of military force against Iran."

In Brief
- James Paterson says the timing of the Medicare breach disclosure was politically motivated.

The Opposition has questioned the timing of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's disclosure that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics portal, as pressure grows for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence.
Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he did not believe it was a "coincidence" that Albanese revealed the incident while attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
"The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did," Paterson told ABC's 7.30.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Paterson, however, played down the severity of the breach itself, describing it as being at the "bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness".
He said Australians should be "alert but not alarmed" about the incident, noting the information accessed was not personal or private Medicare data.
It reportedly occurred on 18 June when an OpenAI agent tasked with researching public medicine spending gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.
The government says the portal contained aggregated health statistics and was separate from systems handling Medicare claims or individual patient records.
OpenAI detected the activity on 11 August but did not notify the Australian government until 10 September, when it sent an email to a Services Australia inbox.
Albanese publicly revealed the breach on Thursday after speaking with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman in New York.
The prime minister criticised both the length of time it took OpenAI to inform Australia and the way the notification was made.
Government examining legal options
The federal government has established a task force to investigate the incident, including whether Australia's existing laws and reporting requirements are adequate to deal with autonomous AI systems.
The review will also consider whether OpenAI breached Australian law and whether stronger penalties or liability rules are needed for companies whose AI agents cause harm.
Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Friday the government was examining what legal consequences could follow the incident, amid calls for OpenAI to be held accountable.
The government is also investigating whether activity linked to OpenAI agents affected systems belonging to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Victoria's Department of Health.
Calls for stronger AI safeguards
The breach has added to debate over how Australia regulates increasingly autonomous AI systems.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the incident demonstrated the need for stronger rules around transparency and incident reporting.
He told the ABC Australia could not be left "entirely at the mercy of foreign AI companies".
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie also called for safeguards to ensure AI systems were fit for purpose, telling ABC Radio National Breakfast that Australia needed to make sure "AI serves humanity, not the other way around".
The government has said it plans to develop national AI standards, with findings from the investigation expected to inform its approach to future regulation.

Cambodian Authorities Investigating Scamming Sites Linked to Sanctioned Tycoons, Senior Official Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:46:00 UTC
09:46:00 KST

Online scamming sites linked to two sanctioned Cambodian tycoons are among those being investigated by the Cambodian authorities, a senior official said yesterday, as the country concluded a two-day anti-scam conference.
In an interview with Nikkei Asia, Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the government’s ad hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, said that compounds linked to the businessmen Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are being investigated as part of the government’s ongoing anti-scam crackdown.
“For those two tycoons who have compounds that are linked to scams, they are being investigated,” Sinarith said, referring to the properties.
Asked for details of the investigations, Sinarith said that “investigations were ongoing at all suspect compounds and that investigators were still determining the complicity of individuals linked to locations allegedly used for online scams,” in Nikkei’s paraphrase.
As Nikkei’s correspondent Ananth Baliga noted, Sinarith’s comments mark “the first time the government has admitted such well-connected people are associated with investigations into scam operations.”
Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are not minor figures. Both were important allies and financial buttresses of Prime Minister Hun Sen during his 38-year rule, and have remained prominent figures under his son, Hun Manet, who took over the prime ministership in 2023. Both control corporate empires based in (although not confined to) the western provinces of Koh Kong and Banteay Meanchey, respectively, and are also long-serving senators for the Cambodian People’s Party.
Sinarith’s comments came on the second day of the two-day International Conference on Combating Online Scams, which the Cambodian government hosted in Phnom Penh this week.
The conference, which was co-sponsored by Interpol, the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime, and China’s Lancang Mekong Cooperation mechanism, was intended to promote global collaboration in the fight against cyber-scams. It also marked the culmination of an anti-scam campaign that Cambodia’s government launched last year, in response to rising pressure from foreign governments, including the United States and China, over the industrial-scale scamming operations that were operating, with apparent impunity, across the country.
Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are among the group of politicians and prominent businesspeople who are alleged to have abetted and/or profited from this wave of cyber-criminality. Both are alleged to own properties where thousands of trafficked workers were held in prison-like conditions by criminal syndicates and were forced to run scams on victims across the globe.
In addition to the independent media reporting alleging such connections, Ly Yong Phat was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department in 2024 for his role “in serious human rights abuse related to the treatment of trafficked workers subjected to forced labor in online scam centers.”
Kok An followed him onto Treasury’s Specially Designated Nationals list in April of this year, when Treasury claimed that he had used his “political connections” to protect a network of scam operations that have “stolen millions of dollars from U.S. victims” through “digital asset investment fraud and other scams.”
Authorities in Thailand have also investigated both tycoons for their ties to online scamming syndicates and money laundering. They have denied any connection to cyber-scam operations.
However, while the Cambodian government’s current crackdown has resulted in the shuttering of dozens of scam compounds and the deportation of tens of thousands of foreign nationals, there have been no signs that it will investigate the allegations against well-connected individuals.
Indeed, the government has defended Ly Yong Phat and Kok An from claims of their involvement in criminal activity, particularly those made by authorities in Thailand, whom they accused of weaponizing the investigations in the context of last year’s border conflict. In 2024, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs described the U.S. sanctions against Ly Yong Phat as “politically motivated.”
Critics of the crackdown say that this is evidence that the current crackdown is a reputation-management exercise rather than a genuine attempt to hold protected figures to account, let alone to alter the political economy that gave Chinese scamming syndicates such a foothold in Cambodia in the first place.
With his comments to Nikkei, Sinarith was clearly trying to address these sorts of concerns – and perhaps to initiate a campaign to have the two businessmen removed from the U.S. sanctions list. However, saying that the compounds allegedly owned by or connected to Ly Yong Phat and Kok An are the subject of investigation does not automatically mean that there will be a full accounting of their alleged role.
Based on several decades of precedent, the likelihood is that these investigations will peter out once the world’s attention has moved on.

At least 41 die as boat capsizes in DRC’s Lake Tanganyika
About 100 people, as well as cargo, were reportedly on board the vessel when it sank on Lake Tanganyika.
At least 41 people have died, and 49 others have been rescued, after a boat capsized on Lake Tanganyika in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Norris Mulongoyi, the provincial transport minister for DRC’s Tanganyika province, told The Associated Press news agency that search operations were under way to locate the remaining passengers.

list of 3 items

The boat was reportedly carrying about 100 people and cargo when it capsized near the Congolese village of Mapera.
The vessel was travelling from the port of Kigoma in Tanzania to the city of Kalemie in DRC when it sank on Thursday.
A survivor identified as Annie Moyoni told Radio Okapi, a UN-backed Congolese broadcaster, that passengers were awakened at about 1am and found the boat tilting to one side.
It is unclear what caused the vessel to capsize, but hundreds of people have been killed in boat disasters in the DRC in recent years, according to the AP. Vessels are often overloaded and lack life jackets.
For many in the DRC, travelling by boat is the cheapest and most affordable way to get around. The country is one of the poorest in the world and lacks sufficient infrastructure for its more than 100 million people.
The sinking was the second loss of a Congolese vessel on the Kigoma-Kalemie route in less than a month.
On August 28, the Congolese vessel MV Pacifique caught fire and exploded at the port of Kigoma while loading fuel, according to Radio Okapi.
Six crew members were killed, and a seventh was reported missing, Radio Okapi said, citing port authorities. The vessel operated between Kigoma and Kalemie and was used to transport fuel.
At least 20 people also died when a wooden boat carrying students returning from state exams sank in central DRC in July.

Brazil’s Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro still essentially tied in new poll

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has maintained a two-percentage-point lead over Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, his main challenger, in a potential run-off ahead of October’s presidential election, a Datafolha poll has shown.
In poll results released Thursday, Lula would receive 47 percent of the vote compared with 45 percent for Bolsonaro in a simulated run-off. A previous Datafolha poll last week had Lula leading Bolsonaro by 46 percent to 44 percent.
The result also represents a technical tie as it falls within the poll’s margin of error of 2 percentage points.
In a first-round scenario, Lula leads with 40 percent of the vote, followed by Bolsonaro (36 percent), Augusto Cury (5 percent), Ronaldo Caiado (4 percent) and Renan Santos (3 percent).
The previous poll showed the leftist president with 39 percent against the right-wing senator’s 36 percent.
Senator Bolsonaro is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election defeat to Lula.
Lula is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term as Brazil’s president.
If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of valid votes in the first round, the two frontrunners advance to a run-off.
Datafolha surveyed 2,002 people between September 22 and 23.
Earlier this week, two other polls showed similar results.
A Quaest poll released on Monday showed Bolsonaro with 42 percent of voter support in a potential run-off, versus 41 percent for Lula.
Meanwhile, a BTG Pactual/Nexus poll has Lula receiving 46 percent of voter support, compared with 45 percent for Bolsonaro in a potential run-off.

Dutch prime minister slams 'attempts to undermine' ICC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:35:08 UTC
09:35:08 KST

Melike Pala
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
 Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten on Thursday condemned "attempts to undermine" the International Criminal Court (ICC), warning such actions threaten the broader international legal order.
"Take the attempts we’ve seen to undermine the International Criminal Court - which is based in my country, in my city. This undermines the international legal order as a whole, and that affects us all," Jetten said in an address to the UN General Assembly in New York.
Jetten stressed that the ICC was established to combat impunity and called for the international community to defend the court and other institutions underpinning international law.
"I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order," he said.
The Dutch premier said the international legal order was facing growing pressure, citing violations of international law and human rights as well as the undermining of institutions established to protect people and populations.
He also pointed to the humanitarian suffering in Gaza and Sudan, among other conflicts.
"When major powers choose to pursue only their own interests, it is tempting to respond defensively," Jetten said, urging countries instead to pursue their "common interest" through international cooperation.
He called on middle powers to take the lead in fostering cooperation and said countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America should have a fuller role in global decision-making.
Jetten also highlighted artificial intelligence as an area requiring international cooperation, asking whether decisions over the technology should be left to "a small group of companies and countries" or addressed collectively through the UN.

====================================================================================================

Viral squishy toy trend putting children in hospital with burns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:32:10 UTC
09:32:10 KST

Squishy toys leaving children with burns as manufacturer asks Australian Border Force to help stop counterfeits
In short:
Viral squishy toy microwave stunts driven by social media are resulting in children suffering severe burns.
One manufacturer has asked Australian Border Force to stop counterfeits from entering the country.
Experts say most of the toys are safe if they are used as intended.
They are soft, often sparkly, a sensory delight and the current must-have for children around the world.
But what the viral squishy toys are made of is often not disclosed and a social media trend has put dozens of Australian children in hospital with serious burns.
Squishies are squeezable toys usually made from a thermoplastic rubber outer shell and filled with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), maltose — a sugar-like substance — gels, beads and other materials.
They come in a range of shapes and sizes, from cubes to capybaras, and can be purchased anywhere from large department stores to small pop-up shops and online.
Demand for the toys has driven a rise in counterfeits that often do not disclose their contents, leading one manufacturer to ask the Australian Border Force (ABF) to stop them from entering the country.
Dangerous microwave trend
Even when the toys disclose their make-up and undergo safety testing, however, they are not completely risk-free.
A viral online trend has children microwaving squishies, resulting in serious injuries.
A Sydney Children's Hospitals Network spokesperson said between January and September this year, 11 children were referred to the Burns and Plastics Treatment Centre at the children's hospital at Westmead for burns caused by heated squishy toys.
"Children were aged between 6 and 12 years old with burns ranging from mid to deep burns on the face, neck, chest, arms and hands," the spokesperson said.
"Some children sustained burns that required skin grafts and longer-term scar treatment."
Queensland Children's Hospital paediatric emergency physician Veevek Thankey said that, since April, he was aware of at least 13 burn cases linked to squishy toys being heated.
"The biggest issue that we've seen is actually the burns themselves as opposed to the actual reactions to the content that's present within these toys," he said.
Dr Thankey said most of the issues have been with burns to the hands or face, which require "intensive management".
He said that because the gel liquid becomes sticky, burns can occur extremely fast.
If an incident occurs, Dr Thankey said the most effective first aid was to remove any of the gel from the skin and place the affected burn area under cool running water for 20 minutes.
A Tasmanian Department of Health spokesperson confirmed its burns unit was aware of a small number of injuries caused by these toys.
Other health jurisdictions were unable to confirm if there were any reports of injuries related to the toys.
Counterfeit concerns
The sudden popularity of the toys has led to a boom in counterfeits.
It is something Schylling, the manufacturer behind NeeDoh, has taken extremely seriously, asking the ABF to seize counterfeit products entering the country.
William Valentine, the distributor of NeeDoh in Australia, confirmed it had taken steps to combat counterfeit products, including registering its intellectual property with the ABF Notice of Objection scheme.
"Counterfeit products don't just infringe on our intellectual property — they bypass the rigorous design, manufacturing, quality control and independent safety testing that authentic NeeDoh products undergo before reaching consumers," managing director Benjamin Halls said.
"That's why we take the growing issue of counterfeit toys so seriously."
Mr Valentine said the company was also working with local counsel to identify sellers of counterfeit products and take appropriate legal action.
Consumer watchdog the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) confirmed it has been liaising with several domestic and international regulators in relation to squishy toys, along with online marketplaces and businesses.
It said there were mandatory standards regarding the levels of lead and other chemicals contained in products, and warned of consequences if businesses fail to comply.
Counterfeits seized globally
In the UK, the Office for Product Safety and Standards issued a recall for Samsons Cash and Carry Squeezy Dumplings after they were found to contain an excess concentration of benzene — a chemical linked to leukaemia.
Thousands of toys, including squishy toys, were seized in shops across north-east Lincolnshire. Another 81 were seized from a retailer on the Isle of Man.
In the US, the Consumer Product Safety Commission has also issued a warning about counterfeit squishy toys, with 55 shipments of noncompliant squishy toys stopped at US ports, preventing more than 355,000 units from entering the country.
A professor of analytical chemistry at RMIT, Oliver Jones, said that while the unknown chemical make-up of squishy toys can be concerning, they were most likely made from the same materials.
"It's just that the manufacturing quality and the amounts [of chemicals] that might be left over in the final product could be worse if you've got one of these counterfeit ones that have been made at short notice without proper oversight and brought onto the market here," he said.
Dr Jones said other qualities, such as the thickness of the material on the outside of the toy and its robustness, were also concerns for knock-offs.
The ACCC recommended consumers avoid toys with strong chemical smells, weak seams, loose beads and leaking parts and to look for clear safety information, including ingredient or material information.
However, Dr Jones said most of these toys were made at a quality standard.
"If you bought it from a reputable shop … and it doesn't smell and it's got listing of what's in it and so forth, I wouldn't be particularly worried as long as it's used in the way it's intended," he said.
"Even if it's like the best quality made toy in the world, if you put it in the microwave, that's an extra risk.
"And I'd certainly be a bit careful about leaving them in hot cars, just to be on the safe side.
"We just have to be careful that when something does go wrong, then we learn from it. And if we can improve safety with better data on what's in the toy and how it's been manufactured, that can't be a bad thing."

EU sounds alarm over Trump diesel ban threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:32:04 UTC
09:32:04 KST

EU sounds alarm over Trump diesel ban threat
A US ban on diesel exports could squeeze the EU’s energy market, which is already strained by reduced Russian supplies due to sanctions and disruptions in flows from the Middle East, officials in Brussels have warned.
European Commission spokesman Olof Gill told Politico on Thursday that Brussels was concerned by reports that Washington could halt diesel exports for 90 days, warning that any disruption “would risk negatively impacting both sides.”
The US has supplied about a third of Europe’s diesel imports this year, with its share rising to around half in August, according to government data. Prices at the pump have already reached record highs in Germany and the Netherlands.
Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said Brussels was monitoring the markets and security of supply “very, very closely,” noting that the US was a “major supplier” of both diesel and liquefied natural gas as part of the bloc’s “diversification strategy since 2022.”
Trump backed the idea of restricting exports on Tuesday as US diesel prices hit a record $6.52 a gallon ($1.72 per liter). “I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” he told reporters ahead of a meeting with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky.
Trump has also repeatedly urged Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, saying the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage.
The issue was raised during talks between Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in New York on Wednesday. According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, Lavrov said Ukrainian attacks on energy and cross-border infrastructure were deliberately contributing to instability in global energy markets.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to stabilize its domestic market. The measures run through January, although direct producers have been permitted to export diesel, marine fuel and gasoline since September.
Supplies have also been squeezed by the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that normally carries around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Gulf diesel and gasoline exports fell to just over a quarter of pre-war levels in August, according to the International Energy Agency.
The EU has sharply reduced purchases of Russian energy since the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Russia’s share of the bloc’s gas imports plunged from 45% to 12% by 2025, while its share of oil imports dropped from 27% to about 2%.
Moscow has blamed the EU’s decision to cut Russian energy imports as a key factor behind the crisis. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said last week that Europe was facing “the worst energy crisis in history,” describing the situation as “self-made.”

Retiring Dolphin lauded as one of NRL's toughest ahead of prelim final
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:03:31 UTC
09:03:31 KST

Retiring Dolphin Ray Stone has been lauded by coach Kristian Woolf over his toughness ahead of what could be his final NRL game.
Woolf said Stone, 29, is "in the top group" when it comes to the toughest players in the league.
What's next?
Stone will be in action when the Dolphins host the Roosters in the preliminary final at Lang Park from 7:50pm AEST on Friday night. ABC Sport will live blog the match.
Ray Stone has claims to being the toughest man in the NRL.
Not that the Dolphins' warrior would care two hoots for the title as he nears retirement at the end of the 2026 season at the tender age of 29.
But there was a reason coach Kristian Woolf singled him out at last year's presentation night for playing the last six rounds with a broken hand and final 15 rounds with needles in both shoulders.
He had off-season shoulder surgery after pushing himself to play when the Dolphins had multiple forwards on the injured list.
Stone is one of those players who performs when busted. When fit and relatively injury-free, though, he is even more dangerous.
"There are a lot of tough men who play our game but he is in the top group,"
Woolf said.
"It is not just his toughness, it's his commitment to the team that I really admire.
"He is just a guy who refuses to let his teammates down. It doesn't matter if it is playing injured, he is making an effort on a kick-chase, getting into a tackle or a carry.
"I love his hit-ups off the kick-off. I get a kick out of watching those because he runs so hard. He is just committed to the team. That is what we are going to miss."
Stone has been linked to a boxing career but AAP understands he has obtained multiple tickets in trade areas and will only get in a ring if he sees fit. He can hold them up, as the saying goes.
"It is probably based on family time for me," Stone said, when asked why he was calling time.
"The kids are getting a bit older and I am quite busy on weekends so I want to be a part of that."
Woolf wanted him on deck in 2027.
"I have spoken to him a number of times and asked if I could change his mind but he has got other things in life he wants to do," the coach said.
"I respect that about him. He knows what he wants. He has pushed himself through the pain."
Stone was the second player signed at the Dolphins after starting his NRL career at Parramatta, where he played 31 matches in five seasons. At the Dolphins, he has notched 81 games in four years.
"The reason I came up here was for opportunity," he said.
"I was in and out of first-grade at Parramatta where we had a strong team and I spoke to Wayne Bennett about coming here and he said I'd be more of a consistent first-grader."
The warhorse, who plays mostly off the bench, has scored eight tries for the Dolphins but, like an old-school footy player of the past, he doesn't smile after any.
"It's not something I stress about," Stone said, through gritted teeth.
"I like to leave all my celebrating until after the game when the boys have got the result."
He's done plenty of that this year, with the Dolphins winning 16 of their last 18 matches ahead of the preliminary final against Sydney Roosters.
"This year I've been a lot healthier and the squad has too, which has definitely helped our middle rotation," Stone said.
"Last year, pretty much our whole starting pack was in rehab. The minutes have been distributed a lot more which has helped me stay healthy."
Woolf is just glad to have Stone in the team after he missed the early rounds with his shoulder recovery.
"We did miss him too. He is a small man in a big man's world who plays so tough," Woolf said.
"He is loved, respected and will be missed next year.
"He is going to leave a legacy that people don't realise. There are no discipline issues around Ray. He turns up and gets his job done every day of every week."
AAP

New eye-tracking study reveals how followers use gaze to show conscientiousness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
00:00:13 UTC
09:00:13 KST

An eye-tracking study found that more conscientious followers appear to use their gaze strategically when speaking, directing it at a leader’s eyes to support their own arguments. This behavior makes those individuals appear more conscientious to observers, indicating that they may be using eye contact to signal their reliability. The paper was published in the Journal of Applied Social Psychology.
Eye gaze is one of the most powerful forms of nonverbal communication because it helps people both gather information and convey information to others. Looking directly at another person can attract attention, increase engagement, and influence how social interactions unfold. Although avoiding eye contact is sometimes interpreted as a sign of dishonesty, gaze behavior is more complex and can communicate many different social meanings.
In workplaces, leaders use eye contact to signal confidence, involvement, and leadership ability. Followers can also use gaze to communicate qualities about themselves. One particularly important trait in organizational settings is conscientiousness, a personality trait that predisposes individuals to reliability, persistence, and effective task performance. Gaze may therefore act as a subtle behavioral signal through which followers convey attentiveness, engagement, and conscientiousness to leaders and colleagues.
Study author Simon Liegl and his colleagues hypothesized that more conscientious followers direct their gazes at their leader’s eyes more frequently. By doing so, they use gaze to signal their conscientiousness, leading others to perceive them as such. The researchers proposed that this gaze behavior mediates the association between how a person perceives their own conscientiousness and how observers perceive it.
The study included 39 university students (21 of whom were men) with an average age of 24. To participate, they were required to have normal or corrected-to-normal vision using soft contact lenses.
During the study, participants completed a negotiation task while the researchers measured their eye movements using mobile eye-tracking glasses. The researchers used specialized software to map each recorded gaze point to a separate static image of the other people in the room on a frame-by-frame basis. This allowed them to map precisely where participants directed their gazes at any given moment.
In the negotiation task, participants interacted with three research assistants who acted as fellow participants. One assistant always acted as the leader, while the real participant and the other two assistants were placed in follower roles. Although the real participants were told that roles had been assigned randomly, the assistants followed carefully standardized behaviors so that differences in the interaction would mainly reflect the real participant’s choices. The followers had to argue for one preferred form of compensation, such as higher pay or more vacation, while opposing the alternatives preferred by the others.
The discussion took place over four rounds, with the leader making offers and each follower presenting arguments in turn. The mobile eye-tracking glasses allowed the researchers to measure where and how much the participants looked at the leader and the other followers during these interactions.
Participants also completed standardized questionnaires to assess their self-perceived charisma and personality traits, such as the Big Five. Additionally, the research assistants rated the participants’ charisma and personality based on their observations.
The results showed that participants who described themselves as more conscientious tended to look at their leader’s eyes more frequently, especially when speaking. Furthermore, participants who directed more eye gazes at the leader and other negotiators, both while listening and while speaking, tended to be rated as more conscientious by the observers. This indicates that other people interpret these frequent gazes as a signal of reliability and diligence.
Interestingly, participants’ openness to experience (a personality trait reflecting curiosity, imagination, preference for novelty, and receptiveness to new ideas) was associated with making less eye contact when speaking.
“Importantly, more conscientious followers appear to specifically instrumentalize their gaze when speaking and direct it at the leader to support their own arguments. Thus, this study underscores the importance of investigating followers’ signaling of their traits and abilities, identifies eye-directed gaze as a potential signal of conscientiousness, and further emphasizes the significance of gaze behavior as a particularly potent social cue in the organizational context,” the study authors concluded.
The research contributes to the scientific understanding of nonverbal behavior in social interactions. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on a small group of students. The results of studies on larger or different demographic groups might vary.
The paper, “Eyes on the Leader: Gaze Behavior as a Cue for Follower Conscientiousness,” was authored by Simon Liegl, Thomas Maran, Marco Furtner, and Pierre Sachse.

Pezeshkian says he met with Khamenei face to face, supreme leader healthy, giving direction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:59:17 UTC
08:59:17 KST

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that he had met with Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei approximately a month ago for several hours and that Khamenei was "completely" healthy and was giving directions to the Iranian leadership in a Fox News interview with Bret Baier, aired on Thursday evening.
"The implementation of the policies is in the hands of the administration and the government, but the consultations and the directions come from there [Khamenei]," Pezeshkian said.
Khamenei has not been seen publicly since the start of the war, when he succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as supreme leader following Ali Khamenei's assassination.
Pezeshkian previously claimed he met with Mojtaba Khamenei in August on Iranian state television, saying the two spoke for seven hours on issues facing Iran, including affordability, unemployment, sanctions, unity, and wartime resilience.
Iran willing to move forward with peace agreement before midterm elections, Pezeshkian says
Pezeshkian said that Iran was willing to make a deal with the US before the US midterm elections in November, and indicated that Iran wanted to return to the Memorandum of Understanding which was signed by both Iran and the US in June before collapsing in July, while speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
"We do not seek war. Rather, whenever they attack us, we are forced to defend ourselves. We never started a war. But if they wish to keep fighting with us, we will respond strongly, resolutely," Pezeshkian said in his interview.
Iran is also willing to dilute its highly enriched uranium and has never wanted a nuclear weapon, according to Pezeshkian.
"Our martyred esteemed supreme leader, he had announced several times that from a religious decree, it is unholy, it is religiously illegal to have weapons of mass destruction," Pezeshkian said.
When asked why the nuclear material had not been inspected by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and was stored beneath Pickaxe Mountain, Pezeshkian blamed US military activity as the reason the UN watchdog has not been able to conduct an investigation since 2025.

UC Berkeley offers Israeli dance scholar position after legal settlement over denied job
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:58:58 UTC
08:58:58 KST

For more than nine months, UC Berkeley has failed to honor a legal settlement with an Israeli dance scholar who was denied a teaching position due to her nationality.
In response to a J. inquiry, a university spokesperson said the delay was caused by “internal miscommunication.” The university now promises that the scholar, Yael Nativ, will receive the job offer she was guaranteed in the December 2025 settlement “no later than the week of Sept. 28.”
“We deeply regret this unfortunate delay and look forward to welcoming Dr. Nativ back to our campus,” UC Berkeley spokesperson Dan Mogulof said in a statement.
Nativ said she received an apology for the delay and the promise of an imminent job offer in a Sept. 21 email from a university administrator.
“It’s always a surprise when I get emails from them because the correspondence was so little to none,” Nativ said. “I’m so tired of this case.”
UC Berkeley professor cites student anger in decision not to rehire Nativ
Nativ, a sociologist specializing in Israeli dance, taught in UC Berkeley’s dance department during spring 2022 as a visiting professor through the Helen Diller Institute for Jewish Law and Israel Studies. Her course focused on contemporary dance in Israel through social, political, and cultural perspectives.
The institute invited Nativ to reapply for another year of teaching. But after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, SanSan Kwan, chair of the dance department, informed Nativ that she would not be rehired. In November 2023, Kwan told Nativ in a WhatsApp message: “My dept cannot host you for a class next fall. Things are very hot right now, and many of our grad students are angry. I would be putting the dept and you in a terrible position if you taught here.”
The university’s civil rights office investigated the matter and concluded that Nativ was discriminated against based on her Israeli identity.
Nativ sued the university, with representation from the Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law, in August 2025. When the two sides settled the lawsuit in December 2025, the university acknowledged its wrongdoing and committed to apologizing to Nativ and inviting her back to campus.
UC Berkeley apology followed by delay in job offer
UC Berkeley Chancellor Rich Lyons apologized to Nativ over Zoom on Feb. 3, but no job offer arrived.
The lapse was publicized by Malcolm Feeley, a retired UC Berkeley Law professor, who wrote about Nativ’s case in a Sept. 16 article in the Jewish Review of Books.
“Justice delayed is justice denied. This is justice delayed in the extreme,” Feeley said in an interview. “It takes a concerted effort of badgering to get [the university] to move an inch.”
In a statement to J. following the publication of Feeley’s article, Mogulof said the university hadn’t sent Nativ a job offer due to a misunderstanding among administrators about who was responsible for doing so.
Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost Ben Hermalin will personally ensure the offer will come within the next two weeks, according to Mogulof.
Nativ went on to work as a research fellow at Ben-Gurion University in Israel after she left Berkeley. She said her main goal since the lawsuit has been to hold UC Berkeley accountable, not to land a job.
“It wasn’t urgent for me to go [back to campus]. It’s more about making a point, getting my justice,” she said. “But if they invite, I will consider.”
This story was first reported by J. The Jewish News of Northern California and is reprinted with permission.

Trump-Xi summit: Four key takeaways from the Washington, DC, meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:51:56 UTC
08:51:56 KST

Trump-Xi summit: Four key takeaways from the Washington, DC, meeting
Trump and Xi seek stable US-China ties at the White House, but differences over Iran, Taiwan and trade remain unresolved.
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping seemed to put sources of tension between their countries to the side during the second day of Xi’s three-day visit to the United States, where he met with Trump and toured the White House.
Trump touted what he described as a “great meeting” with Xi on Thursday, as the two superpowers seek greater dialogue despite differences over issues such as Iran, Taiwan, AI and trade.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump and Xi summit will focus on ‘stabilising’ ties, experts say
- list 2 of 3Trump-Xi summit: Here’s what’s on the agenda, and why it matters
- list 3 of 3‘Hostile, but hooked’: What’s behind the US-China trade truce extension?
“From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people,” Trump said.
Here are a few key takeaways from Xi’s second day in the US.
Emphasis on stable ties
When Trump first returned to the White House, he announced severe tariffs on Chinese goods that quickly set off a trade war between the world’s two largest economies and warnings of wider fallout around the globe.
Despite such a rocky start, Trump and Xi have sought to dial back tensions and improve their personal ties, even if there is an understanding that core areas of disagreement aren’t likely to change.
The US president has sometimes talked about China’s status as a rising power as a source of admiration, even as those changes bring it into competition with the US.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump told reporters on Thursday, without offering further details.
For his part, Xi stated on Thursday that the US and China should take steps to avoid the “Thucydides Trap”, a term used by international relations scholars regarding the risk of conflict between a rising power and an existing power.
“It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses,” Xi said, adding that both countries were deeply interconnected and should engage in “healthy” competition that is “kept within bounds”.
Iran war hangs over visit
While Xi’s visit is focused on improving ties with Trump and the US, several issues have also been at the centre of discussions between the two leaders. One is the US war on Iran, which was launched by the US and Israel in February and has led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and surging global energy prices.
Trump has called on China to support US efforts to isolate Tehran economically and reopen the strait, which was open before the war. Beijing, Iran’s largest trading partner, has been hesitant to get involved.
No breakthroughs on the issue were reported during talks between Trump and Xi on Thursday, with the Chinese president stating that he supported the US and Iran returning to an interim agreement that was supposed to pave the way for a larger peace deal.
That truce broke down shortly after it was announced in June.
Visit gets mixed reception from US lawmakers
While Xi’s visit to the US has been marked by pomp and ceremony, some Democratic and Republican lawmakers have complained that the spectacle amounts to a celebration of a US rival.
“Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party,” said Republican Senator Roger Wicker.
That line of criticism was shared by Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, who said that Trump “always deludes himself into thinking that, by ingratiating himself with authoritarians, he’s somehow going to get his way”.
Others said that diplomacy between the US and China is a positive thing that will help the two powers avoid potentially disastrous conflict.
“I’m glad this meeting is happening; diplomacy is key,” Republican Senator Rand Paul said in a social media post. “Talk more, war less.”
Xi urges Trump not to recognise Taiwan independence
US ties with Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, remain a core flashpoint in relations between Washington and Beijing.
During their meeting on Thursday, the Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported that Xi urged Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence and handle the issue “prudently”. The White House has yet to release its own summary of the talks and remarks on Taiwan.
The Chinese leader is likely to continue pressing Trump to avoid acts that Beijing views as provocative.
Trump stated after a meeting with Xi in May that he would postpone final approval of a $14bn arms package for Taipei, and has called arms sales a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
That transactional approach has angered some in Washington, who see US promises of military aid to Taiwan as a core commitment.
But the US has long taken an expedient approach to relations with Beijing and Taipei, seeking stronger ties with China as it emerged as an economic powerhouse and maintaining an official policy of encouraging a peaceful resolution of the dispute without taking either side.
Taiwan has expressed concern that China could use coercion, both economic and military, to bring the island under its control.
A May Economist/YouGov poll found that people in the US are much more likely to view Taiwan as an ally of the country than China. Asked whether the US should prioritise good relations with Beijing or preventing China from seizing control of Taiwan, respondents were split 36 percent to 35 percent.
Less than 40 percent of those polled said the US should be prepared to use military force to stop China from controlling Taiwan.

Iran seeks deal with US, not war: President Pezeshkian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:48:05 UTC
08:48:05 KST

Diyar Guldogan
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Iran does not seek war with the US and remains prepared to pursue a negotiated agreement, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday as tensions between the two countries continue.
In an exclusive interview with Fox News' Bret Baier, Pezeshkian was asked if Iran was choosing war or a deal.
“We do not choose war. The war was imposed on us. We do not seek war,” Pezeshkian said.
He said Iran remains willing to move forward with an agreement with Washington, referring to the June memorandum that called for a final peace deal within 60 days but collapsed due to differences over navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
“We did reach an agreement with your president (Donald Trump),” he said. “Based on that, we are willing and still wish to move forward.”
The Iranian president said it is America that must choose whether it wants to end the war or not.
Asked whether Iran would give up it's 60% enriched uranium, Pezeshkian the country would comply with its obligations under international law and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
“Yes,” he said. “Within the framework of international law, based on the Non-Proliferation Treaty, whatever we are supposed to adhere to, we will.”
The interview also addressed Iran's regional relationships, including its ties to Hezbollah and the Houthis.
When Baier asked whether Iran would stop arming Hezbollah and the Houthis as part of a deal, and whether it would tell the Yemeni rebel group to stop attacking Saudi Arabia, Pezeshkian said the Houthis act independently.
“The Houthis are responsible for their own actions,” he said. “They don't take directions from us.”
Pezeshkian also rejected the suggestion that Iran had closed the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically important waterway through which a fifth of world's oil passed before the war.
Baier questioned Pezeshkian about Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen publicly since replacing his father, Ali Khamenei, killed in US-Israeli strikes in late February.
Pezeshkian said he met Khamenei in person almost a month earlier, and spent about seven hours with him.
Asked whether the supreme leader was healthy and able to govern, Pezeshkian responded: “Very much so, completely.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:39:15 UTC
08:39:15 KST

In brief
- Albanese has used UN address to launch Australia’s 2029-30 Security Council campaign and push for reform.
- He backed global AI rules and stronger Pacific representation as major powers dominated talks.
In a week where the civilian death toll from wars in multiple continents continues to climb, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has appealed for the 193 member states of the United Nations to ensure the quest for peace is not left to the "loudest voices".
"Clearly, the multilateral system we have all known and benefited from is under immense strain," he told the United Nations General Assembly in his key speech of this US trip.
"To protect the peace, to create a world of human dignity, to do justice to the UN’s mission, we must embrace change and reform."
Earlier this week, Albanese officially launched Australia’s bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council in 2029 and 2030.
His message from the podium echoed that of his key middle power partners, Canada’s Mark Carney and the European Commission’s Ursula Von der Leyen.
