====================================================================================================

Intelligence and personality traits do not predict inattentional blindness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:00:49 UTC
07:00:49 KST

People’s intelligence and personality traits do little to predict whether they will notice an unexpected object while concentrating on another task, according to a study published in Royal Society Open Science. The findings suggest that inattentional blindness may depend more on the demands and design of a situation than on stable differences between individuals.
Inattentional blindness occurs when people fail to see something that is clearly visible because their attention is directed elsewhere. A person counting ball passes in a video, for example, may miss an unusual figure moving through the scene. The failure does not necessarily mean the person has poor eyesight or low intelligence. Instead, attention is limited, and the brain prioritizes information relevant to the task at hand.
Previous research has examined whether some people are consistently better at noticing unexpected events. Possible predictors have included intelligence, working memory (the ability to hold and manipulate information over short periods) and personality traits such as openness or absorption (a tendency to become deeply immersed in sensory and imaginative experiences). However, earlier studies often involved small numbers of participants and produced inconsistent results.
The new research was designed to provide a stronger test. Led by Daniel J. Simons of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, the researchers conducted two large online studies across multiple countries. One study examined cognitive ability and included 1,000 participants in the final analyses. The second examined personality and also included 1,000 participants.
Participants completed three inattentional blindness tasks. In one, they judged the length of lines while an unexpected shape briefly appeared. In another, they counted the movements of shapes while an unexpected object traveled through the display. In the third, they searched for a target number among symbols while another object appeared in the scene.
Participants in the cognitive ability study completed tests of visual reasoning and working memory. Those in the personality study completed measures of the Big Five personality traits (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and open-mindedness), absorption, attention-related symptoms (specifically those related to ADHD) and perfectionism-related characteristics.
The proportion of people who noticed the unexpected object varied between 39% and 66%, depending on the task. In the counting task, about 45% of participants noticed the unexpected object in both the easier and more difficult conditions. This did not reproduce the common finding that a harder main task reduces noticing.
People who noticed an unexpected object in one task were slightly more likely to notice one in another task. However, the relationship was weak, suggesting that there may be a small tendency for some people to notice more often without indicating a strong, stable “noticer” personality.
Some cognitive measures were associated with noticing in particular conditions. For example, higher scores on certain reasoning and working memory tests were linked with slightly greater noticing in the easier condition. But these relationships were small and inconsistent. A measure that predicted more noticing in one condition sometimes predicted less noticing in another.
Personality produced even less evidence of a reliable relationship. None of the personality measures consistently predicted noticing. When the researchers combined the full set of cognitive or personality measures, the models explained very little of the differences between participants.
The authors concluded: “Collectively, we found evidence that individual differences in some cognitive abilities weakly and inconsistently predicted noticing, but little or no evidence that individual differences in personality predicted noticing.”
Some limitations are to be noted. For example, the online format limited experimental control, and the sample included relatively few older adults. Also, noticing an unexpected object is difficult to measure repeatedly because individuals may remember the task and deliberately search for the object the next time.
The study, “Do individual differences in cognitive ability or personality predict noticing in inattentional blindness tasks?”, was authored by Daniel J. Simons, Yifan Ding, Connor M. Hults and Brent W. Roberts.

Trump tells countries to quit ICC. Few follow his lead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:56:55 UTC
06:56:55 KST

Trump tells countries to quit ICC. Few follow his lead
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 24 - President Donald Trump urged countries to leave the International Criminal Court immediately, calling it "evil" and "a rogue institution," but only Naoero, a tiny Pacific island nation formerly known as Nauru, has followed suit during the UN General Assembly this week.
Trump's appeal on Tuesday capped an escalating US campaign against the Hague-based court, which Washington says oversteps its authority by claiming jurisdiction over citizens of countries, including the United States and Israel, that have not ratified its founding treaty known as the Rome Statute.
While a handful of countries have moved to leave the ICC, many governments, particularly in Europe, have rallied to defend the Netherlands-based court as a cornerstone of international justice. Parties to the statute include 125 countries.
Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten, addressing the General Assembly on Thursday, said the court is "under attack" and at risk, without mentioning the United States.
"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?" he asked. "And I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order." The remarks drew loud applause from delegates.
The US has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on court staff, and officials have prepared sanctions that could undercut the court's ability to operate, sources familiar with the matter said.
'DISMANTLE THE ICC'
In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio launched a diplomatic push to "dismantle the ICC — brick by brick, if necessary," claiming the court posed a threat to American service members and those carrying out Trump's deportations of migrants and strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats.
Trump has said the campaign is aimed at protecting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, against whom the ICC issued arrest warrants in 2024 alongside his then-defense minister and a Hamas military commander over the Gaza war.
Since Rubio announced the campaign, Venezuela and Chad have announced plans to withdraw from the court. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger announced their exits the previous year, denouncing the court as an instrument of "neocolonial repression."
Naoero President David Adeang said in his speech to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday he would formally withdraw his country from the Rome Statute due to the ICC’s “increasing irrelevance.”
"Naoero joins a growing number of nations standing up for their sovereignty against the ICC’s illegitimate overreach,” US Assistant Secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs Michael DeSombre said on X after meeting the island nation's deputy foreign minister.
DEFENDING THE COURT
The European Union rallied behind the court and officials have discussed drawing up a blocking statute in response to the potential US sanctions.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters this week the bloc had options to defend the court.
"We have the tools in our toolbox when it gets really serious, how to defend ICC, and here (at the UN) we are rallying countries behind supporting the ICC functioning and the accountability part because it's not only a European issue; it's much broader than that,” she said.
Tomoko Akane, the ICC president already under US sanctions, is a Japanese national. Japan's government called the proposed sanctions "very unfortunate" and dispatched an official to The Hague to discuss how it could support her.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi noted Japan’s support for the ICC in her address to the General Assembly on Tuesday.
“Since the end of the Second World War, Japan, as a peace-loving nation, has attached great importance to the rule of law in the settlement of any disputes,” Takaichi said.
Brian Finucane, a senior adviser at the International Crisis Group, said many countries remain invested in the ICC's mission of accountability, limiting the impact of Washington's campaign against the court. He noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin targeted the ICC after it issued a warrant for his arrest.
“The Trump administration has managed to align itself with Putin in terms of, you know, imposing targeting ICC personnel with sanctions, and of course, Putin would also benefit from the destruction of the court,” Finucane said. REUTERS

Infantino calls for 'culture of dialogue' amid resignation calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:56:11 UTC
06:56:11 KST

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino calls for 'culture of dialogue' amid continued push for his resignation
In short:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino says he wants to create a "culture of dialogue" at the governing body amid a continued push for his resignation.
Despite widespread opposition, Infantino is still clinging to the role and shows no signs of wanting to step down.
What's next?
Infantino faces an election challenge ahead of a March 18 vote by FIFA members.
FIFA's embattled president, Gianni Infantino, says he is committed to a fresh culture of openness at the football body that is "not about generating positive headlines".
Two months into a deep rift in global soccer over Infantino's now-dropped $4.2 billion ($6 billion) World Cup sell-off plan, he offered his critics this week an independent review of how FIFA is run and makes decisions.
"I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other," he wrote in an Instagram post from Jeddah in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the Arabian Gulf Cup.
Infantino will chair an October 15 meeting of the 37-member FIFA Council that will also be asked to approve consultation with the 211 member federations and six continental soccer bodies on "how to further strengthen FIFA's decision-making processes".
The 211 members already effectively own FIFA, a Switzerland-based not-for-profit that has at least $5 billion in cash reserves after a financially successful men's World Cup in North America.
FIFA's ruling council includes three vice presidents — European football leader Aleksander Ceferin, North America's Victor Montagliani and Asia's Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa — who have led opposition to Infantino during the furore over his proposal to create a commercial spin-off part-owned by investors fronted by Josh Kushner.
"There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting one another," Infantino wrote on Thursday, local time, about the council meeting in Zurich. "This is not about generating positive headlines; it is about doing what is right for the game."
Infantino's presidency since 2016 has created most turmoil when proposing multi-billion-dollar commercial plans without fully consulting continental bodies like UEFA, which succeeded in stopping them.
Flying FIFA solo toward close ties to Trump
FIFA has often seemed an executive one-man leadership as Infantino built closer ties to US President Donald Trump around this year's World Cup. FIFA created a peace prize to award Trump last year and allowed United States striker Folarin Balogun to evade a mandatory ban at the tournament after intervention from the White House.
Infantino's secretive plan to sell at least 20 per cent of FIFA's commercial rights in a deal anchored by Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law, provoked the soccer body's biggest crisis since anti-corruption arrests in 2015 that led to trials in New York.
The 211 national federations were offered $20 million each to approve the creation of the FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary. UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation countered by saying FIFA could afford to give each federation a $10 million dividend just from its reserves.
Now Infantino, who faces an election challenge ahead of a March 18 vote by FIFA members in Morocco, insists he is ready to listen to soccer officials.
"I have never been more determined and committed in doing that," he wrote on Instagram.
"FIFA is always engaged. I am always engaged, and I want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere."

Netanyahu brings ‘killer pager’ to UN (VIDEO)
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held up a pager at the UN General Assembly, invoking the deadly 2024 covert sabotage operation against Hezbollah in Lebanon, which killed dozens and severely wounded thousands, including women and children.
Thousands of pagers carried by Hezbollah members exploded across Lebanon on September 17, 2024, followed by hundreds of weaponized walkie-talkies the next day. The attacks killed dozens and injured up to 4,000 people, including numerous civilian bystanders, healthcare workers, and their families. Israel later acknowledged responsibility for the operation.
Speaking at the General Assembly on Thursday, Netanyahu held up a pager, saying: “You remember the beepers? Remember these? Hezbollah certainly remembers them.”

Police arrest actors, politicians protesting against Netanyahu outside UN
NEW YORK – Police arrested at least 30 people, including actors and politicians, as they protested outside the United Nations headquarters on Sept 24 against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of his speech at the UN General Assembly.
Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon, Emmy winner Hannah Einbinder, Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York City council member Chi Osse were among those arrested.
“What’s being done to Gaza, the obliteration of an entire society, in our name, with our tax dollars, this is our responsibility to speak out against, and Netanyahu has no right to use the platform of the United Nations to justify these atrocities,” said Manijeh Moradian, a 50-year-old university professor of Iranian and Jewish heritage, who took part in the protest.
At the General Assembly, Netanyahu defended Israel’s actions in the region, seeking to counter growing international isolation ahead of elections he could lose, as dozens of delegates streamed out of the hall.
The rally was organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, a Jewish activist group that supports Palestinians. Around 200 people gathered outside the UN in identical white T-shirts with printed slogans saying “Fund people not bombs”, “No war” and “Free Palestine”.
The group blocked traffic, and police ordered them to leave through loudspeakers. Some people moved to the pavements, but the core group of protesters remained seated on the pavement and continued chanting anti-Netanyahu slogans as police officers, who arrived on bicycles, surrounded them.
One by one, officers pulled protesters from the group, tied their hands behind their backs with zip ties and escorted them to police buses. The activists chanted “Netanyahu, go to hell” outside the buses. REUTERS

Dinners, cars, and moving away: The extreme sacrifices Aussies make to buy a home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:51:05 UTC
06:51:05 KST

in brief
- Australians lead global peers in cutting spending for property deposits.
- High interest rates keep most buyers cautious until market conditions ease.
Australians are willing to cut back their spending in record numbers to afford a property, affirming the ongoing value of home ownership, new data shows.
More than 75 per cent of residents were willing to cut their spending back to afford a home, a Cotality survey released on Friday revealed.
Australians were more likely to do so than their Canadian, United States, and United Kingdom peers, for whom the figures sat below 70 per cent.
The percentage was higher for Gen Z Aussies than any other age group.
Levels of discretionary spending, like eating out, owning a car, and even moving from the family home into a sharehouse, have dropped among young adults in recent years.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The number of 26-to-29-year-olds living with their parents climbed from 19.6 per cent in 2012 to 21.9 per cent in 2024, the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia Survey revealed on Thursday.
Young men were almost 10 per cent more likely to be staying home than women.
But it wasn't just first-time buyers making significant financial sacrifices to climb the ladder.
Millennials — the largest buyer cohort in the world — are readily forgoing small luxuries to afford homes large enough for their families.
Prospective buyers were selling their second car or putting off holidays while their children were young, Capital Buyers Agency owner Claire Corby said.
"For many, it's around delaying things like going away, or reducing things like dinners out," she said.
"People are leaving where they want to live and buying in cheaper markets."
Most Australians would not be persuaded to participate in the housing market until mortgage interest rates hit a 4.9 per cent average, the data revealed.
The average rate for an owner-occupier in August 2026 was 6.3 per cent, meaning the market is likely to stay quiet for some time and allow bold buyers to swoop in.
"People are being conservative and cautious," Corby said.
"A lot of it is about personality."
Only a quarter of Australians reported they could feel financially comfortable while paying up-front housing costs, and just 26 per cent said they could cover monthly repayments without changing their lifestyle, the Cotality survey showed.
Corby said it was important for buyers to consider what a property needed to do for them within a certain duration and work backwards.
She spoke with clients who were not willing to stretch their mortgage ceiling given the volatility of rates.

Xi calls for translating new vision of China-U.S. relationship into action
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
05:48:40 CST
06:48:40 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for translating the new vision of a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability into action and finding the right way for the two major countries to get along with each other.
Xi made the remarks when meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House.
Xi pointed out that the exchange of visits between the heads of state of China and the United States in less than half a year is unprecedented in the history of China-U.S. ties.
He and Trump have maintained communication through various channels and worked together to steer the giant ship of China-U.S. relationship, Xi said.
Noting that in May this year, he and Trump agreed to work toward building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, Xi said that the new vision reflects the realities of China-U.S. ties, embodies the expectations for the future, and is an important step toward finding the right way for the two countries to get along with each other.
The two sides need to work toward a relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences, and promises of peace, Xi said.
He noted that China and the United States should, and fully can, achieve mutual benefit and win-win results through practical cooperation, help each other succeed through healthy competition, properly manage differences by seeking common ground while respecting differences, and build peace by fostering mutual trust, so that a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability can better benefit the two peoples and people around the world.
Xi stressed that the economic and trade teams of the two countries held a new round of consultations and reached a new joint arrangement, which is good news for industries and people of both countries, as well as the global economy.
Noting that cooperation is a two-way street, Xi said a stable China-U.S. economic and trade relationship requires both expanding the list of cooperation, and shortening the list of problems.
As long as the two sides uphold the spirit of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit, a way out of problems can be found, Xi said.
Xi expressed hope that the two sides will work in the same direction, stay committed to the principle of mutual benefit and win-win cooperation, and promote the sustained, stable and sound development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations.
Xi said that while China and the United States, as both major countries in AI, compete in AI, they have even more reasons to cooperate.
The two sides should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other, Xi said, adding that the two sides can continue to engage in dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and work together to prevent the misuse and abuse of AI.
The two sides should maintain human control over AI technologies, uphold a people-centered approach and the principle of using AI for good, and ensure that AI serves human progress, he added.
Xi stressed that the Chinese side's position on safeguarding national reunification and territorial integrity is clear-cut.
It is hoped that the U.S. side will adhere to the correct position of opposing "Taiwan independence," and handle the Taiwan question with caution, so as to lay a solid foundation for China-U.S. strategic cooperation and the development of bilateral relations, Xi said.
For his part, Trump said that the state visit of Xi to the United States is a great visit, adding that both the United States and China are major countries, and that he and Xi are good friends and have maintained in-depth and close communication.
The U.S.-China relations will surely be handled well under the leadership of the two heads of state, he said.
The latest round of economic and trade consultations between teams of both countries achieved new outcomes, said Trump, calling on both sides to continue dialogue to reach a better agreement.
Noting that AI bears on the future of humanity, Trump said that the United States and China should maintain dialogue and strengthen cooperation on this issue.
Both heads of state also exchanged views on major international and regional issues including the Middle East situation, Ukraine crisis and Korean Peninsula.
The two leaders also confirmed that the two countries will support each other in hosting the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting and the G20 Leaders' Summit. ■

Over 6,500 Palestinians displaced in West Bank since 2023: UN
China
Unknown Publisher

05:48:30 CST
06:48:30 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- More than 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced from their homes in the West Bank since 2023 due to settler attacks or access restrictions, UN humanitarians said Thursday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said an updated map showed the locations of communities displaced and sites of more than 6,000 settler attacks since 2023 that caused casualties, property damage or both.
According to OCHA, 49 communities have been fully displaced and 83 partially displaced. About 88,000 trees and saplings, a source of livelihood for many, and more than 3,100 vehicles have also been damaged.
"Palestinians across the occupied Palestinian territory must be protected and allowed to access their homes, olive groves, workplaces, schools and essential services in safety and dignity," OCHA said, stressing that "Perpetrators of attacks must be held to account."
Separately, the UN Population Fund reported high levels of gender-based violence against women and girls in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, according to OCHA.
Reported incidents rose by over 30 percent in the second quarter of this year from the previous quarter, with women and girls facing denial of resources, opportunities and services, as well as emotional, physical and sexual violence, including forced or early marriage, the report said. ■

Croatian court approves extradition in Nord Stream bombing case
Nord Stream sabotage suspect to be extradited from Croatia; court ruling faces appeal with final decision still pending
A Croatian court has approved the extradition of a Ukrainian man wanted in Germany in connection with the 2022 undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
The man was arrested on a European warrant in the northern Croatian town of Pula in August while reportedly working on a Hollywood dramatisation of the attack, according to the AFP news agency.

On Thursday, his lawyer, Ljubo Pavasovic Viskovic, said the court approved the extradition on September 18.
Pavasovic Viskovic added that the ruling is not final and will be appealed, so it is unclear when or whether the extradition will take place.
German prosecutors identified the man as Vladimir Z.
They said the suspect was a “trained scuba diver” who was part of a team that allegedly “planted explosives” on the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm.
The undersea blasts on September 26, 2022, damaged the pipelines, which had been built to carry natural gas from Russia to Germany under the Baltic Sea.
In July, German federal prosecutors filed charges against a former Ukrainian army officer in connection with the explosions.
Prosecutors accuse Vladimir Z of working closely with another Ukrainian identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K. He was detained in August 2025 during a raid on the bungalow in an Italian village where he was staying with his family. He was then extradited to Germany in November last year.
Serhii K is due to face trial at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court on October 14, and the proceedings could continue through February 2027.
The Nord Stream attacks came months after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, destroying three of the four pipelines of the major energy link at a time when European countries were trying to gradually wean themselves off Russian energy.
German investigators believe a Ukrainian state agency ordered the attack to deprive Russia of revenues to finance its invasion of Ukraine.
The case is politically awkward for Germany and Ukraine, as Berlin has been one of Kyiv’s strongest supporters in its fight against Russia.
German government officials, when asked about the issue, have pointed to the judiciary’s independence.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said his government knew nothing about any plan to blow up the pipelines.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed allegations that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza as “the biggest lie of the century” during a defiant address to the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday, as scores of delegates walked out in protest.
“Here's the simple truth. Israel didn't commit genocide. Israel prevented genocide,” Netanyahu said, calling the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) “the most moral army in the world.” He pointed to Israel’s facilitation of food aid and polio vaccination campaigns in Gaza, saying “Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way.”
Israel faces allegations of genocide in a case brought by South Africa before the International Court of Justice. The court has ordered Israel to take provisional measures under the Genocide Convention but has not ruled on whether Israel has committed genocide. The case remains pending.
In September 2025, an independent U.N. commission of inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide, and the International Association of Genocide Scholars said Israel’s policies and actions met the legal definition of the crime. Israel has rejected the findings.
Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘spreading lies’
Netanyahu sharply criticized New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani during his speech, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and placing him among “all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers.”

He reiterated his claims that the mayor supports Hamas and has “incit[ed] riots against New York Jews.” Mamdani has denied supporting Hamas. “Mr. Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can’t silence me and you can’t silence the truth,” Netanyahu said.
In response to Netanyahu’s remarks, Mamdani accused the Israeli leader of using his speech to “repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians.”

Netanyahu’s remarks come amid heightened concern about antisemitism in New York, where anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 57% of all reported hate crimes in 2025, according to NYPD data. Mamdani has rejected accusations of antisemitism and proposed increasing the city’s hate-crime prevention budget from $3 million to $26 million. His administration has also maintained a dedicated Mayor’s Office to Combat Antisemitism.
The dispute stretches back to Mamdani’s mayoral campaign. A longtime critic of Israel’s military actions in Gaza, Mamdani has repeatedly condemned Netanyahu, calling him “a war criminal and an architect of a horrific genocide of the Palestinian people.” He also vowed to have Netanyahu arrested under an International Criminal Court warrant issued over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Mamdani later acknowledged that the city lacked the independent authority to execute the warrant and called on the federal government to arrest Netanyahu instead.
Netanyahu praised President Donald Trump, saying Israel has “no greater partner.” He pointed to the joint U.S.-Israeli operation that he said had destroyed much of Iran’s nuclear program after the two countries launched their war against Iran in February. He called attacking Iran “one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as Prime Minister.”
Netanyahu also accused Qatar of spending billions of dollars to finance universities and the Al Jazeera media network as part of an effort to “brainwash young minds to hate Israel, America and the West.” He also criticized the country for hosting Hamas leaders. Netanyahu went on to accuse Turkey of being a “super-spreader of antisemitic lies” and condemned Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan for also hosting Hamas leaders. Turkey and Qatar are yet to respond to the statement.
Outside the United Nations, several hundred protesters gathered with chants of "stop arming Israel, let Gaza live" and "stop arming Israel, let Iran live" ahead of Netanyahu’s speech.
Abbas addresses UN by video after visa denied
In a prerecorded address shown at the U.N. General Assembly earlier Thursday, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas said that “the Palestinian people face one of the most dangerous times of its history.”
“How much longer will some states continue to remain silent on Israel or supply it with the weapons that it uses against our people?” Abbas said. He accused Israel of “ethnic cleansing” and a “genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe.”
The U.S. denied Abbas and other Palestinian officials visas to attend the assembly in person for the second consecutive year, accusing the Palestinian Authority of “glorifying terrorism.” Abbas condemned what he called the “unlawful punitive measures” and called on the Trump administration to lift the restrictions on his delegation and on the U.N. to grant Palestine “full membership” in the international organization. He also called for the State of Palestine to be granted full U.N. membership.
According to the Gaza Health Ministry, more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas terror attack on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel and saw about 250 others taken hostage.
Since the ceasefire was signed in October 2025, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed according to the ministry. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. Data from the IDF suggests a Palestinian civilian death rate of 83%.
The U.N. in October estimated that Gaza required $70 billion to reverse the damage caused by two years of war to its infrastructure.
What other world leaders have said at the U.N.
The war in Gaza has been a major focus for world leaders addressing the U.N. in New York this week.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, whose nearly decade-long tenure leading the international body comes to an end at the start of next year, said during his address on Tuesday that Gaza has experienced “a scale of killing and destruction unlike anything I have witnessed in all my years as Secretary-General.” He added that Israel’s “violence, displacement and settlement expansion” raised the “specter of ethnic cleansing.”
Trump said the war in Gaza was over. He took credit for ending it, “saving untold thousands of lives,” and brokering the return of the remaining hostages held in Gaza. But key elements of the peace agreement Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’ disarmament, a long-term plan for governing Gaza, and the delivery of humanitarian aid—remain largely stalled.
Other world leaders called for greater international action over the continuing suffering in Gaza. French President Emmanuel Macron asked “what is our credibility worth if we remain inactive on Gaza?” during his speech on Tuesday. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the same day: “We will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution, the best hope for peace and stability for both nations, comes under attack.”

Xi, in lavish Trump summit, urges 'human control' over AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:42:59 UTC
06:42:59 KST

Xi, in lavish Trump summit, urges ‘human control’ over AI
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — China’s president issued a call from the White House on Thursday for artificial intelligence to remain “under human control” as the world’s two superpowers race for technological supremacy.
Xi Jinping’s remarks reflect growing concern within China over whether governments in Washington or Beijing will be able to contain a technology with potentially transformative capabilities, according to a U.S. official.
Lawmakers and AI industry leaders urged President Trump to use his summit with Xi this week to pursue a safety framework for AI, which researchers warn could soon surpass human understanding.
But Trump preempted the meeting with a post on social media stating he had no intention of negotiating limits on AI development.
“A big day with President Xi of China,” Trump wrote. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also. Our guardrail is the DOJ!”
After offering Xi a lavish welcome on the White House grounds, Trump made a passing reference to AI. “The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” he said.
But Xi gestured to substantial concerns, noting AI first among priorities to discuss between the two nations.
President Trump’s decision to greet Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington rather than receiving him at the executive residence shows how far Trump is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
“Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence,” Xi said. “We have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good — and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control, and serves the well-being of the people.”
The two held a private meeting with aides in the Oval Office after participating in a military review in the Rose Garden and exchanging gifts in the Blue Room.
In the evening, a guest list of top banking and technology leaders — including AI industry executives — were scheduled to attend a state dinner in the East Room of the White House.
“Given Trump’s statements going into the summit about not wanting guardrails, I have tepid expectations about tangible outcomes” on AI, said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“The most likely scenario seems to be the establishment of a hotline — though how useful that will be depends on who will be staffing it, and how much each government prioritizes it,” Mehta added, “and likely some discussions about issues blocking cooperation, like distillation, with a promise to engage in ongoing dialogue.”
Earlier in the week, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with his Chinese counterpart primarily to discuss AI development, according to U.S. officials.
“What we discussed was setting up a mechanism — so it’s going to be called the U.S.-China AI Dialogue. We’ve agreed to meet again,” Bessent said Monday. “The U.S. has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries, and we want a shared vision of common goals, and common threats.”
While Trump’s team has remained divided over whether — and how extensively — to regulate AI, Bessent has favored a cautious approach, advocating modest, voluntary guardrails that have shaped administration policy in recent months.
China, too, has shown increasing willingness to open channels of communication on AI, despite deep distrust between the two sides.
Two American AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are widely viewed to be developing the most advanced AI models in the world, leading at the frontier of technological breakthroughs.
Both have begun to use their most sophisticated models to train the next generation, in a process known as recursive self-improvement. Researchers and industry experts believe the first company to master that process could set off an exponential cycle of progress, pulling so far ahead that competitors can no longer catch up.
But those same companies also fear what they’re creating: machines capable of continuously improving their own intelligence, pushing AI development beyond human control.
Leaders from the two companies have called on Beijing and Washington to cooperate, warning that geopolitical competition could thwart the two sides from preventing a human catastrophe.
In his remarks, Xi said that China and the United States “stand to gain from cooperation, and will both lose in confrontation.”
“We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one, and should be kept within bounds,” the Chinese president said. “It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses. China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict, and no confrontation between us.”
“Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention,” he continued, adding a historical reference to rising powers challenging established ones: “The Thucydides trap can be overcome.”
Xi’s trip to Washington follows just months after Trump traveled to Beijing for a state visit in May, where the U.S. president was greeted with a similarly imperial welcome.
The leaders emerged from that summit with few deliverables. But Trump left Beijing declaring the trip a success, emphasizing the importance of his personal relationship with Xi, China’s most powerful leader in generations.
A bipartisan group of Congressional leaders is pushing for a 20% federal tax credit for film and TV production, a move they say will help bring filming back to the U.S.
This time, Trump himself greeted Xi on the tarmac upon his arrival at Joint Base Andrews — a rare honor reserved in recent decades only for Catholic popes — before pulling out several red carpets and draped ceremonies for the Chinese leader.
The pageantry seen during the state visit has served China’s long-standing desire for respect and dignity on the international stage, said Jessica Chen Weiss, the director of the Johns Hopkins SAIS Institute for America, China and the Future of Global Affairs.
“Trump is someone who loves spectacle, and right now the spectacle is working in both leaders’ favor,” Weiss said.
For Xi, the ceremonies have offered a chance to demonstrate that relations with the United States remain under control and that China is being treated as a significant global power, she argued.
The state visit comes at a time when Americans are appearing to warm up to China, according to recent polls. A survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs recently found that a majority of Americans say the United States should have friendly engagement and cooperation with China.
“I tend to think we focus too much on the optics,” Weiss said. “But I also think treating China as a significant player on the world stage is not a concession. It’s appropriate if we want a stable relationship and is hardly something to worry about.”

Insane catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:20:56 UTC
06:20:56 KST

A remarkable one-handed diving catch from all-rounder Marco Jansen has helped South Africa claim a 67-run win over Australia in a one-day clash in Durban.
Jansen was named the Player of the Match after scoring 75 off 59 deliveries with the bat before picking up one wicket with the ball. Mitch Marsh top scored for Australia with 60 off just 36 deliveries.
What's next?
South Africa leads 1-0 in the three-match series ahead of the second ODI in Johannesberg on Sunday night AEST.
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an incredible catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.
The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.
Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.
After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.
"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."
The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.
Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.
He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.
The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.
Loading Twitter content
Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.
The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.
So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.
The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.
Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.
All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.
All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.
The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

Pedro Sánchez, at Harvard: "Some of the algorithms behind technologies such as AI have not been designed to serve us, but to enslave us"
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:19:00 CEST
06:19:00 KST

Pedro Sánchez, at Harvard: "Some of the algorithms behind technologies such as AI have not been designed to serve us, but to enslave us"
President's News - 2026.9.24
Harvard University, Cambridge (United States)
The President of the Government of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, has taken part in the John F. Kennedy Jr. Forum, the main platform for political debate and the exchange of ideas at the Institute of Politics at Harvard University's Kennedy School. In his speech, he highlighted the need to promote regulation capable of addressing the risks that tech oligarchies pose to democracies.
The President of the Government of Spain began his speech by referring to the legacy of Louis Brandeis, a Harvard-trained jurist regarded as one of the architects of the American rule of law, drawing a parallel between the late 19th-century struggle against large monopolies and the challenge posed today by the 'new technological oligarchies'. He recalled that Brandeis "believed that prosperity should be shared" and that the only way to guarantee this was to "prevent large concentrations of economic power".
Building on this premise, Pedro Sánchez warned that many of the algorithms underpinning these technologies "are not designed to serve us; they are designed to enslave us". He has also asserted that their purpose is "to undermine our critical thinking, distort public debate and turn our attention into profit", destroying our rights and institutions with the aim of advancing a political agenda that serves only a select few.
He also emphasised that each of these technologies "is controlled by a handful of men who publicly scorn the democratic institutions, laws and liberal values that have guided our societies since the end of the Second World War".
Pedro Sánchez warned of the lack of oversight, transparency and accountability among companies that are developing increasingly powerful capabilities. He therefore urged people to ignore those who claim that deregulation will lead to greater competitiveness, "because speed is useless if we are heading in the wrong direction". In this vein, he emphasised that we need to "find a way to ensure that these technologies benefit us, the citizens, and not just a handful of tech oligarchs".
The Spanish model
In this regard, President Sánchez made it clear that his position is not one of rejection of technological progress. He pointed out that, over the last eight years, the Government of Spain has invested more than 40 billion euros in the development and adoption of technologies such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing, and has championed their potential to tackle challenges such as climate change, demographic decline and inequality. "I am not suggesting that we get rid of these technologies. I am saying that we must control and oversee them", he emphasised. "We should also slow down their development until we find a way to make this technology safe and to channel its power towards the goals we truly have as a society", he added.
Pedro Sánchez outlined the main measures adopted by his Government in this area, including the criminalisation of algorithmic manipulation, restricting access to social media for those under the age of sixteen, the creation of public tools to combat hate speech, and the legislative proposal to hold platform executives legally accountable, emphasising that "those who create the risk and benefit from it must also take responsibility".
He also highlighted that Spain was the first Western country to adopt a Charter of Digital Rights and that it has established Europe's first Artificial Intelligence Supervisory Agency.
Finally, the President of the Government of Spain emphasised the need for joint action, "because the digital space is like the atmosphere: there is only one. If we want to save it, all our countries must act together". He also called on Harvard students and lecturers not to be blinded by money or by the promises of large tech corporations, and to become actively involved in championing democratically controlled technological development.
During the day, President Pedro Sánchez met with the Dean of Harvard College, David Deming, and the Dean of the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, Hopi Hoekstra, as well as holding a meeting with Spanish students and researchers. He also met with the Governor of Massachusetts, Maura Healey, with whom he discussed the challenges faced by those who defend social and democratic rights, gender equality and the rights of migrants.

Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:11:49 UTC
06:11:49 KST

Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
NEW YORK, Sept 24 - Finnish President Alexander Stubb said on Thursday he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defenses to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
"That's why ... I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers, either in the occupied territory of Ukraine or in Russia for strategic purposes because that would save lives," Stubb said.
The Finnish leader, a staunch ally of Ukraine who also has good relations with US President Donald Trump, made the remark in an interview with Reuters in New York where world leaders have converged for the annual gathering at the United Nations.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy used the event to press hard for ceasefires that would cover strikes on targets related to energy infrastructure and vessels in the Black Sea. Russia has given no public indication it wants to see such arrangements.
Four-and-a-half years since the full-scale Russian invasion, the Ukrainians fear Moscow plans to systematically target and destroy power and heating sites in the depth of winter. Russia's use of ballistic missiles hit record levels this summer.
Only Ukraine's Patriot air defenses are able to intercept such missiles, but ammunition is severely depleted and it is unclear where new supplies could come from.
Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine's battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones.
Starlink does not work over Russian territory, but Ukrainian officials believe turning it on for Ukraine's use inside Russia would allow its weapons to strike mobile ballistic launchers located within several hundred kilometres of the border.
Looking ahead to winter, Stubb said there were three things that Ukraine needed.
"One is air defenses and even Starlink would be to a certain extent a good air defense there. And the second one is energy installations for the winter."
"The third one is money. So those are the things that we're working on. We're working on putting up a winter package because I don't see the war ending, you know, before the winter."
Stubb said it was good that US-led peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine had restarted in August with the visits of US envoys to both Moscow and Kyiv.
"I still think that the easiest solution would be to call an unconditional ceasefire, basically stop the killing, as President Trump reiterated in his speech in the UN General Assembly," he said.
Such a step, he continued, would be followed by negotiations on security, territory, reconstruction and compensation and other topics.
The war could be frozen along the line of contact with 30-kilometre buffer zones east and west, he said, adding that the next best option was the idea of the partial ceasefire on energy and grain related targets. REUTERS

Death toll reaches 42 after vessel sinks in Indonesia’s Java Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:02:57 UTC
06:02:57 KST

Faisal Mahmud
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
The death toll from the sinking of the KM Virgo Transport 8 in Indonesia's Java Sea has risen to 42 after search and rescue teams recovered 14 more bodies from inside the vessel, media reports said Thursday.
The victims were retrieved during diving operations inside the wreckage, state-run Antara News Agency reported, citing Mohammad Syafii, the head of the National Search and Rescue Agency (SAR), or Basarnas.
“The joint SAR team's efforts have once again yielded results,” said Syafii.
He said divers from the Basarnas Special Group, the Indonesian Navy and other search and rescue units recovered all 14 bodies from inside the ship.
The bodies were initially transferred to the KN SAR Pacitan search and rescue vessel for emergency handling before being flown to Banjarmasin.
A Basarnas HR-3604 helicopter and an Indonesian Navy Panther helicopter were used to transport the victims, according to the Antara News Agency.
Upon arrival in Banjarmasin, the bodies were handed to the Disaster Victim Identification team and authorities for medical identification and additional procedures.
As of Thursday, authorities had found 150 people from the vessel's passenger manifest.
Of them, 108 survived, while 42 were confirmed dead.
Search and rescue operations are continuing for 93 people who are missing, according to the latest figures.

PARIS, September 24. /TASS/. Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries are worsening the problem of fuel prices in Europe, French President Emmanuel Macron said in an interview with TF1 and France 2 television channels.

Federal politics: Taylor signals support for changing laws to charge OpenAI over hack — as it happened

Loading
More than half of complaints against AFP 'finalised' without investigation, figures show
More than half of all allegations made against Australian Federal Police officers have been "finalised" without investigation due to the use of discretionary powers the national watchdog says pose a risk of "denying procedural fairness".
Figures released by the AFP to the national inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at First Nations people reveal the number of complaints made against officers in the last five years.
Since July 2021, 512 complaints have been made about AFP officers' conduct, with 1,213 individual allegations identified.
Of those allegations, 643 were "finalised", without investigation, using a broad discretionary power available to the AFP under section 40TF of the legislation.
Read the full story from national Indigenous affairs correspondent Dana Morse in the link below.
PM sidesteps questions on US banning diesel exports
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has sidestepped questions about the idea of the US banning diesel exports from the US.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday, local time, he backed the idea of a ban on diesel exports from the US, which has been floated by some Republican politicians ahead of the midterm elections in November.
A leading energy analyst has warned that Australia could be looking at diesel rationing within weeks and prices topping $4 a litre.
Albanese has told News24 "trade between the United States and Australia is a good thing".
"That's why we have a free trade agreement. What happens with barriers impact the country and can hurt the country that's imposing them. But the United States domestic policy is, of course, a matter for the United States," Albanese says.
Albanese says digital duty of care will not shut down free speech
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has denied the government's digital duty of care legislation will shut down free speech.
Labor's proposed digital duty of care could let Australians opt in or out of algorithmically recommended social media content.
It also sets out expectations for all online platforms, including social media, AI chatbots and search engines, to proactively protect Australians from harmful content.
The Trump administration has warned the Albanese government that the policy would be "extraterritorial censorship of protected speech".
But Albanese says the digital duty of care is the opposite of the government getting involved.
"This is about giving Australians power and empowering them for them to determine what they receive on their device," Albanese says.
Australia must 'lean in' on artificial intelligence development: Albanese
Anthony Albanese says Australia can't be defined by its relationships with other countries and must speak up for the nation's interest.
Asked if he was concerned the US president isn't open to any further guardrails on artificial intelligence, the PM has sidestepped the question.
But he says Australia has to "lean in" on AI and its development.
"It is up to Australia to not be defined by our relationships just with other countries, to speak up for Australia's national interests and to engage constructively will continue to engage constructively, with both the United States and China," Albanese says.
"We want to be a part of the development, because what that will do is enable us to have a say in how this is rolled out."
PM defends timing of disclosure of OpenAI agent hack
The prime minister has defended the timing of when the federal government informed the public of the OpenAI agent hack.
Nationals frontbencher Bridget McKenzie suggested today that there were political reasons the PM announced the hack yesterday.
Anthony Albanese says that's "nonsense" and the government released the details as soon as it could.
"Imagine if we had said there's been a data breach, but we don't know what has been sourced. We don't know if your personal information is out there," Albanese says.
"That would have created a great deal of anxiety, which was unnecessary. We had to ascertain the facts. And then we made the statements as a matter of urgency. We also provided briefings to the opposition, as is appropriate."
No personal details compromised in OpenAI agent hack, Albanese says
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says personal details weren't accessed in the OpenAI agent hack revealed yesterday.
The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
Speaking in an interview with News24 from New York, Albanese says there is no evidence of any harm being done in the incident.
"That doesn't mean that it's not serious, because it is an example of the implications that we have been warning of," Albanese says.
"Indeed, AI companies themselves have warned of that the potential for this new technology to go in directions without human direction, without human control."
Ayres defends work of AI Safety Institute
Tim Ayres has defended the work of the AI Safety Institute following the recent OpenAI agent hack on a Services Australia portal.
The institute was established to examine new artificial intelligence capabilities, along with emerging risks and harms.
Asked on News24 whether the institute was reactive rather than proactive, Ayres says it is responsible for securing AI investment in Australia.
The industry minister says the cybersecurity approach across government is a responsibility of departments and ASD.
"It is to secure onshore investment in AI training, in particular because that is an important sovereign capability for Australia, and that means questions like pre-launch testing," Ayres says.
Taylor indicates support for changing laws to charge OpenAI for breach
A taskforce has been assembled to review whether Australia can prosecute OpenAI after its agent breached a Medicare data portal.
So if the review suggests the law needs updating, would the Coalition agree to this? Angus Taylor appears open to it.
"We haven't seen any proposal yet for the government," he says.
"What I will say is that I've long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it.
"But we'll wait and see what the government has in mind."
Taylor questions timing of PM's reveal of OpenAI hack
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is on the Gold Coast this morning, where he's again spruiking the opposition's plan to slash the fuel excise.
He stopped by a petrol station to fill up a car and used it as an opportunity to give the PM a whack for attending the UN General Assembly while fuel prices were so high.
The focus of the press conference quickly turns to the OpenAI agent hack of a Medicare data portal.
Taylor says the breach is "serious". But he questioned the timing of the prime minister's announcement.
"It seems to be terribly coincidental, doesn't it. He's swanning about New York at black tie dinner events, getting this Global Citizen of the Year award. And he wanted to say something, so he held off," the Liberal leader says.
"I mean, this stuff matters and it should be timely. The government should be talking about it as soon as it knows about it."
Albanese and his office were briefed on the hack over the weekend. The breach occurred in June, but Services Australia was not told by OpenAI until September 10.
Taylor also called on the government to start using AI to identify vulnerabilities in our cybersecurity defences.
Albanese meets with Greece's PM on sidelines of UN
Anthony Albanese has caught up with Greece's prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, on the sidelines of the United Nations.
The Greek PM delivered his speech to the UN General Assembly just before Albanese stepped up to the podium to deliver his address.
Key Event
Australia a 'reliable, practical and transparent' partner, PM says
In conclusion, the PM says Australia's geography gives the country a unique perspective as a Pacific nation connected to South-East Asia, the Indian Ocean and Antarctica.
Anthony Albanese says addressing climate change and accepting the science has been an entry point for engaging with the Pacific.
He says Australia is a "reliable, practical and transparent" partner.
"We listen with respect, we partner as equals, and we protect what matters most," Albanese says.
"We engage across regions, listen to different perspectives, and build trust.
"Australia helped create the United Nations to bring an end to an era of destructive conflict. And to build something better, for all of us."
Key Event
Albanese says decision to recognise Palestine was 'considered'
On Australia's decision to recognise the State of Palestine, Anthony Albanese says the decision was "considered" and in step with its partners.
Albanese says the decision was motivated by the "determination" to end the "cycle of violence".
He says Australia will continue to speak out against actions that damage prospects of peace in the region.
"We know the only viable path to peace and security in Palestine, in Israel and in the broader Middle East, is through a two-state solution," Albanese says.
"We will continue to speak out against actions that damage that prospect of peace, including illegal settlements in the West Bank.
"Just as we continue to oppose any role for the terrorists of Hamas in Palestine's future."
And on the conflict between the US and Iran, Albanese says Australia has been consistent in calls for a ceasefire and for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen.
PM reaffirms Australia's opposition to Russian invasion of Ukraine
Anthony Albanese has used his address to the United Nations General Assembly to reaffirm Australia's opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The prime minister says Australia this week endorsed the 2026 International Crimea Platform joint statement.
He says it reaffirms Australia's respect for Ukraine's sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity.
"We oppose Russia's continued illegal, unprovoked and immoral invasion of Ukraine and reiterate our calls for Russia's immediate, complete and unconditional withdrawal and an end to attacks upon civilians and civilian infrastructure," Albanese says.
Key Event
Albanese says AI must be subject of public discussion now
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says artificial intelligence must now be the subject of public discussion.
The prime minister says while it has the potential to improve people's lives and productivity, it carries risks.
He's also spoken about the recent OpenAI data hack that affected a Services Australia portal.
"Recently an Artificial Intelligence agent infiltrated an Australian government website. This is unacceptable. And it is why Australia has been leading the way in establishing Australian Standards for AI," Albanese says.
"Standards to ensure AI will work and deliver for people — not the other way around. We can't ignore AI or prevent it."
World must 'embrace change and reform', Albanese says
Anthony Albanese says the world must "embrace change and reform" to create a world of human dignity.
He says Australia doesn't believe in abandoning multilateralism, but rather reforming it to adapt to challenges ahead.
The PM says Australia seeks to amplify the voices of mid-sized states to ensure Security Council decisions are informed by a wide range of perspectives.
He says Australia stands for a "safer world" where "no country dominates, and no country is dominated".
"In our region, the Indo-Pacific, we are elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice, free from coercion," Albanese says.
"So that our partners can address the big issues confronting them: economic security, human development, energy security, transnational crime, sovereign capabilities, trade and investment, and science and technology."
Key Event
PM makes his pitch for Australia's seat on UN Security Council
The prime minister is now making his pitch for Australia's non-permanent seat at the UN Security Council from 2029 to 2030.
Anthony Albanese says Australia wants to respond to the world's challenges by partnering to make a difference.
He says if Australia is successful, it will listen with respect, partner as an equal and protect what matters most.
"As a member of the UN Security Council, Australia will safeguard the rules that protect us all by upholding international law, including the UN Charter, and the sovereignty of all states," Albanese says.
"We will amplify the voices of small states and middle powers to ensure a wider range of perspectives shape the Council's decisions.
"We will work to prevent crises, resolve conflicts and protect civilians through diplomacy, peacebuilding and practical action."
Key Event
Albanese says UN mission can't be entrusted alone by great powers
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says from artificial intelligence to climate change, the world is being confronted by challenges predecessors could never have imagined.
He says the world can rise to meet new challenges now to reaffirm national sovereignty and shared humanity.
Albanese says smaller countries need to take more responsibility for the world's challenges.
"We understand the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers, or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone," Albanese says.
"Nor can it be sub-contracted to the world's richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology.
"Then, now, and always, shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us."
Albanese begins speech to UN General Assembly
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just taken to the podium at the United Nations General Assembly in New York to speak.
He's started by saying that eight decades ago, the citizens and leaders of nations around the world made "solemn promise" to never repeat the horrors of World War II and nuclear weapons.
Albanese has urged world leaders to "lean in" and strengthen and modernise the fundamental parts of the UN system.
"Sovereignty, prosperity and peace are never guaranteed—they must be created, nurtured and protected by each generation," Albanese says.
"We know that the surest way to minimise the potential for conflict is to create the prosperity, opportunity and economic justice on which lasting peace depends."
Key Event
Albanese to address UN General Assembly soon
We expect Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to step up sometime soon to address the United Nations General Assembly.
It's understood he'll urge nations to come together and cooperate to confront the major challenges facing the world, including climate change, emerging technologies like AI and the breakdown of international rules.

Arab lawmaker criticizes exclusion of Arab lists from Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
20:56:22 UTC
05:56:22 KST

Khaled Yousef, Mohammad Sio
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Arab member of the Israeli Knesset Ayman Odeh on Thursday criticized the Central Elections Committee’s decision to bar Arab electoral lists from running in the Oct. 27 parliamentary election. 
Israeli Army Radio quoted Odeh as saying: “All the Kahanists are allowed (to run the elections), but representatives of the Arab population are prohibited from competing.” 
Palestinian citizens make up around 21% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million. 
The term “Kahanism” refers to a far-right Israeli ideology associated with Meir Kahane, an Israeli-American rabbi and politician who founded a movement known for its extremist views. 
On Wednesday, the Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify the Joint Arab List and the United Arab List, or Ra’am, as well as Knesset member Ofer Cassif and Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh from running in the election. 
Critics of the decisions say the exclusions are part of efforts by Israel’s right wing to prevent Arab parties from influencing the formation of the next government, as polls show neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc nor the opposition securing the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. 
By contrast, the Central Elections Committee on Thursday rejected a request to disqualify the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.  
Odeh expressed hope that Israel’s Supreme Court would overturn the disqualification decisions and allow the barred candidates and lists to contest the election. 
Earlier Thursday, Cassif also criticized both the government and the opposition in a post on US social media company X following his disqualification. 
“The Kahanists in both the government and the opposition are afraid of the power of our voice,” said Cassif, a lawmaker with the Joint Arab List. 
“Our voice is the only one that offers a genuine alternative to racist, militaristic and bloodthirsty discourse,” he added. 
Cassif is known for his opposition to the Netanyahu government’s policies toward Palestinians, particularly Israel’s genocide in Gaza since 2023. 
The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. 
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022. He is also standing trial on corruption charges, which he denies.

Church of England leader honored cleric linked to Pakistani gang – Telegraph

Unknown Publisher

Church of England leader honored cleric linked to Pakistani gang – Telegraph
A Pakistani Muslim cleric honored by Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally has been accused of protecting an alleged extortion gang linked to abductions and torture, The Telegraph reported on Thursday.
The head of the Church of England withdrew an interfaith award from Tahir Ashrafi, Pakistan’s special envoy on interfaith harmony, last week, just six days after presenting it to him.
According to The Telegraph, Ashrafi’s brother allegedly leads a so-called “blasphemy gang” in Pakistan that entraps young men online and blackmails them with threats of prosecution under the country's blasphemy laws. The newspaper said the group was behind “a huge surge” in the number of people jailed for blasphemy in recent years. Blasphemy can carry the death penalty in Pakistan.
Ashrafi has publicly defended his brother and called a judge investigating the alleged gang a “dog,” according to the British newspaper.
Pakistan’s National Commission for Human Rights has said the group used women operating under pseudonyms to lure men into making blasphemous statements online. Those targeted were then frequently detained by “private individuals rather than law enforcement,” subjected to torture and denied access to legal assistance, according to the state human rights watchdog.
Relatives of alleged victims told The Telegraph they were “shocked” to see Ashrafi receive the British award. They claimed the cleric played the “good cop” while his brother acted as the “bad cop,” entrapping and rounding up victims. The newspaper said the relatives were granted anonymity because of fears of reprisals.
Ashrafi has denied any wrongdoing.
The controversy comes amid heightened scrutiny in Britain of crimes linked to gangs involving men of Pakistani heritage, following years of revelations about organized child sexual exploitation in towns and cities across the country.
An inquiry funded by Restore Britain MP Rupert Lowe reported in June that it had identified evidence of grooming gangs operating across 149 of the UK’s 317 local authority districts. The report determined that a “bare minimum” of 250,000 women and girls were raped by grooming gangs since the year 2000, and that senior politicians helped the gangs escape prosecution.

UK premier rules out early general election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:49:36 UTC
05:49:36 KST

Burak Bir
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday that he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing that doing so would throw “the country into a backward-looking process.”
In interviews with BBC and ITV regional political editors, Burnham said his focus is on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses, adding that there are no plans for a general election before 2029.
Asked whether the next election would be held in 2029, he replied: “Yes, that’s when the next election will be.”
“All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead,” Burnham said.
The next general election must be held by August 2029, although the prime minister can choose to call it earlier.
His remarks came as recent polling suggested Labour’s position had improved since Burnham replaced Keir Starmer in July.
According to a YouGov poll conducted for Sky News and The Times and published Thursday, Britain is on course for a hung Parliament if an election were held now, with no party projected to secure an overall majority and Labour expected to win the most seats.
“I see all the speculation and it just races ahead,” Burnham said when asked whether he would be tempted to call an early poll.
He added: “No election anytime soon. I’m focused on the job as prime minister, doing what I said I would do.”
The prime minister said he wants to use the upcoming annual Labour Party Conference to say more about “the direction” in which he wants to take the country.
“The focus is on that, helping people with the cost of living, helping businesses with the cost of running a business,” he said.
“These have got to be the priorities right now, rather than throwing the country into a backward-looking process where we’re arguing again amongst ourselves.”
On small boat crossings, Burnham said his goal is that he does not “want to see any crossings at all.”
His remarks came two days after at least 781 migrants crossed the English Channel to reach the UK, the highest single-day total recorded this year.
Despite the continued arrivals, overall Channel crossings have declined this year.
More than 18,500 migrants have crossed the Channel so far this year, down 45% from the same period in 2025.

The only goal of the game was scored towards the end of the first half with a header by Belgian "Anderlecht" striker Danylo Sikan.
It should be added that Ukraine's national team will play its next match on 28 September, also away, against Georgia.
Previously
Before the match, Ukraine national team head coach Andrea Maldera spoke about the players' condition. The coach noted that Dynamo forward Matviy Ponomarenko had fallen slightly ill, while Olympiacos striker Roman Yaremchuk was troubled by a knee injury.

Bill Gates warned of the threat of AI capable of causing a billion deaths

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25

Bill Gates warned of the threat of AI capable of causing a billion deaths
Kyiv • UNN
Bill Gates called on governments to regulate AI through legislation because of the risk of abuse. He considers self-regulation by technology companies insufficient.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates stated that artificial intelligence is powerful enough to contribute to events that could result in the deaths of a billion people. UNN reports this with reference to Axios and Forbes.
He called for statutory regulation of the technology, emphasizing that companies’ self-regulation is insufficient.
Details
In a conversation with television host Kristen Welker, Gates drew attention to the danger of people with malicious intentions using the latest artificial intelligence tools.
"AI is certainly powerful enough to lead to events that, you know, will cause a billion deaths," he said.
According to the Microsoft co-founder, the combination of modern AI’s capabilities and people’s malicious intentions creates an unprecedented threat. Gates also spoke in favor of the government’s involvement in establishing rules for artificial intelligence developers. In his view, policymakers and law enforcement agencies should participate in determining mandatory protective and monitoring measures.
He emphasized that voluntary restrictions imposed by technology companies themselves are insufficient. When asked whether appropriate legislation was needed, Gates answered in the affirmative.
Context
In August, Gates published an essay on his website about the risks of artificial intelligence development. Among the threats, he listed job losses, the spread of fraud and disinformation, the facilitation of cyberattacks, and growing bioterrorism risks. He also warned that the technology could exacerbate inequality if its benefits were concentrated in the hands of a limited number of people.
At the same time, the Gates Foundation announced its intention to direct at least $1 billion over two years toward expanding access to AI. The funds are intended for projects in education, healthcare, agriculture, and digital infrastructure development.
Reminder
The heads of leading AI companies warned the UN about the risks of artificial intelligence to humanity.

The Russian attack destroyed the "Sushiya" warehouse along with all its inventory
Kyiv • UNN
As a result of the Russian attack on September 25, the "Sushiya" company's warehouse containing goods and packaging was destroyed. The restaurants and delivery service continue to operate.
On Friday, September 25, a warehouse belonging to the "Sushiya" restaurant chain was destroyed as a result of a Russian attack, along with all its stock and packaging. The company reported this on social media, UNN reports.
Details
At the same time, it is noted that all restaurants and delivery services continue to operate.
We will do everything possible to restore the necessary supplies as quickly as possible, provide a full menu, and ensure uninterrupted operations. We express our sincere condolences to our logistics partners. We ask for your understanding and support
We would like to remind you
In Kyiv region, on September 25, one of the warehouses of McDonald’s logistics partner was damaged as a result of a Russian drone attack by the Russian armed forces. The company confirmed that no one was injured and that the chain’s restaurants continue to operate as usual.
